Clement names no emperor, but attests the exile-and-return and the aged John governing the Asian churches, and elsewhere notes that John, called back to episcopal work, was still vigorous in extreme old age. 4

Tertullian , arguing that the great churches keep the apostles' own teaching, appeals to Rome, “where the Apostle John was first plunged, unhurt, into boiling oil, and thence remitted to his island-exile.” It is the earliest witness to the Roman boiling-oil legend (later localized at the Latin Gate) and, in the same breath, to the Patmos exile — told as an ordeal survived, in the manner of the martyr-deliverance stories. 5

The apocryphal Acts of John — part of the “Leucian” romance-corpus, and marked by encratite and docetic tendencies — supplies the most famous scenes: John raising the dead (Drusiana), wrecking the temple of Artemis at Ephesus by a word, and at the last his own peaceful “falling asleep” in a grave he digs himself. (The poisoned-cup ordeal, often pictured with John, is not in this work — it is attached to him only by the later apostle-lists and the Golden Legend .) It is romance-hagiography of low biographical value, condemned in antiquity for its heresy, and is cited here only as an early witness to how John was venerated — never as history. On the reliability of this whole layer, see the apo…

Victorinus, in the earliest surviving commentary on Revelation, states plainly that John saw the Apocalypse while “condemned to the labour of the mines by Cæsar Domitian” on Patmos, and published it “when grown old” after his release — the first witness to attach the vision itself, by name, to Domitian and to date John's old age accordingly. His testimony is treated at length on the companion timeline for the date of Revelation (where he appears as a witness in his own right ); it matters here because the Domitianic exile is one of the load-bearing supports of the old-age-at-Ephesus tradition. 7

Eusebius gathers the tradition into a single connected account: John banished to Patmos under Domitian, released under Nerva, and living on at Ephesus until Trajan; the governor of the Asian churches; the seer of Revelation (whose authorship, however, Eusebius is willing to assign to the “other” John). He quotes Irenaeus and Clement, and preserves Polycrates of Ephesus (c. 190), who lists among Asia's buried luminaries “John, who was both a witness and a teacher, who reclined upon the bosom of the Lord … He fell asleep at Ephesus.” And it is Eusebius who, reading Papias, first argues for two Johns and “two tombs in Ephesus, each … called John's.” 8

Jerome , in On Illustrious Men , condenses the Greek tradition for the Latin West: John wrote his Gospel last, at the bishops' request, against Cerinthus and the Ebionites; “in the fourteenth year … after Nero, Domitian having raised a second persecution he was banished to the island of Patmos, and wrote the Apocalypse”; released after Domitian's death, he “returned to Ephesus,” and, “continuing there until the time of the emperor Trajan, founded and built churches throughout all Asia, and, worn out by old age, died in the sixty-eighth year after our Lord's passion and was buried near the same city.” 9

Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend gathers the medieval life: John summoned to Rome and cast into a cauldron of boiling oil before the Latin Gate, from which he came out unhurt; his exile to Patmos and the writing of the Apocalypse; the poisoned-cup challenge before the temple of Diana (Aristodemus's ordeal), which he drinks unharmed; the raising of the dead; and his tranquil death in a grave dug at his word, his body afterward not found. It is cited here as late medieval hagiography, more than a millennium after the events, gathering the boiling oil, the poisoned cup, and the peaceful death into a single story. 10

ar.q: Did John die of old age at Ephesus?
ar.c: Unlike his brother James, whose death Acts records, John's end is not told in the New Testament. The claim weighed here is the church's settled memory: John outlived every other apostle, spent his last decades governing the churches of Roman Asia from Ephesus, was exiled for a time to Patmos, and died peacefully, an old man, in the reign of the emperor Trajan (98–117), and was buried at Ephesus. 1
ar.a: Sound. That John lived to old age and died a natural death at Ephesus under Trajan is early, multiply and independently attested, and anchored in the local memory of the church that held his grave. The embellishments (the priestly plate, the two tombs, the boiling oil) can be pared away without disturbing the core, and the sole contrary tradition does not hold. This is mainstream and well-grounded — the default against which every rarer claim abo…

ar.q: Was John martyred early, with his brother James?
ar.c: Against the mainstream memory of a peaceful old age, a minority of critics — classically Eberhard Schwartz (1904) and Julius Wellhausen — has argued that John the son of Zebedee was martyred, and possibly martyred early, like his brother James (killed by Herod Agrippa, c. 44). The thesis was often pressed to sever the apostle from the Fourth Gospel and the long Ephesian career the tradition assigns him. 1
ar.a: Weak. The early-martyrdom thesis has a real proof-text and a claimed early source, and so is more than a bare guess — but on its best available case it does not hold. The “cup” saying does not require it; the Papias notice reaches us only through late, self-contradictory epitomes; and it must overturn a strong, early, independent, and local tradition of John's old age at Ephesus, which it cannot. It fails on the evidence, not because a martyrdom …

ar.q: Was Papias's “John the elder” a second John?
ar.c: In the one surviving sentence of his preface, Papias names a John twice — once among the apostles whose words the elders reported, and again, after Aristion, among “the disciples of the Lord” still speaking in his own day, whom he calls “the presbyter John.” The claim weighed here is Eusebius's inference, revived by many moderns: that these are two men, an apostle John and a distinct “John the elder,” both at Ephesus — with the corollary that the Johannine corpus may be divided between them (the Gospel to the apostle, the Revelation and/or the short epistles, whose author calls himself “the el…
ar.a: Contested. Whether Papias's “John the elder” is a second John — and how, if so, the Gospel, epistles, and Revelation divide between the two — is genuinely disputed, with weighty considerations and real proponents on each side and no consensus. The internal, stylistic evidence favours more than one hand; the external, early attestation favours one apostolic John in Asia; and the decisive text is a single sentence patient of both readings. It is le…

ds.t: Judas Iscariot
ds.q: Judas Iscariot is the one apostle everyone remembers for a single act — the betrayal — and the one whose story the New Testament tells at both ends: a name and a father at the start, and, uniquely among the Twelve, two accounts of his death. He stands last in every list, always tagged “who also betrayed him”; John adds that he kept the disciples’ purse and pilfered from it; the Synoptics fix his price at thirty pieces of silver. Then he dies — but the two death-notices do not read alike. Matthew has him fling the silver into the temple and hang himself , after which the priests buy a potter’s field with the blood-money and call it “the field of blood”; Acts has Judas himself buy a field and …

tl.t: The New Testament gives Judas more than most of the Twelve: a surname (“Iscariot,” most likely ’îsh-Qêriyôth , “man of Kerioth” in Judah — perhaps the one Judean among Galileans), a father (Simon), a role (keeper of the common bag, and, John says, a thief), and a crime (handing Jesus over for thirty pieces of silver). It also, alone among the apostles, records his death twice. Matthew has Judas repent, throw the silver into the temple, and “ hanged himself ”; the priests then buy the potter’s field for the blood-money, so the field is called “the field of blood” and the whole tied to a prophecy of “Jeremy.” Acts, in Peter’s speech, has Judas himself “purchase a field with the reward of iniqu…

Papias , among the earliest post-apostolic writers, preserves a third account of Judas’s end, surviving as a quotation in Apollinaris of Laodicea: not a hanging and not a plain fall, but a grotesque swelling — “his body having swollen to such an extent that he could not pass where a chariot could pass easily, he was crushed by the chariot, so that his bowels gushed out.” It keeps the gushing bowels of Acts but supplies a new cause, and later writers (Theophylact) piled on further horrors — worms, a stench, blindness. Within a generation or two of Acts, the manner of Judas’s death was already multiplying. 2

tl.w: The Gospel of Judas (2nd c.; Coptic copy c. 300)
tl.t: Against the whole canonical picture stands a 2nd-century Gnostic text that turns the traitor into the hero. Denounced by Irenaeus about 180 and lost until a Coptic copy was published amid great publicity in 2006, the Gospel of Judas makes Judas the one disciple who truly knows Jesus — “you are from the immortal realm of Barbelo” — and, on its first reading, casts the betrayal as a service Jesus himself commanded, freeing his spirit from the flesh. (A revisionist school reads the Sethian author as in fact damning Judas.) It is late, Gnostic, and dependent on the canonical Gospels: no witness to the historical Judas, but a vivid witness to how a sect reimagined him. 3

By the high Middle Ages Judas had acquired a full fabulous life. Jacobus de Voragine’s Golden Legend (c. 1260), telling it as the preamble to the life of Matthias, gives an Oedipus-tale: an infant exposed on the sea after a dream that he would “destroy their people,” who grows up to kill his own father and unknowingly marry his mother before coming to Christ for mercy — a story Voragine himself twice brands apocryphal and “not authentic.” Dante meanwhile fixed Judas at the absolute bottom of Hell, head-first in the central mouth of Satan, in the ring named Giudecca for him. It is late legend — church and poetic imagination, a millennium and more after the events — not history. 4

Critical study returns Judas to the two spare, divergent death-notices and asks the obvious questions. On the manner of death, much turns on two observations: that each notice sits close to an Old Testament pattern — Matthew shadowing the traitor Ahithophel, who “hanged himself” (2 Samuel 17:23), and Acts using the very words of Wisdom 4:19 for the ruin of the ungodly — and that Acts’ famous “headlong” is a translator’s gloss for a word that means “prostrate,” so that it may describe the state of the body rather than a rival cause of death. Scholars divide accordingly between one death told twice and two independent traditions. On the field, the divergence over who bought it and why it is na…

ar.q: Matthew’s hanging and Acts’ bursting: one death, told twice
ar.c: [Matthew:] And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself… [Acts:] and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out. — Matthew 27:5 and Acts 1:18 . The reading weighed here is that these are two descriptions of a single death — Matthew giving how Judas died, Acts the state in which his body was found — and not two incompatible reports. A third witness, Papias , adds a swelling so gross that Judas “could not pass where a chariot could pass easily” and burst — neither hanging nor a fall. 1
ar.a: Plausible. Two questions have to be kept apart. The popular apologetic case — a decomposing body, a snapped rope, a cliff above the Hinnom — is the weaker one: its forensic prop rests on a citation no one can find, its lexical prop was refuted in 1933, and its topographical prop has no advocate in the literature. The interpretation those props are meant to serve stands on its own without them. Acts does not say Judas fell from a height; it says h…

ar.q: Matthew’s priests and Acts’ Judas: one purchase, one name
ar.c: [Matthew:] And they [the chief priests] took counsel, and bought with them the potter’s field, to bury strangers in. Wherefore that field was called, The field of blood, unto this day… [Acts:] Now this man [Judas] purchased a field with the reward of iniquity… and it was known unto all the dwellers at Jerusalem; insomuch as that field is called in their proper tongue, Aceldama, that is to say, The field of blood. — Matthew 27:7–8 and Acts 1:18–19 . The reading weighed here is that these are two notices about one plot of ground — one purchase, made with Judas’s betrayal-money and so reckoned hi…
ar.a: Plausible. Two questions, again, have to be kept apart. The popular apologetic case rests partly on props that fail: there is no documented Jewish law making the field Judas’s in title, there is no causative in the Greek, and there were not two fields. The interpretation those props were meant to serve does not need them. On the buyer the case is strong enough to be near settled: ektēsato does not mean “bought,” Luke never uses it of a cash purch…

ar.q: Why does Matthew credit the thirty-pieces oracle to “Jeremy the prophet”?
ar.c: Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying, And they took the thirty pieces of silver… and gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord appointed me. — Matthew 27:9–10 . The wording is substantially that of Zechariah 11:12–13 (thirty pieces of silver; cast to the potter) — not Jeremiah. The charge: Matthew has misremembered his source and named the wrong prophet, a plain error in the text. 1
ar.a: Sound. Matthew’s ascription to “Jeremy” is best read as a deliberate composite citation — Zechariah’s words within a Jeremian frame of potter, field, and innocent blood, credited to the governing prophet — not as a misremembered source. The composite reading is coherent, well-grounded, and the majority explanation among Matthean specialists, and the bare-error charge is the weaker alternative. The one residual open question is why Jeremiah is nam…

ar.q: Matthew’s repentant Judas and Acts’s silence: conflict, or omission?
ar.c: [Matthew:] Then Judas… repented himself… saying, I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood… [Acts:] …this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas by transgression fell, that he might go to his own place. — Matthew 27:3–4 and Acts 1:25 . Alongside the three famous tensions between the two death-notices — the manner of death, who bought the field, and why it bears its name — a fourth is sometimes urged: Matthew shows a Judas stricken with remorse, while Acts’s account (Peter’s speech) gives no hint of it, calling him only one who “fell” from his ministry to “his own place,” who…
ar.a: Sound. Taken as a charge of contradiction — “Matthew says he repented, Acts says he did not” — the objection fails outright, because Acts does not say he did not. Peter’s speech names Judas’s fall in a single clause to explain a vacant office; it neither asserts nor denies anything about his state of mind, and its bleak language (“transgression,” “reward of iniquity”) is a verdict Matthew’s own scene shares, since in Matthew it is Judas who confe…

ar.q: Judas’s remorse: true repentance, or despair? — and could he have been forgiven?
ar.c: Matthew did not use metanoeō , which means a genuine change of mind and will… but metamelomai , which merely connotes regret or sorrow. He did not experience spiritual penitence but only emotional remorse. — a representative modern statement of the popular reading (John MacArthur, “Did Judas Repent?”). 1 The interpretation weighed here is the one that statement serves: that when Matthew 27:3–5 says Judas “repented himself” ( metamelētheis ), brought back the thirty pieces, confessed “I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood,” and then went and hanged himself, it describes a gen…
ar.a: Sound. That Judas felt real remorse but never reached saving repentance — because it collapsed into despair and self-murder instead of turning back to Christ — is the church’s near-unanimous reading (Chrysostom, Origen, Jerome, Theophylact, Leo, Aquinas) and squares with the text as it stands: a genuine confession, a returned bribe, and then a noose rather than a plea for mercy. It is confirmed by contrast, in the Judas/Peter foil Matthew plainly…

ds.t: Matthew
ds.q: Matthew is the apostle the church remembered as a writer . Where most of the Twelve are names in a list and nothing more, Matthew is called from a toll-booth in a scene the Gospels tell three times — and then, from the second century on, is credited with the first Gospel, “composed in the Hebrew tongue.” Two puzzles sit at the head of his story. The first is his name: the man Matthew’s Gospel calls “Matthew” at the receipt of custom is called Levi in the very same scene by Mark and Luke, so that the church has had to ask whether Matthew and Levi are one man under two names. The second is his book: Papias’s famous notice that “Matthew put together the oracles in the Hebrew language” launched …

tl.t: The New Testament names Matthew in all four lists of the Twelve, and tells one story about him: his call. As Jesus “passed forth from thence, he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him” — a tax-collector, a publican , left his toll-booth at a word. Matthew’s own Gospel alone adds the detail that he was a publican when it lists him among the Twelve: “Matthew the publican.” Mark and Luke tell the identical call-scene — the same booth, the same words, the same rising and following — but name the man Levi , “Levi the son of Alphaeus” in Mark, a “publican, named Levi” in Luke, who then makes Jesus “a great feast …

tl.w: Papias on the Hebrew oracles, and the patristic chain (c. 125, reported c. 325)
tl.t: The earliest word about Matthew’s book is a single sentence of Papias of Hierapolis (c. 125), preserved by Eusebius: “So then Matthew wrote the oracles in the Hebrew language, and every one interpreted them as he was able.” From this seed grew a unanimous patristic tradition of a Semitic Matthew. Irenaeus (c. 180): “Matthew also issued a written Gospel among the Hebrews in their own dialect.” Origen (c. 230, via Eusebius): the first Gospel “was written by Matthew, who was once a publican, but afterwards an apostle… for the converts from Judaism, and published in the Hebrew language.” Eusebius himself: Matthew, “who had at first preached to the Hebrews, when he was about to go to other people…

tl.w: Clement of Alexandria: a hint that Matthew was not martyred (c. 200)
tl.t: Against the later martyr-legends stands an early and awkward note. Clement of Alexandria (c. 200), discussing what it means to “confess” Christ, quotes the Valentinian Heracleon’s observation that not all the saved confessed with the voice before the authorities — “of whom are Matthew, Philip, Thomas, Levi, and many others,” who confessed instead by their lives. The passage implies that Matthew was not put to death for the faith — the earliest datum we have on how his life ended, and it points away from martyrdom. (It also, incidentally, lists “Matthew” and “Levi” as if two men — a wrinkle for the identity question.) It is a slender and second-hand thread, but it is early, and it sits at odd…

Jerome , opening his catalogue of Christian writers, gives the compact Latin summary that fixed the Western picture of Matthew. He identifies the apostle without hesitation: “Matthew, also called Levi, apostle and aforetimes publican, composed a gospel of Christ at first published in Judea in Hebrew for the sake of those of the circumcision who believed, but this was afterwards translated into Greek though by what author is uncertain.” Jerome adds that “the Hebrew itself has been preserved until the present day” in the library at Caesarea, and that he had been permitted to copy a text of it used by the Nazarenes of Beroea — a claim that entangles the “Hebrew Matthew” with the apocryphal Gosp…

tl.w: The mission-field and the apostle-lists (uncertain date, mutually dependent)
tl.t: Where Matthew went after Judea, the tradition cannot decide. The line that reached the Greek historians sends him to Ethiopia : Rufinus and Socrates Scholasticus, expanding Eusebius’s scheme of the apostles’ allotted regions, assign “Ethiopia” to Matthew, and it is Ethiopia that the medieval West would inherit. But the apostle-lists — the late, mutually-copying Greek and Latin catalogues of where each apostle preached and died — scatter him widely: to Parthia and Persia , to Macedonia , to the cannibal “man-eaters” on the Black Sea, dying variously by the sword, by fire, or in peace at Hierapolis. No consistent memory survives; the mission-field of Matthew is church legend of low evidential …

Jacobus de Voragine’s Golden Legend gathers the full medieval romance of Matthew in Ethiopia: the apostle confounds two sorcerers, Zaroes and Arphaxat, and their serpents; he raises the son of King Egippus and converts the land; he consecrates the king’s daughter Iphigenia and her virgins to God; and when the next king, Hirtacus, wishes to marry her and is refused, he has Matthew struck down at the altar — the martyrdom the Latin church settled on, and the source of his emblems, the angel and the sword or spear. It is late hagiography, twelve centuries after the events, weaving the apostle-lists and lost Acts into a single tale; but it is the form in which the West received Matthew the marty…

Critical study leaves Matthew’s biography thin and his book contested. On the man: that the tax-collector of the call-story is the apostle Matthew, and that Matthew is the Levi of Mark and Luke, is the majority view and probably right — the scene is one scene, told thrice — though it rests on harmonizing two names and cannot be proved. On the book: few today think our Greek Matthew is a translation from a Hebrew original, since it demonstrably uses the Greek Mark and the Greek Old Testament; the debate is instead over what Papias’s “oracles” ( logia ) were — the canonical Gospel, a lost sayings-source, a collection of messianic proof-texts — and whether the whole “Hebrew Matthew” tradition i…

ar.q: Was Matthew’s Gospel first written in Hebrew?
ar.c: So then Matthew wrote the oracles in the Hebrew language, and every one interpreted them as he was able. — Papias of Hierapolis (c. 125), in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.39.16 . The claim under test is that the Gospel of Matthew was originally composed in a Semitic language — Hebrew or the Aramaic often called “Hebrew” — for Jewish believers, and that our Greek Matthew is a translation of that lost original. 1
ar.a: Contested. That Matthew wrote first in Hebrew is affirmed by an early and unanimous line of Fathers and is not improbable for a Jewish-Christian gospel; but the Greek Matthew we have reads as a Greek work built on Greek sources, Papias’s “oracles” may not mean the Gospel, and the later witnesses may merely echo him. A real dispute between patristic testimony and internal evidence, with no settled resolution.

ar.q: Was Matthew the tax collector the same man as Levi?
ar.c: And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the receipt of custom, and said unto him, Follow me. And he arose and followed him. — Mark 2:14 . The claim under test is the traditional identification: that the tax-collector called from the toll-booth — whom Matthew’s Gospel names Matthew and Mark and Luke name Levi — is one man, so that the apostle Matthew and the publican Levi are the same person under two names. 1
ar.a: Plausible. The identification of Matthew with Levi is coherent, economical, and the majority view, and — resting on one call-scene told three times rather than on silence — it is the stronger of the Gospels’ two apostle-identity questions and is probably correct. But it is an equation no Gospel states, “Levi” never appears among the Twelve, and one early witness lists the two names apart. A probable identification, not a demonstrated fact.

ar.q: Was Matthew martyred in Ethiopia?
ar.c: …and thus he received the crown of martyrdom. — the Golden Legend , life of St Matthew. The claim under test is the traditional martyrdom: that Matthew, after converting Ethiopia and consecrating the virgin Iphigenia, was killed at the altar on the order of King Hirtacus, who wished to marry her — the death the Latin West assigned him, dated by tradition to about the year 68. 1
ar.a: Weak. The Ethiopian martyrdom under King Hirtacus is late, detailed only in medieval legend, and set on mission-traditions that do not agree; the earliest surviving hint of Matthew’s death points instead to a natural end. A martyrdom somewhere cannot be excluded, but this particular account does not hold on its evidence.

ds.t: Matthias
ds.q: Matthias is the one apostle added to the Twelve after the Ascension — and the only one whose calling the New Testament describes in full: between the Ascension and Pentecost, Peter proposed that the empty place of the fallen Judas be filled by a man who had “companied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us,” from the baptism of John to the day of the Ascension; two were put forward, Joseph Barsabbas Justus and Matthias, the company prayed, cast lots, “and the lot fell upon Matthias.” After that verse the New Testament never mentions him again. Everything else — where he preached, how he died, even whether he was some better-known figure under another name — is late…

tl.t: Matthias enters the New Testament at a single scene and leaves it at the same one. In the days between the Ascension and Pentecost, Peter stood among some hundred and twenty believers and proposed that the “office” ( episkopē ) vacated by Judas be filled; the replacement had to be an eyewitness of the whole of Jesus’ public life — “of these men which have companied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John, unto that same day that he was taken up from us” — and a witness of the resurrection. Two men met the test: Joseph called Barsabbas Justus, and Matthias. The company prayed to the Lord “which knowest the hearts of all men” to sho…

The first writer after the New Testament to say anything of Matthias uses his name for a book. Clement of Alexandria three times quotes a Traditions of Matthias ( Paradōseis Matthiou ) — “Wonder at what is before you,” the saying runs, “laying this down first as the foundation of further knowledge” — and reports that “Matthias also taught that we ought to fight against and abuse the flesh, and not give way to it for the sake of pleasure.” Clement cites the work respectfully but does not treat it as Scripture, and the sect of the Basilidians who leaned on it he counts among the heretics. In the same Stromateis Clement preserves a second, stranger notice: retelling the story of the repentant t…

Eusebius gives Matthias two brief notices, and they pull in opposite directions. In Book 1 of the Ecclesiastical History he passes on the tradition — which he is the first to record — that Matthias, “who was numbered with the apostles in the place of Judas,” and Barsabbas Justus with him, had first been among the Seventy whom Jesus sent out ahead of him: a tidy way of satisfying Peter’s requirement that the man have followed Jesus from the beginning. In Book 3, cataloguing the books the church rejected, he lists a “Gospel of Matthias” among the forgeries “cited by the heretics under the name of the apostles” — with the Gospels of Peter and Thomas — works “to be cast aside as absurd and impio…

tl.w: The apocryphal Acts of Andrew and Matthias (2nd–4th c.)
tl.t: Where the sober record stops, romance takes over. The Acts of Andrew and Matthias — among the Anthropophagi , “the man-eaters” — opens with the apostles casting lots for their mission-fields; the lot sends Matthias to a city of cannibals who blind, drug, and fatten their captives to eat them on the thirtieth day. Matthias is imprisoned and his eyes put out; Christ sends Andrew across the sea to rescue him, and after a run of miracles the city is converted. It is heroic legend of no biographical worth — and it does not even hold his name steady: many manuscripts and the Anglo-Saxon Andreas built on it call the hero “Matthew,” the better-known evangelist, so that the very text meant to celebra…

tl.w: The apostle-lists and the Golden Legend (c. 6th–13th c.)
tl.t: The late catalogues supply the mission and the death the earlier sources withhold, and cannot agree on either. The apostle-lists — the Synopsis ascribed to Dorotheus, Nicephorus, and their kin — send Matthias to preach “in Ethiopia,” meaning not Africa but Colchis on the eastern Black Sea (the harbour of Hyssus, the mouth of the Phasis), among “barbarians and man-eaters,” and bury him at Sebastopolis by the Temple of the Sun. On his death the traditions splinter: stoned by the Jews at Jerusalem and then beheaded with an axe (whence the axe in his images); crucified in Colchis; or, in Pseudo-Hippolytus, dead of old age at Jerusalem. The medieval West, following the Golden Legend , kept the st…

Critical study leaves Matthias almost exactly where the one Gospel verse found him. The Traditions and the Gospel of Matthias are judged second-century pseudepigrapha that merely borrowed a safely obscure apostolic name; the Acts of Andrew and Matthias is romance, and its wandering between “Matthias” and “Matthew” a textbook case of hagiographic name-drift; the mission to Colchis and the several deaths are late, mutually exclusive, and unattested before the list-literature, so that surveys of the apostles’ fates rank the evidence for any particular end of Matthias among the very weakest. What can be said with confidence is only this: after Judas fell, the Eleven filled the Twelve by lot with…

ar.q: Was Matthias’s election legitimate, or was Paul the “true” twelfth apostle?
ar.c: And they gave forth their lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles. — Acts 1:26 . The interpretation under test reads this verse as a false step. On it, the risen Christ had told the apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:4–8); instead, impatient Peter convened an election ten days early and resolved it by the Old-Covenant device of the lot — acting “in the flesh” before the Spirit came. The proof, its advocates say, is in the sequel: Matthias vanishes from the record without a further word, while the man “called… by the will of God”…
ar.a: Weak. That Matthias’s election was a mistake, and Paul the intended twelfth apostle, is a minority reading that the passage actively resists: no censure, a legitimately sacred lot, the Spirit’s ratification at Pentecost, Paul’s failure of the eyewitness test, and Paul’s own witness to an intact “twelve.” The mainstream verdict — that the Eleven rightly filled their number and that Paul’s was a separate and later apostolate to the Gentiles — holds…

ar.q: Was Matthias the same man as Zacchaeus, or as Barnabas?
ar.c: It is said, therefore, that Zaccheus, or, according to some, Matthew, the chief of the publicans… — Clement of Alexandria, Stromateis 4.6 . Two identifications are on the table. (a) Matthias = Zacchaeus. Clement’s aside — whose Greek runs Zakchaion… hoi de Matthian phasi , “Zacchaeus, or, as some say, Matthias” — is read as evidence that the apostle chosen by lot was the repentant publican of Luke 19 under a second name; a later strand (the Apostolic Constitutions ) even makes “Zacchaeus” a first bishop. (b) Matthias = Barnabas. Because the rejected candidate in Acts 1 was “Joseph called Barsa…
ar.a: Weak. Neither the Zacchaeus nor the Barnabas identification stands. The first rests on one hedged, textually-variant line in Clement and contradicts Matthias’s defining qualification; the second confuses Matthias with the rejected candidate Barsabbas and then with Barnabas beyond him. Matthias is best left as Acts leaves him: a disciple from the beginning, chosen by lot, and otherwise unknown — not a better-known man in disguise.

ds.t: Paul
ds.q: Paul is the apostle we know best and the one whose end the New Testament leaves half-told. Almost half of Acts follows him, and thirteen letters carry his name — so his origin (a Pharisee of Tarsus, a Roman citizen, “a Hebrew of Hebrews” who had persecuted the church before the risen Christ arrested him on the Damascus road), his three missionary journeys, the Jerusalem council, and his arrest and voyage under guard to Rome are documented as no other apostle’s life is. But Acts stops with Paul in his own hired house at Rome, preaching “no man forbidding him,” and says nothing of how he died — so for once the tradition that grew up around an apostle is filling not a total silence but a single…

tl.t: No apostle is drawn in the New Testament so fully. Saul of Tarsus in Cilicia — a Roman citizen by birth, of the tribe of Benjamin, “a Hebrew of Hebrews,” a Pharisee schooled in Jerusalem “at the feet of Gamaliel,” a tent-maker by trade — first appears consenting to the stoning of Stephen and “making havock of the church.” On the road to Damascus the risen Christ struck him down and made a persecutor into “a chosen vessel” and apostle to the Gentiles. Three missionary journeys carried him across Asia Minor and Greece; the Jerusalem council (Acts 15; Galatians 2) settled that his Gentile converts need not be circumcised; and a riot at the Temple ended in his arrest, his appeal “unto Caesar” as…

The first writer after the New Testament to speak of Paul’s end is Clement, bishop of Rome , writing to Corinth perhaps thirty years after the event, in the city where it happened. Setting Peter and Paul before his readers as “the greatest and most righteous pillars” martyred in “our own generation,” Clement writes that Paul, after “seven times” imprisoned, exiled, and stoned, “taught righteousness to the whole world, and came to the extreme limit of the west, and suffered martyrdom under the prefects.” The notice is short but weighty: a Roman Christian, within living memory, attests Paul’s martyrdom at Rome, and — on the natural reading of “the extreme limit of the west” from the vantage of…

tl.w: The Acts of Paul and Acts of Paul and Thecla (c. 160)
tl.t: Where the sober record thins, romance fills in. The second-century Acts of Paul — whose most famous episode is the tale of Thecla, the noble virgin of Iconium who follows Paul, survives fire and beasts, and baptizes herself — is orthodox in aim but legendary in substance; Tertullian reports that its author, a presbyter in Asia, was deposed for composing it “from love of Paul.” It is prized for one thing above all: the earliest physical portrait of the apostle, “a man small in size, bald-headed, bandy-legged, well-built, with eyebrows meeting, rather long-nosed, full of grace — for sometimes he seemed like a man, and sometimes he had the countenance of an angel.” Its closing Martyrdom has Pau…

Writing from Carthage, Tertullian points inquirers to the churches the apostles founded, and to Rome above all — “how happy is its church, on which apostles poured forth all their doctrine along with their blood! where Peter endures a passion like his Lord’s, where Paul wins his crown in a death like John’s.” The comparison is exact and deliberate: John here is John the Baptist, beheaded — so Tertullian, our earliest explicit witness to the manner of death, has Paul executed by the sword, the end Roman law reserved for a citizen, as against Peter’s cross. In the Scorpiace he is blunter still — “that Paul is beheaded… a birth suited to Roman citizenship” — and names Nero as the emperor who fi…

Eusebius gathers the threads and adds the physical monuments. Following Acts, he notes that Paul was “sent bound to Rome” under Festus and spent two years in open custody; but he then records the tradition — behind the Pastoral epistles — that Paul was acquitted at that first trial, “sent again upon the ministry of preaching,” and only on a second visit to Rome “suffered martyrdom under Nero.” For the death itself he cites hard evidence: Paul “was beheaded in Rome itself,” and the Roman presbyter Gaius (c. 200) could already point to the apostles’ graves — “I can show the trophies of the apostles: for if you will go to the Vatican or to the Ostian way, you will find the trophies of those who…

In his catalogue of Christian authors, Jerome opens the entry on Paul with a biography and closes it with the fullest early statement of the martyrdom. He dates the death precisely — “in the fourteenth year of Nero,” the same day as Peter — and names the place of burial: Paul “was beheaded at Rome for Christ’s sake and was buried in the Ostian way,” where the basilica of San Paolo fuori le Mura stands over the traditional tomb. Jerome also states the release-and-second-imprisonment openly — Paul was “dismissed by Nero, that the gospel of Christ might be preached also in the West” — and reads 2 Timothy’s “I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion” as Paul’s own word on Nero. With Jerome th…

Critical study leaves the core of the tradition standing and trims its extensions. That Paul was executed at Rome under Nero, in the mid-60s, is among the best-attested facts of apostolic history — multiply and independently witnessed (Clement, Ignatius, Dionysius of Corinth, Gaius, Tertullian, Eusebius, Jerome) within a century and a half, with no rival account of a different death anywhere — so that surveys of the apostles’ fates grade Paul’s martyrdom, with Peter’s and James’s, at the very top of the scale. That the death was by beheading is early (Tertullian) and coheres with his Roman citizenship, though it is one step less firm than the fact of martyrdom. The Spanish mission and the re…

ar.q: Was Paul beheaded at Rome under Nero?
ar.c: The tradition, in its classic form, has two parts. First, the fact: Paul died a martyr at Rome under the emperor Nero, in the persecution of the mid-60s. Second, the manner: he was beheaded — put to the sword, the execution Roman law reserved for a citizen — whereas Peter , no citizen, was crucified . Jerome fixes the date in Nero’s fourteenth year (A.D. 67/68) and the burial on the Ostian way, where San Paolo fuori le Mura stands. This page weighs both parts, and distinguishes the firm core from the legendary embellishment that later gathered around it. 1
ar.a: Sound. Paul’s execution at Rome under Nero is among the best-attested facts of apostolic history — early, multiple, independent, and unrefuted, and anchored to a tomb venerated continuously from the second century to the sarcophagus dated to the first or second century beneath San Paolo fuori le Mura. The beheading by the sword is early enough and is the very death Roman law reserved for a citizen, and stands as the mainstream verdict even if a h…

ar.q: Did Paul reach Spain?
ar.c: Paul told the Roman church, before his arrest, that Rome was only a stop on the way to the western edge of the empire: Whensoever I take my journey into Spain, I will come to you: for I trust to see you in my journey… When therefore I have performed this, and have sealed to them this fruit, I will come by you into Spain. — Romans 15:24, 28 . The interpretation under test holds that Paul actually did it: acquitted at the trial with which Acts leaves him, he sailed west to Spain, came back east to the churches of the Pastoral epistles (Crete, Miletus, Troas, Nicopolis — none of them reachable wi…
ar.a: Contested. Whether Paul reached Spain is a genuine open question on which the disciplines pull apart: the early literary evidence (Clement at Rome, the Muratorian canon, the Acts of Peter , the release-tradition and the wider patristic chorus, the Pastorals) leans toward a Spanish mission — and leans harder once Clement’s phrase is read from its Roman vantage — while the historical-critical evidence leans against : the silence of Acts, the absenc…

ds.t: Simon Peter
ds.q: Simon Peter stands first in every list of the Twelve, and the traditions about him are the fullest and the best-attested of any apostle. This page is not a life of Peter so much as a history of what the church remembered about him — his origin and family, his name, his mission, and above all his death — set out earliest source first, so that the spare notices of the New Testament, the early Roman witnesses, the great compiler Eusebius, and the late legend can each be weighed on its own date. This is a biographical tradition-timeline : its “witnesses” are the datable sources that report on Peter, and the contested questions — did he really lead and die at Rome? was he crucified head-downward?…

tl.t: The New Testament gives Peter a fuller portrait than any other apostle. He is Simon, son of Jonah, a fisherman of Bethsaida and Capernaum and the brother of Andrew; at their first meeting Jesus renames him — “thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone” (Greek Petros ) — and later builds a saying on the name: “thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church.” 1 He is married — the Gospels heal his wife's mother, and Paul notes that “Cephas” travelled with a believing wife. 2 He heads the Twelve, preaches at Pentecost, and leads the Jerusalem church through Acts 1–12, until Paul “withstood him to the face” at Antioch over table-fellowship with Gentiles. Of his e…

Clement of Rome , writing to Corinth within a generation of Peter's death, gives the earliest notice of his martyrdom. Peter and Paul are “the greatest and most righteous pillars” of the church who were “persecuted and put to death”: Peter “endured not one or two, but numerous labours, and when he had at length suffered martyrdom, departed to the place of glory due to him.” Clement names neither the manner nor the place — but he writes from Rome, treating both deaths as recent and famous. 4

On his own way to martyrdom, Ignatius writes ahead to the Roman church, “I do not, as Peter and Paul, issue commandments unto you” — a passing appeal that assumes both apostles had once taught with authority at Rome. It is an early, incidental confirmation of the Roman tradition. 5

The apocryphal Acts of Peter — a second-century romance — supplies the two most famous scenes of Peter's death: the Quo vadis , in which the fleeing apostle meets Christ on the road (“Lord, whither art Thou going?” — “I am going to Rome to be crucified”) and turns back; and his crucifixion head-downward, at his own request, “for I am not worthy to be crucified like my Lord.” This is hagiographical legend of little biographical worth, but it is an early and valuable witness to how Peter was already being venerated , and it is the wellspring of the inverted-cross tradition. 6

Tertullian of Carthage points converts to Rome, “how happy is its church … where Peter endures a passion like his Lord's!” — the earliest explicit statement that Peter died by crucifixion . He does not, however, specify that the cross was inverted. 7

Gaius, a Roman churchman under Pope Zephyrinus, answers a rival by pointing to the apostles' graves: “I can show the trophies ( tropaia ) of the apostles. For if you will go to the Vatican or to the Ostian way, you will find the trophies of those who laid the foundations of this church.” Preserved by Eusebius, this is the earliest reference to a monument marking Peter's tomb on the Vatican hill — the “Trophy of Gaius” that twentieth-century excavation would recover beneath St Peter's Basilica. 8

Origen , quoted by Eusebius, is the first writer to record the specific manner: Peter preached to the dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Bithynia, Cappadocia, and Asia, and “at last, having come to Rome, he was crucified head-downwards; for he had requested that he might suffer in this way.” With this the detail long carried by the romance Acts enters a named theologian. 9

Eusebius gathers the scattered notices into the first connected account. Peter came to Rome under Claudius to confront Simon Magus; Mark, “a follower of Peter,” set down his preaching as a Gospel; and under Nero “Paul was beheaded in Rome itself, and … Peter likewise was crucified” — a report Eusebius says is confirmed by the apostles' names in the Roman cemeteries, by Gaius's trophies, and by Dionysius of Corinth, who wrote that Peter and Paul “taught together in like manner in Italy, and suffered martyrdom at the same time.” 10

Jerome condenses the whole Greek tradition into one compact Latin life. Peter, son of John, of Bethsaida, brother of Andrew and chief of the apostles, was bishop of Antioch, preached to the dispersion, then “pushed on to Rome in the second year of Claudius to overthrow Simon Magus, and held the sacerdotal chair there for twenty-five years until … the fourteenth year of Nero.” He was crucified “with his head towards the ground and his feet raised on high, asserting that he was unworthy to be crucified in the same manner as his Lord,” and lies “buried at Rome in the Vatican near the triumphal way.” 11

ar.q: Did Peter lead and die at Rome?
ar.c: It is, therefore, recorded that Paul was beheaded in Rome itself, and that Peter likewise was crucified under Nero. This account of Peter and Paul is substantiated by the fact that their names are preserved in the cemeteries of that place even to the present day. — Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2.25 . The claim to be weighed: Peter came to Rome, led its church, and died a martyr there in the mid-60s.
ar.a: Sound. That Peter ministered at Rome and was martyred there under Nero is as well-attested as almost anything in first-century church history outside the New Testament itself: an unbroken, independent, early literary tradition converging with a continuously venerated tomb, and no competing claim anywhere. The New Testament's silence is the one genuine gap, but the “Babylon” greeting and Jesus' death-prophecy in John 21 sit comfortably with the tr…

ar.q: Was Peter crucified head-downward?
ar.c: … my cross ought to be fixed head down most, so as to direct my feet towards heaven; for I am not worthy to be crucified like my Lord. Then, having reversed the cross, they nailed his feet up. — Acts of Peter and Paul 41, source . The claim has two parts that the tradition welds together but the evidence pulls apart: that Peter was crucified upside-down (the posture ), and that he asked for it out of unworthiness to die as Christ did (the motive ). 1
ar.a: Plausible for the posture; weak for the request. That Peter was martyred at Rome is sound , and that he died by crucifixion is well grounded in Tertullian and Origen. That the cross was inverted is coherent and unrefuted — inverted crucifixion was an ordinary Roman cruelty, and Origen's early, possibly-independent notice gives it a real foothold — but the silence of the earlier sober witnesses keeps it short of proven. What does not hold is the c…

ds.t: Philip
ds.q: Philip was a fisherman’s town-fellow of Andrew and Peter, of Bethsaida, one of the first Jesus called and, in John’s Gospel, the man who fetched Nathanael and later voiced the disciples’ bafflement at the loaves and at the Greeks who came seeking Jesus. The New Testament names him in all four lists of the Twelve and then, as with most of the apostles, tells nothing of where he went or how he died. What the church came to “know” grew up afterward — and Philip’s case carries a complication all its own: the earliest sources that place him in Asia may have confused him with a different Philip, the deacon and evangelist of Acts, whose four prophesying daughters look suspiciously like the daughter…

tl.t: The New Testament gives Philip a clear but modest place. He is of Bethsaida, “the city of Andrew and Peter,” one of the first Jesus calls with the plain word “Follow me,” and at once he finds Nathanael: “We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write.” He appears three times more, all in John — tested by Jesus before the feeding of the five thousand (“Whence shall we buy bread?”), approached by the enquiring Greeks, and answered at the Last Supper when he asks, “Lord, shew us the Father” (“he that hath seen me hath seen the Father”) — and he is named in all four lists of the Twelve. Of his mission or death the New Testament says nothing. It also names a second Phili…

tl.w: Papias of Hierapolis, preserved by Eusebius (c. 110–130)
tl.t: Papias , bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia and a collector of the oldest apostolic memory, is the earliest witness to a Philip at Hierapolis. Eusebius reports that Papias “received a wonderful narrative from the daughters of Philip” — his neighbours — among them the raising of a dead man and the story of Justus Barsabas surviving a draught of poison. Eusebius calls this figure “the Apostle Philip,” and this notice is the root of the whole Asian tradition. But Papias’s own words (as Eusebius gives them) speak only of “Philip” and his daughters — and daughters at Hierapolis are exactly what Acts attaches to the evangelist . Here, at the very first link, the identity is already in question. 2

tl.w: Polycrates of Ephesus and the Dialogue of Gaius, preserved by Eusebius (c. 190–210)
tl.t: Polycrates , bishop of Ephesus, writing to Victor of Rome in the Quartodeciman controversy, lists the “great lights” buried in Asia and names first “Philip, one of the twelve apostles, who sleeps in Hierapolis, and his two aged virgin daughters, and another daughter who lived in the Holy Spirit and now rests at Ephesus.” A generation later the anti-Montanist Dialogue of Gaius, quoting the Montanists’ own appeal, points to “four prophetesses, the daughters of Philip, at Hierapolis… their tomb is there and the tomb of their father.” These two early, independent Asian witnesses fix Philip’s home, grave, and daughters at Hierapolis — and disagree on their number and character (Polycrates’ three,…

The apocryphal Acts of Philip — a late romance in which Philip journeys with Bartholomew and his sister Mariamne (accompanied by a talking leopard and kid) to “Ophiorymos,” the “city of the serpent,” identified with Hierapolis — supplies the martyrdom the earlier sources lack. Philip converts the proconsul’s wife Nicanora, is arrested, and is executed by being hung head-downward : the soldiers “pierced Philip’s ankles… put the cords through his ankles, and hung him head downwards on a tree,” from which he preaches and, in some manuscripts, calls down destruction on his persecutors until Christ rebukes him. It is hagiographical romance of low biographical value, but it is the wellspring of Ph…

The tradition’s one physical anchor is the great octagonal martyrium of St Philip on the hill above Hierapolis (modern Pamukkale, Turkey), a fifth-century pilgrimage shrine long known to excavators. In 2011 the Italian archaeologist Francesco D’Andria announced that, some forty metres from the martyrium, he had uncovered a fifth-century church built around a first-century Roman tomb — which he identified as Philip’s original grave, emptied when the relics were carried (he suggests) to Constantinople and then Rome. The find confirms what the texts already showed — that by the fourth century a Philip was venerated as a martyr and buried at Hierapolis — but a tomb cannot say which Philip lay in…

ar.q: Was Philip crucified head-downward at Hierapolis?
ar.c: And he ordered to bring clubs and strong cords; and after piercing Philip’s ankles they brought hooks, and put the cords through his ankles, and hung him head downwards on a tree that was before the door of the temple… — the Acts of Philip (ANF vol. 8). The claim: Philip died a martyr at Hierapolis, crucified or hung head-downward under the city’s proconsul after converting his wife. 1
ar.a: Weak. Keep the two questions apart. The burial of a Philip at Hierapolis is solid history; a martyrdom there is possible but unproven — the early sources attest a grave and, later, a cult, not a killing, and Polycrates’ “fell asleep” neither proves nor disproves one. But the titled claim is narrower and weaker still: that Philip was crucified head-downward hangs on the late Acts of Philip alone, an image visibly borrowed from Peter and unsupporte…

ar.q: Which Philip dwelt and died at Hierapolis — the apostle or the evangelist?
ar.c: …among these are Philip, one of the twelve apostles, who sleeps in Hierapolis, and his two aged virgin daughters, and another daughter who lived in the Holy Spirit and now rests at Ephesus. — Polycrates of Ephesus, in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.31 , 3. The claim under test is the one the ancient sources make and the whole Asian tradition rests on: that the Philip remembered at Hierapolis — with his grave, his daughters, and (later) his martyrium — was Philip the apostle , one of the Twelve, and not Philip the deacon and evangelist of Acts. 1
ar.a: Contested. That the Hierapolis Philip was the apostle is asserted by two early and local witnesses and was undoubted in antiquity; that he was really the evangelist is the natural inference from the four-prophesying-daughters signature of Acts, and is the judgment of much modern criticism. Each reading survives the other’s best objection; the daughters’ own count and character are reported inconsistently, betraying a conflation already complete i…

ds.t: Simon the Zealot
ds.q: Simon the Zealot is, with James the son of Alphaeus, among the most silent of the Twelve. He stands eleventh in every list — next to last, just before Judas Iscariot — and the New Testament tells us nothing of him but a single word of description: Matthew and Mark call him “the Cananaean,” Luke and Acts “the Zealot.” The two are the same epithet, not two facts: “Cananaean” is not “of Cana” nor “Canaanite” but the Aramaic qan’ana , “zealous,” which Luke simply renders into Greek as zēlōtēs . What that zeal was — membership in the revolutionary party that would later fight Rome, or a plain devotion to the Law — is the one real question the name raises, and it is weighed below. Everything else …

tl.t: The New Testament names Simon four times, always in the same place — eleventh in the third group of four, immediately before Judas Iscariot — and never otherwise. It gives him no saying, no deed, no mission, no death: only a surname that marks him off from that other Simon, Simon Peter. Matthew and Mark write “Simon the Cananaean” ( ho Kananaios ); Luke and Acts, in the same slot, write “Simon called Zelotes.” These are not two men nor two facts but one epithet in two languages: “Cananaean” transliterates the Aramaic qan’ana (“zealous”), and Luke translates it for Greek readers as zēlōtēs . That the word does not mean “from Cana” or “Canaanite” is settled; what the “zeal” denotes — a former …

Where the Gospels give a name only, the late apostle-lists — Pseudo-Hippolytus On the Twelve Apostles , Pseudo-Dorotheus of Tyre, and their Byzantine and Latin kin — supply a mission and a death, and cannot agree on either. One strand sends Simon far into the north and west — the Black Sea coast, Egypt and North Africa, and even Britain; another keeps him in the East, in Persia or the Caucasus. Worse, the lists cannot even keep his person distinct: Pseudo-Hippolytus writes that “Simon the Zealot, the son of Clopas, who is also called Jude, became bishop of Jerusalem after James the Just, and fell asleep and was buried there at the age of 120 years” — which is not the apostle Simon at all but…

tl.w: The Latin Passio and the Golden Legend (c. 1260)
tl.t: The Western Church settled on one of these strands and made it the standard story. The Latin Passio Simonis et Iudae , retold in Jacobus de Voragine’s Golden Legend (c. 1260), pairs Simon with Jude/Thaddaeus, sends the two together into Persia — Simon “preached in Egypt,” Jude “in Mesopotamia,” “and from thence came they into Persia” — to confront the sorcerers Zaroes and Arphaxat and to die together in a pagan temple at Suanir, where the priests “ran upon the apostles and hewed them to death.” From this joint martyrdom the West keeps their common feast on 28 October, and Western art gave Simon a saw as the emblem of his death — from the parallel tradition, reported as far back as the Greek …

Critical study leaves Simon nearly as blank as the Gospel lists found him, and turns the two live questions over to the tools that grade them. On the epithet , most now doubt that “the Zealot” can mean a card-carrying member of the revolutionary party: Josephus dates the organized Zealots to the war of 66–70, a full generation after Jesus called Simon, so the surname more likely means “zealous for the Law” — though Martin Hengel’s study of a longer-running “freedom movement” reaching back to Herod keeps the political reading alive, and the question stays genuinely open. On the travels , the verdict is harder: the mission-traditions are late, mutually contradictory, and geographically impossi…

ar.q: Where did Simon the Zealot preach and die — Persia, Britain, or elsewhere?
ar.c: … according to the Greeks, he preached on the Black Sea, in Egypt, Northern Africa, and Britain, while, according to the Latin Passio Simonis et Judae … Simon laboured in Persia, and was there martyred at Suanir. — Catholic Encyclopedia, “St. Simon the Apostle,” summarizing the sources. The claim under test is whether any of the rival mission-and-death traditions can be established as historical — most often the Western favourite, that Simon evangelized Persia with Jude and was martyred there (sawn asunder, or crucified at Suanir), and secondarily the British legend that made him a founder-apo…
ar.a: Weak. The mission-and-death traditions of Simon the Zealot are late, contradictory, and carried by the least trustworthy sources in the apostolic dossier, which confuse even his person. That he evangelized somewhere is plausible; that it was Persia, or Britain, or Egypt, and that he was sawn, crucified, or hacked down there, is not what the evidence shows.

ar.q: Was Simon the Zealot the same man as Simeon son of Clopas, the second bishop of Jerusalem?
ar.c: Simon the Zealot, the son of Clopas, who is also called Jude, became bishop of Jerusalem after James the Just, and fell asleep and was buried there at the age of 120 years. — Pseudo-Hippolytus, On the Twelve Apostles 11. In one sentence the catalogue makes the apostle Simon the Zealot identical with Simeon son of Clopas, the second bishop of Jerusalem whom Hegesippus reports martyred under Trajan at 120. The claim under test is that identity: that the silent eleventh apostle and the long-lived kinsman-bishop are one man, so that Simon the Cananaean was the Lord’s cousin who took the Jerusalem …
ar.a: Contested. The equation of Simon the Zealot with Simeon son of Clopas is genuinely advanced and cannot be dismissed: it is old (Pseudo-Hippolytus, the Chronicon Paschale , an apocryphal apostle- Preaching ) and carried by a real family argument — if Alphaeus is Clopas, Simon son of Clopas is the brother of James son of Alphaeus, explaining their juxtaposition in the lists. But it leans on the least reliable stratum of the apostolic record, and th…

ar.q: Was Simon “the Zealot” a member of the revolutionary party?
ar.c: … Simon called Zelotes… — Luke 6:15 (cf. Acts 1:13 ; and “Simon the Canaanite,” Matthew 10:4 , Mark 3:18 ). The claim under test is the strong, popular reading of the surname: that “the Zealot” identifies Simon as an actual member of the Zealots — the armed nationalist party that sought to expel Rome and establish a Mosaic theocracy — so that Jesus’ circle held a reformed revolutionary alongside Matthew, who had collected Rome’s taxes. (The weaker, uncontested point — that the epithet derives from the zeal-word and not from “Cana” — is common ground and is set out on the New Testament detail p…
ar.a: Contested. That Simon was “zealous” is certain; whether the word marks him a member of the revolutionary party is genuinely disputed and not resolvable on the present evidence. The strict party-membership reading founders on the late date of the named faction (Meier); a looser political reading survives on Hengel’s longer chronology of the freedom movement. No discipline’s verdict overrides the other’s here, and the Gospel gives nothing further t…

ds.t: Thaddaeus / Jude
ds.q: Alone among the Twelve, this apostle cannot be securely named . He stands tenth in every list, in the third group of four — but Matthew and Mark call him “Thaddaeus” (some manuscripts “Lebbaeus”), while Luke and Acts, in the same place, call him “Judas of James,” and John lets a “Judas, not Iscariot” ask a single question at the Last Supper. The church long ago harmonized these into one apostle of several names, and then reached further and identified him with Jude the author of the Epistle of Jude — though that Jude names himself “brother of James” and is usually reckoned a brother of the Lord, one of the “brethren” the Gospels keep apart from the Twelve. Around this silent, many-named figu…

tl.t: The New Testament gives this apostle a fixed place and an unfixed name. In the third group of four he stands tenth — and where Matthew and Mark write “Thaddaeus” (the Received Text of Matthew “Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus”), Luke and Acts write “Judas of James.” John, without listing the Twelve, names a “Judas, not Iscariot” among them, giving this apostle the one saying the Gospels record from his lips. Of his mission, his labours, or his death the New Testament says nothing at all. Distinct from him in its own telling is Jude the author of the short epistle, who calls himself “brother of James” — naming him with the “brethren of the Lord” (James, Joses, Simon, and Judas) whom the …

tl.w: Eusebius and the letters of Abgar (c. 325)
tl.t: The earliest connected story attached to a “Thaddaeus” is the legend of King Abgar of Edessa, which Eusebius gives in full, claiming to translate the correspondence of Abgar and Jesus from the royal archives. Yet his Thaddaeus is not one of the Twelve: Eusebius twice calls him “one of the seventy,” sent to Edessa by the apostle Thomas — “Thomas, one of the twelve apostles… sent Thaddeus, who was also numbered among the seventy disciples of Christ, to Edessa.” The Syriac source behind the tale, the Doctrine of Addai , names the missionary “Addai” and likewise reckons him one of the seventy-two. So the very first “life of Thaddaeus” belongs, on its own telling, to a lesser figure of the same n…

What the New Testament left as a tangle, Jerome tied into a single knot. Commenting on the apostle-list of Matthew, he took Thaddaeus, Lebbaeus, and Luke’s “Judas of James” to be one man — “he is called Judas son of James by the evangelist Luke, and elsewhere is named Lebbaeus… one must believe he had three names” — and, elsewhere, folded in Jude the Lord’s brother and the epistle-writer as well, so that a single Judas carried the apostolate, the kinship to Jesus, and the canonical letter. The first of these harmonizations (that the list-names denote one apostle) is a sound instinct; the second (that this apostle is the Lord’s brother and wrote the epistle) revives the same cousin-machinery …

tl.w: The apostle-lists and the Golden Legend (uncertain date; c. 1260)
tl.t: Where the New Testament gives no mission and no death, the late catalogues supply both — and pair Jude with Simon the Zealot. The apostle-lists scatter his labours across Mesopotamia, Persia, and Armenia and cannot agree; the Edessene strand collapses him into Addai of the seventy. Jacobus de Voragine’s Golden Legend (c. 1260) gives the fullest form, sending Simon and Jude together into Persia to confront the sorcerers Zaroes and Arphaxat and to die in a pagan temple, where the priests “ran upon the apostles and hewed them to death.” From this joint martyrdom the Western Church keeps their feast on 28 October, and Western art gave Jude a club and Simon a saw as the emblems of their deaths. I…

Critical study keeps the two knots apart and answers them differently. The first — that Thaddaeus, Lebbaeus, and “Judas of James” name one apostle of the Twelve — is widely accepted as the most economical reading of four parallel lists, confirmed in part by John’s independent “Judas not Iscariot,” though it remains an inference. The second — that this apostle wrote the Epistle of Jude — is generally rejected: the apostle is “Judas son of James,” while the epistle-writer is a brother of James who sets himself apart from the apostles, and so is better identified with Jude the brother of the Lord. The Abgar mission, on its own sources, belongs to Addai of the seventy, not to the apostle, and re…

ar.q: Did the apostle Thaddaeus found the church of Edessa?
ar.c: Thomas, one of the twelve apostles, under divine impulse sent Thaddeus, who was also numbered among the seventy disciples of Christ, to Edessa, as a preacher and evangelist of the teaching of Christ. — Eusebius, Church History 1.13.4 . The claim under test is the popular identification — often attached to the apostle Jude/Thaddaeus — that this Thaddaeus, the healer of Abgar and founder of the Edessene church, is the apostle Thaddaeus of the Twelve, so that the wordless apostle acquires a famous mission and a kingdom converted. 1
ar.a: Weak. The Abgar tradition anchors Edessa’s claim to an apostolic founder, and in its strongest form — the Armenian confession of the apostle Jude/Thaddaeus — it is cherished and living still; but its own earliest witnesses, Eusebius and the Doctrine of Addai , name the Edessene founder Addai, one of the seventy, sent by the apostle Thomas, the letters that dramatize it are apocryphal, and even the Armenian tradition attaches the apostle to Armeni…

ar.q: Did the apostle Jude write the Epistle of Jude?
ar.c: Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James, to them that are sanctified by God the Father… — Jude 1 . The claim under test is the traditional identification — made doctrine by Jerome and long standard in the West — that the author of this letter is the apostle of the Twelve variously called Thaddaeus and “Judas of James.” If it holds, the silent tenth apostle turns out to have left a canonical epistle. If it fails, the epistle belongs to a different Jude — Jude the brother of the Lord — and the apostle remains as wordless as the Gospel lists leave him. 1
ar.a: Weak. That the apostle “Judas of James” wrote the Epistle of Jude held in the Latin West through Jerome’s fusion of the Judases, but it does not hold on its own evidence: the apostle’s name points to a son of James, the epistle-writer names himself a brother of James, and that writer sets himself apart from the apostles. The letter belongs to Jude the brother of the Lord, a distinct man — which leaves the apostle Thaddaeus / Judas-of-James withou…

ar.q: Are Thaddaeus, Lebbaeus, and Judas of James one and the same apostle?
ar.c: Judas saith unto him, not Iscariot, Lord, how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world? — John 14:22 . The four lists of the Twelve divide into three fixed groups of four; in the third group, after James the son of Alphaeus, Matthew and Mark name “Thaddaeus” (Matthew’s Received Text “Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus”), while Luke and Acts, in exactly that place, name “Judas of James.” The claim under test is the harmonization that has stood since antiquity: that these are not three or four apostles but one, a single member of the Twelve who bore more than one …
ar.a: Plausible — indeed probably right. That Thaddaeus, Lebbaeus, and Judas of James name one apostle of the Twelve is the most economical reading of four parallel lists, is confirmed in part by John’s “Judas not Iscariot,” and rests on the manuscript truth that Lebbaeus and Thaddaeus are two bynames, not two men. It falls short of certainty only because the lists give different names in the slot and no text equates them — a harmonization coherent and…

ds.t: Thomas
ds.q: Thomas is the apostle whom the Gospels let us hear speak. Where the others are only names in a list, John gives him three lines — the loyalty that says “Let us also go, that we may die with him,” the bafflement that asks “how can we know the way?” and above all the doubt that will not believe the resurrection until it touches the wounds, breaking at last into the highest confession in the Gospel, “My Lord and my God.” His name is not a name either: Thomas (Aramaic te’oma ) and its Greek gloss Didymus both mean “the Twin,” and the Syriac church would call him Judas Thomas and wonder whose twin he was. Beyond the New Testament, Thomas carries the best-developed missionary tradition of any apos…

tl.t: The New Testament names Thomas in all four lists of the Twelve, but only John’s Gospel lets him act and speak. When Jesus resolves to return to Judea though the Jews there had sought to stone him, it is Thomas who rallies the rest: “Let us also go, that we may die with him.” At the Last Supper he interrupts with the honest question “Lord, we know not whither thou goest; and how can we know the way?” — drawing out the answer “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” And after the resurrection he is the disciple who was not there, who swears he will not believe “except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails… and thrust my hand into his side,” and who, when Jesus offers him exactly that…

tl.w: Origen, preserved by Eusebius: Parthia (c. 230, reported c. 325)
tl.t: The earliest tradition of where Thomas went is the soberest. Origen , in a lost commentary on Genesis quoted by Eusebius, gives the apostles’ “division of the world”: “Parthia… was allotted to Thomas as his field of labor, Scythia to Andrew, and Asia to John.” This is a bare geographical notice, without marvels — the Parthian empire of Persia, not yet India. Eusebius elsewhere preserves a second early strand: the Edessene legend that “after the ascension of Jesus, Judas, who was also called Thomas, sent” the apostle Thaddaeus to King Abgar of Edessa — the first link, however legendary, between Thomas and the Syriac East that would become the heartland of his cult. 2

tl.w: The Acts of Thomas (c. 220–240, Syriac, Edessa)
tl.t: The Acts of Thomas is the fullest and most famous of the apocryphal Acts , and the wellspring of the India tradition. Written in Syriac at Edessa in the early third century, it opens with the apostles dividing the world by lot: India falls to Thomas, who refuses until the risen Christ sells him as a slave-carpenter to a merchant buying for the Indian king Gundaphar . Commissioned to build the king a palace, Thomas gives the money to the poor and tells him he has raised a palace in heaven instead. The tale runs on through miracles and conversions to a martyrdom: under King Misdaeus , whose wife and son Thomas had baptized, the apostle is led to a hill and run through with spears by four soldi…

tl.w: Ephrem the Syrian and the shrine at Edessa (4th c.)
tl.t: By the fourth century Thomas had a tomb-cult in the Syriac world. Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), who lived out his last decade at Edessa, sings in his hymns of the apostle martyred in India whose bones a merchant carried back to Edessa — picturing even the demons dismayed that the apostle they thought slain in India had come to trouble them at Edessa. An early Syriac martyrology fixes the memory: “3 July, St. Thomas who was pierced with a lance in India. His body is at Urhai [Edessa], having been brought there by the merchant Khabin. A great festival.” And about 384 the pilgrim Egeria, on her way through Mesopotamia, “straightway repaired to the church and memorial of Saint Thomas” at Edess…

Jacobus de Voragine’s Golden Legend gathers the medieval Thomas: the palace built in heaven for King Gundaphorus, the raising of the king’s dead brother who had seen it, the mission to a second Indian king Mesdeus, the idol shattered, and the martyrdom by the spears (or swords) of the pagan priests. It is late hagiography, a thousand years and more after the events, drawing on the old Acts and the apostle-lists; but it is the form in which the Latin West received Thomas, and the source of his emblem, the carpenter’s square. 5

Critical study grades Thomas’s tradition as the strongest of the apostolic missions outside Peter and Paul — which is not to say secure. The living witness is the Mar Thoma or Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala, an ancient community that traces its founding to Thomas’s landing at Muziris (Cranganore) in AD 52 and his martyrdom at Mylapore, near modern Chennai, about AD 72, with his tomb at San Thome. Sean McDowell, weighing each martyrdom account on a probability scale, rates Thomas’s death in India “more probable than not” — below the near-certain deaths of Peter, Paul, and James, but well above the apostles for whom nothing early survives. The anchor is Gundaphar’s recovered historicity; th…

ar.q: Was Thomas the twin brother of Jesus?
ar.c: These are the secret sayings which the living Jesus spoke and which Didymos Judas Thomas wrote down. — incipit of the Gospel of Thomas . The double epithet “Didymos… Thomas” — Greek and Aramaic for “twin” — together with the personal name “Judas,” gives the Syriac Judas Thomas ; and a strand of eastern tradition took the “twin” to mean the twin of Jesus himself. 1
ar.a: Weak. The name is genuine and old: Thomas was called “the Twin,” and the Syriac church did call him Judas Thomas . But the claim that he was the twin brother of Jesus is a sectarian elaboration — unknown to the four Gospels, which name Jesus’ brothers without him; at odds with the church’s understanding of the Incarnation; and attested only in gnostic and Syriac texts that had a doctrinal motive to assert it. As a reading of what “the Twin” meant…

ar.q: Did Thomas evangelize India?
ar.c: Parthia, according to tradition, was allotted to Thomas as his field of labor… — Origen, in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.1 . The earliest notice sends Thomas to the Persian East; the fuller tradition — the Acts of Thomas , the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala, the Edessa cult — sends him to India and a martyr’s death there. The question is whether that fuller tradition preserves a genuine mission or an elaborated legend. 1
ar.a: Plausible. Uniquely among the apocryphal missions, Thomas’s has a hard historical anchor in the recovered king Gundaphar, a broad and independent chorus of fourth-century fathers naming India specifically, a sea-route that made the voyage ordinary commerce, a continuous Indian church that claims him, and an early Edessene cult of his relics — a coherent reading, not ruled out on any front, and rated by serious scholarship as more likely than not.…

ds.t: The Apostles
ds.q: The apostles were the men Jesus chose to be with him and to be sent out in his name — the word apostolos (ἀπόστολος) means “one sent.” The Gospels name twelve; after one of them, Judas Iscariot, betrayed Jesus and died, the remaining eleven chose Matthias to fill his place; and the risen Christ afterward called Paul, “as to one born out of due time.” This page introduces the group and opens onto a separate timeline for each figure — tracing, earliest source first, how the church's memory of who he was, where he preached, and how he died took shape across the centuries.

xs.w: The four lists of the Twelve
xs.t: The New Testament gives four lists of the Twelve — in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Acts. They agree in dividing the names into three fixed groups of four, each group always headed by the same man (Peter, Philip, and James son of Alphaeus), and they agree that Judas Iscariot comes last. Two names vary: where Matthew and Mark have “Thaddaeus” (some manuscripts “Lebbaeus”), Luke and Acts have “Judas son of James”; and the Simon whom Matthew and Mark call “the Cananaean” Luke and Acts call “the Zealot.” Acts, listing the Eleven after the resurrection, omits the dead Judas Iscariot. 1

Between the Ascension and Pentecost, Peter stood up among the believers and proposed that another take the “office” (ἐπισκοπή) left empty by Judas's fall. Two men were put forward; the company prayed and cast lots, “and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.” 2

xs.w: Paul, born out of due time
xs.t: To the Twelve and Matthias the tradition adds Paul, who never followed Jesus in Galilee but met the risen Christ on the road to Damascus. He called himself an apostle “as to one born out of due time” — “the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle” — yet one who “laboured more abundantly than they all.” 3

The Twelve as the Gospels name them, followed by Matthias and Paul. The bare identifications below are those the New Testament itself gives; the traditional identifications — several of them debated (Bartholomew as Nathanael, Matthew as Levi, Thaddaeus as Jude) — are weighed on the individual pages as they come online. 4 .html">Name and add its "> heading + one-line description under the "The apostles" family

xs.w: on docs/index.html, plus its slug to DOCTRINE_NAMES in toc.js. Once >=2 apostle pages exist, add the "Related doctrines:" cluster breadcrumb to each member summary and to this hub (family: "The apostles"). --> Simon Peter — the fisherman of Bethsaida and Capernaum, always named first. Andrew — Simon Peter's brother, who first brought him to Jesus. James, son of Zebedee — with his brother John, surnamed by Jesus a “son of thunder”; the first of the Twelve to be martyred. John — son of Zebedee, brother of James; “the disciple whom Jesus loved,” the last of the Twelve to die. Philip — of Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Peter. Bartholomew — traditionally identified with Nathanael. Thomas — called Didymus, “the Twin.” Matthew — the tax collector (publican); traditionally identified with Levi. James, son of Alphaeus — sometimes distinguished as James “the Less.” Thaddaeus / Jude — the apostle Matthew and Mark call Thaddaeus (or Lebbaeus) and Luke and Acts call Judas son of James. Simon the Zealot — called “the Cananaean” in Matthew and Mark. Judas Iscariot — who betrayed Jesus, and whose place among the Twelve Matthias took. And, added to the Twelve: Matthias — chosen by lot to replace Judas Iscariot. Paul — the apostle to the Gentiles, called last of all on the Damascus road. Beyond the Twelve
xs.t: The apostolic circle did not end with the Twelve. Luke's Gospel records that Jesus also appointed “other seventy” (seventy-two, in many manuscripts) and sent them out ahead of him, two by two, into every town he meant to visit. 5 Standing near the same circle are figures the early church remembered as co-workers of the apostles — Mark and Luke, the evangelists; Barnabas, Paul's first companion; and James the brother of the Lord, who led the church at Jerusalem. Their traditions belong to the same story and may in time join the timelines here.

xs.w: The sources, and how far to trust them
xs.t: Every one of these timelines draws on the same layered body of evidence, and the layers are of very uneven historical worth. It is worth setting the ladder out once — earliest witness first, latest last — because the same caution applies each time a legend of an apostle's travels or death is weighed. The rule followed throughout is simple: date a source, name it, and signal its reliability the same way wherever it recurs, and never let a vivid late legend pass as early fact. The reliable core — the New Testament The four Gospel lists, the Acts of the Apostles, and Paul's own letters (especially Galatians 1–2) are the bedrock. They are also spare: the only apostle whose death the New Testamen…

ds.t: The site of the Ascension: the Imbomon and the Chapel of the Ascension
