In Prae-Adamitae (Amsterdam, 1655; English Men before Adam , 1656) he argued that men existed before Adam, Adam being "the first and father of the Jews, not of all men," and drew from it the consequence that the Deluge — a punishment of the Jews' sins — "overflow'd only Palestine, and the Land of the Jews," sparing the pre-Adamite Gentile nations "that dwelt in China, America, the South, or Greenland. " 30 He denied the Flood's universality , not its realit…

ar.q: Was patristic allegory of the Flood a denial of its history — and did any named ancient writer deny it?
ar.c: "Who was the first Saint to say the Flood story did not really happen?" — the challenge presumes the answer is no one : Origen, Clement of Alexandria, Ambrose, and Augustine are routinely filed as "allegorists," yet they read the Flood on multiple levels, affirming the historical event and its figurative sense. Calling them "allegorists" does not make them deniers of the history. The challenge is a staple of popular debate over Genesis. The argument turns on a single equivocation: the assumption that to read a narrative figuratively is to read it instead of historically. Against that, the ques…
ar.a: Sound. The interpretation this argument serves — that the patristic allegory of the Flood was layered atop an affirmed history rather than substituted for it, and that no named ancient Christian writer denied the Flood's historicity — holds on the primary texts. Augustine states the two-level reading as a rule and rejects both the bare-history and the figure-only errors ( City of God 15.26–27); Philo and Origen, the heaviest allegorists, keep the…

ar.q: Was the Flood's historicity ever "essential to the faith" — a defined dogma, or universally assumed but never defined?
ar.c: A common defense of denying the historical Flood is that its historicity "wasn't seen as essential to the faith." Against that defense one may press a suspicion: that the hedge is an evasion, since a narrative woven so deep into Scripture cannot be merely optional. The suspicion and the hedge it answers are the two halves of one doctrinal-status question: was the Flood's historicity ever conciliar, creedal, or otherwise defined — so that denying it is a faith matter — or was it universally assumed but never formally defined , the ordinary situation for a narrative-historical claim, so that den…
ar.a: Contested. The doctrinal-status question has no clean yes-or-no answer, and the two disciplines that bear on it pull opposite ways. By the lights of strict dogmatic theology — what carries a solemn definition whose denial is formal heresy — the hedge holds: the Flood's historicity is in no creed, defined by no council, and untouched by the one modern decree (1909) that bound the historical sense of Genesis, which reaches only chapters 1–3; geogra…

ar.q: Who first denied the historical Flood — and is the first real denial early-modern, not patristic?
ar.c: "Who was the first Saint to say the Flood story did not really happen?" — and the answer pressed is that none did: the first serious denial of the universal, historical Flood is a modern development. It is not patristic, not scholastic, but early-modern, and it spreads with the geology and biblical criticism of the seventeenth century and after — so "literalism" on the Flood is the inherited Christian reading and its denial is the innovation. The claim has two parts that must be weighed separately: (i) the negative point that no patristic or medieval writer denied the historical Flood (establi…
ar.a: Sound. The interpretation this argument serves — that the first real denial of the historical, universal Flood is early-modern (La Peyrère, 1655), with geology and higher criticism mainstreaming the local and then the non-historical readings, so the patristic-to-early-modern continuity is unbroken and "no ancient Saint denied it" holds — is well-grounded and close to consensus. The hinge falls in the seventeenth century and after, exactly as the …

ar.q: Did the tradition require a geographically global Flood, or only an anthropologically universal one?
ar.c: The common claim that the Flood "wiped out human life on earth" elides a distinction the tradition keeps: between an anthropologically universal Flood (all humans outside the ark died) and a geographically global one (water over the entire planet). A Father or Doctor could affirm the historical, humanity-destroying Flood without holding the modern global-geology picture, so the slogan "global flood" smuggles in more than the consensus carried. The distinction is sorted this way by the Catholic Encyclopedia 's "Deluge" article (1908), which affirms anthropological universality as binding while …
ar.a: Contested. The interpretation is strong by one discipline's lights and weak by another's, which is precisely the contested case. As a claim about doctrinal status it is sound: anthropological universality was the firm point, and the orthodox writers who limited the Flood's extent (Augustine reporting the Olympus exemption, Cajetan, Tostatus) show strict geographic globality was never a fixed requirement of the faith — so one can affirm the histor…

ar.q: Was reading the Flood as real history the universal Christian position until the 19th century?
ar.c: "Who was the first Saint to say the Flood story did not really happen?" … Noah, the Ark, and a flood that wiped out all human life except the eight in the ark were treated as historical fact by every Doctor of the Church, all the scholastics, and all the Fathers, East and West — so biblical literalism on the Flood is the historic Christian belief, not a modern American-fundamentalist invention. The challenge is a staple of popular debate over Genesis: posed as "who was the first Saint to deny the Flood?", it presses the thesis that none did. The thesis bundles three sub-claims: (i) the pre-mod…
ar.a: Sound. The interpretation the thesis serves — that the Christian tradition read Noah's Flood as a real historical event, with no Saint denying it before the early-modern period, so the historicity reading is the inherited position rather than a nineteenth-century invention — holds, and is close to consensus: the patristic and scholastic witnesses read it as history, the older Catholic scholarship affirms the unanimity in so many words, and the fi…

ds.t: The Christian Theology of Friendship
ds.q: Christianity did not invent the philosophy of friendship — it inherited one. Long before the gospel, the classical world had thought friendship ( philia , amicitia ) through to a fine point: for Aristotle it was a species of virtue, or could not exist without it, and its highest form belonged only to the good, who love the friend for his own sake and become, in the old phrase, “a single soul in two bodies”; for Cicero, writing his Laelius de Amicitia as Rome's republic died, true friendship could exist only among the good and was the one thing whose usefulness no one doubted and whose loss no wealth could repair. This is the material the church received. The belief that develops on this page…

tl.t: Christian reflection on friendship begins from a book it did not write. In the eighth and ninth books of his Nicomachean Ethics Aristotle set down the analysis the West would use for two thousand years: that “without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods,” and that friendship comes in three kinds — for utility, for pleasure, and, highest of all, the “perfect friendship” of “men who are good, and alike in virtue,” who “wish well alike to each other qua good.” 18 Only this third kind is friendship in the full sense, for only the good love the friend for his own sake rather than for use or delight; and in it each finds in the other “another self” ( heteros autos ), …

What Aristotle argued in Greek, Cicero recast in Latin — and it was Cicero’s Laelius de Amicitia , written in 44 BC as the republic collapsed around him, that the Latin fathers actually read. He defines friendship as “a complete accord on all subjects human and divine, joined with mutual goodwill and affection,” insists that “friendship can only exist between good men,” and ranks it above every external good: “with the exception of wisdom… nothing better than this has been given to man,” for you might “take the sun out of the sky” as soon as friendship from life. 20 The true friend is “as it were a second self” ( alter idem ), and — the limit the fathers would seize on — friendship is given …

Beside the treatises stands a portrait. Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390), in the funeral oration he preached over his friend Basil the Great ( Oration 43 , c. 381), left the tradition’s most celebrated description of a real Christian friendship — the lived exemplar the theorists analyze. Meeting as students at Athens, the two led a single life bent on virtue: they knew only two roads, “the one leading to our sacred buildings… the other to secular instructors,” leaving the “feasts, theatres, meetings, banquets” to others; they competed only in yielding first place to each other, “envy we knew not,” and so “seemed to have one soul, inhabiting two bodies.” 22 It is the classical ideal — Aristo…

The first great Christianizer of the classical ideal is Ambrose, and he does it in the open. His De Officiis Ministrorum (“On the Duties of the Clergy,” c. 389) is a deliberate rewriting of Cicero’s De Officiis — same title, same three-book plan — and just as Cicero had ended with the honourable, Ambrose ends his last book with a treatment of friendship ( amicitia ) that reworks the Laelius for a clergy. He keeps the whole classical frame: friendship “which maintains virtue is to be preferred… to wealth, or honours, or power” yet never to virtue itself; the friend is a “second self”; candour and rebuke are owed (“rebukes are good, and often better than a silent friendship”); and nothing dish…

Where Ambrose defined the third term, Augustine makes it existential. Book IV of his Confessions (c. 397–400) tells not a theory but a bereavement: the death of an unnamed boyhood friend, and a grief so total that “I wondered still more that I, who was to him a second self, could live when he was dead… my soul and his soul were but one soul in two bodies.” The classical praise-words are all there — the “second self,” the “one soul in two bodies” — but Augustine turns them into a diagnosis: the grief had cut so deep because “I had poured out my soul upon the dust, in loving one who must die as if he were never to die.” 26 From this he draws the central correction of Cicero’s autonomous virtue…

Where Ambrose Christianized Cicero’s theory, John Cassian (c. 360–435) writes the Christianized practice . His whole Conference 16 — the First Conference of Abbot Joseph, titled On Friendship — is the great early-monastic treatise on the subject, and it presses the question the philosophers never had to: not what friendship is, but why it fails , and what makes one last. Cassian sorts the bonds that unite men — recommendation, bargain, shared pursuit, and blood — and finds them all “common both to the good and bad,” dissolved by time or distance; only one is indissoluble, the love owed “not… to the reason of some bargain, or the necessities of nature, but simply to similarity of virtue,” whi…

The arc reaches its Christian summit in the Cistercian abbot Aelred of Rievaulx (1110–1167), whose De Spirituali Amicitia ( Spiritual Friendship ) is the medieval classic on the subject — a three-book dialogue that is a deliberate, self-conscious rewriting of Cicero’s Laelius with Christ installed as friendship’s beginning, middle, and end. Aelred keeps the whole classical apparatus — the prologue’s recollection of a boy’s love of Cicero, the very definition (“friendship is agreement in things human and divine, with good will and charity”), the three-book plan — but tests it against Scripture and reroots it in Christ: friendship must “begin in Christ, continue with Christ, and be perfected b…

The arc reaches its modern terminus in a self-conscious heir. C. S. Lewis (1898–1963), in the “Friendship” chapter of The Four Loves (1960), names his forebears outright — “that Philia which Aristotle classified among the virtues [and] that Amicitia on which Cicero wrote a book” — and takes up their high estimate against a modern world that, he argues, “ignores” friendship: “To the Ancients, Friendship seemed the happiest and most fully human of all loves… The modern world, in comparison, ignores it… few value it because few experience it.” 33 His restatement turns on four claims. Friendship is “the least natural of loves… the least instinctive, organic, biological… and necessary” — and ther…

ar.q: Was the David–Jonathan bond a covenant friendship?
ar.c: I will now cite you from the Scriptures a wonderful instance of friendship. Jonathan, the son of Saul, loved David, and his soul was so knit to him, that David in mourning over him says, “Thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women.”… Such friendship I would wish all to entertain both towards the living and the dead. — John Chrysostom, Homilies on 2 Timothy 7, link . 1 The Old Testament’s set-piece of the two knit souls (1 Samuel 18–20; 2 Samuel 1:26) is read on this view as Scripture’s own paradigm of covenant friendship — a bond of sworn loyalty and steadfast affection ( ḥesed ) …
ar.a: Sound. That the David–Jonathan bond is a covenant friendship — sworn loyalty and steadfast ḥesed in the Near-Eastern idiom, expressed with real and demonstrative affection — is the mainstream, best-supported reading, and the only one the text received for its first two thousand years. The “love” is the treaty-allegiance vocabulary of these books, the “covenant” is a formal oath renouncing a throne, the robe is investiture, and “passing the love o…

ar.q: Was the David–Jonathan bond a homoerotic relationship?
ar.c: I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan: very pleasant hast thou been unto me: thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women. — 2 Samuel 1:26 (KJV), link . 1 A genuinely-advocated modern reading holds that the David–Jonathan narrative (1 Samuel 18–20; 2 Samuel 1:26) depicts a romantic or erotic bond, not merely covenant friendship: the two “knit” souls, the disrobing, the parting kiss, Saul’s furious rebuke, and above all David’s lament that Jonathan’s love “surpassed the love of women” are read as an eroticized register the narrator did not trouble to hide. The interpretation …
ar.a: Weak. On its best available form — Ackerman’s methodologically self-aware reading of the narrative’s eroticized rhetoric — the interpretation does not hold: it must read eros where the covenant idiom of these books already accounts for the language, it depends on an active/passive apparatus whose own logic (via Nissinen) yields “homosocial, not homoerotic,” and even granted whole it describes a rhetorical coloring in the service of dynastic polit…

ar.q: Grounding friendship in faith rather than virtue: a development of the classical ideal, or a change of subject?
ar.c: This is the fruit of friendship; and so faith may not be put aside for the sake of friendship. He cannot be a friend to a man who has been unfaithful to God… For there can be no friendship between diverse characters. — Ambrose of Milan, On the Duties of the Clergy III.22.132, link . 1 The classical philosophers grounded true friendship in virtue and reserved it for the good, who love the friend for his own sake. Ambrose keeps that frame but reroots the bond in faith : the fellowship of the virtuous becomes a fellowship of the faithful, with God himself a party to it. Aelred of Rievaulx carries…
ar.a: Plausible. On its best available form — the two-tier reading, where a supernatural friendship with and in God is added above the natural friendship of the virtuous rather than substituted for it — the Christian rerooting is a coherent development of the classical ideal and not a change of subject: Cicero’s own definition already made the divine one of the things friends must share, Aristotle’s “love the friend qua good” transfers cleanly once God…

ar.q: Is preferential friendship taken up and perfected by charity, not abolished?
ar.c: Accordingly, since there is a communication between man and God, inasmuch as He communicates His happiness to us, some kind of friendship must needs be based on this same communication… The love which is based on this communication, is charity: wherefore it is evident that charity is the friendship of man for God. — Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II q.23 a.1. 1 Against the reading that sets agape over against philia, the mainstream of the tradition holds that charity does not abolish preferential friendship but takes it up and perfects it. Charity is itself a friendship — the supernatural…
ar.a: Sound. That charity takes friendship up and perfects it, rather than abolishing it, is the mainstream Christian reading and is well grounded and unrefuted: the incarnate love of God kept particular friends, the gospel names friendship the highest love and offers it to the creature, charity is itself the friendship of man for God, and an ordering of the loves secures the primacy of neighbor-love without opposition. What keeps it honest — and what …

ar.q: Are exclusive “particular friendships” a danger to communal charity, to be discouraged in community life?
ar.c: The law of love does not allow particular friendships and companionships in this common dwelling. For it is inevitable that particular affections should injure greatly the common harmony… But if anyone be found to have greater feelings of affection towards a monk that is a brother, or a kinsman, or no relation, however plausible his excuse, let him be chastened as an injurer of the commonweal. For excessive affection towards one person plainly shows a corresponding deficiency as regards others. — Basil of Caesarea, An Ascetic Discourse ( Sermo Asceticus ), trans. W. K. L. Clarke. 1 The thesis,…
ar.a: Contested. The thesis is strong by the lights of communal discipline and weak by the lights of theology, and the dispute is internal to the monastic tradition itself, which supplies both the prohibition and its defence. The danger it names is real and patristically grounded — Basil forbids particular friendships by name and has the offender chastened, and the peril of faction, jealousy, and privatized affection is genuine — so the caution is soun…

ar.q: Does Christian charity (agape) stand in tension with — even against — preferential friendship (philia)?
ar.c: Passionate preferential love is another form of self-love… self-denial’s love, in contrast, loves the neighbor… the beloved… he loves as himself is not the neighbor; the beloved is the other I… the neighbor is the first you. — Søren Kierkegaard, Works of Love (1847), II.B. 1 The Christian love-command sets neighbor-love as a duty owed to everyone as such , even the enemy: “if ye love them which love you, what thank have ye? for sinners also love those that love them.” 2 On the reading weighed here, friendship and erotic love — chosen for the beloved’s qualities, returned in kind, confined to t…
ar.a: Weak. The thesis is right that a tension exists and that preferential love needs neighbor-love as its foundation and its judge; that much is genuine, and it is carried — as a positive principle rather than an antithesis — by the reading that charity takes friendship up and perfects it . But the claim that makes this a rival reading, and not merely a caution — that agape stands against friendship, which is a self-love to be dethroned — does not ho…

ar.q: Does classical virtue-friendship survive the Christian transformation, or is it superseded?
ar.c: The best of classical friendship was transformed and found a secure purpose in Christianity. — Carolinne White, Christian Friendship in the Fourth Century , link . 1 This is the interpretive question that ties the whole timeline together. For Aristotle and Cicero, true friendship is possible only among the virtuous and rests on shared virtue — the friend is “another self” ( heteros autos ), “a second self” ( alter idem ). 2 When the fathers baptize amicitia — Ambrose, Cassian, Augustine, Aelred — does that core thesis survive intact (friendship still grounded in virtue, now specified as Christ…
ar.a: Sound. On its best available form — the transformed-yet-continuous reading — the classical ideal of virtue-friendship is taken up and elevated by the Christian tradition, not superseded: the fathers rewrote Cicero rather than repudiating him, carried the entire classical apparatus (the second self, candour, the ban on wrongdoing, the ranking above external goods, like-loves-like) over intact, deepened its ground from virtue-in-general to the God …

xs.t: Before the fathers could Christianize amicitia they had a Scripture to read, and it gave them more than a stray proverb: a paradigm friendship told at length, a Lord who renames his followers “friends,” a patriarch styled “the friend of God,” a body of wisdom on choosing and keeping friends, and one hard warning that not every friendship is safe to have. This is the layer every witness below builds on. David and Jonathan — the covenant of two souls The Old Testament’s set-piece of friendship is the bond of David and Jonathan. At their first meeting “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul,” and the two “made a covenant, because he loved hi…

ds.t: The Garden of Gethsemane
ds.q: Four evangelists put the agony and the arrest in a garden, and each names the place a little differently. Matthew and Mark call it “a place called Gethsemane”; Luke says only that Jesus went “as he was wont, to the mount of Olives”; John says he crossed “the brook Cedron, where was a garden.” No evangelist gives a wall, a gate, or a distance. This page traces how the church knit those four descriptions into one location, kept it, built on it, split it into rival denominational plots, and finally let the spade test its most famous relic — the ancient olive trees.

tl.w: The Gospels name the place four ways (1st century)
tl.t: Every later identification has to reconcile four descriptions. Matthew: “Then cometh Jesus with them unto a place called Gethsemane.” 1 Mark, nearly the same: “they came to a place which was named Gethsemane.” 2 Luke gives no name but a habit: Jesus went “as he was wont, to the mount of Olives… And when he was at the place.” 3 John gives neither name nor mount but a garden across a watercourse: “he went forth with his disciples over the brook Cedron, where was a garden… And Judas also, which betrayed him, knew the place: for Jesus ofttimes resorted thither with his disciples.” 4 The name itself is a clue and a puzzle: Gethsemane transliterates a Semitic gat shemanim , “oil-press” — the insta…

tl.w: Origen: Gethsemane as a real named estate (c. 246)
tl.t: A full century before any gazetteer or pilgrim, the earliest surviving commentator already reads Gethsemane as a genuine place . Origen, expounding Matthew, notes that Jesus came “to an estate called Gethsemane” — the Greek chōrion , a farm or landed estate — and insists the name was not set down “without reason”: “the name of this estate which is called Gethsemane is of use for making this place clear.” 6 That an Alexandrian reading in the mid-third century treats Gethsemane as a real, interpretable farm-estate (the gat shemanim , “oil-press,” that the grotto's archaeology later recovers) is the earliest textual anchor for the site's identity. Two honest limits keep it modest: Origen declin…

tl.w: Eusebius: the first gazetteer entry — a place of prayer (c. 325)
tl.t: The earliest topographical notice is in Eusebius's Onomasticon , his gazetteer of biblical places. The Gethsemane entry places the site “at the foot of the Mount of Olives” and records that the faithful of his own day resorted there to pray — the first evidence that the spot was already a station of devotion, a generation before any church is attested on it. 7 (The entry's own wording preserves two stages: the Greek notes that “even now the faithful fervently utter prayers” on the spot, and Jerome's Latin recension of the same work adds that “now a church has been built over it” — the open place of prayer of Eusebius's day already sanctuaried by Jerome's.) What Eusebius fixes is the general …

The oldest surviving Christian travel diary, written by an anonymous pilgrim from Bordeaux the very year he travelled, climbs the Mount of Olives and notes two monuments there — the basilica Constantine raised “where the Lord taught his apostles before his passion” (the Eleona), and nearby “a little hill, where the Lord went up to pray” with Moses and Elijah (the Transfiguration) — but he names no Gethsemane and no site of the agony or the betrayal. 8 The silence is worth pausing on. By 333 the mount was already monumentalized at its summit, yet the agony-garden was not yet a marked pilgrim station with a church of its own. Eusebius's “place of prayer” and Egeria's “graceful church” a half-c…

tl.w: Egeria: the “graceful church” and the Holy-Thursday procession (c. 384)
tl.t: By the 380s the site is fully built and fully liturgical. The pilgrim Egeria describes the Maundy-Thursday night procession descending from the summit: “at the first cockcrow they come down from the Imbomon with hymns, and arrive at the place where the Lord prayed, as it is written in the Gospel… There is in that place a graceful church,” where the Gospel of the agony is read; “and then all… go down with the Bishop… with hymns to Gethsemane.” 9 Two things enter the record here. This is the first firm evidence of an actual church (the ecclesia elegans ) on the prayer-spot — the building later archaeology finds beneath the modern basilica. And Egeria already distinguishes two stations: “the pl…

tl.w: John Chrysostom: the brook Cedron and the habitual garden (c. 391)
tl.t: The eastern preacher supplies what the western topographers do not: a vivid reading of John's arrest-topography. Expounding John at Antioch, Chrysostom dwells on the crossing — Jesus “departed beyond the brook Cedron, where was a garden… He journeyeth at midnight, and crosseth a river, and hasteth to come to a place known to the traitor… and placeth Himself in the garden as in a prison.” 10 And against any thought that the garden was a hiding-place he presses John's own note that it was a familiar haunt: “Judas knew the place” because Jesus “often resorted thither with His disciples… especially in mountains and gardens, seeking a place free from disturbance.” Chrysostom names no Gethsemane, …

Jerome, who had translated Eusebius's gazetteer and lived in Palestine, supplies the philology. On Matthew he notes: “Gethsemane means ‘very fertile valley,’ in which he ordered the disciples to sit for a little while and wait for the Lord to return, while he prayed for everyone alone.” 11 The gloss is an etymology, not a survey — and it is arguably the wrong one (the “oil-press” derivation fits the Semitic better) — but it shows the site's name being actively interpreted by the church's leading Latin scholar, and it is the reading that carried into the medieval commentators, who read the “valley of fatness” as an allegory of humility and charity rather than as a datum of location.

The four Gospel descriptions had to be shown to be one place, and it is Augustine who does the harmonizing in his Harmony of the Gospels : the Mount of Olives “is this place, whose name Matthew and Mark called Gethsemane: and there we understand there to have been a garden, which John commemorates” — adding, on the authority of an earlier commentator, that “that village is situated at the foot of the Mount of Olives.” 12 This is the move that makes a single site out of four evangelists: Luke's mount, Matthew and Mark's Gethsemane, and John's garden are declared one and the same ground. Every later map of the place assumes Augustine's synthesis.

tl.w: The grotto and the garden: an early fork (4th–8th centuries)
tl.t: Roughly 100 m north of the modern garden, beside the Tomb of the Virgin , is a natural cave — itself an ancient oil-press — venerated from the fourth century as the place the disciples waited and slept while Jesus prayed, and where Judas came to betray him. In the fourth century the grotto was floored with white mosaic and turned into a funerary chapel; forty-two graves, dated to the fifth to eighth centuries, were later cut through its floor. 13 This matters for the whole tradition: the earliest localized devotion may have clustered on the cave (a sheltered, datable station) rather than on the open olive-plot shown today — the split Egeria's two-station procession already implies. Whether t…

tl.w: “Shown to this day”: Bede and Rabanus keep the memory (8th–9th centuries)
tl.t: The Latin West kept reporting the site as a living, visible place. The Venerable Bede , drawing on the pilgrim reports, writes: “The place of Gethsemane is shown to this day, where the Lord prayed, at the foot of the Mount of Olives, now a church built above it.” 14 A century later Rabanus Maurus harmonizes the Gospel names as Augustine had and confirms the fabric still stood: John's brook-Cedron garden “is the same as this Gethsemane… a place where He prayed at the foot of mount Olivet, where is a garden, and a Church now built.” 15 Neither is an eyewitness — both transmit what pilgrims reported — but together they show the identification unbroken from Egeria's church down through the early…

tl.w: “Campus Florum” and the four rival gardens (13th century onward)
tl.t: Where the ancient sources fixed the general spot, the later centuries multiplied the exact ones. From the thirteenth century the traditional enclosure appears under the name Campus Florum , “the field of flowers.” 16 And the single “place where the Lord prayed” hardened into four separate plots, each held by a different church, all within a few hundred metres at the western foot of the mount: the Roman Catholic (Franciscan) garden beside the Church of All Nations, over the “Rock of the Agony”; the Eastern site by the Tomb of the Virgin to the north; the Greek Orthodox plot to the east; and the Russian Orthodox orchard beside the Church of Mary Magdalene. 17 The general location was never ser…

tl.w: The Church of All Nations rises over the old foundations (1919–1924)
tl.t: The dominant modern site is the Franciscan Basilica of the Agony, or Church of All Nations, built 1919–1924 by the architect Antonio Barluzzi directly over the bedrock — the “Rock of the Agony” — where Jesus is remembered to have prayed. The 1919 excavation that preceded it, directed by Fr. Gaudence Orfali, uncovered beneath the site the remains of two earlier churches on the same spot: the fourth-century Byzantine basilica — Egeria's ecclesia elegans — and a twelfth-century Crusader chapel (the Church of St. Saviour), abandoned in 1345. 18 The dig is the physical confirmation of the written chain: the modern basilica stands on the ruins of the very church Egeria walked into on Holy Thursday…

tl.w: The spade tests the olive trees (2015): the relic deflated
tl.t: The garden's most venerated feature is its gnarled ancient olive trees, revered by pilgrims — a devotion first attested only in the sixteenth century 19 — as survivors that witnessed the agony. Two lines of evidence tell against that. First, the historical: Josephus records that in the Roman siege of AD 70 “all the trees that were about the city had been already cut down,” the whole landscape “before adorned with trees and pleasant gardens” reduced to “a desolate country every way, and its trees… all cut down” for some ninety furlongs around. 20 Second, the scientific: a 2015 study led by Italy's National Research Council radiocarbon-dated the oldest wood of three of the garden's trees to AD…

ar.q: Did the garden's ancient olive trees witness Jesus' agony?
ar.c: The Garden of Gethsemane's most venerated feature is its cluster of eight enormous, gnarled olive trees. Pilgrims are shown them as living witnesses of the Passion — trees that stood, or grew directly from trees that stood, in the grove where Jesus “ofttimes resorted” with his disciples and where he prayed on the night of his arrest. 1 The devotion is powerful and old-feeling, but it is not itself ancient: the trees are first singled out for veneration only in the sixteenth century, long after the enclosure had acquired its medieval name Campus Florum (“field of flowers”) in the thirteenth. 2
ar.a: Weak — for the strong relic-claim that the garden's ancient olives witnessed the agony. It is a beloved tradition that the evidence trims: Josephus felled the first-century trees, radiocarbon dates the oldest surviving trunks to the Crusader twelfth century, and a shared genotype marks the eight as a single medieval replanting. The defensible residue is a different and much more modest claim — that Gethsemane has borne olives across the centuries…

ar.q: Which of the four rival Gethsemane sites is the authentic garden?
ar.c: Every claimant honours the same Gospel data — Luke's Mount of Olives, John's garden across the brook Cedron, Matthew and Mark's “place called Gethsemane” 1 — and every claimant sits on or at the western foot of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron from the Old City, exactly where those texts put it. The dispute is therefore not over miles but over metres : four churches maintain four separate walled plots within a short walk of one another, and each is shown to pilgrims as “the” garden of the agony. The question weighed here is whether the evidence lets us pick one of them out as the authent…
ar.a: Contested — with a two-level verdict that should be kept distinct. The general location (the western foot of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron) is sound : attested from the fourth century, matching the Gospel topography, and archaeologically anchored. But identifying one of the four denominational plots as the authentic garden is at best plausible and cannot be adjudicated on present evidence — there is no first-century marker and no decisiv…

ar.q: Was the agony in the grotto or the open garden?
ar.c: The Gospels fix a general ground — the Mount of Olives, across the brook Cedron, a garden the disciples knew 1 — but they do not fix a single point within it. Modern pilgrimage puts the whole memory in one place: the walled open-air garden beside the Church of All Nations, with its gnarled olives. Yet a hundred metres to the north, beside the Tomb of the Virgin, is a natural cave — the Grotto of Gethsemane — venerated from the fourth century as the spot where the disciples waited and slept while Jesus withdrew to pray, and where Judas came to betray him. 2 The question weighed here is which cl…
ar.a: Plausible. The grotto is a credible — perhaps the earliest datable — locus of Gethsemane devotion, and the strongest form of the claim is not “the cave, not the garden” but a grotto-and-garden pair, both authentic at adjacent spots: the cave for the disciples' lodging and the betrayal, the open ground a stone's throw off for Jesus' prayer. That reading fits the Gospel scene, the cave's fourth-century veneration, its character as an oil-press, and…

ds.t: The Two Genealogies of Jesus (Matthew 1 vs. Luke 3)
ds.q: Related doctrines: Hard passages — see also Who Killed Goliath? (2 Samuel 21:19) · How Tall Was Goliath? (six or four cubits) · Solomon's Stalls: 40,000 or 4,000? (1 Kings 4:26 vs. 2 Chronicles 9:25) · Ahaziah's Age: 22 or 42? (2 Kings 8:26 vs. 2 Chronicles 22:2) · The Bronze Sea: 2,000 or 3,000 Baths? (1 Kings 7:26 vs. 2 Chronicles 4:5) · What Jesus Wrote on the Ground (John 8:6) · The Death of Judas (Matthew 27 vs. Acts 1) · Naming the Wrong Prophet (Mark 1:2; Matthew 27:9) · Baptized for the Dead (1 Corinthians 15:29)

tl.t: Irenaeus , the earliest witness here, does not yet weigh the clash between the two lists; his eye is on where Luke's ascending line ends. Luke traces the pedigree of Jesus back past Abraham to "Adam, which was the son of God," and Irenaeus makes that Adam-ward reach the hinge of his recapitulation theology: Christ the Second Adam "has summed up in Himself all nations dispersed from Adam downwards, and all languages and generations of men, together with Adam himself" — which is why, unlike Matthew, Luke climbs all the way to the head of the race. He is also the first datable reader to count the list, reckoning it at "seventy-two generations" — fewer than the received text's, and so an early s…

Julius Africanus , the Christian chronographer, gives the solution that fathered all the rest. In his Letter to Aristides he first sweeps away the easy answer that Matthew traces a "royal" line and Luke a "priestly" one — both descents run through the royal tribe of Judah, so that reading "establish[es] the truth by a false statement." 4 His own account rests on Israel's law of levirate marriage (Deut. 25:5): Jacob and Heli were half-brothers by one mother, Estha, but different fathers (Matthan of Solomon's line, Melchi of Nathan's); when Heli died childless, Jacob "raised up seed to him" and begot Joseph — "his own son by nature, but the son of Heli by law." So Matthew names the natural fat…

Eusebius is the reason Africanus's letter survives: he quotes it at length in his Church History , prefacing it with the note that "many suppose" the two genealogies "are at variance with one another," and that "every believer, in ignorance of the truth, has been zealous to invent some explanation." 7 He endorses the levirate solution as the best available and draws from it a further point the later tradition would seize on: since the Law forbade marriage across tribes, Joseph's Davidic descent "virtually" shows Mary too "to be of the same tribe with him." 8 Elsewhere he reads Luke's guarded "as was supposed" as the Evangelist reporting "the common opinion of many, not his own," and notes th…

The anonymous Latin commentator known as Ambrosiaster is the tradition's early dissenter: he examines the levirate solution and rejects it as "neither plausible nor useful for anything." 10 On his reading the two lists "fork" from David: Matthew descends through Solomon to Jacob and Joseph, Luke ascends through Nathan from Heli, and Joseph and Heli are simply two men "of one and the same stock" — kinsmen, so that "in the same sense in which Jesus was called Joseph's son, he was also Heli's son," and of all their common tribe. 11 His target is the heretic Photinus, who made Christ begin only with Mary; the genealogy, ascending past Adam to God, proves the Son "before all flesh." 12

Jerome , in his Commentary on Matthew , names the objector: "this passage is objected to us by the Emperor Julian in his Discrepancy of the Evangelists . Matthew calls Joseph the son of Jacob, Luke makes him the son of Heli." 13 Julian, he replies, "did not know the Scripture manner — one was his father by nature, the other by law" — the levirate answer, for which Jerome points the reader to "Africanus the chronologist, and Eusebius of Caesarea," who "have disputed [it] more fully." 14 To the further question why Joseph's line is given at all, since he was not Jesus's father, Jerome answers that Scripture does not trace genealogies through women, and that Joseph and Mary "were of the same tr…

Augustine , in the Harmony of the Gospels , lays out three ways the doubled father might be resolved — a maternal grandfather, an adoptive father, or the levirate — and prefers adoption : it is "most probable that Luke took the origin by adoption," for Matthew's insistent "begat… begat" marks natural descent to Jacob, while "more easily is a man said to be his son by whom he was adopted." 16 He finds a fitting sense in it: Luke gives the genealogy at the baptism and runs it up to God, "as thus more clearly pointing Him out as the Priest that should make atonement," since "by adoption we are made the sons of God." 17 (In his later Retractations Augustine withdrew his over-firm rejection of th…

The Venerable Bede , in his Commentary on Luke , carries the harmonizing tradition into early-medieval Latin learning — gathering the earlier answers rather than minting a new one. To "the knotty question… how Joseph could have had two fathers," he gives Africanus's levirate solution almost whole (Estha married in succession by a Solomon-line and a Nathan-line husband, Jacob and Heli half-brothers, Jacob raising seed to the childless Heli), so that Matthew's "Jacob begot Joseph" and Luke's "son of Heli" stand "both… validated and intact"; and he notes, tellingly, that Africanus's own copy named "Melchi" where the received Luke has Matthat, "because either his copy had it so" — the very manus…

John of Damascus , gathering the Greek tradition in An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith , restates Africanus's levirate scheme almost verbatim — Matthan of Solomon's line and Melchi of Nathan's by one wife, Jacob and Heli brothers, Jacob raising seed to the childless Heli, so "Joseph… is by nature the son of Jacob, of the line of Solomon, but by law the son of Heli of the line of Nathan." 21 But he adds what the Gospels leave silent: a descent for Mary , through Nathan's line by way of "Panther… Barpanther … Joachim," Mary's father — so that the Virgin herself is shown to be of David's house, and the demonstration of Joseph's tribe (whom the law required her to marry within) doubles as…

Raymond E. Brown , the leading modern scholar of the infancy narratives, closes the timeline with the critical verdict. He holds that neither list is a biographical record: "the Lucan genealogy is no less theological in purpose than Matthew's and no freer of historical difficulties," and it "scarcely constitutes an exact record of Jesus' biological ancestry." 23 The genealogies, he concludes, "tell us how to evaluate Jesus" but "nothing certain about his grandparents." And he dismisses the harmonization that began with Africanus: "the theory of a levirate marriage solves so little and has so many difficulties that it should be abandoned as a solution." 24

ar.q: Did Jesus's kinsmen (the desposynoi ) preserve a genuine family genealogy?
ar.c: “A few of the careful, however, having obtained private records of their own, either by remembering the names or by getting them in some other way from the registers, pride themselves on preserving the memory of their noble extraction. Among these are those already mentioned, called Desposyni, on account of their connection with the family of the Saviour. Coming from Nazara and Cochaba, villages of Judea, into other parts of the world, they drew the aforesaid genealogy from memory and from the book of daily records as faithfully as possible.… And let this suffice us, for, although we cannot of…
ar.a: Contested. The thesis genuinely divides along a seam, and honesty requires rating each side of it. That Jesus's kinsmen preserved a real Davidic family tradition — that they were self-conscious Davidides whose descent was a live, publicly checkable claim — is well-grounded and early, resting on the strongest evidence the question affords: a Palestinian source (Hegesippus) reporting a named, dated family examined as Davidides against the backdrop …

ar.q: Does the curse on Jeconiah (Jeremiah 22:30) bar the Messiah's throne-claim?
ar.c: Two intertwined objections fall on Matthew's list in particular. (1) The curse. Matthew routes the royal line through Jeconiah (Coniah / Jehoiachin), the king on whom Jeremiah pronounced a sentence that seems to disqualify the whole line from the throne: "Thus saith the LORD, Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper in his days: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah." — Jeremiah 22:30 (KJV). If no descendant of Jeconiah may sit on David's throne, how can the Messiah inherit that throne through a line that runs stra…
ar.a: Plausible. The conclusion is well-grounded and close to the mainstream: the Jeconiah curse does not bar Matthew's royal genealogy, because Jeremiah's sentence is time-limited to the reigning pre-exilic monarchy (Jeconiah did have sons, and the line is expressly rehabilitated at Haggai 2:23), and the demonstrably schematic 3×14 list confirms that Matthew is tracing a theological throne-succession rather than a bare pedigree. It falls short of soun…

ar.q: Both genealogies are Joseph's — one father natural, one legal
ar.c: "Thus neither of the evangelists is in error, as the one reckons by nature and the other by law… Heli dying childless, Jacob raised up seed to him and begat Joseph, his own son by nature, but the son of Heli by law. Thus Joseph was the son of both." — Julius Africanus, Epistle to Aristides §§ II, VI, link . The assertion is that both lists give Joseph's ancestry, and the two fathers named for him — Jacob in Matthew, Heli in Luke — are a natural father and a legal one. Africanus supplies the legal father by levirate marriage (Deut. 25:5); Augustine supplies him instead by adoption. Either way t…
ar.a: Contested. As a demonstration that the two genealogies can both be Joseph's without contradiction, the reading holds — and for that limited defensive purpose it is the strongest of the harmonizations, invoking a real biblical institution rather than an invented one. But it does not rise to a probable reconstruction of what actually happened: the levirate form depends on an unverifiable tradition its own author flags as unattested, doesn't fit the…

ar.q: Matthew the royal (legal) succession, Luke Joseph's natural line — both of Joseph
ar.c: "Matthew gives the legal descendants of David—the men who would have been legally the heir to the Davidic throne if that throne had continued—while Luke gives the descendants of David in that particular line to which, finally, Joseph, the husband of Mary, belonged." — J. Gresham Machen, The Virgin Birth of Christ (1930), link . The thesis is not (as with the levirate reading) that a single marriage event doubled Joseph's father, but that the two lists differ along their whole length because they are two different kinds of list: Matthew traces the legal line of succession to David's throne — wh…
ar.a: Plausible. This is the strongest of the harmonizations on the point where the levirate reading is weakest: it rests on a demonstrable fact about Matthew's list — a schematic throne-succession that omits real kings — and so explains the near-total divergence of the two lines and the Jeconiah curse together, rather than pinning everything on one unattested marriage. It is coherent and not ruled out. It falls short of probable because its own final …

ar.q: Why does Luke ascend to Adam and “the son of God”? — the purpose of Luke’s genealogical structure
ar.c: “Wherefore Luke points out that the pedigree which traces the generation of our Lord back to Adam contains seventy-two generations, connecting the end with the beginning, and implying that it is He who has summed up in Himself all nations dispersed from Adam downwards, and all languages and generations of men, together with Adam himself. Hence also was Adam himself termed by Paul ‘the figure of Him that was to come.’” — Against Heresies 3.22.3, ANF 1 (also newadvent.org ). 1 The interpretation weighed here: Luke, unlike Matthew, does not begin at Abraham and climb down to Jesus but starts at J…
ar.a: Sound. The interpretation, stated in its load-bearing form — Luke’s genealogy is theologically composed, its ascent past Abraham to “Adam… the son of God” at the baptism deliberately framing Jesus as the new head of the human race and answering the divine sonship just declared from heaven — holds up. It is near-consensus across confessional and critical readers alike; it is grounded in the earliest datable comment on the list (Irenaeus); it draws…

ar.q: Does Luke give Mary's genealogy rather than Joseph's?
ar.c: "And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli." — Luke 3:23 (KJV), link . The reading proposes that this verse is really the head of Mary's family tree: "Heli" is Mary's father, and Joseph is named only as his son-in-law ("son of Heli" = son by marriage). On this construction Matthew gives Joseph's own line (through Solomon) and Luke gives Mary's (through Nathan), so Jesus has a genuine biological Davidic descent — through his mother — and the two lists never really competed, because they are the pedigrees of two …
ar.a: Weak. The goal it serves — Mary's Davidic descent — is legitimate and well-attested, but the means are not: the "Heli = Mary's father, Joseph his son-in-law" construction contradicts Luke's plain statement that Joseph "was the son of Heli," names no woman, and was unknown to the entire early church, which read the list as Joseph's. It is best seen as a modern shortcut to a conclusion the older tradition secured differently (through the tribal-mar…

ar.q: Is Mary of David's line — and does Jesus's Davidic descent by blood depend on it?
ar.c: "…concerning his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh." — Romans 1:3 (KJV), link ; cf. 2 Timothy 2:8 ("Jesus Christ of the seed of David") and Acts 2:30. The proof-text is read to require that Jesus inherit David's blood physically — kata sarka , "according to the flesh." But the Gospels are emphatic that Joseph was not Jesus's natural father (Matt. 1:18–25; Luke 1:34–35). So the argument runs: if the Davidic descent is a matter of flesh and blood, and it does not come from Joseph, it can only come through Mary — which means Mary herself must be…
ar.a: Plausible. Keep the two questions apart. Was Mary of David's line? — well-attested and probably true: it is early (Ignatius couples Davidic seed with the virgin birth), it is the natural reading of Romans 1:3 once Joseph is removed as natural father, and it commands near-unanimous consent; only the specific pedigree (Joachim, the Panther line) is late and legendary. Does Jesus's Davidic descent by blood depend on it? — this is the contestable hal…

ar.q: Are Matthew's and Luke's Shealtiel and Zerubbabel the same two men?
ar.c: "Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel" (Matthew 1:12). "…Zorobabel, which was the son of Salathiel, which was the son of Neri" (Luke 3:27). "…Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah…" (Haggai 1:1; cf. Ezra 3:2). Between David and Joseph the two genealogies scarcely touch: they run through different sons of David (Solomon in Matthew, Nathan in Luke) and disagree at nearly every name. The single conspicuous exception is a Shealtiel (Salathiel) whose son is Zerubbabel — a pair standing in both lists at the same point, the hinge of the Babylonian exile and return. Th…
ar.a: Contested. Keep the two questions the lead poses apart. Are they the same two men? — near-certainly yes: this is the one post-exilic Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and Matthew's Shealtiel is even confirmed as Jeconiah's son by 1 Chronicles 3:17; that identity is sound. Does the shared pair therefore support the royal-succession reconciliation? — no more than the reconciliation supports itself. The divergent fathers (Jeconiah vs. Neri) can be made o…

tl.t: The oldest translation of the verse already reads "four." The Septuagint 's 1 Kingdoms (= 1 Samuel) 17:4 has the champion come out of Gath "his height four cubits and a span." 5 The reading is carried by the great uncials Vaticanus and Alexandrinus and by the Lucianic recension, so "four" was very probably the number in the Old Greek from the start — the Greek tradition's steady witness against the later Masoretic "six." 6

tl.w: 4QSam a — the Dead Sea Samuel scroll (mid-1st c. BC)
tl.t: The decisive witness is Hebrew. 4QSam a , the Samuel scroll from Qumran and by a thousand years the oldest surviving Hebrew copy of this verse, reads "four cubits and a span" — agreeing with the Greek against the medieval Masoretic Text. 7 Its discovery is what turned the question: the shorter number is no longer a Greek peculiarity to be discounted, but the reading of the oldest Hebrew manuscript we possess.

Josephus , retelling the duel in the Antiquities , describes the champion as "a man of vast bulk, for he was of four cubits and a span in tallness." 8 Writing in Greek from a Hebrew source, he is an independent first-century witness — neither Qumran scroll nor Septuagint codex — that the number known in his day was four.

With Jerome 's Latin the "six" enters and fixes the Western Bible. Translating from the Hebrew of his day, he renders 1 Samuel 17:4 "his height was six cubits and a span" ( sex cubitorum et palmo ) — the Masoretic number, which through the Vulgate became the giant every Latin reader would know. 9

The rabbinic tradition works entirely from the Masoretic Hebrew, and so from "six cubits and a span." The Talmud 's Goliath haggadah (Sotah 42b) elaborates that text — his descent from Orpah, his taunts, his fall — without a hint of the shorter reading. 10 Tellingly, the rabbis reserve genuinely cosmic giant-scale for Og of Bashan , not for Goliath, whose six cubits they take as an ordinary—if formidable—man's height. 11

The Latin West reads "six" as plain text and mines it for allegory. Bede , in his Commentary on Samuel , takes the giant "six cubits and a palm high" as a figure of the devil, who "boasts to be similar to the Most High" and so counterfeits the perfection God measures in six days of work — tying the six cubits to the six days of creation and to Ezekiel's measuring-reed "of six cubits and a palm." 12 He shows no awareness that any manuscript ever read four: for him "six" simply is the text.

tl.w: The Masoretic codices — Aleppo and Leningrad (c. 930–1010)
tl.t: The earliest complete Hebrew Bibles — the Aleppo and Leningrad codices , the manuscripts behind every printed Hebrew Bible — both read "six cubits and a span" ( shesh ammot wa-zaret ). 13 They are the base of the "six" that stands in the Hebrew text and in the translations made from it — but they are also, by a thousand years, later than 4QSam a , which reads four.

tl.w: J. Daniel Hays and the modern text-critics (2005)
tl.t: Modern criticism reopens the case for "four." J. Daniel Hays , gathering the witnesses (4QSam a , Vaticanus, Josephus, the Lucianic Greek), argues that "four cubits and a span" is the original reading and the Masoretic "six" a later inflation — the giant swelling in transmission — a verdict shared in the main by the text-critical consensus (McCarter, Tov, Ulrich). 14 The reading is not unopposed: Clyde Billington and William Barrick defend the Masoretic "six" (Billington reading the Greek "four" as a conversion into Egyptian royal cubits, and putting Goliath near eight feet), so the "which number is original" question remains genuinely argued. 15

ar.q: Is "four cubits and a span" the original reading of 1 Samuel 17:4 (the Masoretic "six" a later inflation)?
ar.c: "Therefore, in conclusion, I suggest that we accept 'four cubits and a span' as the most likely original reading. I also suggest that this reading should be reflected in our Bible translations, relegating the variant reading of 'six cubits and a span' to the notes and/or the margins…" — J. Daniel Hays, "Reconsidering the Height of Goliath," JETS 48/4 (2005): 701–714 , link , at 713–714. 1 The reading this serves: the autograph of 1 Samuel 17:4 gave Goliath's height as "four cubits and a span" (about 6′9″), and the "six cubits and a span" (about 9′9″) that stands in the Masoretic Text—and, thro…
ar.a: Sound. On the question the argument actually decides—which reading is earliest—"four cubits and a span" wins on the ordinary criteria of the discipline: it is the reading of the oldest Hebrew witness (4QSam a ), independently confirmed in the Greek and by Josephus, against a "six" that surfaces in Hebrew only in medieval codices; the parablepsis mechanism and the David-versus-Saul literary logic reinforce it; and it is the mainstream judgment of …

ds.t: Who Killed Goliath? (2 Samuel 21:19)
ds.q: Related doctrines: Hard passages — see also How Tall Was Goliath? (six or four cubits) · Solomon's Stalls: 40,000 or 4,000? (1 Kings 4:26 vs. 2 Chronicles 9:25) · Ahaziah's Age: 22 or 42? (2 Kings 8:26 vs. 2 Chronicles 22:2) · The Bronze Sea: 2,000 or 3,000 Baths? (1 Kings 7:26 vs. 2 Chronicles 4:5) · What Jesus Wrote on the Ground (John 8:6) · The Two Genealogies of Jesus (Matthew 1 vs. Luke 3) · The Death of Judas (Matthew 27 vs. Acts 1) · Naming the Wrong Prophet (Mark 1:2; Matthew 27:9) · Baptized for the Dead (1 Corinthians 15:29)

tl.t: Josephus is the earliest witness to feel the difficulty, and the earliest to smooth it. Retelling 1 Samuel 17 he keeps David the slayer of the named Goliath, "cut off his head with his own sword… but David carried the head of Goliath into his own tent." 3 Yet when he reaches the giant-wars of 2 Samuel 21, he renders the Elhanan of verse 19 as "Nephan his kinsman," who "fought in a single combat with the stoutest of all the Philistines, and slew him" — and the name Goliath never recurs in Book 7. 4 By reserving the name for David's victim and leaving Nephan's giant anonymous, he leaves his narrative with a single Goliath, killed by David: the harmonization achieved by silent omission.

The Aramaic Targum Jonathan makes explicit what Josephus implied: Elhanan simply is David. Reading the strange patronymic as a bundle of titles, it renders the verse "And David the son of Jesse, weaver of the curtains of the sanctuary, killed Goliath the Gittite, the wood of whose spear was like a weaver's heddle rod." 5 It is a solution by exegesis, not emendation: the consonants stand, but "Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite" becomes a description of David, and the verse restates 1 Samuel 17 instead of competing with it — the fountainhead of the rabbinic Elhanan-=-David reading.

The Christian-Latin form of the same identification. The Quaestiones Hebraicae in libros Regum et Paralipomenon , read for centuries as Jerome 's but now judged spurious, translates "Elhanan" as Adeodatus ("God-given") and argues from the etymologies — and from the chapter's closing note that the giants "fell by the hand of David" — that "Adeodatus is David himself… called Adeodatus because he was chosen by God for the kingdom." 6 Tellingly, its parallel note on 1 Chronicles 20:5 takes the other harmonizing road — David killed Goliath, Elhanan killed Goliath's brother — so the two Christian solutions to the crux sit unreconciled in one book. (The authorship and date are uncertain; the c. 400…

Rashi , the pre-eminent medieval Jewish commentator, fixes the Targum's reading as standard: "Elhanan — David. We know that it was David who killed Goliath in Shmuel I, 17:51, consequently this Elhanan must be David." 7 He glosses the patronymic through the same "weaver of the sanctuary curtains" image — a single Goliath, and 2 Samuel 21:19 a poetic byname for David.

Radak reports both answers — the Chronicles-harmonization (the man slain was Goliath's kinsman) and the Targum's identification of Elhanan with David — and then does what the harmonizers rarely do: he confesses the identification puzzles him. Having quoted the Targum's "David… killed Goliath," he adds, "but as to why [Scripture] called David 'Elhanan,' I do not know the reason for it." 8 His candor at the seam is the medieval tradition's admission that the authoritative reading does not really explain the odd name.

With Benjamin Kennicott , the Oxford Hebraist whose manuscript collations founded modern Old Testament text-criticism, the verse becomes a demonstration that the printed Hebrew is not inerrant. "Goliath the Gittite was slain by David," he reasons, "and therefore there must have been a Mistake of some Transcriber here"; the reading of 1 Chronicles 20:5 — "Elhanan… slew Lahmi the Brother of Goliath" — is "plain and consistent," and "these words have evidently been corrupted into the words now found in Samuel." 9 He reconstructs the corruption letter by letter, and so opens the case that Chronicles preserves the original.

Julius Wellhausen , in his monograph on the text of Samuel, isolates the mechanical fault — "the spelling Jaare instead of Jair … was probably occasioned by the following oregim ('weavers'), whose accidental intrusion from the line below is easy to recognize" — but warns against the easy fix of importing the Chronicler's smoother text, "given his tendency to avoid archaisms." 10 He thus reverses Kennicott's direction: the Chronicler is a reviser, so Samuel is likely primary and Chronicles the correction.

The standard conservative commentary of Keil & Delitzsch reaches Kennicott's verdict by the opposite instinct — to restore, not to concede. The two verses "presuppose the same original text, so that the difference can only have arisen from an error in copying"; therefore "we must regard the reading in the Chronicles as the correct one, and alter our text accordingly; since the assumption that there were two Goliaths is a very improbable one." 11 Chronicles is original; Samuel is emended to match it, and David remains the sole slayer of Goliath.

S. R. Driver 's Notes gives the classic argument for the reverse. Weighing the two readings, he finds it "scarcely credible that a scribe having before him a text identical with that of [Chronicles]… could, with the knowledge of I 17 that he must have possessed, have so altered… it as to make it state that 'Elhanan… slew Goliath of Gath!'" — whereas "a motive for the correction of the text of Samuel by the Chronicler… is obvious." 12 On the principle of the harder reading, Samuel is prior and Chronicles the harmonization — the line that becomes the modern majority.

The International Critical Commentary of Henry Preserved Smith states it in a sentence: "Elhanan ben Jair the Bethlehemite slew Goliath the Gittite; the harmonistic purpose of the Chronicler in making the victim the brother of Goliath is evident." 13 He even reads the difficulty back onto 1 Samuel 17, noting that Elhanan's deed "would weigh somewhat against the present form of that narrative."

The Anchor Bible commentary of P. Kyle McCarter carries the Samuel-is-primary line to its strongest form. The Chronicler's "'Laḥmi, the brother of Goliath'" is "a scribal error with the effect of harmonizing this notice with I Samuel 17"; and beyond the text, "there is no doubt that the tradition attributing the slaying of Goliath to Elhanan is older than that which credits the deed to David," the contradiction "eliminated in the targumic and midrashic literature by identifying David with Elhanan." 14 On this reading the champion of 1 Samuel 17 was originally anonymous, and "Goliath" was drawn into that story from Elhanan's older notice.

Michael S. Heiser presents the crux to a popular audience as ordinary scribal transmission, not contradiction: "somewhere along the chain of copying… one scribe made a mistake in 2 Sam 21:19," so that the verse is "a defective reading… the result of a scribe's sincere effort to cope with a problematic manuscript," resolved by 1 Chronicles 20:5. 15 He sides with the toward-Chronicles direction — but, unlike the ancient harmonizers, grants that the Masoretic verse is genuinely in error, defending Scripture through the doctrine of transmission rather than by denying the fault.

The most careful recent treatment, by Tyndale House's Kaspars Ozoliņš , resists both tidy camps. Laying out three possibilities, he judges the most plausible reconstruction to be that "Elhanan the Bethlehemite actually killed the brother of Goliath, who himself was left unnamed" — both texts descending from a shared original that each branch garbled, "Lahmi" being not a real name but a scribal slip for "the Bethlehemite" — while stressing that "we are still left with uncertainty" and that "scribes copying the Hebrew Bible rarely made deliberate changes to their text." 16 He closes the timeline as its most explicit voice for a measured uncertainty over any slogan for "David, full stop" or "El…

ar.q: Is "Elhanan" in 2 Samuel 21:19 simply another name for David himself?
ar.c: "Elhanan — David. We know that it was David who killed Goliath in Shmuel I, 17:51, consequently this Elhanan must be David." — Rashi on II Samuel 21:19 , via Sefaria . The reading this serves: there is no contradiction between 1 Samuel 17 and 2 Samuel 21:19 because the "Elhanan" of the later verse is David under another name — so the same man, David/Elhanan, killed Goliath, and 2 Samuel 21:19 merely restates the duel of 1 Samuel 17 rather than competing with it. On this reading the strange patronymic "son of Jaare-oregim, the Bethlehemite" is not a father's name but a bundle of epithets for Da…
ar.a: Weak. The interpretation is coherent only as pious harmonization: it dissolves the crux by declaring Elhanan to be David, an identification no verse supports, that a separate Bethlehemite Elhanan among the Thirty tells against, that the Gob setting of David's later wars tells against, and that even its medieval transmitter (Radak) could not explain. Its historical importance is real and independent of its truth — it is the earliest witness to the…

ar.q: Was Elhanan the original slayer of Goliath, the deed later transferred to David?
ar.c: "Deeds of obscure heroes tend to attach themselves to famous heroes, and there is no doubt that the tradition attributing the slaying of Goliath to Elhanan is older than that which credits the deed to David. The contradiction in the tradition was eliminated in the targumic and midrashic literature by identifying David with Elhanan…" — P. Kyle McCarter, II Samuel (Anchor Bible 9; Doubleday, 1984), p. 450 . The reading this serves is the reverse of the harmonizers': 2 Samuel 21:19 preserves the original tradition — Elhanan the Bethlehemite was the historical slayer of the giant Goliath — and the…
ar.a: Contested. Two claims must be kept apart. The textual claim — Samuel prior, Chronicles a harmonization — is well-grounded and widely held; taken alone it would rate higher. But the historical-transfer claim that rides on it — Elhanan the real slayer, David's victory a later attribution — is an inference beyond the evidence: no manuscript attests it, it presupposes a contested reading of 1 Samuel 17, and the same textual facts are equally explaine…

ar.q: Is 2 Samuel 21:19 a scribal corruption, its original naming Goliath's brother?
ar.c: "The solution to the contradiction between 2 Sam 21:19 and 1 Chr 20:5 is recognizing that 2 Sam 21:19 is a defective reading since it is the result of a scribe's sincere effort to cope with a problematic manuscript." — Michael S. Heiser, "Who Killed Goliath — David or Elhanan?" (reproducing "Clash of the Manuscripts," Bible Study Magazine, 2014) , link . The reading this serves: David remains the sole slayer of the Goliath of 1 Samuel 17; the Elhanan of 2 Samuel 21:19 killed a different Philistine giant, and the Masoretic verse that seems to make him kill "Goliath" is a copyist's error to be c…
ar.a: Contested. On its best case — Ozoliņš's "both texts corrupt from an original naming the brother of Goliath" — the reading is coherent, economical, and leaves David the slayer of 1 Samuel 17's champion without treating Chronicles as flawless; it is strong by the lights of careful conservative text-criticism and may well be the single most probable account of the three texts. But it is genuinely disputed, not settled: the mainstream critical judgme…

ds.t: The Great Apostasy (did the church wholly fall, needing a restoration?)
ds.q: The Great Apostasy thesis holds that the church founded by the apostles did not merely err here and there but defected wholesale after their death — losing valid authority, ordinances, and true doctrine — so that no legitimate church survived until it was restored in a later age. It is the load-bearing premise of every restorationist movement: if the apostolic church still stood, there was nothing to restore. In its Latter-day Saint (Mormon) form the claim is stated sharply — the young Joseph Smith is told in his First Vision account to join none of the churches, “for they were all wrong,” their creeds “an abomination” and their professors “all corrupt” — and it is the foundation on which th…

tl.t: The thesis begins in the apostolic writings themselves — and so does the objection to it. Paul foretells that “that day shall not come, except there come a falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed” (2 Thessalonians 2:3), warns the Ephesian elders that “after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you” and that “of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things” (Acts 20:29–30), and writes that “in the latter times some shall depart from the faith” (1 Timothy 4:1). 2 These are the restorationist proof-texts. Set against them are the same writings’ promises of the church’s permanence: Christ builds his church so that “the gates of hell shall not prevail against…

The earliest counter-voice is not a rebuttal of the thesis — no one had yet proposed it — but a case built on its exact contradictory. Arguing against Gnostics who claimed a secret , interrupted apostolic tradition, Irenaeus answers that the true faith has been kept in full public view, unbroken , through the succession of teachers in every apostolic church: the succession is “most abundant proof that there is one and the same vivifying faith, which has been preserved in the Church from the apostles until now , and handed down in truth” ( Against Heresies III.3.3), while the heretics’ systems are recent inventions that “cannot trace their origin up to the apostles” (III.4). Where a Restorati…

The Gallic monk gives the Latin church its classic test for telling catholic truth from heresy — the “Vincentian canon,” that we hold “what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all ” ( Commonitory ch. 2). The rule is a test of continuity : it works only if there is an unbroken, self-identical faith to appeal to, and Vincent says so plainly — the church “never changes… does not lose her own” (ch. 23), holding a doctrine that “has continued one and the same through the several successions of ages… and so will continue for ever” (ch. 24). A faith interrupted and later restored would fail the canon by definition: it would not have been believed “always.” His whole method presupposes the …

The Reformation supplies the thesis’s fiercest apostasy-language and, in the same breath, its clearest limit. Luther brands the papacy the Man of Sin of 2 Thessalonians 2 — “the Pope is the very Antichrist, who has exalted himself above, and opposed himself against Christ” ( Smalcald Articles II.4). 6 Yet he flatly denies that the true church had ceased to exist: under the papacy, he writes, “there are the true holy Scriptures, true baptism, the true sacrament of the altar, the true keys to the forgiveness of sins, the true office of the ministry… I contend that in the papacy there is true Christianity, even the right kind of Christianity.” 7 This is the partial or reformable model: a corrup…

Two centuries before the Latter-day Saints, the founder of Rhode Island reached the total position from Puritan premises. Williams came to regard established Christendom’s church, baptism, and worship as “a whole forme of Antichristian worship” and false ( Christenings Make Not Christians , 1645). 8 Having helped gather a Baptist congregation at Providence, he withdrew even from it, judging that there was “none upon earth that could administer baptism” “for the want of a called administrator,” and became a “Seeker” who — as the hostile Cotton Mather reports, and as modern scholarship summarizes — held that the apostasy since Constantine had engulfed Christendom and that the true church could…

The Latter-day Saint Restoration rests the whole edifice on the total-apostasy premise. Joseph Smith ’s First Vision account has him told to join no church, “for they were all wrong… all their creeds were an abomination… those professors were all corrupt” (Joseph Smith—History 1:19). 10 The Doctrine and Covenants frames the age as one of universal straying — men “have strayed from mine ordinances, and have broken mine everlasting covenant” — a loss the newly organized body is raised to repair as “the only true and living church upon the face of the whole earth” (D&C 1:15, 30). 11 The claim is the strong one: not corrupt doctrine only, but a broken priesthood requiring literal restoration by …

The systematic Latter-day Saint statement is Talmage ’s The Great Apostasy , which gathers the New-Testament prophecies and the patristic-to-medieval innovations into a single case. Its thesis is unqualified: the primitive church “lost its power, authority, and graces as a divine institution, and degenerated into an earthly organization only” (Preface), so that “succession in the priesthood was broken; and… the Church, as an earthly organization operating under divine direction and having authority to officiate in spiritual ordinances, ceased to exist” (ch. II). 12 Talmage supplies the fullest form of exactly the two sub-claims weighed below — the historical rupture and the scriptural predic…

Against the rupture stands the modern study of how doctrine actually moved. John Henry Newman argued that Christian teaching legitimately develops — “to live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often” — and set out seven “notes” to tell a genuine development from a corruption. 14 Even the strongest scholarly declension narrative — Adolf von Harnack’s “acute secularising or hellenising of Christianity” — reads church history as one continuous process within a surviving body, not a church that vanished; and J. N. D. Kelly and Jaroslav Pelikan describe the ante-Nicene centuries as a fixed apostolic outline whose “theological explication was to a large extent left unfettered” — co…

ar.q: Do the New Testament prophecies foretell a total falling-away?
ar.c: the Church gradually drifted into a condition of apostasy… [as] the Apostasy Foretold — James E. Talmage, The Great Apostasy (1909), ch. II heading and text , link . Restorationist writers read a cluster of New-Testament texts — 2 Thessalonians 2:3 (“a falling away first”), Acts 20:29–30 (“grievous wolves… of your own selves shall men arise”), 1 Timothy 4:1 (“some shall depart from the faith”), 2 Timothy 4:3–4, and Amos 8:11 (“a famine… of hearing the words of the LORD”) — as predicting a total apostasy: the whole church falling away, so that a restoration becomes necessary.
ar.a: Weak. The prophecies foretell a real, even severe apostasy — a falling-away of many and the rise of a man of sin — but not the extinction of the church, which is the reading a Restoration requires. The partial quantifiers of the warning-texts, the countervailing promises of permanence in the same corpus, and the misapplication of Amos 8:11 together mean that as a prediction of a total falling-away the argument overruns its evidence. It supports, …

ar.q: Is baptism for the dead (1 Corinthians 15:29) a lost apostolic ordinance restored?
ar.c: Else what shall they do which are baptized for the dead, if the dead rise not at all? why are they then baptized for the dead? — 1 Corinthians 15:29 (KJV). 1 On the Latter-day Saint reading this clause is direct biblical evidence that the earliest church baptized the living on behalf of their dead as a real, saving ordinance — an ordinance later lost in the general apostasy and restored through Joseph Smith, who made proxy baptism a temple rite and called it “the most glorious of all subjects belonging to the everlasting gospel.” The sub-claim weighed here is not whether the practice can be re…
ar.a: Weak. That the church once possessed proxy baptism for the dead as a saving ordinance, lost it, and needed it restored is not established by 1 Corinthians 15:29 on its best case. The surface reading grants only that some baptism-on-behalf-of-the-dead may lie behind the clause — but the sole proxy rite the ancient record actually names, it condemns as heretical (Marcionite, Cerinthian) and forbids by canon, so the “ancient attestation” the argumen…

ar.q: Do Christ’s promises guarantee the church against a total apostasy?
ar.c: upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. — Matthew 16:18 (KJV), with Matthew 28:20 (“lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world”). 1 The argument is the mainstream church’s standing answer to the Great Apostasy thesis: Christ pledged that the powers of death and hell would not prevail against the church he founded, and that he himself would remain with it to the very end of the age. If those promises hold, then at no point between the apostles and now was there no church — a wholesale defection in which all valid authority, ordinan…
ar.a: Sound. Christ’s promises that the gates of hell will not prevail and that he is with his church “all the days… unto the end” do, on their minimum and mainstream sense, guarantee that the church will never be wholly overcome or cease to exist — the indefectibility the fathers read off the clause and the systematic tradition after them affirmed. That guarantee is the direct contradictory of the total apostasy a Restoration requires, and the restora…

ar.q: Was priesthood authority restored by angelic ministration after a total apostasy?
ar.c: The messenger who visited us on this occasion and conferred this Priesthood upon us, said that his name was John, the same that is called John the Baptist in the New Testament, and that he acted under the direction of Peter, James and John, who held the keys of the Priesthood of Melchizedek, which Priesthood, he said, would in due time be conferred on us… — Joseph Smith—History 1:72 (Pearl of Great Price), churchofjesuschrist.org . The Latter-day Saint answer to the Great Apostasy ’s lost authority is a literal two-stage restoration : because a total apostasy severed the line of priesthood suc…
ar.a: Weak. The interpretation is not weak for being miraculous; it is weak on ordinary evidence. Its foundation — a total apostasy that severed priesthood succession — does not hold, so the restoration answers a need the record does not establish. And the restoration’s own historical case is thin: the named, dated, two-stage narrative appears years after the traditional 1829 dating, entering the canon only with the 1835 expansion of an earlier text; i…

ar.q: Did the church wholly apostatize after the apostolic age?
ar.c: We affirm that with the passing of the so-called apostolic age the Church gradually drifted into a condition of apostasy, whereby succession in the priesthood was broken; and that the Church, as an earthly organization operating under divine direction and having authority to officiate in spiritual ordinances, ceased to exist. — James E. Talmage, The Great Apostasy (1909), ch. II , link . The asserted event is a total one: not that the church erred, innovated, or declined, but that it ceased to exist as an authoritative body, its priesthood succession broken , so that nothing but “an earthly or…
ar.a: Weak. The strong, total-rupture form of the Great Apostasy — the only form that grounds a restoration — does not hold on its best available case: the continuous, footnoted record shows a church that developed and argued rather than one that ceased to exist, and the strongest scholarly critiques of doctrinal change concede a surviving body. The lesser claim folded inside it — that real corruptions and innovations occurred — is a genuinely differen…

ds.t: The Veneration of Images and Icons
