The interpretation weighed here is Origen’s: that when Paul names Pharaoh’s two magicians — figures the Old Testament never names — he is not merely echoing a floating legend but citing a particular written work , the apocryphal Book of Jannes and Jambres . A second, distinct question rides on the same book and is best kept separate: given that no Old-Testam…
ar.a: Contested — on whether Paul quoted the written book. The strong form of Origen’s claim (a direct, exclusive dependence of 2 Timothy 3:8 on the Book of Jannes and Jambres ) is neither established nor refuted: for it stand the earliest reader who addressed the question, a real and early book on exactly these figures, and a Latin Father who knew its plot; against it stand the names’ wide currency before and apart from the book (the Damascus Document…

ar.q: Where do the names “Jannes and Jambres” come from — and why does Jambres become Mambres?
ar.c: JANNES AND JAMBRES (more correctly Mambres… also… Yoḥanai and Mamre): Names of two legendary wizards of Pharaoh “who withstood Moses” (II Tim. iii. 8)… — Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), “Jannes and Jambres.” The interpretation weighed here is the mainstream one behind that entry: the names of Pharaoh’s magicians belong to a real, early, Semitic-Jewish onomastic tradition — forms with regular by-development and a knowable sense (“Yoḥana,” a by-form of John; “Mamre/Mambres,” the opposer or rebel) — from which Paul, in 2 Timothy 3:8 , simply cites a pair his readers already knew, rather than coining …
ar.a: Plausible — with its core claim sound. That the names of Pharaoh’s magicians descend from a genuine, pre-Christian Jewish onomastic tradition — a tradition old enough that Paul cites it without explanation and wide enough to reach pagan Rome — is well-grounded: the Damascus Document ’s pre-Pauline naming and the cross-lingual stability of “Jannes” put that beyond serious doubt, and the Latin Mambres is a regular variant of Jambres, not a second n…

ar.q: Were Jannes and Jambres the sons of Balaam?
ar.c: And when they had gone Pharaoh sent for Balaam the magician and to Jannes and Jambres his sons , and to all the magicians and conjurors and counsellors which belonged to the king, and they all came and sat before the king. — Sefer ha-Yashar (the mediaeval “Book of Jasher”), ch. 79, Internet Sacred Text Archive . The interpretation weighed here is the traditional identification behind that line: that the two magicians who “withstood Moses” ( 2 Timothy 3:8 ) were the literal kin of Balaam — his sons, or at least his household attendants — so that the Exodus contest and the attempted cursing of I…
ar.a: Weak — as a literal claim about kinship. That Jannes and Jambres were the sons of Balaam (or even his household servants) does not hold on its best available evidence: the identification is confined to the tradition’s latest and most legendary layers — the most expansive Targum, the fragmentary apocryphon, the mediaeval Book of Jasher , and the modern compilations — and is unknown to the Damascus Document , to Paul , to the pagan writers , and to…

ds.t: The Japanese-Israelite theory: a lost tribe in the East?
ds.q: The Japanese-Israelite theory (Japanese Nichiyu dōsoron , “the common ancestry of the Japanese and the Jews”) holds that the Japanese — or a priestly or imperial class within them — descend from the Ten Lost Tribes of Israel , carried east after the fall of Samaria until they reached the islands of Japan. Proponents rest the case on two kinds of resemblance: ritual parallels between Shinto practice and the worship of ancient Israel (a portable shrine likened to the Ark of the Covenant, a mountain festival read as the binding of Isaac, priestly linen and salt purifications), and linguistic ones — Japanese words and names derived from Hebrew by sound-resemblance, the same folk-etymology method…

tl.w: A Jesuit ties the Lost Tribes to the East — then recants (1608)
tl.t: The earliest thread runs back to João Rodrigues (1561–1634), the Portuguese Jesuit interpreter who spent decades in Japan. In his História da Igreja do Japão (c. 1608) he floated the idea that an East-Asian people descended from the Lost Tribes — though he applied it to the Chinese , not the Japanese, arguing that Confucius and Laozi had drawn on Judaism. He is a precursor rather than a proponent of the Japan theory: he abandoned the notion, concluding instead that Japan had been peopled by ordinary migration from the Asian mainland (from Zhejiang and by way of Korea). His false start is worth recording only because it shows the lost-tribes-in-the-East impulse already stirring in the early m…

tl.w: Nicholas McLeod launches the Japan theory (c. 1875–1878)
tl.t: The theory in its Japanese form was the work of Nicholas McLeod (a Scot of the Isle of Skye, active in Japan in the 1870s–80s), a former herring-trader turned missionary. In a privately printed book — Epitome of the Ancient History of Japan (Nagasaki; the cover title of the fuller edition reads Japan and the Lost Tribes of Israel ), with a companion volume of Illustrations issued at Kyoto — he argued that Japan’s aristocratic and priestly “holy class” descended from the deported tribes. He identified Japan’s legendary early king “Osee” (whom he placed c. 730 BC) with Hoshea , the last king of Israel (d. 722 BC), matched the founding emperor Jimmu to Moses, and filled his pages with parallels…

tl.w: P. Y. Saeki makes the Hata clan a “Jewish-Nestorian” tribe (1908)
tl.t: The theory entered Japanese scholarship through Peter Yoshirō Saeki (1871–1965), a Waseda University professor and the leading Japanese authority on the Nestorian (Church of the East) mission in China. In a 1908 book on the Chinese Nestorians he added an appendix, “Regarding Uzumasa,” proposing that the Hata clan (秦氏) — immigrants who reached Japan from Korea around the third century — were a Jewish tribe that had converted to Nestorian Christianity in Central Asia before travelling east. His key prop was a piece of wordplay: the Kyoto district of Uzumasa , where the Hata settled, he parsed as concealing “Ishu” (Jesus) and “masa” (messiah). (The name in fact has a documented origin unrelated…

tl.w: Oyabe Zen’ichirō traces the emperor to the tribe of Gad (1929)
tl.t: The most ambitious pre-war statement came from Oyabe Zen’ichirō (1867–1941), a Yale-trained scholar who had lived among the Ainu. His Nihon oyobi Nihon kokumin no kigen (“The Origin of Japan and the Japanese,” 1929) traced the Japanese to the Hebrews and made the imperial line itself descend from the tribe of Gad — reading the title mikado as mi (“honourable”) + Gad. He argued that the portable mikoshi shrine derived from the Ark of the Covenant, and marshalled the ritual parallels that would become standard. The book ran to a sixth edition within months and was presented to the Imperial Household — a measure of how respectable the idea had briefly become in an age of surging Japanese nation…

tl.w: Bishop Juji Nakada gives it a Christian-Zionist turn (1933)
tl.t: Juji Nakada (1870–1939), co-founder and first bishop of the Japan Holiness Church, folded the common-ancestry idea into a Christian-Zionist theology. In Japan in the Bible (Tokyo, 1933) and related preaching he held that Japan had a providential destiny bound up with Israel’s restoration — the Japanese, as kin of the ancient Israelites, being divinely appointed to a role in the last-days gathering of the Jews. Nakada shows how quickly the theory passed from antiquarian speculation into the pulpit of a large Japanese Protestant body, where the question was no longer merely historical but prophetic. 6

tl.w: Ikurō Teshima founds the Makuya movement (1948)
tl.t: The theory found its most enduring institutional home in the Makuya (“Tabernacle”) movement, founded in May 1948 by Ikurō Teshima (1910–1973), a businessman shaped by Uchimura Kanzō’s “Non-church” Christianity who took the Hebrew name Abraham. Teshima read the near-simultaneous births of his movement and the modern State of Israel (the same month) as a single act of Providence; Makuya teaches a historical bond between the Japanese and ancient Israel through the dispersion of the Lost Tribes, and expresses it concretely — members have worn vests marking descent from the seafaring tribe of Zebulun, made pilgrimages to Jerusalem, and sent young people to Israeli kibbutzim, and Teshima led Japan…

tl.w: Joseph Eidelberg builds the linguistic case (1980)
tl.t: The fullest linguistic version came from Joseph Eidelberg (1916–1985), an Israeli engineer and former army officer who, after spending about a year living at a Shinto shrine, published The Japanese and the Ten Lost Tribes of Israel (1980; Japanese translation 1984, which sold tens of thousands of copies and spawned a television series). Eidelberg derived hundreds of Japanese words, songs, and names from Hebrew: Yamato from a Hebrew phrase for “the people of God,” the imperial style Sumera Mikoto as “His Majesty of Samaria,” and much else, tracing a migration-route for the tribes from Samaria across Asia to the archipelago. His work — extended in the posthumous The Biblical Hebrew Origin of t…

The theory’s most widely read contemporary vehicle is the work of Arimasa Kubo (b. 1955), a Tokyo pastor and head of Remnant Publishing, whose essay “Israelites Came to Ancient Japan” (first published in 1999, then freely circulated on his website) has been reposted across the internet and translated widely. Kubo’s signature argument is the Ontohsai festival at the Suwa Taisha shrine in Nagano, which he reads as a re-enactment of the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22), pointing to the local place-name Moriya as an echo of Moriah ; he adds the standard parallels — the omikoshi as the Ark, the yamabushi ’s forehead box as Jewish phylacteries, the two-chamber shrine as the Tabernacle. “Apparently,” …

tl.w: The historians read it as a Western projection (1991–2002)
tl.t: Modern scholarship treats the theory as a construction rather than a lineage. Ben-Ami Shillony, in The Jews and the Japanese: The Successful Outsiders (1991), documents both the philo-Semitic enthusiasm behind it and its strange coexistence with antisemitism; David Goodman and Masanori Miyazawa, in Jews in the Japanese Mind (1995), trace how Japanese Christians, having redefined themselves as the “real” Israel, could in the same culture absorb the Protocols of the Elders of Zion (introduced to Japan in the 1920s) — a paranoia that culminated in the Aum Shinrikyō cult’s antisemitic tract on the eve of its 1995 sarin attack; and Jacob Kovalio’s The Russian Protocols of Zion in Japan (2009) ana…

tl.w: The genetics point to East Asia (2019–2021)
tl.t: The last witnesses are the population-genetic studies, which place Japanese origins firmly in East Asia. On the now-standard account — extended to a “tripartite” model by Cooke and colleagues in Science Advances (2021) — the Japanese descend from the indigenous Jōmon hunter-gatherers (a lineage deeply diverged from the mainland some 15,000–20,000 years ago), the Yayoi rice-farmers who arrived from the Korean peninsula and Northeast Asia, and a further East-Asian influx in the Kofun period. The Y-chromosome record tells the same story: Japanese paternal lineages are dominated by the Jōmon marker haplogroup D (the D-M55 line, all but unique to Japan) and the Yayoi haplogroup O (shared across E…

ar.q: Were the Hata clan a Jewish-Nestorian tribe?
ar.c: The Hata clan was a large group of ancient immigrants to Japan… They were originally a part of the Ten Lost Tribes of Israel… The name Uzumasa had come from Ish-Mashiah, which meant Jesus Christ in Aramaic, the language that the ancient Eastern Christians used. — Arimasa Kubo, “The Ancient Christians in Kyoto and the Hata Clan,” stating in its modern popular form the thesis first argued by P. Y. Saeki in 1908. The interpretation has a definite shape, distinct from the general descent claim: a subset of the Japanese — the immigrant Hata — were a Jewish tribe who adopted Nestorian Christianity i…
ar.a: Unsupported. The Hata thesis is the most concrete form of the Japanese-Israelite theory — it names a real clan and a real road, and it deserved weighing on its own rather than being left as a footnote to the general descent claim — but it does not survive the weighing. Its distinctive contribution, the Nestorian migration channel, is ruled out by chronology: the Hata reached Japan before the Church of the East existed and long before it reached t…

ar.q: Do Japanese words and names derive from Hebrew?
ar.c: The argument runs that Japanese still carries its Hebrew ancestry in its vocabulary. The showpieces span several kinds. Names of the nation and its ruler: Yamato (Japan) from a Hebrew phrase for “the people of God” (or from Yahweh); the imperial style Sumera Mikoto as “His Majesty of Samaria” (Eidelberg); mikado (emperor) as mi (“honourable”) + Gad, the tribe (Oyabe), or from Hebrew migdol ; samurai as “men of Samaria” or from Hebrew shomer , “guard” (Edward Odlum). Place-names of the Hata district: Uzumasa from Aramaic “Ishu Mashiach” (Jesus Messiah); the well called Isarai from “Israel”; the…
ar.a: Unsupported. The philological proof does not hold: the Hebrew–Japanese matches are folk etymologies that fail the test of regular sound-correspondence, the two languages are unrelated, and every showpiece ( samurai , Uzumasa , torii , the songs) has a documented Japanese origin. It is rated unsupported — the same verdict as the Anglo-Saxon “Saxon = Isaac’s sons” philology, whose method it exactly repeats — because, once examined, it supplies no e…

ar.q: Are the Japanese descended from the Ten Lost Tribes of Israel?
ar.c: Twenty-seven centuries ago, ten Hebrew tribes were exiled by the Assyrians and vanished somewhere beyond the mist-shrouded mountains of the East… a close examination of their traditions suggests the possibility that the Japanese are the descendants of the Ten Lost Tribes of Israel. — Joseph Eidelberg, The Japanese and the Ten Lost Tribes of Israel , stating the thesis in its modern form. In its strongest version the interpretation runs: when Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel (c. 722–719 BC), the deported tribes did not assimilate but migrated east across Asia and reached the Jap…
ar.a: Unsupported. The identification of the Japanese with the Ten Lost Tribes has no footing in documented history, historical linguistics, or genetics. Its central mechanism — reading Shinto ritual and Japanese words as Israelite survivals — is resemblance-hunting that fails on examination, and its prophetic and comparative “evidence” assumes the conclusion. It is rated unsupported rather than weak — a step below the Pashtun verdict — for the reason …

ar.q: Do Shinto rituals preserve ancient Israelite worship?
ar.c: Apparently, no other country but Japan has a festival illustrating the biblical story of Abraham and Isaac. — Arimasa Kubo, “Israelites Came to Ancient Japan,” on the Ontohsai festival at Suwa Taisha. The argument runs that Shinto has preserved, under a native surface, the cult of the Ark and the Temple. Its showpieces are: the omikoshi , a gold-overlaid portable shrine carried on two shoulder-poles and topped by a golden bird, likened to the Ark of the Covenant (1 Chron. 15:15); the Ontohsai festival at Suwa Taisha in Nagano, where a boy is bound to a pillar and a priest approaches with a kni…
ar.a: Unsupported. The ritual proof does not hold. Its parallels are selected from two rich cultic systems, so a long list proves little; the resemblances that are distinctive enough to matter turn out, where they can be dated, to be documented indigenous developments (the Nara-period mikoshi , the medieval tokin , the Edo-period torii and lanterns); and the single most impressive case, the Ontohsai, rests for its Israelite reading on a folk etymology …

ds.t: Jerome and Augustine: a correspondence across the Mediterranean
ds.q: This is the story of a friendship built entirely out of letters. Augustine of Hippo (c. 354–430) and Jerome (c. 347–420) — the two greatest Latin churchmen of their age — never met. For a quarter-century they wrote to each other across the sea between Roman Africa and Bethlehem, and the exchange began badly: a respectful young bishop's criticism of the famous old scholar's exegesis, letters that went astray or circulated behind Jerome's back, and a decade of prickly, wounded, half-suspicious replies. Yet it ended as one of the warmest friendships of the early Church, the two men allied against a common enemy and longing, across the miles, to embrace.

tl.w: Augustine opens the correspondence — and the letter is lost (c. 394/395)
tl.t: Not long after his ordination, Augustine — soon bishop of Hippo — wrote to Jerome , then in his monastery at Bethlehem, opening the correspondence with a respectful but pointed objection to Jerome's commentary on Galatians. Jerome had read Paul's rebuke of Peter at Antioch (Gal 2:11–14) as a staged, mutually-agreed performance — a “useful” pretense in which neither apostle really erred. To Augustine that opened a fatal breach in the truthfulness of Scripture: For it seems to me that most disastrous consequences must follow upon our believing that anything false is found in the sacred books: that is to say, that the men by whom the Scripture has been given to us, and committed to writing, did…

tl.w: A second letter, and a request for a “palinode” (c. 397)
tl.t: Some two years later Augustine wrote again, pressing the same objection harder and asking Jerome outright to recant the reading — to sing, in the Greek phrase, a palinode : Wherefore I beseech you, apply to the correction and emendation of that book a frank and truly Christian severity, and chant what the Greeks call παλινῴδια. — Augustine, Letter 40 (to Jerome), §7 . This letter also miscarried in delivery — but a copy escaped into circulation, passing through many hands in Italy and at Rome long before it ever reached Bethlehem. Criticism of Jerome's work was being published to the world behind his back. 2

tl.w: “A book against you”: Augustine denies the rumour (402)
tl.t: Word reached Augustine that Jerome had been told something worse than criticism — that the African bishop had written and published a whole book against him. Augustine wrote at once to deny it: … I have heard that some brethren have told your Charity that I have written a book against you and have sent it to Rome. Be assured that this is false: I call God to witness that I have not done this. — Augustine, Letter 67 (to Jerome), §2 . Where he did differ, he insisted, he had written “not with a view of contradicting you, but only of stating my own views,” and he begged for correction in return — and simply for contact: “Do not refuse to write me in return, however seldom.” 3

tl.w: Jerome's guarded first reply: an unauthenticated letter and “do not challenge a veteran” (402)
tl.t: When Jerome at last answered (402), friendship and suspicion were mixed — and the first thing he raised was not the exegesis but the paperwork. He had never received a letter from Augustine; what he had were the loose copies of the palinode letter, brought east by a deacon named Sisinnius, and he would not treat an unsigned copy as authentic: … by our brother Sysinnius, deacon, copies of a letter addressed by some one apparently to me have come hither. … Although the style and the method of argument appeared to be yours, I must frankly confess to your Excellency that I did not think it right to assume without examination the authenticity of a letter of which I had only seen copies … — Jerome…

tl.w: A trusted courier at last: the asterisks, the Septuagint plea, and the riot at Oea (403)
tl.t: In 403 Augustine tried again, this time by a bearer he trusted to get an answer — the deacon Cyprian, “a most faithful servant and minister of God” — and he enclosed fresh copies of both earlier letters, since “I suppose that they never reached you.” He also opened a second front. Jerome's older Latin Old Testament, made from the Greek, had marked with asterisks and obelisks every word present in the Hebrew but missing from the Greek and the reverse; the new version straight from the Hebrew abandoned that scrupulous apparatus, and Augustine wanted to know why: it “perplexes any thoughtful reader.” Behind the technical question lay the larger worry — that a Latin Bible following the Hebrew wo…

tl.w: Jerome's grievance: the letter is all over Rome, but not with me (403/404)
tl.t: Jerome's patience frayed. He had still, he protested, never received an authenticated letter from Augustine — yet the criticism was everywhere: I am at a loss to express my surprise that the same letter is reported to be in the possession of most of the Christians in Rome, and throughout Italy, and has come to every one but myself, to whom alone it was ostensibly sent. — Jerome, Letter 105 (to Augustine), §1 . He suspected the whole exercise was a bid for fame at his expense, and asked to be left alone — to have his critic “desist from annoying an old man, who seeks retirement in his monastic cell.” 6

tl.w: Augustine owns the letter and asks pardon — and grieves the quarrel with Rufinus (404)
tl.t: Augustine's answer of 404 finally closed the authenticity question and, with it, nine years of misdirected post. He acknowledged the palinode letter as his own and did not defend himself: … it remains for me to confess, as I now do, my fault as having been the first to offend by writing that letter which I cannot deny to be mine. Why should I strive to swim against the current, and not rather ask pardon? — Augustine, Letter 73 (to Jerome), §3 . He set out plainly how the years had been lost: “I remember writing to your Holiness regarding these words in the Epistle to the Galatians when I was young; and behold I am now advanced in age, and have not yet received a reply, and a copy of my lette…

tl.w: Jerome's great reply: Hebrew verity and the Antioch defense (404)
tl.t: Then came Jerome's long-delayed answer to all three earlier letters. On the translation he defended his “Hebrew verity”; on Galatians he stood his ground, insisting that in reading the Antioch scene as a prudent arrangement he had only followed the Greek fathers before him — Origen above all, and “John, who has long governed the Church of Constantinople” (Chrysostom). Peter, he argued, had neither truly sinned nor Paul truly rebuked; the apostle only seemed to keep the law: … Peter was thoroughly aware of the abrogation of the law of Moses, but was compelled by fear to pretend to observe it. — Jerome, Letter 112 (to Augustine), §8 . And he begged the younger man to leave him in peace: “have …

tl.w: Augustine's irenic answer: only the canonical books are without error (405)
tl.t: Augustine's reply (405) conceded nothing on Galatians but framed the whole disagreement with a principle that would outlast them both. He held Scripture inerrant — and reserved that reverence for Scripture alone: For I confess to your Charity that I have learned to yield this respect and honour only to the canonical books of Scripture: of these alone do I most firmly believe that the authors were completely free from error. And if in these writings I am perplexed by anything which appears to me opposed to truth, I do not hesitate to suppose that either the manuscript is faulty, or the translator has not caught the meaning of what was said, or I myself have failed to understand it. — Augustin…

tl.w: The thaw: “letters not of controversy, but of mutual charity” (405)
tl.t: With that, the heat went out of the quarrel. Jerome's next note struck a wholly different key, proposing they lay down their arms: … let there be sincere brotherliness between us; and henceforth let us exchange letters, not of controversy, but of mutual charity. — Jerome, Letter 115 (to Augustine), §1 . “Let us, if you please,” he added, “exercise ourselves in the field of Scripture without wounding each other.” 10

tl.w: Rome falls, and Jerome starts sending inquirers to Augustine (410)
tl.t: Alaric took Rome in August 410, and the shock reached Bethlehem in the form of refugees. Jerome had promised his readers a commentary on Ezekiel; he could not write it: … at the time when I had just begun to dictate the proposed exposition, my mind was so much agitated by the devastation of the western provinces of the empire, and especially by the sack of Rome itself by the barbarians, that, to use a common proverbial phrase, I scarcely knew my own name; and for a long while I was silent, knowing that it was a time for tears. — Jerome, Letter 126 (to Marcellinus and Anapsychia), §2 . In the prefaces to that commentary he described the monastery overwhelmed — “the quiet of the monastery has …

tl.w: Allies against Pelagius; Orosius carries the letters (c. 415–416)
tl.t: A few years later the two were allies. When the Pelagian controversy broke, Augustine sent the young Spanish priest Orosius east to Jerome (415), carrying two long letters that consulted the old scholar as an authority — one on the origin of the soul , one on the meaning of James 2:10. Jerome, whose own Bethlehem community was already under threat from Pelagian partisans, answered with unguarded warmth: I am resolved to love you, to look up to you, to reverence and admire you, and to defend your opinions as my own. — Jerome, Letter 134 (to Augustine), §1 . He welcomed Orosius, he wrote, “both on his own account and in obedience to your request” — but he would not answer the two treatises at …

tl.w: The Pelagians sack the monasteries at Bethlehem (416–417)
tl.t: After the synod of Diospolis acquitted Pelagius, partisans of his cause fell on Jerome's monasteries. Augustine reported it — carefully, at second hand, and from a great distance — in the closing chapter of his account of the synod: Certain followers of Pelagius are said to have carried their support of his cause after these judicial proceedings to an incredible extent of perverseness and audacity. They are said to have most cruelly beaten and maltreated the servants and handmaidens of the Lord who lived under the care of the holy presbyter Jerome, slain his deacon, and burnt his monastic houses; while he himself, by God's mercy, narrowly escaped the violent attacks of these impious assailan…

In his last letters Jerome, embattled and aging, hailed Augustine as the Church's champion against the Pelagians: Go on and prosper! You are renowned throughout the whole world; Catholics revere and look up to you as the restorer of the ancient faith, and — which is a token of yet more illustrious glory — all heretics abhor you. — Jerome, Letter 141 (to Augustine) . And across the sea he longed for a reunion that could never come: “if it were possible, I would take the wings of a dove and fly to be folded in your embrace.” Their “co-operation and … leadership,” he wrote in 419, had “succeeded in strangling the heresy of Celestius.” 15

tl.w: Jerome dies; Augustine enrols him among the authorities (420–430)
tl.t: Jerome died at Bethlehem in 420. Augustine outlived him by a decade and honoured him to the last. Answering Julian of Eclanum about a year after Jerome's death, he set against the Pelagians a bench of dead witnesses — ten bishops and, punctiliously, one presbyter: “Irenaeus, Cyprian, Reticius, Olympius, Hilary, Ambrose, Gregory, Innocent, John, Basil, to whom I add, whether you wish it or not, the priest Jerome.” He anticipated the obvious objection — that Jerome was a combatant in this very war — by restricting himself to what Jerome had written “free from all partisanship, before your damnable doctrine sprang up.” The correspondence that began as a young man's challenge to a prickly elder …

ar.q: The clash at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14): a real rebuke of a genuine error?
ar.c: But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed. For before that certain came from James, he did eat with the Gentiles: but when they were come, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision. And the other Jews dissembled likewise with him; insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation. But when I saw that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, I said unto Peter before them all, If thou, being a Jew, livest after the manner of Gentiles, and not as do the Jews, why comp…
ar.a: Sound. That Peter genuinely erred at Antioch and that Paul genuinely, truthfully, and publicly corrected him is the plain sense of Galatians 2 and has become the settled verdict of later interpretation; Augustine won the exegetical argument, and his companion principle — that inerrancy belongs to the canonical books alone, and that admitting one dutiful falsehood there unravels the whole — became the classic Latin statement of the point. The riva…

ar.q: The clash at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14): a staged pretense, in which neither apostle really erred?
ar.c: But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed. For before that certain came from James, he did eat with the Gentiles: but when they were come, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision. And the other Jews dissembled likewise with him; insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation. But when I saw that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, I said unto Peter before them all, If thou, being a Jew, livest after the manner of Gentiles, and not as do the Jews, why comp…
ar.a: Weak — a pedigreed and self-qualified reading that does not hold on its best case. The “economy” interpretation carried the authority of Origen and the Greek fathers and answered a real apologetic worry, and Jerome himself never pressed it as more than a reported opinion; those facts keep it honourable and explain why so careful a tradition held it. But it does not survive the words Paul actually wrote: the vocabulary of fault, the oath of Galati…

ar.q: Should the Latin Old Testament be translated from the Hebrew rather than the Septuagint?
ar.c: … it would have been but fair to have given me credit for the same fidelity in the Old Testament; for I have not followed my own imagination, but have rendered the divine words as I found them understood by those who speak the Hebrew language. — Jerome, Letter 112 (to Augustine), §20 . Against Augustine 's repeated request that he simply put the Greek Seventy into good Latin, Jerome held that the base text of a Latin Old Testament must be the Hebrew original. 1
ar.a: Sound. Translating the Old Testament from the Hebrew rather than from the Greek was the right call and is now the near-universal practice; Jerome's reasons for it — the collapse of any single Septuagint text, the compounding of error through a double translation, and the New Testament's own citations of Hebrew readings — are good ones, and Augustine, whose objections were mostly pastoral, conceded the scholarly half of the case himself. Two quali…

ar.q: The plant of Jonah 4:6: the castor-oil plant, and neither “gourd” nor “ivy”?
ar.c: And the LORD God prepared a gourd, and made it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shadow over his head, to deliver him from his grief. So Jonah was exceeding glad of the gourd. — Jonah 4:6 (KJV) . The Hebrew word is qiqayon , a word that occurs nowhere else in the Bible. The Septuagint made it κολοκύνθη, “gourd,” and the Old Latin followed with cucurbita ; Aquila and the later Greek revisers made it κισσός, “ivy,” and Jerome's Vulgate followed them with hedera . That single word emptied a church: when a bishop at Oea read Jerome's version aloud, the congregation rioted, and he had to re…
ar.a: Sound. That the qiqayon of Jonah 4:6 is the castor-oil plant is the mainstream lexical judgment, resting on the Egyptian and Akkadian cognates, the rabbinic identification, and Jerome's own eyewitness description of the shrub — and the bottle-gourd alternative, though not absurd, has only the Septuagint's guess and the shape of a field-booth behind it. Certainty is not available for a word that occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, and the sensible mo…

ar.q: Is the churches' settled text a legitimate constraint on a new translation?
ar.c: … my only reason for objecting to the public reading of your translation from the Hebrew in our churches was, lest, bringing forward anything which was, as it were, new and opposed to the authority of the Septuagint version, we should trouble by serious cause of offence the flocks of Christ, whose ears and hearts have become accustomed to listen to that version to which the seal of approbation was given by the apostles themselves. — Augustine, Letter 82 (to Jerome), §35 . The claim is that a translator is answerable not only to the original but to the receiving church: a text long read, chante…
ar.a: Contested. Judged as translation theory the question has no settled winner, and the two disciplines that judge it disagree. By the lights of textual scholarship Augustine loses: accuracy is what a translation is for, and a rule that freezes a known error because congregations are used to it cannot be defended. By the lights of pastoral and liturgical practice he wins, and has largely been followed — the Gallican Psalter outlived the Hebraica veri…

ds.t: Who Was Jethro?
ds.q: Jethro is the great Gentile mentor of the Hebrew Bible — a Midianite priest, outside the covenant and the line of Abraham, who shelters the fugitive Moses, gives him a wife, and, when the exodus is done, blesses the LORD, offers Him sacrifice, and teaches Israel’s deliverer how to govern. Moses first meets him at the well in Midian, where he drives off the shepherds who trouble the priest’s seven daughters and is taken into the household: “Moses was content to dwell with the man: and he gave Moses Zipporah his daughter” ( Exodus 2:21 ). It is while “Moses kept the flock of Jethro his father in law, the priest of Midian” that he comes “to the mountain of God, even to Horeb” and the burning bu…

tl.w: The biblical portrait (Exodus 2–18, with Numbers 10 and the Judges echoes)
tl.t: The whole later tradition grows from a handful of scenes and a tangle of names. Moses, a fugitive from Egypt, sits down by a well in Midian and defends the seven daughters of “the priest of Midian” from the shepherds who would drive them off; brought home, he is taken into the household and married to Zipporah, who bears him Gershom, “for he said, I have been a stranger in a strange land” ( Exodus 2:16–22 ). The priest is here called Reuel ; a chapter later, keeping “the flock of Jethro his father in law, the priest of Midian,” Moses leads it “to the backside of the desert” and comes “to the mountain of God, even to Horeb” — the site of the burning bush ( Exodus 3:1 ). So the outsider priest…

tl.w: The rabbis (the Mekhilta and Sifrei, 3rd c.; the Talmud, c. 500–600; Exodus Rabbah)
tl.t: Where the rabbis made Balaam the paradigm of the wicked gentile, they made Jethro the paradigm of the righteous one, and four traditions carry the portrait. First, Jethro is one of Pharaoh’s three counsellors on the plan to afflict the Hebrews: “Balaam, who advised … was killed. Job, who was silent … was punished by suffering. Yitro, who ran away as a sign of protest, merited that some of his children’s children sat in the Sanhedrin in the Chamber of Hewn Stone” — a measure-for-measure legend that judges three men by what each does with the same evil (b. Sotah 11a; b. Sanhedrin 106a; Exodus Rabbah 1:9). 4 Second, his confession “Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods” ( Exodus 18:…

tl.w: The Fathers (Origen, 3rd c.; Gregory of Nyssa, Chrysostom, Augustine, 4th–5th c.; Gregory the Great, 6th c.)
tl.t: Where the rabbis made Jethro the paradigm proselyte, the Fathers made him a figure — and a scandalous one, for here a Gentile priest instructs the man to whom God spoke “face to face.” Origen felt the shock and turned it into a charter for Christian learning: Moses “accepted counsel from Jethro the priest of Madian … He hears not the one who speaks, but what he says. Whence also we, if perhaps now and then we discover something said wisely by the Gentiles, ought not immediately to despise what is said … we should ‘prove all things and hold fast that which is good’” — the personal form of the same motif he calls, in his Letter to Gregory , the “spoiling of the Egyptians,” the Church’s licit p…

tl.w: The Islamic tradition and the Druze (the Qur’an, 7th c.; the tafsir; the Druze veneration, 11th c. onward)
tl.t: The latest and largest tradition about Jethro is also a living one. The Qur’an sends the prophet Shu‘ayb (شعيب) to the people of Midian (Madyan) and to the “companions of the thicket” ( Ashab al-Aykah ): he preaches the worship of the one God and honest weights and measures — “O my people, worship Allāh… fulfill the measure and weight and do not deprive people of their due” — is mocked, and his people are destroyed by earthquake, shriek, and a canopy of fire ( Qur’an 7:85–93 ; 11:84–95 ; 26:176–191 ; 29:36–37 ). The Qur’an never names Shu‘ayb as Moses’ father-in-law; but the commentary tradition — al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, the Qisas al-Anbiya (“Stories of the Prophets”) — widely identifies the …

tl.w: Modern scholarship (a survey) — the source-critical, epigraphic, and history-of-religions grading of the whole tradition
tl.t: Set against the ancient and living witnesses, critical study grades the whole Jethro tradition, and four results recur. First, the source-critical one: the father-in-law’s three names — Reuel , Jethro , Hobab , plus the Kenite of Judges — are read as a redactional seam where the Pentateuch’s sources were joined ( Reuel and Jethro commonly split between the J and E strands), against the harmonizing seven-names and father-and-son readings. Second, and most consequential, the history-of-religions one: the same Midianite-priest-of-Yahweh datum anchors the Kenite/Midianite hypothesis — that Israel first received the worship of YHWH not by Jethro’s conversion but from his desert people — proposed …

ar.q: Was Jethro a true convert to the God of Israel, or a henotheist?
ar.c: There was no idolatry in the world that Yithro did not come across and did not worship … Now I know that greater is the L–rd than all the gods. — the Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael, reading Exodus 18:11 as the verdict of a man who had exhausted every alternative cult and, finding each empty, turned to the God of Israel: the archetypal seeker who converts. 1 On this reading Jethro is a true proselyte — not a man who merely added a greater God to a standing pantheon, but one who abandoned the idols he had sampled and gave his allegiance to the LORD alone. The interpretation is weighed here on its bes…
ar.a: Contested. The question divides because two true things about the same scene point opposite ways, and the text supplies no third thing to break the tie. What Jethro does — offer a burnt offering and sacrifices to the LORD, preside at a covenant meal Aaron and the elders share, confess Him newly and gladly — is the conduct of a man who has turned to Israel’s God, and grounds the ancient reading of him as the paradigm proselyte. What Jethro says — …

ar.q: Did Israel receive the worship of YHWH from Midian? — the Kenite/Midianite hypothesis
ar.c: The Israelites derived their belief in Yahweh from the Midianites through the intermediary of the Kenites. — the Kenite hypothesis in its classic form, as summarized in the standard reference literature. 1 The observation the reading is built on is the text’s own and is genuinely arresting: Jethro, an outsider and “the priest of Midian,” blesses the LORD, pronounces Him “greater than all gods,” and offers Him burnt offering and sacrifice, presiding over a covenant meal with Aaron and all the elders of Israel “before God” ( Exodus 18:10–12 ). On the ordinary reading Jethro is a convert who now …
ar.a: Contested. The two disciplines that weigh this reading return opposite verdicts, and neither can overrule the other. By the lights of the history of religions and the epigraphic record the hypothesis is strong: it unifies the Midianite-priest datum, the southern theophany, the archaic poetry, and the Kenites’ standing favour under one cause, and it is anchored by a genuine external attestation of a Yahweh-connected desert people — strong enough t…

ar.q: Is the Qur’anic Shu‘ayb to be identified with Jethro?
ar.c: And to [the people of] Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu‘ayb. He said, “O my people, worship Allāh; you have no deity other than Him… So fulfill the measure and weight and do not deprive people of their due…” — Qur’an 7:85 (Saheeh International). The prophet here sent to Midian is, on the identification, the same man the Torah calls Jethro: “Now Moses kept the flock of Jethro his father in law, the priest of Midian” ( Exodus 3:1 ). Both are righteous men of Midian in the age of Moses; and Islamic tradition, from the early commentators onward, took them for one figure, so that retellings of th…
ar.a: Contested. The question divides because the answer depends on which claim is on the table, and the evidence points opposite ways for the two. Taken as a claim about the same figure — that the Qur’anic prophet of Midian and the biblical priest of Midian are the tradition’s one righteous Midianite monotheist of Moses’ age, assimilated across the two scriptures — the identification is well-motivated, attested from the early commentators, and held as…

ar.q: One father-in-law, not a seam — the three names harmonized
ar.c: Reuel was probably not identical with Jethro: and Hobab was the brother-in-law, not the father-in-law, of Moses; the Hebrew word translated in the King James Version “father-in-law,” signifying simply any relation by marriage. — Albert Barnes, Notes on the Bible , on Numbers 10:29 . 1 The harmonizing thesis, in its strongest form, is not that one man improbably bears three unrelated names but that the text describes a single Midianite priestly household consistently: Reuel and Jethro are the one father-in-law, and Hobab is a second in-law of the same family — no seam, and no error, once the el…
ar.a: Plausible. The received text can be read as one internally consistent portrait — Reuel and Jethro the one father-in-law, Hobab an in-law of the same household — and every load-bearing step draws on a genuine breadth in the Hebrew rather than on invented harmony, so the claim of a bare contradiction fails and no seam is required . What the reading cannot supply is a single, non-optional construal: it leaves open whether Hobab is the father-in-law …

ar.q: The three names as a redactional seam
ar.c: J names Moses’ father-in-law as Reuel or Hobab, whereas E knows him as Jethro, priest of Midian. — the source-critical account, as stated in the Encyclopaedia Judaica treatment of Jethro. 1 On this reading the puzzle that the harmonizers labor to dissolve is not a puzzle at all but a datum: the received Pentateuch is a composite, and the alternation of names is one of the ordinary marks by which its once-separate strands still show. The interpretation is weighed here, not any single proponent.
ar.a: Contested. By the lights of source criticism the redactional reading is the better explanation of the whole pattern: the names sort by stratum, the Horeb correlation and the Midianite/Kenite doubling converge on the same seams, and the account needs none of the selective looseness a harmony requires. But it is not a fact about the text so much as a verdict about a chosen model: it presupposes the Documentary Hypothesis, which remains genuinely di…

ds.t: Who Was Job?
ds.q: No book of the Old Testament wrestles God so openly as the book of Job, and no figure in it is harder to place in time or on a map than its hero. Scripture introduces him without a genealogy and outside the line of Israel: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil” ( Job 1:1 ). A Gentile of the nations who fears God from the first — with no story of conversion or of coming to Israel — Job is the born-righteous pole of a figure that recurs across the Hebrew Bible, the God-fearing Gentile whose faith the New Testament reads as a foretype of the Gentile church: where Rahab, Naaman, and the Queen of Sh…

tl.w: The biblical portrait (the book of Job, with Ezekiel and James)
tl.t: The whole later tradition grows from a single book and two brief backward glances at it. The book of Job opens by placing its hero outside Israel and beyond easy dating: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil” — the greatest of “the men of the east,” with seven sons, three daughters, and vast flocks ( Job 1:1–3 ). Heaven itself repeats the verdict when the LORD asks the Satan, “Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil?” ( Job 1:8 ). On that testimony the wager turns: Job is stripped of ch…

tl.w: The Septuagint appendix to Job (Job 42:17b–e) — Job is Jobab, king of Edom (c. 2nd–1st century BC)
tl.t: The first readers to try to place Job were the Greek translators, and their answer is the fountainhead of everything after. Where the Hebrew ends at the hero’s death, the Old Greek adds a paragraph absent from the Hebrew — conventionally Job 42:17a–e — that first affirms Job will “rise again” and then, citing “the Syriac book,” supplies the biography the canon withholds: “his name before was Jobab ,” he “dwelt in the land of Ausis” (Uz) “on the borders of Idumea and Arabia,” he married an Arabian wife, and he was “the son of his father Zare, one of the sons of Esau… so that he was the fifth from Abraam.” The appendix then reproduces the Edomite king-list of Genesis 36:31–35 and slots the her…

tl.w: The Testament of Job — Job the patient king who battles Satan (c. 1st century BC–1st century AD)
tl.t: The next reader to take up Job did far more than place him: he rewrote the whole story. The Testament of Job , a Greek Jewish work of the turn of the era, is cast as the dying Job’s deathbed address to his children, and it presupposes the Septuagint’s reading — Job says outright, “before the Lord had named me Job, I was called Jobab… I am of the sons of Esau,” living in the land of Ausitis (Uz). Onto that frame it builds three developments the canonical book never made. First, Job is a king and an anti-idolatry hero: puzzling over the idol his people worship, he is told by an angel that it belongs to Satan and that to destroy it means war — and he does it anyway (“I rose up in the night and …

tl.w: The rabbinic debate (b. Bava Batra 14b–16b) — did Job exist? when did he live? (opinions c. 2nd–4th century, redacted c. AD 500)
tl.t: Where the Greek and the Testament answered the open questions, the rabbis of the Talmud reopened them all. The long discussion of Job at the foot of tractate Bava Batra is the classic Jewish reckoning with the man of Uz, and it is remarkable chiefly for how little it settles. Its most famous line denies Job’s existence outright: a sage sitting before Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani declared that “Job never existed and was never created… his story was a parable,” and, pressed, likened the opening “there was a man in the land of Uz” to the “two men in one city” of Nathan’s parable to David ( 2 Samuel 12:3 ). The Gemara answers that Job’s verse, unlike Nathan’s, gives a name and a homeland — “Rather, …

tl.w: Tertullian — Job the “hero” and instrument of God’s victory, the pattern of patience (c. 200)
tl.t: The first Christian to enroll Job on this timeline does so not to place him but to praise him. In the closing chapter of his treatise On Patience , the Latin apologist Tertullian holds up the man of Uz — unnamed but unmistakable — as the supreme human example of endurance kept “as well in spirit as in flesh, as well in mind as in body”: a “hero” whom “neither the driving away of his cattle… nor the sweeping away of his children… nor… the agony of his own body” could estrange “from the patience and the faith which he had plighted to the Lord.” Tertullian frames the ordeal as a Roman triumph over the devil — “What a bier for the devil did God erect in the person of that hero!” — with Job answe…

tl.w: Origen of Alexandria — Job the athlete who wrestles the devil (c. 245)
tl.t: With the Christian commentators the questions of land and lineage largely drop away and the drama of Job’s endurance takes their place — and it is Origen, the earliest reader on this timeline, who sets the pattern. He reads Job’s cry for a hearing as the shout of a wrestler mid-bout — “I cried out like an athlete in the stadium… if I do not bring my fight to a close, I will not get my crown” — and, on the whirlwind speeches, re-voices the heavenly wager as words God speaks back to the victorious sufferer: “A slanderer conspired against you… But, on the contrary, you were victorious.” The ordeal purifies rather than merely punishes, refining Job “like gold… in a melting pot.” It is the first …

tl.w: Ephrem the Syrian — the man of Uz who lived 248 years, a type of Christ (c. 370)
tl.t: The Syriac tradition’s earliest sustained reading, transmitted under Ephrem’s name, does what neither the Greek nor the Talmud had: it puts a number on the ageless hero. Reading the doubled restoration as a doubling of Job’s remaining years, it reckons his life at 248 years — a Peshitta computation that fits the patriarchal longevity the Septuagint appendix had presupposed. It takes Job as a real man of Uz whom the devil, “convinced by the evidence of the facts,” could “never [bring] to blasphemy,” and — most consequentially — reads the blameless sufferer as a type of the sinless suffering Christ, whose “Redeemer lives” is prophecy of “the future manifestation of Emmanuel in the flesh.” (The…

tl.w: Didymus the Blind — the “marked pillar” of perseverance (c. 377)
tl.t: Didymus, head of the Alexandrian school, reads Job in the spiritual key of his city: the man is deliberately set before “his contemporaries and his successors” as an “image of perseverance—like a marked pillar,” an athlete who “prays that he himself may win the crown in the competition.” The Satan, meanwhile, can strike only within bounds — “no one is tempted without God’s permission… given [only] with restrictions” — so that Job’s ordeal is a permitted, purposeful testing rather than fate or accident. His recovered commentary (lost until the 1941 Tura papyrus find) says nothing of Job’s place or era, but hands the Alexandrian athlete-of-endurance Job on intact. 12 Full text and context →

tl.w: Ambrose of Milan — Job the “good athlete” whose bold complaint keeps faith (c. 388)
tl.t: The Latin West’s great bishop gives Job a whole treatise. His four-book The Prayer of Job and David ( De interpellatione Iob et David ) pairs Job with David as the two saints who show how a righteous man may plead with God under undeserved affliction — taking as its problem the oldest scandal of faith, that “the unjust prosper… and the just [are] frequently afflicted in this world.” Ambrose answers it by reading Job as “a good athlete” and “champion of Christ” permitted to be tested “so that … he could become more glorious and reach the crown through trials,” and — his distinctive move — by taking Job’s bold complaint itself as righteous speech, not a lapse from patience: even while “he felt…

tl.w: John Chrysostom — the patient sufferer, and the wife as the devil’s tool (c. 390)
tl.t: Chrysostom’s running Commentary on Job gives the tradition its fullest pastoral portrait. Job’s mourning is “not… a defeat” but “a sign of victory,” a wisdom that never speaks “a single inappropriate word”; the devil, permitted to test him, unwittingly “bore witness to him from above… without realizing what he was doing”; and Job’s wife, urging him to curse God, is the devil’s own instrument — “when indeed the wife of Job speaks, a Devil is at work.” Chrysostom reads Job as a righteous man who lived before the Law, offering sacrifice as his own priest, and who even “knew the doctrine of resurrection.” He is the great witness to the moral Job — the patient sufferer whom James had already made…

tl.w: Julian of Eclanum — the literal, historical Job (c. 425)
tl.t: Against the allegorists stands Julian, the exiled Pelagian bishop, who reads Job in the literal, historical manner of the Antiochene school he drew on. Job and his friends are real men in a real dispute, argued “according to the rules of debating”; the wager is the devil’s calculated escalation to test “Job’s own person”; and even the monstrous verses are kept first to “the faithful understanding of the story” (Job’s “giants” are merely “wild beasts”) before any spiritual sense is allowed. Julian offers no Christ-typology of Job at all — the exact counter-position to the Syriac reading and to the christological Moralia Gregory the Great would build; that refusal to allegorize is itself his c…

tl.w: The later Greek homilists and catenists — Hesychius of Jerusalem and Olympiodorus (c. 430–515)
tl.t: Two later Greek readers carry the patient-athlete Job into the fifth and sixth centuries. Hesychius of Jerusalem (c. 430), in his Homilies on Job , casts Satan as “the betrayer” defeated in single combat who, “after ripping Job’s body with his blows, as a last… resource… leads his wife against Job,” while Job’s pains only “made him appear to be a powerful fighter… deserv[ing] crowns and happiness” — and he reads Job’s “his brothers did not believe in him” prophetically of Christ. 16 The Alexandrian deacon Olympiodorus (c. 515), in his catena commentary, notes in passing that Job “also was a king before” his crown was taken, and reads Behemoth and Leviathan as the devil whom Christ defeats — …

tl.w: Gregory the Great — the Moralia in Job : Job as type of Christ and of the Church (c. 590)
tl.t: The Latin West’s reading of Job is settled, for a thousand years, by one enormous book. Gregory’s Moralia in Job — thirty-five books begun as spoken conferences to his monks at Constantinople and finished after he became pope (c. 578–595) — is the single most influential patristic treatment of the man of Uz and the fountainhead of medieval moral theology. Gregory expounds the book in three senses at once, “first historically, then in an allegorical, and lastly in a moral sense”: he keeps Job a real man, a Gentile saint holy in a heathen land (“who knows not that Uz is a land of the Gentiles?… he was good among bad men”), and upon that history builds his allegory. Its two governing moves fix …

tl.w: Ishodad of Merv — the Antiochene critical reading: a poem, before the Law (c. 850)
tl.t: The East Syriac bishop Ishodad preserves the rationalizing reading of “the Interpreter” (Theodore of Mopsuestia), and in doing so brings the timeline’s contested questions back to the surface among Christians. Job “lived before the law,” known to God by nature; the book may be a poetic composition whose author “reported many statements in the name of Job, of his friends and in the name of God himself that are not appropriate to them,” as against those “who assert that this book was written by the divine Moses”; and the heavenly council where Satan speaks “never took place in reality” but is “reported in a narrative style for the edification of the listeners.” Here the Christian East stages t…

tl.w: Modern scholarship (a survey) — date, provenance, and the folktale-frame / poetic-core question
tl.t: Set against the ancient witnesses, critical study grades the whole Job tradition, and four results recur. First, the composition : the book is widely read as joining an old prose folktale frame (the wager and the losses, Job 1–2 ; the rebuke of the friends and the doubled restoration, 42:7–17 — the patient Job of legend, already proverbial by Ezekiel 14 ) to a later, more radical poetic core , the dialogues in which an impatient, protesting Job arraigns God — with the Elihu speeches (chs. 32–37) often taken as a still-later insertion. This is the literary counterpart to the ancient historicity debate: a real man of legend versus a poet’s parable of protest. Second, the date of the book : pro…

ar.q: Was Job a historical man, or the hero of a didactic parable?
ar.c: The book of Job presents its hero with the flat assurance of history — “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright” ( Job 1:1 ) — and then tells of him things that read like anything but a chronicle: a wager struck in the LORD’s court with “the Satan,” losses tallied in round thousands, and a restoration that returns exactly double. His earliest readers felt the strain at once. The Greek translators and the Septuagint appendix tried to place him — a great-grandson of Esau, Jobab king of Edom — while the rabbis of Bava Batra reopened the prior qu…
ar.a: Contested. The historical/parable question genuinely resists resolution to either pole, and has since its earliest readers staged it: strong by the received tradition’s lights (the book names a man and a land, James treats him as a real example, the Fathers and the rabbinic majority assume he lived) and strong by the critical reading’s (the schematic doubled numbers, the staged heavenly wager, the wisdom-dialogue genre, the legendary company of N…

ar.q: Is Job the same man as Jobab, king of Edom?
ar.c: The Hebrew book of Job gives its hero a name and a homeland but no genealogy, no era, and no royal office: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job” ( Job 1:1 ). The Greek translators filled all of that in at a stroke. Where the Hebrew closes at Job’s death, the Old Greek adds a paragraph — conventionally Job 42:17a–e — that names his former name as Jobab , sets his home “on the borders of Idumea and Arabia,” runs his line back through Esau to Abraham, and slots him into the Edomite king-list of Genesis 36:31–35 as Bela’s successor: “after Balac, Jobab, who is called Job .” In th…
ar.a: Weak. On its best available case the identification of Job with Jobab king of Edom does not hold as a claim about one historical man. Its supports are two, and both give way: the Greek near-homonymy Iōb / Iōbab dissolves in Hebrew, where ’ Iyyob and Yobab are different names from different roots; and the only text that asserts the equation is the Septuagint appendix , a paragraph absent from the Hebrew (and from the Peshitta and the Job Targums) …

ar.q: Where was the land of Uz? Edom, the Hauran, or north Arabia?
ar.c: Unlike Job’s era , which the book leaves wholly open, his place is named in the first verse — “There was a man in the land of Uz” ( Job 1:1 ) — and then never explained. Uz is a real toponym, but the Bible attaches the name to more than one line and more than one region, and the book of Job adds only atmospheric clues: Job is “the greatest of all the men of the east” ( Job 1:3 ), raided by Sabeans from the south and Chaldeans from the north-east ( Job 1:15 , 17 ), and surrounded by neighbours from Teman, Shuah, and Naamah ( Job 2:11 ). From these the tradition drew three broad answers. The sou…
ar.a: Contested. Where the land of Uz lay is genuinely disputed, but the dispute has a clear favourite: the southern, Edomite locale — Edom and the desert border it shares with north Arabia. The decisive evidence is scriptural and points one way: Lamentations sets the “daughter of Edom” dwelling “in the land of Uz” ( Lamentations 4:21 ), and Job’s friend Eliphaz is a Temanite ( Job 2:11 ) from an Edomite district proverbial for wisdom ( Jeremiah 49:7 ;…

ar.q: When did Job live? The patriarchal age, the days of Moses, or later?
ar.c: The book of Job places its hero with great care in space — “a man in the land of Uz” ( Job 1:1 ) — and with none at all in time . It names no king, no dynasty, no war, no covenant, nothing that would peg him to a reign; and this silence is exactly what the later tradition tried to fill. Three broad answers were given. The oldest and most widely held sets Job in the patriarchal age , the world of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (or just before), inferred from the book’s own archaic-looking details. A rabbinic strand instead placed him in the days of Moses — or, in a variant, the generation of the spi…
ar.a: Plausible. The patriarchal-age placement is the best-supported reading of the book’s own evidence and is probable as to milieu: the “hundred and forty years” and the doubled-lifespan computation, the family-priest sacrifice with no Levitical cult, the flock-wealth and the archaic qesitah , and the complete absence of Israel, the Exodus, Sinai, and the Temple all converge on a pre-Mosaic, patriarchal world, and that convergence — recognized by the…

ds.t: Justification
ds.q: Justification is the doctrine of how a sinner is set right with God — the question the Reformation split the Western Church over. All sides agree it is by grace and turns on Christ; they divide on two axes. The first is what justification is : a forensic act in which God declares the believer righteous, crediting (“imputing”) to him the righteousness of Christ received by faith, a verdict kept distinct from the moral renewal (sanctification) that follows (the Protestant reading); or a transformative one in which God makes the sinner inwardly righteous, infusing grace and charity so that he is really, not merely reckoned, just — a righteousness then increased through grace-enabled good works …

tl.t: Clement of Rome , writing to Corinth, states the seed of the later doctrine in the plainest form: “we, too, being called by His will in Christ Jesus, are not justified by ourselves , nor by our own wisdom, or understanding, or godliness, or works which we have wrought in holiness of heart; but by that faith through which, from the beginning, Almighty God has justified all men.” The chapter’s own heading — “We are justified not by our own works, but by faith” — makes the emphasis unmistakable; yet the very next chapter urges good works, so Clement holds both without the later systematic tension. 1

tl.w: John Chrysostom — faith opens the door “to the world” (c. 391)
tl.t: John Chrysostom , preaching through Romans, reads 3:28 (“a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the Law”) as Paul’s deliberate universalizing move: “he does not say, a Jew, or one under the Law, but after leading forth his discourse into a large room, and opening the doors of faith to the world, he says ‘a man,’ the name common to our race.” For Chrysostom faith is what admits Gentile and Jew alike; the Greek fathers preach justification by faith warmly, without dividing it from the transformation of the believer. 2

tl.w: Augustine against Pelagius — justified “freely by His grace” (c. 412–427)
tl.t: Augustine , forced by the Pelagian crisis to define grace, insists that no one is justified by law or by his own will: “they are justified freely by His grace” — and “in Him only is the ungodly man justified,” to whom “on believing… faith is reckoned for righteousness.” Yet Augustine’s “justify” already means to make righteous ( iustum facere ), an inward healing wrought by the love God pours into the heart; and his principle that God, rewarding the saints, “crowns His own gifts, not your merits,” is quoted by both later camps. He is the father each side claims — sola gratia to the Reformers, infused righteousness to Trent. 3 4

The founding Lutheran confession states the Reformation thesis: men “cannot be justified before God by their own strength, merits, or works, but are freely justified for Christ’s sake, through faith , when they believe that they are received into favor, and that their sins are forgiven for Christ’s sake… This faith God imputes for righteousness in His sight.” Justification is here a received verdict — forgiveness and imputed righteousness grasped by faith — not a quality infused. 5

tl.w: The Council of Trent, Session VI (1547)
tl.t: Trent answered with the Catholic definition and its anathemas. Justification is “not remission of sins merely, but also the sanctification and renewal of the inward man , through the voluntary reception of the grace and of the gifts, whereby man of unjust becomes just” (Ch. VII) — a real infusion, increased by good works, which “truly merit” eternal life (Ch. XVI). Its canons condemn the Protestant reading by name: anathema on any who says “that by faith alone the impious is justified” (can. 9), or justified “by the sole imputation of the justice of Christ… to the exclusion of the grace and the charity” poured into the heart (can. 11), or that justifying faith is mere “confidence in the divi…

Against Trent the Reformed confessions sharpened imputation into a defining doctrine. The Church of England’s Thirty-Nine Articles , Article XI, hold “we are accounted righteous before God, only for the merit of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ by Faith, and not for our own works or deservings… that we are justified by Faith only, is a most wholesome Doctrine.” The Westminster Confession (XI.1) makes the forensic point explicit against infusion: God justifies “ not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous … by imputing the obedience and satisfaction of Christ unto them, they receiving and resting on him… by …

tl.w: The Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999)
tl.t: Four and a half centuries later the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church signed, at Augsburg, a Joint Declaration claiming “a consensus on basic truths of the doctrine of justification”: “By grace alone, in faith in Christ’s saving work and not because of any merit on our part, we are accepted by God and receive the Holy Spirit, who renews our hearts while equipping and calling us to good works” (§15). On its own account “the corresponding doctrinal condemnations of the sixteenth century do not apply to today’s partner” — a contested claim to have dissolved the old anathemas by distinguishing the senses in which each side meant them, not by either side reversing its confession. …

ar.q: Is justification an imputed, forensic righteousness?
ar.c: “Those whom God effectually calleth, he also freely justifieth: not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous; not for anything wrought in them, or done by them, but for Christ’s sake alone; nor by imputing faith itself, the act of believing, or any other evangelical obedience to them, as their righteousness; but by imputing the obedience and satisfaction of Christ unto them, they receiving and resting on him and his righteousness by faith.” — Westminster Confession of Faith XI.1 (1646), the-highway.com . 1 The …
ar.a: Contested. The forensic-and-imputation reading is not a mere polemical construct: the law-court sense of “justify,” the reckoning verbs of Romans 4, the crediting of righteousness to the ungodly apart from works, and the exchange of 2 Corinthians 5:21 give it a real and defensible base in Paul. What it cannot claim is a clean sweep: Paul’s “made righteous” language and the “charity poured forth” feed the rival infusion reading ; the crisp justifi…

ar.q: Is justification an infused, transformative righteousness?
ar.c: “Justification… is not only a remission of sins, but also the sanctification and renewal of the inward man, through the voluntary reception of the grace and of the gifts, whereby man of unjust becomes just, and of an enemy a friend, that so he may be an heir according to hope of life everlasting.” — Council of Trent, Session VI (1547), Decree on Justification, Chapter VII , papalencyclicals.net . 1 The advocated interpretation: to justify is to make just. The grace of justification is a real quality infused into the soul — the “charity… poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Ghost” (Rom 5:5) —…
ar.a: Contested. The infusion reading has the stronger claim on Paul’s “made righteous” and “charity poured forth” language, on the renewal texts, and on the pre-Reformation concept of justification, which the fathers did not sever from the healing of the person. What it must concede is the forensic grain the rival reading presses: “justify” is court-language, Romans 4 credits righteousness to the ungodly apart from works and against debt, and Trent’s …

ar.q: Does James 2:24 (“not by faith only”) overturn justification by faith alone?
ar.c: “Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only.” (Jas 2:24) “Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.” (Jas 2:17) — The Epistle of James , James 2:24 , 2:17 . 1 The advocated interpretation: Scripture itself, in the only verse that names “faith only,” teaches that a man is not justified by faith only but also by works — so the Reformation’s sola fide is contradicted at its own key phrase, and justification cannot be by faith to the exclusion of works.
ar.a: Contested. James 2:24 is the one verse that uses “faith only,” and it denies it, so it genuinely refutes a bare-assent sola fide and rightly qualifies every version of the doctrine — the Reformers themselves conceded that the justifying faith is never workless. But it does not overturn the considered Protestant reading, because James and Paul demonstrably use “faith,” “works,” and “justify” in different senses (living versus dead faith; ground ve…

ar.q: Does Romans 3:28 teach justification by faith alone — and was Luther right to add “alone”?
ar.c: “So halten wir nun, dass der Mensch gerecht werde ohne des Gesetzes Werke, allein durch den Glauben.” (“So we hold that a man is justified without the works of the law, alone through faith.”) — Martin Luther , rendering Romans 3:28 in his German New Testament (1522). Luther defended the added word in his Open Letter on Translating ( Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen , 1530), conceding that “the word solum is not in the Latin or Greek text,” but arguing that “the text itself and the meaning of St. Paul demand and require it forcefully,” as idiomatic German for an exclusive sense. 1 The advocated interp…
ar.a: Contested. Split the claim and each half is clear. That Romans 3:28 excludes the works of the law from the ground of justification is Paul’s own, stated and repeated — that core is sound, and the “faith alone” way of expressing it has real patristic precedent. But the stronger claim — that the verse by itself establishes the whole Reformation sola fide , and that Luther’s inserted “alone” is simply Paul’s meaning — remains genuinely disputed: the…

ds.t: The Lemba of southern Africa: a lost tribe with a genetic signal?
ds.q: The Lemba (Vhalemba, and by their own names Mwenye / Vamwenye , Basena , or vaRemba ) are a Bantu-speaking people scattered across Zimbabwe, the Limpopo and Venda regions of South Africa, Mozambique, and Malawi — perhaps fifty to eighty thousand in all — who hold a tradition of ancient Israelite or Jewish descent . They recite a migration out of a northern city called Sena (“We left Sena, we crossed Pusela, we came to Africa and there we rebuilt Sena”), and they keep a cluster of observances that struck every outside observer as Judaic: strict endogamy , refusal to eat with or take food from non-Lemba (the likely sense of vaRemba , “the people who refuse”), male circumcision , avoidance of p…

tl.w: The oral tradition and its first writing-down (1940)
tl.t: The Lemba story was purely oral until the twentieth century. Its earliest sustained transcription is a chapter, “Ngoma-lungundu and the Early Invaders of Venda,” contributed by the Lemba writer M. F. Mamadi to N. J. van Warmelo’s Ethnological Publications No. 8 (Pretoria, 1940 ). It sets down the migration formula (“We left Sena… we rebuilt Sena”), the crossing of the unlocated Pusela , the food and marriage rules, the twelve clans under the Buba, and the wanderings of the ngoma lungundu , “the drum that thunders” — too holy to touch the ground, borne on poles, and said to have gone before the people to show them where to camp and to strike down their enemies. The variety of glosses the Lemb…

tl.w: Tudor Parfitt goes to find Sena (1992)
tl.t: The claim moved from folklore to a testable hypothesis through the British historian Tudor Parfitt of SOAS, later “the British Indiana Jones.” Commissioned by the Lemba leader Professor M. E. R. Mathivha — president of the Lemba Cultural Association, who that same year privately published The Basena/Vamwenye/Balemba to consolidate the scattered clans into a single Jewish “nation” — to “go and find Sena,” Parfitt retraced the migration route and, while working among the Jews of Yemen, located the ruins of a town actually named Sena in the eastern Wadi Hadramaut, whose irrigation system failed around the tenth or eleventh century. His Journey to the Vanished City: The Search for a Lost Tribe o…

tl.w: Spurdle and Jenkins: the first Y-chromosome evidence (1996)
tl.t: The first genetic test came from Amanda Spurdle and Trefor Jenkins of the University of the Witwatersrand: “The origins of the Lemba ‘Black Jews’ of southern Africa,” American Journal of Human Genetics 59 (1996). Reading Y-chromosome markers (YAP, p12F2, p49a/TaqI), they found that a substantial share of Lemba paternal lines — on their reckoning more than half , against about forty per cent of clearly sub-Saharan African origin — carried a Semitic (Middle-Eastern) signature, a strong result for a real male-line contribution from the north. But at that resolution the marker could not tell Jewish from other Semitic ancestry: it established a Middle-Eastern input, not a Jewish one. 4

tl.w: Thomas, Parfitt, et al.: the Cohen Modal Haplotype and the Buba clan (2000)
tl.t: The high-water mark for the Jewish reading is Mark Thomas, Tudor Parfitt, Karl Skorecki, Neil Bradman, David Goldstein, and colleagues, “Y Chromosomes Travelling South: The Cohen Modal Haplotype and the Origins of the Lemba,” American Journal of Human Genetics 66 (2000): 674–686. Analysing 399 Y chromosomes at higher resolution, they reported the Cohen Modal Haplotype (CMH) — a six-marker profile then thought distinctive of the Jewish priestly line — in 8.8 per cent of all Lemba Y chromosomes, and, strikingly, in seven of the thirteen men of the priestly Buba clan (about 54 per cent), a concentration “significantly associated” with Buba membership. Two-thirds of Lemba Y chromosomes (67.6 per…

tl.w: Parfitt’s myth-history and le Roux’s fieldwork (2002–2003)
tl.t: Parfitt then supplied his own critical counterweight in The Lost Tribes of Israel: The History of a Myth (London: Weidenfeld & Nicolson, 2002), a source-critical study arguing that “lost tribe” identifications are, across history, largely constructed myths — a caution he turned on the Lemba themselves. The fullest fieldwork is Magdel le Roux ’s The Lemba: A Lost Tribe of Israel in Southern Africa? (Pretoria: UNISA Press, 2003), which keeps the title a question: le Roux documents the customs at first hand (including a new-moon ceremony she found paralleled nowhere else), traces the “merchants of Sena” to the Sabaean and Swahili trade world, and concludes the Lemba’s Jewishness is culturally r…

tl.w: Parfitt and Egorova: genetics, media, and identity (2005–2006)
tl.t: The historian Tudor Parfitt and anthropologist Yulia Egorova made the Lemba one of two case studies (with the Indian Bene Israel ) in Genetics, Mass Media and Identity (Routledge, 2006), following a 2005 journal treatment. Their argument is that the DNA studies did not simply “confirm” an origin legend; rather, the way the results were portrayed in the mass media — received as “irreproachably objective” hard science — reshaped how the Lemba understood themselves and how outsiders saw them. It is the same critical frame this wiki reaches for with the Anglo-Saxon and Japanese versions elsewhere in this family: a reminder that a genetic headline is a social event as much as a scientific one. 7

tl.w: Parfitt and the ngoma lungundu as the Ark (2008)
tl.t: In The Lost Ark of the Covenant (New York: HarperOne, 2008) Parfitt pressed the boldest form of the claim: that the biblical Ark was essentially a drum-like ritual object and that the Lemba ngoma lungundu is its descendant — “the dwelling place of God, carried on poles, forbidden to touch the ground and connected with death, fire, smoke and noise.” The surviving drum, which Parfitt rediscovered in a Harare museum storeroom, radiocarbon-dates to about AD 1350; he reconciled this with Lemba lore that the original had exploded and been remade (“the son of the original”). The thesis drew sharp skepticism — the Zimbabwean historian Rob Burrett noting that wooden drums are integral to African cult…

tl.w: Tofanelli and Hammer: the CMH loses its Jewish specificity (2009)
tl.t: The evidential picture shifted when the marker itself was re-examined. Sergio Tofanelli and colleagues, “J1-M267 Y lineage marks climate-driven pre-historical human displacements,” European Journal of Human Genetics 17 (2009), found that the short Y-STR motifs “previously used to trace Arab or Jewish ancestries” were “unsuitable as diagnostic markers for ethnicity” — the original six-marker CMH recurs broadly across the Middle East, its spread tracking the diffusion of Islam as much as anything Jewish. In the same year Michael Hammer and colleagues, “Extended Y chromosome haplotypes resolve multiple and unique lineages of the Jewish priesthood,” Human Genetics 126 (2009), defined a far more …

tl.w: Soodyall: “Lemba origins revisited” — the signal does not survive higher resolution (2013)
tl.t: The file is brought up to date by a re-test with exactly that higher resolution. Himla Soodyall , “Lemba origins revisited: Tracing the ancestry of Y chromosomes in South African and Zimbabwean Lemba,” South African Medical Journal 103 (2013), found the original six-marker CMH in 13.2 per cent (10 of 76) of Lemba men — but the Jewish-specific extended CMH in none of them (“None of the 10 Lemba who were found to have the original CMH had the extended CMH”). Her conclusion: the study “does not support the earlier claims of their Jewish genetic heritage,” and the Lemba’s haplogroup-J chromosomes “are not closely associated with Jewish ancestry” — pointing instead toward Arab traders as the like…

ar.q: Are the Lemba an Arab-Muslim trader stock whose Semitic ancestry and customs were later reframed as Jewish?
ar.c: The Lemba are what the historians of the Zambezi already knew them to be: the descendants of the Muslim trader stratum — Hadrami Arabs and their Swahili partners — who ran the gold and ivory routes inland from the coast, took local wives, and over generations lost their Arabic and their Islam and became a Bantu-speaking people. Circumcision, pork-avoidance, ritual slaughter, endogamy and the Arabic-sounding clan-names are the residue of that Muslim past, not a lost Israelite exodus. The Jewish reading came later. — the Arab-Muslim substrate reading in its strongest form. It shares one premise …
ar.a: Plausible — and, of the two rival readings of the Lemba’s Semitic input, the more probable on current evidence. It rests on a documented population and trade mechanism, explains the customs, clan-names, and self-name without strain, and is favoured by the higher-resolution genetics that dismantled the Jewish-specific reading. It falls short of sound for two honest reasons: the “Judaic” observances are equally compatible with a Yemeni-Jewish sourc…

ar.q: Did the ancestral Lemba build Great Zimbabwe?
