xs.t: The biblical portrait (2 Kings 5, with Luke 4:27) The whole later tradition grows from a single chapter and one saying of Jesus that turns on it. 2 Kings 5 presents Naaman at the height of worldly honour and the depth of affliction at once — “captain of the host of the king of Syria… a great man with his master, and honourable… a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper.” The cure comes through the humblest link in the chain: “a little maid” carried captive out of Israel, waiting on Naaman’s wife, who wishes her master were “with the prophet that is in Samaria.” Sent at last to Elisha, Naaman is met not by the prophet but by a messenger with a bare instruction — “Go and wash in the Jordan se…

ds.t: Who Was Nebuchadnezzar?
ds.q: Nebuchadnezzar II is the great pagan world-emperor of the Hebrew Bible — the Babylonian king who burned Jerusalem and carried Judah into exile, and whom the book of Daniel makes the stage for a drama no other Gentile king receives: the master of the earth driven mad, sent out to eat grass like an ox, and brought back confessing the God of heaven. He enters Daniel as the terror before whom the wise men tremble, dreams the dream of the great image whose head of gold is his own kingdom, and on its interpretation confesses that Daniel’s God is “a God of gods, and a Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets” ( Daniel 2:47 ). When the three young men walk unburnt in his furnace he blesses their God…

tl.t: Everything the later tradition made of Nebuchadnezzar grows from two books read together. In Jeremiah he is the rod of God’s anger, and — astonishingly for a pagan destroyer of the Temple — God’s own servant : “I will send and take… Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant”; “I have given all these lands unto the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant” ( Jeremiah 25:9 ; 27:6 ). The prophet who watched him burn Jerusalem still names him the instrument by whom the LORD works his purpose — a title the Fathers would find as scandalous as it is exact. 1 In Daniel the same king becomes a stage for the God he does not know. He dreams the great image whose head of gold is his o…

tl.w: The Prayer of Nabonidus (4Q242, c. 2nd–1st century BC) — the same story told of a different king
tl.t: Among the Qumran scrolls is a short Aramaic text that reads like Daniel 4 with the names changed. In the Prayer of Nabonidus it is Nabonidus — the last king of Babylon, not Nebuchadnezzar — who “was stricken with an evil disease by the decree of God in Teiman” (Tayma, in Arabia) “for seven years,” who prayed uselessly to “gods of silver and gold, bronze, iron, wood, stone and clay,” and who was pardoned and healed after “a diviner — who was a Jew of the Exiles” told him to “give honour and greatness to the name of the God Most High.” The parallels are dense — a Babylonian king, a seven-year affliction, a Jewish adviser, a turn from idols to the Most High — and the setting fits history: Nabon…

tl.w: The Old Greek and Theodotion (the Greek editions of Daniel 4, c. 100 BC and later) — the confession expanded
tl.t: Daniel survives in two ancient Greek versions, and in chapter 4 they part company. For most of the book the Old Greek and the later Theodotion track a Semitic text near the Hebrew-Aramaic; but chapters 4–6 are the exception — there the Old Greek is a substantially different edition . Its best witness, papyrus 967, even sets chapters 7–8 between 4 and 5; the king’s confession and decree are moved to a greatly expanded form at the end of the chapter; and the Old Greek “expands on the hubris of the king,” adding notes of temple-desecration absent from the other texts. Where the tradition would later ask whether Nebuchadnezzar’s doxology was sincere, the oldest Greek edition had already heighten…

tl.w: Josephus ( Antiquities 10 and Against Apion 1, c. AD 93) — the great builder, and a silence
tl.t: The earliest datable treatment of Nebuchadnezzar after the Bible is also the most revealing for what it leaves out. Josephus retells Daniel at length — the dreams, the image, the furnace — but passes over the seven-year madness in silence, moving straight from the king’s dream-interpretations to his death and his monuments. What he adds instead is the external record: quoting the Babylonian priest-historian Berossus, he reports how Nebuchadnezzar walled Babylon three times about and raised “a pensile paradise” for his Median queen, and notes that “Megasthenes… endeavors to show that this king exceeded Hercules in fortitude.” He gives the reign its length — “when king Nebuchadnezzar had reign…

tl.w: Hippolytus of Rome ( Commentary on Daniel , c. AD 204) — the beast-king who confessed and was restored
tl.t: The earliest surviving Christian commentary on Daniel reads the madness and the recovery as a single lesson in humbling. Hippolytus paints the fall in full: “no longer did the great king and ruler live as a man… but being alone in the desert he ate grass and herbs until his heart was changed and became as a beast… his hair grew as a lion’s and his nails grew large as a bird’s.” And he reads the outcome as genuine repentance: Nebuchadnezzar, “having humbled himself and recognized that he is a man lying under the authority of God… after begging the Lord, obtained from him a good heart, and again his kingdom and glory were reestablished.” The whole ordeal was “an education for the king,” so tha…

tl.w: Ephrem the Syrian ( Commentary on Daniel , c. AD 363) — the ordeal that led him to repentance
tl.t: Ephrem frames the whole story as God’s patient work toward a genuine turn. The king’s boast on the palace terrace comes just when “God was patient and had shown magnanimity by endeavoring to lead him to repentance”; the madness is the mercy that finally reaches him. And Ephrem reads the doxology as real restored piety: “‘My reason returned to me’… I blessed the Most High, who does what he wills” — the God who rules “not only the affairs of human beings… but also those of the spiritual powers.” Through the punishment God “showed that he gives back to each one his properties with justice… and humiliates those who walk in arrogance.” For Ephrem the confession is the point the ordeal was for. 8 …

tl.w: John Chrysostom, with Cyprian and Augustine (homilies and treatises, c. AD 253–420) — the sins redeemed by almsgiving
tl.t: A whole stream of the reception fastened not on the madness but on Daniel’s counsel before it — “break off thy sins by almsdeeds, and thine iniquities by showing mercy to the poor” (Daniel 4:27) — and made Nebuchadnezzar the great proof that mercy to the poor cancels sin. Chrysostom marvels that “after countless sins, after so many transgressions, he is promised that he will be reconciled” if he will give alms, and that “nothing is so strong and powerful to extinguish the fire of our sins as almsgiving.” Cyprian had already drawn the same lesson — the king “suffered the misfortunes… which he might have escaped… if he had redeemed his sins by almsgiving” — and Augustine preached it too (“you …

tl.w: Jerome ( Commentary on Daniel and the letters, c. AD 407) — the doxology of a worldling, and the servant of God
tl.t: Jerome carries the whole figure into Latin, and he is the tradition’s sharpest skeptic of the king’s piety. He grants the historicity of the madness and restoration — defending it against Origenist readers who used it to argue that even the devil, “through repentance… restored to favor,” will one day be reinstated over the angels — but he doubts the doxology is devout: Nebuchadnezzar “expresses [it] like a worldling,” even seeming “to impugn God’s justice, on the ground that he had suffered unmerited punishment.” On Jeremiah he presses the other scandal — the pagan called God’s servant : “Miserable must those Israelites have been compared with whom Nebuchadnezzar was called God’s servant… if…

tl.w: Theodoret of Cyrus ( Commentary on Daniel , c. AD 433) — the reason lost, and grace restored
tl.t: Theodoret gives the fullest Greek reading of the chapter and lands, against Jerome, on a genuine restoration. The madness is a tailored justice: “in his wish to snatch heaven he was driven also from earth”; stripped of reason he “like a wild animal… kept frequenting uninhabited places, filling his stomach with the food of brute beasts.” And the recovery is grace: “thanks to divine grace he was recognized as the person who previously had administered the mighty kingdom.” Theodoret puts the closing praise in the king’s own grateful mouth — “I sing the praises of the one who to my advantage brought on me one condition and the other… capable of humbling those behaving haughtily.” 11 Full detail …

tl.w: The rabbinic tradition (Babylonian Talmud; traditions from c. AD 200, redacted by c. 500) — the blasphemer whose song outsang David
tl.t: Jewish tradition ran the other way from the Christian and made Nebuchadnezzar the arch-blasphemer: the disciple “of Nimrod the wicked,” the “king of Babylon” of Isaiah 14 who said “I will ascend above the heights… I will be like the Most High,” and was answered “yet thou shalt be brought down to hell.” And yet the very same tradition preserves the most extravagant estimate of his praise anywhere in the sources: had an angel not intervened, his doxology would have eclipsed the Psalter. “If an angel had not come and struck him on his mouth… he would have sought to overshadow all the songs and praises that David recited in the book of Psalms.” The blasphemer and the singer are held together — h…

ar.q: The ox-madness of Daniel 4 — a real malady, a legend, or a theological sign?
ar.c: he was driven from men, and did eat grass as oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, till his hairs were grown like eagles’ feathers, and his nails like birds’ claws. — Daniel 4:33 (KJV). The claim to be weighed: that this is not fantasy or mere legend but the description of a genuine, recognizable derangement — a man who believes himself an ox and behaves as one — suffered by the historical Nebuchadnezzar, and that the account is therefore credible history. 1
ar.a: Contested. The three readings are best kept distinct and rated separately, and they do not exclude one another. As a description of a real malady-type , the boanthropy reading is plausible — the condition exists and the symptoms fit, so the account is not incredible on its face. As a claim about a historically attested episode , it is contested , even weak: it is unattested outside Daniel, defended only by an argument from silence, and embedded i…

ar.q: Does Daniel 4 rework a tradition about Nabonidus? (The Prayer of Nabonidus, 4Q242)
ar.c: The words of the p[ra]yer which Nabonidus, king of [Ba]bylon, the great king, pray[ed when he was stricken] with an evil disease by the decree of G[o]d in Teiman. [I Nabonidus] was stricken with [an evil disease] for seven years… A diviner — who was a Jew o[f the Exiles — came to me and said:] ‘Recount and record (these things) in order to give honour and great[ness] to the name of the G[od Most High.’] — The Prayer of Nabonidus (4Q242), trans. F. M. Cross , link . The claim: the story Daniel 4 tells of Nebuchadnezzar — a Babylonian king humbled by God for seven years, brought to acknowledge t…
ar.a: Plausible (broad) / contested (narrow). That Daniel 4 is ultimately rooted in a Nabonidus tradition is well-grounded and close to consensus — the seven-year humbling, the Jewish adviser, the idol-renunciation, and the load-bearing Tayma setting converge on Nabonidus, whose decade in Arabia and whose son Belshazzar shape Daniel 4–5 alike. What the evidence does not establish is that Daniel copied this fragment : the differing king, the differing m…

ar.q: Was Nebuchadnezzar’s final confession a true conversion?
ar.c: And at the end of the days I Nebuchadnezzar lifted up mine eyes unto heaven, and mine understanding returned unto me, and I blessed the most High… Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and his ways judgment: and those that walk in pride he is able to abase. — Daniel 4:34–37 (KJV). The question adjudicated here is what the doxology amounts to : a genuine conversion — the proud king truly turning to the God of Israel — or an acknowledgment wrung from a broken man, real as far as it goes but short of saving faith. 1
ar.a: Contested. That the doxology is a real acknowledgment of God’s sovereignty is not in doubt; that it is a saving conversion is genuinely disputed, and the wiki declines to force it either way. The genuine-conversion reading rests on the plainest features of the scene — a public, self-abasing, doxological confession that crowns an arc of dawning acknowledgment — and it commands the whole reception, from Hippolytus, Ephrem, and Theodoret to the rabb…

ds.t: The Sons of God and the Nephilim (Genesis 6)
ds.q: Genesis 6:1–4 reports that the "sons of God" saw that the "daughters of men" were fair, took wives, and that the Nephilim — rendered giants ( gigantes ) by the Septuagint — "were on the earth in those days, and also afterward." Two questions divide its interpreters:

tl.t: 1 Enoch gives the fullest ancient form of the angelic reading: two hundred angels ("Watchers"), led by Semjaza, descended on Mount Hermon, took human wives, and "bare great giants," while teaching humanity sorcery, metallurgy, and astrology. 1 Critically, it teaches that when the giants die, "the spirits of the giants" become "evil spirits upon the earth" — the origin of demons. 7

The Septuagint , the Greek Torah of Alexandria and the version the New Testament quotes, renders the Nephilim as gígantes — "giants" — and, in many copies (so Augustine testifies), the "sons of God" as "angels of God." 2 As the earliest translational interpretation, it reads Genesis 6 as angelic beings begetting giants.

Sirach (the Wisdom of Ben Sira), reciting God's historic judgments on the proud, names "the old giants… who fell away in the strength of their foolishness," toward whom God "was not pacified" — a second deuterocanonical witness (with Wisdom ) to the destroyed giants of Genesis 6, and the compressed canonical echo of the Enochic scene in which the antediluvian rebels' plea for forgiveness is refused. 8

The Book of Giants , a distinct Enochic work preserved in as many as ten Aramaic copies among the Dead Sea Scrolls, retells the Genesis 6 event from the giants' own side: the offspring of the Watchers and human women, "giants and monsters" who "were seeking to devour many," troubled by dream-visions of the coming Flood, who send the giant Mahway to petition Enoch and are refused. 9 Uniquely, it names the Mesopotamian heroes Gilgamesh and Humbaba among the giants — the clearest Second Temple bridge between the Nephilim and the gods-and-kings of Babylonian tradition, a link Fr. Stephen De Young presses ("the Book of the Giants … identifies Gilgamesh as one of the Nephilim"). 10

Jubilees retells the same event: "the angels of God … took themselves wives … and they bare unto them sons and they were giants." God bound the angels in the depths of the earth and had their giant sons slay one another by the sword. 11 After the Flood, when the dead giants' spirits afflict mankind, the chief spirit Mastema wins God's leave for "the tenth part" to remain and torment the wicked — the 90% / 10% schema behind the Gospel demons' cry, "Have you come to torment us before the time ?" 12

Wisdom names "the proud giants" as those who perished in Noah's flood, 13 and traces idolatry to the deified dead — a dead man "honoured… as a god" with "ceremonies and sacrifices" — a cult that ran to child sacrifice and "secret ceremonies." 14 It is a Second Temple witness both to the giants of Genesis 6 and to the human-sacrifice cult that later interpreters (and Fr. Stephen De Young) attach to them.

Philo identifies the angels of Genesis 6 with the "souls" or "demons" that fill the air, and states plainly that "these giants were sprung from a combined procreation of two natures, namely, from angels and mortal women." 15 Yet he also reads the passage allegorically — men "born of earth," "of heaven," and "of God" — treating giant partly as a moral type of the earth-bound soul (Nimrod). 16

tl.w: The New Testament: Jude & 2 Peter (c. AD 60–90)
tl.t: The New Testament itself attests the angelic reading: Jude speaks of "the angels which kept not their first estate" reserved "in everlasting chains under darkness," and quotes Enoch, "the seventh from Adam," as a prophet; 17 2 Peter sets "the angels that sinned," cast into Tartarus, immediately beside Noah and the flood. 18 The earliest Fathers (Justin, Clement, Tertullian, Origen) read these texts as the Genesis 6 event. (1 Peter 3:19's "spirits in prison," which De Young also enlists, is read by every patristic commentator surveyed here as human — Christ's descent to the dead, or his preaching through Noah — yet much modern scholarship reads it as the imprisoned Watchers, as De Young does;…
Josephus records that "many angels of God accompanied with women, and begat sons that proved unjust," comparing them to the giants of Greek legend. 19

Justin holds that the angels appointed over humanity "were captivated by love of women, and begat children who are those that are called demons," who then enslaved the human race and were mistaken by the poets for gods. 20

Athenagoras , pleading the Christians' cause before Marcus Aurelius, reads Genesis 6 as angelic history: angels set over matter "fell into impure love of virgins," and "of these lovers of virgins … were begotten those who are called giants," whose souls are "the demons who wander about the world." 21

Irenaeus writes that "angels were united with the daughters of the race of mankind; and they bore to them sons who for their exceeding greatness were called giants," and that the angels brought "teachings of wickedness" — leading to the flood. 22 He also offers "Titan" as his leading candidate for the name of 666, tying the Antichrist to the Titan/giant tradition. 23
Clement refers to "the angels who … having sunk into pleasures, told to the women the secrets which had come to their knowledge" — the angelic reading, applied to the origin of forbidden arts. 24

Tertullian speaks of "those angels … who rushed from heaven on the daughters of men," who taught women metallurgy, the properties of herbs, enchantments, astrology, and cosmetics — and whom Christians "are destined to judge." 25 He further treats the Book of Enoch itself as inspired Scripture, defending its survival of the Flood through Noah — the earliest patristic answer to that objection, and (not Jerome, as is sometimes said) the real source of the argument. 25

Julius Africanus is the earliest writer to articulate the Sethite reading: the "sons of God" are "the descendants of Seth … on account of the righteous men and patriarchs," and the daughters are the line of Cain — though he records the angelic view as the alternative. 3

Commodian , in catechetical Latin verse, keeps the whole Enochic sequence: angels "sent down" despised God's laws, were turned by "the beauty of women," and "from their seed giants are said to have been born"; the giants taught the arts, and their dead spirits "now subvert many bodies" and are worshipped "as gods." 26

Origen groups the "sons of God" of Genesis 6 with the fallen beings who "left their own dwelling" and "did not preserve their own principality," reading the episode through the lens of angelic fall. 27

Lactantius , the first systematic Latin theologian, makes the fall the "fountain of errors" of paganism: God's guardian angels were "polluted … by intercourse with women" and "fell to the earth," and their offspring — "neither angels nor men, but bearing a kind of mixed nature" — became the earthly demons, "the authors of all the evils which are done." 28

Eusebius takes the giants born of "the angels of God" and the daughters of men to be daemons whose "spirits have been deified by the subsequent generations of men" — the pagan gods of Greek legend. 29
Ephrem holds the Sethite reading firmly: "[Moses] called the sons of Seth 'sons of God,' … The beautiful daughters of men … were the daughters of Cain." 30

Basil does not adjudicate the origin question but uses the giants morally, as types of prideful strength: "Such was the arrogance of the giants because of their strength. Such also was the God-defying pride of the witless Goliath." 31

Nemesius , commenting on the fall behind Genesis 6, holds that "of the incorporeal beings, only angels fell away, and not all of them, but some only, that inclined to things below" — an angelic framing. 32

Ambrose explicitly rejects the "children of the earth" reading of the poets and "asserts that they were generated from angels and women," the name giant expressing their bodily magnitude — though he draws a moral lesson about flesh over soul. 33

Chrysostom vigorously attacks the angelic reading as "blasphemy" and "the height of absurdity" — angels are nowhere called "sons of God," and being incorporeal they cannot marry — and identifies the sons of God as the descendants of Seth and Enosh. 34

Jerome reports that Aquila rendered the phrase "sons of gods," understanding "the Holy Ones or Angels," and judges that "it is fitting for the name of falling ones to apply to angels" — leaning to the angelic/Hebrew reading. 35 36

Augustine gives the decisive de-mythologized reading: the "sons of God" were "the sons of Seth" who "sunk into this community when they forsook righteousness," the giants were real but ordinary men, and the Enochic writings "about the giants, saying that their fathers were not men" are apocryphal "fables" without canonical authority. 4 He leaves open only whether some aerial spirits can assault women, while denying that God's holy angels fell this way. 37

Cassian follows the Sethite reading: the "seed of Seth … was by reason of its sanctity termed 'angels of God,' or … 'sons of God,'" the daughters were of Cain's line, and their offspring "were termed giants by reason of the size of their bodies and their cruelty." 38
Cyril reads the "sons of the gods" (Aquila) or "sons of the rulers" (Symmachus) as "the descendants of Seth and of Enosh … because of the piety and godliness which was in them." 39
Philoxenus assumes the Sethite reading, treating the episode as the conquest of "the children of Seth" by "the lust of the belly," for which "they were rejected from the household of God." 40

Bede transmits the Sethite reading to the medieval West: "sons of God" are the lineage of Seth, "men" the offspring of Cain; the giants were "men with immense bodies and excessive power," and he notes the Hebrew "fallen ones." 41 42

George Syncellus , a monk of Constantinople, transcribes long Greek extracts of 1 Enoch's "Book of the Watchers" into the antediluvian section of his universal chronicle, treating them as history: the angels ( Egregori ) descended in the days of Jared on Mount Hermon, took the daughters of men, and "bare … great Giants. Now the Giants begat the Naphilim ." 43 He is the latest pre-modern witness here to the angelic reading, and the conduit through whom both the Greek Enoch and Julius Africanus's Sethite fragment survive. (The "apostolic apocryphon" label sometimes attached to him is in fact De Young's gloss, which De Young himself credits to St. Nikephoros I — not Syncellus; its primary basis…

Bonaventure uses the passage typologically rather than to settle its identity: the sons of God taking the daughters of men, alongside Lamech's bigamy, prefigures the lawlessness that brings judgment and points to the Antichrist. 44

Aquinas holds the Sethite reading he inherits from Augustine — the "sons of God" are the line of Seth, and "they were not all giants" — yet he uniquely preserves the incubus tradition: demons do procure intercourse with women, but any offspring "is not the child of a demon, but of a man," begotten from human seed the demon transfers (a "two-source" logic oddly parallel to De Young's). 45 On 1 Peter 3:19 he reads the "spirits in prison" as human, preferring Augustine's "preached through Noah" reading. 46

Margaret Barker , a British Methodist Old-Testament scholar and founder of "Temple Theology," reads the "sons of God" of Genesis 6 as real fallen angels — the "fuller version" of the creation-and-fall story, of which Genesis preserves only a fragment — and identifies those fallen angels with the apostate priesthood ("the priests… were the angels in the temple"). Hers is a scholarly re -mythologizing of the angelic reading, not a symbolic one: contrary to a paraphrase sometimes attached to her (by Taylor Marshall ), she does not reduce the Nephilim to a metaphor for human wickedness, but insists the angel-beings are real and were edited out of the canonical text. 47

Michael S. Heiser (1963–2023), an Old-Testament and Semitic-languages scholar, is the modern source standing behind much of the angelic reading's revival — the "Divine Council" framework that De Young and Wilson both draw on. In The Unseen Realm (2015) and Reversing Hermon (2017) he holds that the "sons of God" are divine beings (not the line of Seth), the Nephilim their giant offspring (the word from Aramaic naphila , "giant," matching the Septuagint 's gígantes ), and the Babylonian apkallu sages the background of 1 Enoch's Watchers; he extends the theme to the post-flood giant clans (Rephaim, Anakim, Og of Bashan ) and reads the conquest of Canaan as a holy war against them. A supernatura…

tl.w: Fr. Stephen De Young (with Fr. Andrew Stephen Damick) (2018–2026)
tl.t: De Young argues for recovering the ancient supernatural reading: the Nephilim are the offspring of demonic spirits and human women, both giant and tyrannical, continuous with the Babylonian apkallu traditions preserved in 1 Enoch and the Book of the Giants . He extends the theme to the later "giant" tribes — the Rephaim (Og of Bashan), the Anakim, the Emim — and reads Israel's conquest as a war against demonic powers, fulfilled when David's men slew the last giants of Gath. 5 In the Lord of Spirits episode "Land of Giants" (with Fr. Andrew Stephen Damick) he adds the mechanism — a pagan sacral-kingship fertility ritual producing a child of "two fathers," so the objection that demons cannot i…

Dr. Taylor Marshall , a Roman-Catholic writer of a Thomist cast, is a third modern proponent of the angelic reading — distinct in confession from De Young (Orthodox) and Wilson (Reformed). He lays out the Enochic Watcher-legend sympathetically (the Watchers copulate with human women and beget the Nephilim), presses the New Testament's own use of it — Jude directly quotes 1 Enoch and 2 Peter borrows its word "Tartarus" — and reads the Wisdom of Solomon as already presupposing the giant-tradition ("the proud giants" perishing in the Flood, Wis 14:6). He does not build out a mechanism for the begetting; his contribution is to commend the angelic reading's antiquity while remaining reserved on i…

Doug Wilson , a Reformed/CREC pastor, is a second modern proponent of the angelic reading: the "sons of God" ( bene elohim ) are celestial beings — never the line of Seth — and the Nephilim their giant offspring (Gen 6:1–8). Against De Young's ritual mechanism he holds a literal-embodiment one — the angels "relinquished their celestial bodies" (Jude 6's habitation ; cf. 2 Cor 5:2) to take human wives — and reads 1 Peter 3:18–20 as Christ heralding victory (not offering the gospel) to those angels imprisoned in Tartarus, framing the Flood as judgment on a "genetic-engineering" / "being-as-God" rebellion of which modern bioethics is the continuation. (He overstates that the Sethite reading "do…

ar.q: 1 Peter 3:19 — the "spirits in prison"
ar.c: De Young enlists 1 Peter 3:19–20 — Christ "went and preached unto the spirits in prison; which sometime were disobedient … in the days of Noah" — as part of the New Testament's angelic chain, reading the "spirits in prison" as the imprisoned Watchers of Genesis 6 / 1 Enoch , alongside Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 ( tartaróō ). On this reading the "proclamation" is one of victory and judgment over the bound rebel powers, not an offer of salvation. This page weighs only the identity of the spirits; the content and purpose of the proclamation that follows from it — a herald of condemnation/victory vers…
ar.a: Contested , not simply weak. A weak leg by patristic-reception lights — no commentator in the database takes it as the Watchers — but a strong one by modern-critical lights, where the Watchers reading may be the majority. This is unlike Jude 6/14 and 2 Peter 2:4, which carry firm support in both eras (and stay on the NT timeline page without qualification). 1 Peter 3:19 is therefore flagged as contested rather than filed cleanly in the angelic co…

ar.q: 2 Peter's "Tartarus" (ταρταρόω) as a Greek/Titanomachy borrowing
ar.c: It's not only this direct quotation of 1 Enoch by Jude, but Jude (and 2 Peter) allude to the fantastical events of 1 Enoch, namely the sexual encounters of fallen angels with human women, which gives birth to the nephilim or "giants." — Taylor Marshall, Angels having Relations with Humans within Jude and 2 Peter and 1 Enoch (2018), taylormarshall.com , where he notes that 2 Peter 2:4 "explicitly uses Enoch's word 'Tartarus'" (the verb tartaróō ) for the imprisonment of the fallen angels. In the 2023 podcast he presses the point further: the word is not Hebrew or Aramaic but Greek — drawn from …
ar.a: Plausible. Marshall is right at the core, and more defensibly here than in his Maccabean-allegory reading: tartaróō really is a Greek Titan-word, and 2 Peter's choice of it over Jude's Enochic "chains and darkness" is a deliberate, audience-facing Hellenization — that much is sound , and it strengthens (not weakens) the case that 2 Peter 2:4 is about the Enochic Watchers. What outruns the evidence is the distinctive step that makes his version a …

ar.q: Og's cities Ashtaroth and Edrei as the seat of the Ugaritic Rapiu (KTU 1.108)
ar.c: Three times the Hebrew Bible plants Og — "the last of the Rephaim" — at a fixed pair of towns: "Og the king of Bashan, which dwelt at Ashtaroth and at Edrei " (Josh 12:4; cf. Deut 1:4; Josh 13:12). ar.a: Sound. Trust the core: KTU 1.108 hails Rapiu, King of Eternity — the divine eponym of the rpʾum / Rephaim — as the god enthroned at ʿṯtrt and hdrʿy , read as Ashtaroth and Edrei (Margulis 1970; del Olmo Lete; Mark S. Smith; Lindquist), Og's own two cities (Deut 1:4; Josh 12:4). The identification is the majority Ugaritological reading, it rests on an undisputed name-link ( rpʾu = the Rephaim) and an independent parallel (Milku seated at Ashtaroth…

ar.q: Does Augustine's case against the angelic reading hold?
ar.c: Augustine is the hinge of the whole timeline: with him the angelic reading of Genesis 6 gives way, for the Latin West, to the Sethite reading. So the live question is not just what he held but whether his case for the turn is good . Fr. Stephen De Young (with Fr. Andrew Stephen Damick) presses the broader thesis that the angelic reading was the original and the Sethite reading a later rationalization, and that the Fathers who turned against the "watchers" — Augustine above all — rejected a misunderstanding rather than the ancient claim. The cutting edge of that thesis, aimed at Augustine, is a…
ar.a: Sound. Augustine's case against the angelic reading is stronger than its sharpest modern critic allows and weaker than a decisive refutation. The "circular argument" charge identifies something real — Augustine does list the angelic-giant content among the marks of a spurious book, and the canon-status of 1 Enoch is genuinely entangled with the reading-history — but it overstates that kernel into a structural assessment the text will not bear: hi…

De Young's "mechanism" is therefore anchored in a genuine ANE institution, and his participatory logic answers the "spirits can't interbreed" objection on its own terms. The ancient form of the thesis in one breath: the Greek gods' wars are the antediluvian giants' remembered quarrels, the myth a distorted recollection of the real primeval history. The modern form sharpens it into a structural map — the Titans imprisoned in…

ar.q: Are the unclean spirits the spirits of the dead Nephilim?
ar.c: On this reading the demonic is not a single category. The "sons of God" (angelic beings) who transgressed in Genesis 6 are one order; their hybrid offspring, the Nephilim, are another; and when those giants died, their disembodied spirits — neither fully angelic nor ordinary human souls — remained on earth as the restless "unclean spirits" that afflict, possess, and are exorcised in the Gospels. The reading answers a real question (where do the Gospels' daimonia come from, and why are they bound to the earth and the tombs?) by importing the Second-Temple etiology of evil spirits. It is logical…

What keeps it from "sound" is that it is genuinely disputed and never settled: the New Testament does not assert the etiolo…

ar.q: The Watcher legend as a coded Maccabean anti-Hellenistic allegory
ar.c: In his 2023 podcast Marshall floats a reading of 1 Enoch's Watcher-and-Nephilim legend as a coded allegory of the Hellenistic crisis in Judea, produced (he says) "in the Maccabean period" and "likely" a Jewish appropriation — a "judaizing" — of the Greek Titanomachy (Zeus and the Olympians against the Titans). 1 He lays out a six-step historicizing map: Greek/Gentile invaders enter the Holy Land from 312 BC; the Greeks impose pagan customs on the Jews; Greek men marry and couple with Jewish women; producing "hybrid … Greek/Jewish children … considered monstrous" — the Nephilim; the need to dri…

What survives is a different, looser interpretation — an early-Hellenistic Jewish myth with anti-Hellenistic overtones (Nickelsburg's Diadochi-era theodicy) that borrows Greek mythic colors (Bremmer's Titan/Prometheus motifs) — and that…

The lone qualification is a matter of precision rather …

ds.t: Who Was Nimrod?
ds.q: Few names built on so few verses have grown so large as Nimrod. Scripture gives him only a genealogical notice — “Cush begat Nimrod: he began to be a mighty one in the earth. He was a mighty hunter before the LORD” — and adds that “the beginning of his kingdom was Babel, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar”, whence went forth the building of Nineveh and its sister cities ( Genesis 10:8–12 ). A prophet later calls Assyria “the land of Nimrod” ( Micah 5:6 ), and the Chronicler repeats his birth ( 1 Chronicles 1:10 ). That is the whole of the biblical Nimrod. Yet from this seed the tradition raised a towering figure: the first king and the first tyrant, the giant-hunter who …

tl.w: The biblical portrait (Genesis 10, Micah 5, and 1 Chronicles 1)
tl.t: The whole later tradition grows from a single genealogical notice in the Table of Nations. In Genesis 10:8–12 , among the sons of Cush son of Ham, “Cush begat Nimrod: he began to be a mighty one ( gibbor ) in the earth. He was a mighty hunter before the LORD: wherefore it is said, Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD.” The notice then makes him the first empire-builder: “the beginning of his kingdom was Babel, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar. Out of that land went forth Asshur, and builded Nineveh, and the city Rehoboth, and Calah, and Resen between Nineveh and Calah: the same is a great city.” So Scripture binds Nimrod to the two great powers of Mesopotam…

tl.w: Josephus — the tyrant who raised the Tower (c. AD 93)
tl.t: The first extra-biblical witness to give Nimrod a character is Josephus , whose Antiquities of the Jews (c. AD 93) fixes the villain-portrait the whole later tradition builds on. His Nimrod is “a bold man, and of great strength of hand” who taught the survivors of the Flood to trust their own courage rather than God, “gradually changed the government into tyranny,” and turned the people from the fear of God into a “constant dependence upon his power.” To this Josephus adds the move Genesis itself does not make: he names Nimrod as the instigator of the Tower of Babel and gives the building a defiant motive found nowhere in the text — Nimrod would “be revenged on God” for the Flood by raising …

tl.w: Theophilus of Antioch — the first Christian to name him, and no tyrant (c. 185)
tl.t: The earliest Christian notice of Nimrod comes from Theophilus of Antioch , whose apology Ad Autolycum (c. 185) narrates “the history after the flood” a generation after Josephus. Following the Table of Nations, he lists Nimrod (“Nebroth”) as king of the first cities of Shinar — Babylon, Erech, Accad, Calneh — and credits him with building Nineveh, Rehoboth, Calah, and Resen in the north, the Nimrod-subject reading of Genesis 10:11 that gives him the whole Mesopotamian sweep. Two things set his witness apart. He passes no moral verdict — Nimrod is simply the first king of the post-Flood cities, neither Josephus’s tyrant nor Ephrem’s blessed hunter, and the crux “a mighty hunter before the LOR…

tl.w: The Targums — the rebel written into the verse (c. 2nd–8th century)
tl.t: The Aramaic Targums read alongside the Hebrew in the synagogue split cleanly on the crux. The restrained Babylonian Onkelos keeps the neutral proverb — Nimrod merely “mighty” and “a mighty hunter before the Lord,” no rebellion implied — while the expansive Pseudo-Jonathan resolves the ambiguity against him inside the translation itself : Nimrod “began to be mighty in sin, and to rebel before the Lord,” a “mighty rebel” the like of whom “there hath not been… from the day that the world was created.” This is the earliest witness to make “ before the LORD” mean flatly “ against the LORD” in the wording of the verse, textualizing the midrashic pun that ties the name to Hebrew marad , “he rebelle…

tl.w: The rabbinic legend — the name, the garments, and the furnace of Ur (c. 3rd–13th century)
tl.t: Classical rabbinic tradition filled the villain out into a biography. His very name is read as an indictment — from marad , “because he caused the entire world to rebel against God during his reign” (b. Eruvin 53a) — and Nimrod is identified with the “Amraphel” of Genesis 14 , the arch-rebel whose “disciple in corruption” is Nebuchadnezzar (b. Pesachim 94b). Pirqe de-Rabbi Eliezer explains how a hunter became the first king: he inherited the coats of skin God made for Adam, at whose sight the beasts fell down before him — and he is the ringleader who proposed the Tower of Babel. 8 The most influential legend of all is his clash with Abraham. Reading “Ur of the Chaldees” ( Genesis 15:7 ) as “…

tl.w: The Pseudo-Clementine literature — Nimrod is Zoroaster, the first magus (c. 3rd–4th century)
tl.t: A wholly different strand runs alongside the Babel-tyrant tradition, and its fullest ancient statement is the Pseudo-Clementine literature — the fourth-century Christian romance fathered on Clement of Rome. Here Nimrod is not the builder of a tower but the founder of magic, star-worship, and idolatry . In the Greek Homilies (IX.4–6) the man is named “Nebrod” — the Septuagint’s spelling of Nimrod — and identified outright with Zoroaster : a giant who “chose, giant-like, to devise things in opposition to God,” a great magician who compelled a star to grant him sovereignty, was struck dead by the fire he had called down, and was then buried, given a temple among the Persians, and worshipped as …

tl.w: Ephrem the Syrian — the hero blessed “in the battles of the Lord” (c. 373)
tl.t: Against the villain-tradition stands the great Syriac exegete Ephrem the Syrian , the earliest voice on this timeline to give the favourable reading of the crux in full. In his Commentary on Genesis he takes “a mighty hunter before the Lord” as plain praise: Nimrod fought “according to the will of the Lord,” driving the scattered nations out to “the regions that had been set apart for them by God” — the executor of the God-decreed dispersal, not the ringleader of Babel. The proverb the Latins read as a byword for infamy, Ephrem reads as a genuine blessing : “One used to bless a chief or a ruler by saying, ‘May you be like Nimrod, a mighty hunter who was victorious in the battles of the Lord.…

tl.w: John Chrysostom — the birth of tyranny, moralized (c. 388)
tl.t: Preaching through Genesis at Antioch, John Chrysostom reads Nimrod as the moralist’s case-study in ambition. Nimrod “in imitation of his forebear did not take due advantage of his natural preeminence but hit upon another form of servitude in endeavoring to become ruler and king” — the very invention of domination , subjecting free people to one man’s power. The fault is not strength but strength “not keeping to its limits… constantly lusting after more and clutching for glory,” and the cities of his kingdom are raised “with a view to ruling over the enemy.” In the next homily Chrysostom widens the same vice into the diagnosis of Babel — the race that “always longs for more… and topples into …

tl.w: Jerome — the first tyrant and the hunter “never read favourably” (c. 391–392)
tl.t: At Bethlehem Jerome fixed the Latin villain-portrait and grounded it in the Hebrew. In the Hebrew Questions on Genesis Nimrod “first seized an unprecedented tyranny among the people” — the first tyrant. In the Commentary on Micah , on the prophet’s “land of Nimrod,” he loads the adversative reading onto the name and the trade: Nimrod means “descending temptation,” he is “the giant and hunter and one who proudly opposes the Lord,” fallen “like lightning from heaven.” His famous line seals the hunter-question for the Latin tradition: “As far as I can recall… I have never read favorably about a hunter” — pairing Nimrod with the two other biblical hunters, Ishmael and Esau , as a single type of …

tl.w: Augustine — Nimrod at the head of the earthly city (c. 420)
tl.t: The weightiest Latin reading is Augustine’s , in the City of God . Working through the Table of Nations and Babel as one movement, he makes Nimrod the emblem of the earthly city — the society founded on domination and pride, set against the pilgrim city of God traced through Shem to Abraham. Babylon, whose name means “Confusion,” is the head of that earthly city, and “we conclude that the giant Nimrod was its founder… its proud and impious founder,” the architect of the tower meant to “reach the sky.” On the crux Augustine is the earliest voice here to name the ambiguity by its Greek word — enantion “means both ‘before’ and ‘against’” — yet he names it only to close it: those who render “a m…

tl.w: Bede — the crux named, and Nimrod made a figure of the devil (c. 720)
tl.t: The Venerable Bede , in his Commentary on Genesis , gathers the whole adversative tradition into one synthesis and gives the timeline its most careful statement of the crux — the one Father to name the ambiguity by its Greek term. “Before the Lord,” he explains, renders enantion , from which “both can be interpreted”: it means “before the Lord who made us” in Psalm 95 but “against the Lord” in Job, and “another version has it that Nimrod was a giant hunter against the Lord.” Bede adopts the hostile reading — the phrase “was added to magnify the crime” of a tyrant who, “neglecting heavenly matters,” sought “lowly things” — while conceding, more honestly than most, that the grammar will bear e…

tl.w: The Latin Middle Ages — the proud giant-king, from Isidore’s encyclopedia to Dante’s hell (c. 7th–14th century)
tl.t: The tradition’s last pre-modern movement is consolidation : the Latin Middle Ages received the patristic Nimrod — the “against the Lord” giant-tyrant, founder of Babylon and its tower — and hardened him into a fixed type , the proud giant-king who authored Babel’s presumption. Isidore of Seville , in the Etymologies (c. 615–630), the reference work of the medieval West, compressed the Fathers to two dictionary sentences: “Nembroth is interpreted ‘tyrant.’ For he first seized an unaccustomed tyranny… and undertook, in impiety, to build a tower against God” (7.6.22), and “first after the flood, Nembroth the giant founded the city of Babylon” (15.1.4) — Jerome and Augustine welded into an entry…

tl.w: Modern scholarship — the name, the missing king, and the hardening of the legend
tl.t: The timeline closes with the critical grading of the whole tradition. Four results recur in modern study , and together they reorganize the question. First, the name : the marad (“rebel”) derivation that drives the villain-legend is a later Hebrew pun, and “Nimrod” is best explained from the Mesopotamian warrior-hunter god Ninurta — which fits both the “mighty hunter” epithet and the Assyrian geography. Second, the historical identity : no Nimrod is attested in any Mesopotamian record, and the mainstream reads him as a legendary composite , the strongest reconstruction (Yigal Levin) folding the memory of Sargon of Akkad and Naram-Sin into one figure, with Enmerkar, Tukulti-Ninurta I, Gilgame…

ar.q: “A mighty hunter before the LORD” — was Nimrod a hero blessed by God, or a rebel against Him?
ar.c: And Cush begat Nimrod: he began to be a mighty one in the earth. He was a mighty hunter before the LORD: wherefore it is said, Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD. — Genesis 10:8–9 (KJV). The whole question hangs on the twice-repeated phrase “a mighty hunter before the LORD ” (Hebrew lifnê YHWH , “before / in the face of the LORD”; Greek Septuagint enantíon Kyríou ). Read as “in the sight of, and so by the favour of” God, it praises Nimrod; read as “over against, in defiance of” God, it indicts him. Nothing else in the notice pronounces on his character, so the moral verdict of th…
ar.a: Contested. The question “hero or rebel?” is genuinely disputed and the text under-determines it. Each moral pole has real advocates and a real grip on the ambiguous lifnê YHWH / enantíon , and no feature of Genesis 10:9 breaks the tie: the favourable reading imports divine approval the idiom need not carry, while the adversative reading imports defiance the idiom need not carry — and the props that made the rebel-reading dominant (the marad pun, …

ar.q: Who was the historical Nimrod — Sargon of Akkad? Tukulti-Ninurta? Gilgamesh? Amenhotep III?
ar.c: Genesis introduces Nimrod not as a name in a “begat” list but as a person with a career: “he began to be a mighty one in the earth… a mighty hunter before the LORD,” whose kingdom began at Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh in Shinar, and out of whose land went the building of Nineveh and Calah ( Genesis 10:8–12 ). Because the notice reads like a scrap of remembered history — a first empire-builder spanning Babylonia and Assyria — a long line of scholars has asked which real Mesopotamian (or, in one fringe proposal, Egyptian) king it remembers. This page weighs that identification-thesis in its s…
ar.a: Contested. Whether a single historical ruler stands behind Nimrod is genuinely disputed, and no candidate is decisive: Levin’s Sargon–Naram-Sin composite is the strongest and has real scholarly backing, but it is itself a fusion of two kings, and the rival identifications (Enmerkar, Tukulti-Ninurta, the god Ninurta) each capture only a fragment while Gilgamesh and Amenhotep III fail. Beneath the contested identification lies a sounder , more mode…

ar.q: Did Nimrod build Babel and its Tower?
ar.c: The tradition makes Nimrod the architect of Babel and the ringleader of its tower — the tyrant who gathered mankind on the plain of Shinar, raised a tower “whose top may reach unto heaven,” and drew down the confusion of tongues. It is one of the two great things later readers said Nimrod founded (the other being astrology and idolatry ). Here the question is narrower than the moral one weighed elsewhere ( was he a hero or a rebel? ): not what kind of man Nimrod was, but whether the Babel-and-Tower episode is rightly attributed to him at all.
ar.a: Plausible. Taken as a whole — Nimrod as founder of Babel and builder of its tower — the interpretation is a coherent canonical synthesis, well short of certainty but well grounded in the shared city and plain and the flashback logic of Genesis 10–11. Its two halves are of unequal strength: that Nimrod founded the city Babel is asserted by the text (Genesis 10:10) and is effectively secure; that he personally raised or led the tower is a reasonabl…

ar.q: Did Nimrod found astrology, idolatry, and the pagan cultus?
ar.c: Alongside the tower (weighed separately ), the second great thing the tradition said Nimrod founded is the pagan religion itself — star-worship, magic, and the making of idols. In its strong form Nimrod is the first magician and the first false god: the giant who compelled the stars, was deified after death, and so began both astrology and idolatry, the root from which every later paganism grew. This is the strand behind the popular modern picture of Nimrod as the fountainhead of “Babylon mystery-religion” (the Two Babylons thesis is weighed on its own page); here the question is the older and…
ar.a: Weak. As a reading of a real tradition it is sound — the Pseudo-Clementines, the rabbinic idol-king, and the medieval chronicles genuinely make Nimrod the first magus, idolater, and astrologer, and the picture is internally coherent. But as an account of the actual origin of astrology or idolatry it does not hold: it has no basis in Scripture (which links Nimrod to empire, never to the stars or idols), its fullest form is a late patristic romance…

ar.q: The “Two Babylons” thesis: is Nimrod the hidden god behind every pagan religion — Tammuz, Ninus, the husband of Semiramis, the “Babylon mystery religion” smuggl…
ar.c: The thesis is Alexander Hislop’s, set out in The Two Babylons; or, The Papal Worship Proved to Be the Worship of Nimrod and His Wife — a pamphlet of 1853 expanded to a book in 1858, and revived in the twentieth century by Jack Chick, by Dave Hunt’s A Woman Rides the Beast , and across a wide field of anti-Catholic and King-James-only media. In its strong form it runs: Nimrod founded Babylon and its mystery-cult; on his death his widow Semiramis deified him and bore a son, Tammuz , whom she declared to be Nimrod reborn — so that Nimrod is also Tammuz, and the two are worshipped across the natio…
ar.a: Unsupported. The defensible kernel is real — Nimrod is tied to Babylon, ancient fertility cults did syncretize, and Revelation does call a great city Babylon — but the Hislop system built on it has no basis. Its keystone marriage of Nimrod and Semiramis is attested by no ancient source and is chronologically impossible (the historical Semiramis, Sammu-ramat, postdates any Nimrod horizon by more than a millennium); its equation of Nimrod with Tamm…

ds.t: Which text did the New Testament quote?
ds.q: When a New-Testament writer cites the Old Testament, which text-form is he quoting — the Greek Septuagint, the proto-Masoretic Hebrew that later stabilized into the medieval Jewish Bible, an already-revised Greek (the kaige / proto-Theodotion recensions), an older Hebrew now recovered at Qumran, or a free rendering owing to none of these? This is a question about the shape of the text , not about the canon (which books count): a writer can quote a book everyone receives while disagreeing with everyone about how its words run. The honest verdict, stated plainly and not to be laundered upward, is two-part. Where the Greek and the Hebrew part ways the Greek New Testament predominantly follows t…

tl.t: The earliest witness reads the divergence as a moral fact, not a textual one. Debating the Jew Trypho, Justin Martyr treats the Greek of "the seventy elders" as the true text and charges "your teachers" with having physically cut passages out of the Scriptures — the "from the wood" of Psalm 96:10 , a Jeremiah descent-oracle — and with misreading the christological proof-texts, above all Isaiah 7:14 's "virgin" ( παρθένος ) against their "young woman." 1 It is the seed of the whole later tradition — but framed as deliberate, recent, anti-Christian tampering, a diagnosis the text-critical evidence would not sustain: his flagship "from the wood" runs the other way (a Christian addition to some …

The first scholar to map the divergences instead of moralizing them. In the Hexapla Origen set six columns side by side — the Hebrew, the Hebrew in Greek letters, Aquila, Symmachus, the Septuagint, and Theodotion — marking with obelisk and asterisk every place the Greek had more or less than the Hebrew. It is the first systematic collation of the Greek against the Hebrew, and its very method concedes the point the corruption-polemic denied: the two traditions genuinely differ, verse by verse. Yet Origen's governing instinct was conservative — keep the text the churches actually use rather than re-edit the Bible down to the synagogue's Hebrew — and where he does charge suppression he charges …

The polarity reverses. Where the Greek Fathers trusted the Septuagint and suspected the Hebrew, Jerome abandoned the Greek as his base and translated the Old Testament afresh "from the Hebrew," appealing throughout his Vulgate prefaces to the Hebraica veritas , the "truth of the Hebrew." He ranked the versions Hebrew > Greek > Latin, debunked the legend of the seventy inspired cells, and — most pointedly for this question — argued that the evangelists and apostles, wherever the Septuagint diverged from the Hebrew, had themselves quoted the Hebrew and not the Greek . That is the exact counter-thesis to the modern consensus, and it flags from the start that "which text did the New Testament us…

Against Jerome, Augustine defended the Septuagint as itself apostolically authoritative — even inspired. In City of God XVIII.42–43 he argues that the same Spirit who spoke through the Hebrew prophets spoke through the Seventy, so that where the Greek differs from the Hebrew both may stand as prophetic; and he notes the plain fact that "the apostles, in their writings, appeal not only to the Hebrew, but also to the Septuagint" — indeed usually to the Greek. His worry was pastoral: Jerome's new-from-the-Hebrew Psalter would unsettle congregations who had prayed the Greek for centuries. The Jerome–Augustine exchange fixes the two poles the later debate would swing between — the priority of the…

tl.w: Swete and the first modern enumerations (c. 1900)
tl.t: The question passes from polemic to statistics. H. B. Swete's Introduction to the Old Testament in Greek (1900) and the Hatch–Redpath Concordance to the Septuagint (1897–1906) gave scholarship its first systematic tabulations of the New Testament's Old-Testament quotations and their agreement with the Greek — the ancestor of every later "how many follow the Septuagint?" count. Swete already framed the two cautions the modern field keeps: that "what counts as a quotation" is a soft edge (totals range from ~300 to ~400 by how one draws it), and that "the Septuagint" the apostles used was not one fixed book but a family of Greek texts, some already revised ( kaige , proto-Theodotion) back towar…

tl.w: Qumran and the recovery of a plural text (post-1947)
tl.t: The Dead Sea Scrolls settled the underlying question the Fathers could only guess at. Among the Qumran biblical manuscripts are Hebrew copies that agree with the Septuagint against the later Masoretic Text — a shorter Hebrew Jeremiah, a fuller Samuel (4QSamuel a ), a Deuteronomy 32 with the "sons of God" line the Masoretic dropped — proving that many places where the New Testament "follows the Greek against the Hebrew" are really cases of the Greek preserving an older Hebrew that a different, equally Jewish text-tradition once carried. The Scrolls thereby dissolve the ancient corruption-charge in both directions: the first-century text was plural, no side had "the" Hebrew, and divergence is …

tl.w: Archer & Chirichigno; Jobes & Silva; Fernández Marcos (1983–)
tl.t: Modern synthesis sets the columns side by side and does the arithmetic honestly. Gleason Archer & Gregory Chirichigno's Old Testament Quotations in the New Testament: A Complete Survey (1983) prints the Masoretic Hebrew, Septuagint, and Greek New Testament in parallel for each quotation and sorts them into categories A–F; the standard textbooks of Karen Jobes & Moisés Silva ( Invitation to the Septuagint ) and Natalio Fernández Marcos ( The Septuagint in Context ) place that data in the wider picture. Their agreed result: most quotations follow "the LXX in one of its known forms," but the much-cited headline "340 of 386 from the Septuagint" is rhetorically inflated — most of that 340 is pass…

ar.q: 1 Corinthians 2:9: “eye hath not seen” — a free rendering of Isaiah, or a lost source Paul quoted?
ar.c: “But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him.” — 1 Corinthians 2:9 (KJV), c. AD 55; Greek ἃ ὀφθαλμὸς οὐκ εἶδεν καὶ οὖς οὐκ ἤκουσεν καὶ ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἀνέβη, ἃ ἡτοίμασεν ὁ θεὸς τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν αὐτόν , introduced by the standard citation formula kathōs gégraptai (“as it is written”). 1 The interpretation this argument serves is the catalog’s classification of the row — that Paul’s wording follows neither received Old-Testament text, a free rendering or conflation owing to non…
ar.a: Contested. Two questions have two answers. First: does Paul’s 1 Corinthians 2:9 reproduce a surviving Old-Testament text? No, securely — it matches neither the Old Greek nor the Hebrew of Isaiah 64:4 (the dropped “no God beside thee,” the reversed senses, “love” for “wait”), so the catalog’s “neither / free / targumic” tag holds and the row sits with the doctrine’s other no-extant-text cruxes. Second: what is the source — a free, conflated Paulin…

ar.q: Amos 9:11–12 at Acts 15:16–18: a Septuagintal “seek the Lord,” and does the Council’s decision depend on it?
ar.c: “… that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name… LXX: … that they may seek me, the remnant of humanity, and all the nations over whom my name has been called… In the book of Acts … James … spoke these words … ‘so that the rest of mankind may seek the Lord, even all the Gentiles who are called by my name.’ … Where the authority of the apostles prevails … all suspicion of various explanations is to be removed.” — Jerome , Commentary on Amos 9:11–12 (c. 406), historicalchristian.faith . 1 Jerome — the champion of the Hebraica veritas , no friend of prefe…
ar.a: Sound. The interpretation this argument serves — that the Jerusalem Council’s proof-text is an LXX-distinctive quotation, following the Septuagint’s “the residue of men might seek after the Lord” where the Greek diverges from the Hebrew “they may possess the remnant of Edom” — holds. Acts reproduces the Greek reading; no rendering of the Hebrew supplies it; and the Hebrew side of the line reads “Edom” wherever it is attested. The row is correctly…

ar.q: Galatians 3:10–13 — the “curse of the law”: does Paul’s argument depend on the Septuagint’s text-form?
ar.c: “We consider it uncertain whether the seventy interpreters [of the Septuagint] have added ‘everyone’ and ‘in all’ or whether it was in the old Hebrew and deleted by the Jews. What makes me suspect this is that the apostle, a man skilled in Hebrew learning, would never have added these words everyone and all as if they were necessary to his meaning … unless they were in the Hebrew copies. Therefore, reading over the Hebrew copies of the Samaritans, I found the word kol written, which means ‘all’ or ‘in all’ and concurs with the Seventy.” — Jerome, Commentary on Galatians 2.3 (c. 386), on Galati…
ar.a: Sound. The interpretation this argument serves — that Paul’s curse-of-the-law proof is Septuagint-shaped at both hinges (the explicit “all” of Deuteronomy 27:26 at Galatians 3:10 , and the reshaped, LXX-based Deuteronomy 21:23 at 3:13 ) — holds: the “all” is genuinely absent from the Masoretic Hebrew and present in the Greek, and 3:13 is a real free -adaptation (catchword ἐπικατάρατος in, “of God” out). Both catalog tags stand. What the tags must…

ar.q: Deuteronomy 32:43 at Hebrews 1:6: “let all God’s angels worship him” — the Septuagint preserving an older Hebrew?
ar.c: “Rejoice, O you heavens, with Him, and let all the angels of God worship Him” and “Rejoice, O you nations, with His people, and let all the angels of God be strengthened in Him.” … by these words He declares that we, the nations, rejoice with His people — to wit, Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and the prophets, and, in short, all of that people who are well-pleasing to God.” — Justin Martyr , Dialogue with Trypho 130 (c. 155), newadvent.org . 1 Justin quotes Deuteronomy 32:43 in its full Septuagintal form — the summons to “the angels of God” to worship — two centuries before Jerome would trans…
ar.a: Sound. The interpretation this argument serves — that Hebrews 1:6’s proof-text is older-Hebrew , the Septuagint preserving a worship-summons the Masoretic Deuteronomy 32:43 lost — holds, and it is arguably the clearest place in the New Testament where a pre-Masoretic Hebrew reading, recovered at Qumran, is put to explicit christological use. The clause is absent from the Masoretic Text, present in the Septuagint, and carried in Hebrew by 4QDeut q…

ar.q: Ephesians 4:8 and Psalm 68:18: “he gave gifts unto men” — a targumic text-form, or Paul’s own reversal?
ar.c: “And elegantly, he placed here, ‘he gave gifts to men,’ whereas in the Psalter it is written, ‘he received gifts from men’ (Ps. LXVII, 19). But there, because it had not yet happened, but was promised for the future, it is said, ‘he received.’ Here, however, since the Apostle writes that he had already given, and the Church was established throughout the world, he does not write ‘received,’ but ‘gave.’” — Jerome , Commentary on Ephesians 4:8 (c. 386), historicalchristian.faith . 1 Jerome is the earliest surviving writer to flag the reversal in so many words; the interpretation this page adjudi…
ar.a: Text-form sound; the pre-existing-targumic-Vorlage mechanism contested. The catalog’s neither / free / targumic tag on Ephesians 4:8 is sound : the citation reverses the “received gifts among men” of both the Masoretic Hebrew and the Septuagint to “gave gifts to men,” and that “gave” is the distinctive reading of the Aramaic Targum and the Syriac Peshitta — the Pauline corpus’s clearest citation shaped by the interpretive (targumic) tradition rat…

ar.q: Habakkuk 2:4 at Romans 1:17 & Galatians 3:11: “the just shall live by faith” — does Paul’s pronoun-less form match either received text?
ar.c: “For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith.” (Romans 1:17) “But that no man is justified by the law in the sight of God, it is evident: for, The just shall live by faith.” (Galatians 3:11) — Paul, Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11 , quoting Habakkuk 2:4 . In both places Paul reproduces the clause ὁ δὲ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται — “the just shall live by faith” — with no possessive pronoun. 1 The interpretation this argument serves is the catalog’s classification: that Paul’s citation matches neither the Masoretic Hebrew (“…
ar.a: Sound. The interpretation this argument serves — that Paul’s “the just shall live by faith” at Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11 reproduces neither the Masoretic “by his faithfulness” nor the Septuagint’s “by my faith” exactly, and that the one verse is quoted in three divergent forms across Romans, Galatians, and Hebrews — plainly holds; the citation is correctly tagged neither / free , and it is the doctrine’s most economical single proof of a plu…

ar.q: Does the Epistle to the Hebrews argue from a Greek Old Testament? (the book-level case)
ar.c: “The number and the length of the quotations are outstanding in the New Testament…. Hebrews is the climax of New Testament citing.” — Martin Karrer, The Epistle to the Hebrews and the Septuagint , stating the premise the thesis builds on: no other New-Testament book quotes the Old Testament so heavily — some two dozen or more formal citations, many of them long, plus a dense field of allusions — and every one is drawn from a Greek text. 1 The interpretation this argument serves is the stronger claim built on that premise: that Hebrews is the New Testament’s clearest demonstration that its theo…
ar.a: Sound. The interpretation this argument serves — that Hebrews is the New Testament’s clearest demonstration that its argumentation, and not merely its wording, is shaped by a Greek Old Testament — holds on the cumulative evidence. It is the most quotation-saturated book in the canon; it draws its proof-texts from a Greek text-form throughout, with no sign of independent recourse to the Hebrew; and a chain of its signature arguments turns on disti…

ar.q: Isaiah 59:20 at Romans 11:26 — the Deliverer “out of Zion” ( ἐκ Σιων ): a form matching neither received text
ar.c: “And so all Israel shall be saved: as it is written, There shall come out of Sion the Deliverer, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob: For this is my covenant unto them, when I shall take away their sins.” (Romans 11:26–27) — Paul, Romans 11:26–27 , quoting Isaiah 59:20–21 (with a closing clause from Isaiah 27:9 ). Paul opens the citation ἥξει ἐκ Σιων ὁ ῥυόμενος — “there shall come out of Sion the Deliverer.” 1 The interpretation this argument serves is the catalog’s classification: that Paul’s citation matches neither the Masoretic Hebrew (“ to Zion”) nor the Septuagint (“ for the sake …
ar.a: Sound. The interpretation this argument serves — that Paul’s citation at Romans 11:26–27 reproduces neither the Masoretic “to Zion” nor the Septuagint’s “for the sake of Zion” exactly, but reads “ out of Zion” (a preposition in no known Isaiah copy) and closes with a clause spliced from Isaiah 27:9 — plainly holds; the citation is correctly tagged neither / free , and it is among the doctrine’s cleanest surface proofs that an apostle could quote …

ar.q: Isaiah 25:8 at 1 Corinthians 15:54: “death is swallowed up in victory” — did Paul quote a revised Greek (a Theodotion/ kaige -type text) against the Old Greek?
ar.c: “So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory . O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?” — 1 Corinthians 15:54–55 (KJV), c. AD 54, welding Isaiah 25:8 to Hosea 13:14 . 1 The interpretation this argument serves is the catalog’s classification of the 15:54 row: that Paul’s “ victory ” reproduces not the “Old Greek” Septuagint of Isaiah 25:8 — which reads the verse in the opposite direction, with death as the conqueror — but an e…
ar.a: Sound. The interpretation this argument serves — that 1 Corinthians 15:54 quotes Isaiah 25:8 from a revised , Hebraizing Greek against the Old Greek — holds, and it is the New Testament’s clearest single demonstration that the apostolic “Septuagint” was a plural family of texts, some already corrected back toward the Hebrew. The Old Greek reverses the verse (death as conqueror); Paul’s passive “death is swallowed up in victory” restores the Hebre…

ar.q: Isaiah 28:11–12 at 1 Corinthians 14:21: “with men of other tongues” — did Paul quote a revised, Hebraizing Greek (Aquila-like), or render the Hebrew himself?
ar.c: “Brethren, be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men. In the law it is written, With men of other tongues and other lips will I speak unto this people; and yet for all that will they not hear me, saith the Lord . Wherefore tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not…” — 1 Corinthians 14:20–22 (KJV), c. AD 55, citing Isaiah 28:11–12 as “the law” (Paul’s regular name for the whole Old Testament). 1 The interpretation this argument serves is the catalog’s classification of the row — that Paul’s wording follow…
ar.a: Contested. Two questions have two answers. First: is Paul’s 1 Corinthians 14:21 a genuine non-Septuagintal, Hebrew-leaning citation — a real counterweight to his Septuagintal lean? Yes, securely — the Old Greek reverses the verse (the heathen the speakers, “contempt of lips”), and Paul restores the Hebrew’s direction (God the speaker, judgment on Israel), so the catalog’s “neither / free” tag holds and the row sits with Paul’s other MT-leaning te…

ar.q: Isaiah 29:13 at Matthew 15:8–9 / Mark 7:6–7: “teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” — does Jesus’ critique of tradition rest on the Septuagint against…

Howbeit in vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.” — Jesus to the Pharisees and scribes, Mark 7:6–7 (parallel at Matthew 15:8–9 ), quoting Isaiah 29:13 in the Septuagint’s form ( μάτην δὲ σέβονταί με διδάσκοντες ἐντάλματα ἀνθρώπων καὶ διδασκαλίας ). 1 The interpretation this argument serves is the catalog’s classification — that the citation is LXX-distinctive , drawn from the Greek text-form at the very point it diverges …

He who entered into mysterious sympathy with our pain which is the fruit of sin, also put himself underneath our pain which is the penalty of sin. In other words the passage seems to teach that Christ endured vicariously our diseases as well as our iniquities… we urge the transgressor to accept the Lord Jesus as his sin-bearer, that he may himself no longer have to bear the pains and penalties of his disobedience. But should we shrink utterly from reasoning thus concerning Christ as our pain…
ar.a: Text-form sub-claim: sound. ar.q: Isaiah 6:9–10 in the New Testament — one verse in two text-forms: does the divine-hardening theology ride on Matthew’s Septuagint against John’s Hebrew?
ar.c: The reading this page weighs has two layers, and they must be kept apart. The lower layer is a text-form observation, and it is correct: Isaiah’s commissioning oracle enters the New Testament in two measurably different forms. The upper layer is the inference some draw from it — that the theology of divine hardening (judicial blinding, reprobation) hangs on that textual fork, so that Matthew’s Septuagint teaches a people who harden themselves while John’s Hebrew teaches a God who hardens them . The one Father who read both texts states the fork exactly: “According to the easy interpretation of…
ar.a: Text-form sub-claim: sound. The same commissioning oracle enters the New Testament in two measurably different shapes. ar.q: Isaiah 7:14 at Matthew 1:23: a Septuagintal “virgin,” and does Matthew depend on it?
ar.c: “… the Hebrew word for ‘virgin’ is ‘Bethula’, which is not written here in the present passage: instead, the word used is ‘Alma’, which all except the Septuagint translated as ‘young woman.’… But if a young woman, as the Jews want, and not a virgin, were to give birth, what sign could it be called, since this name refers to age, not integrity?” — Jerome , Commentary on Isaiah 7:14 (c. 408), historicalchristian.faith . 1 Jerome — the champion of the Hebraica veritas , no friend of laundering the Greek over the Hebrew — concedes the underlying textual fact this argument turns on: at Isaiah 7:14 …

ar.q: Matthew’s formula quotations: do they evidence direct use of a Hebrew (non-Septuagintal) text?
ar.c: “In this it is to be noted that wherever the Evangelist, whether on his own account or in the person of our Lord the Saviour, quotes the testimony of the Old Testament, he does not follow the authority of the translators of the Septuagint but the Hebrew. Wherefore these two forms exist, ‘Out of Egypt have I called my son,’ and ‘for he shall be called a Nazarene.’” — Jerome , Lives of Illustrious Men 3 (c. 393), on Matthew’s gospel. 1 Jerome is the ancient champion of the reading this argument serves: that Matthew’s fulfilment citations follow the Hebrew rather than the Greek, and so prove the …
ar.a: Sound. The interpretation this argument serves — that Matthew’s formula quotations are non-Septuagintal where the Greek and Hebrew diverge, following the Hebrew at Hosea 11:1, and so stand as the doctrine’s diversity counterweight against any “the New Testament = the Septuagint” picture — holds, and is near-consensus from Stendahl onward. The catalog’s “MT-distinctive” tag on Matthew 2:15 is correct: the singular “my son” is the Hebrew’s and not …

ar.q: Psalm 16:10 at Acts 2:27 / 13:35: “see no corruption” — does the apostolic resurrection proof depend on the Greek?
ar.c: “Moreover also my flesh shall rest in hope: because thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption… Men and brethren, let me freely speak unto you of the patriarch David, that he is both dead and buried, and his sepulchre is with us unto this day… he seeing this before spake of the resurrection of Christ, that his soul was not left in hell, neither his flesh did see corruption.” — Peter at Pentecost, Acts 2:26–31 , quoting Psalm 16:10 in the Septuagint’s form ( οὐδὲ δώσεις τὸν ὅσιόν σου ἰδεῖν διαφθοράν ); Paul repeats the same proof verbatim at A…

The interpretation this argument serves — that the apostolic resurrection proof at Acts 2:27 and 13:35 reads a Septuagintal “corruption” ( διαφθοράν ) where the Hebrew Psalm 16:10 reads “the pit” ( šaḥat ) — plainly holds; the citation is LXX-distinctive and correctly tagged. The interesting, queued sub-finding is that the Greek word is the most load-bearing in the entire catalog of apostolic quotations: the vivid empirical prong (“David d…

ar.q: Psalm 40:6 at Hebrews 10:5: a Septuagintal “body,” and does the argument depend on it?
ar.c: “… the things pertaining to the quotation have become unambiguous as far as I am concerned. Changing it he speaks in this way about the person of Christ, saying, ‘I will establish a body ’ instead of ‘I will establish ears .’” — Theodore of Mopsuestia, Fragments on the Epistle to the Hebrews 10.5 (c. 400), stating the divergence outright — the apostle “changing it” reads “body” where the Psalm's Hebrew has “ears.” 1 Eight centuries later Thomas Aquinas, expounding the Psalm, records both readings in the same breath: “‘But you have fashioned ears for me.’ Another reading has, ‘a body .’ And thu…
ar.a: Sound. The interpretation this argument serves — that Hebrews 10:5 is an LXX-distinctive quotation, reproducing and then reusing the Septuagint's σῶμα where the Greek diverges from the Hebrew “ears” — holds. The author quotes the Greek word verbatim and carries it into his conclusion at 10:10; no literal rendering of the Hebrew supplies it; the Hebraizing Greek tradition and Jerome's Hebrew Psalter read “ears” on the other side of the line. The r…

ar.q: Does Revelation’s Old Testament wording reflect a Hebraizing Vorlage or the Septuagint? (the book-level case)
ar.c: “While he writes in Greek, he thinks in Hebrew…. He never quotes the Old Testament according to the Septuagint…; he translates directly from the Old Testament text.” — R. H. Charles, summarizing the position his Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Revelation of St. John (ICC, 1920) argues at length: that the Seer did not borrow an existing Greek version but rendered the Hebrew (and, for Torrey and Trudinger, an Aramaic) text for himself, so that Revelation’s Old-Testament wording is a window onto a Semitic Vorlage , not onto the Septuagint. 1 The interpretation this argument serves is th…
ar.a: Contested. The interpretation this argument serves — that Revelation’s Old-Testament wording reflects a Hebraizing/Semitic Vorlage rather than the Septuagint — is genuinely and independently advocated, was for most of the twentieth century the majority view, and rests on real data (the pervasive Semitisms, the MT-distinctive “pierced” of 1:7, the Theodotionic Daniel allusions). It is strong by the lights of Semitic-syntax study and weak by the li…

ar.q: Does the Epistle to the Romans argue from a Greek Old Testament? (the book-level case)
ar.c: “This follows the Septuagint text, for in our text, which follows the Hebrew truth, it says the just man lives by his faith.” — Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Romans , at Romans 1:17 , opening the letter with the observation that turns into a refrain: Paul quotes a Greek Old Testament, and where it diverges from “our text” (the Hebrew-based Vulgate) Aquinas keeps flagging the fork — “the Apostle takes these words according to the Septuagint” (Romans 9:33), “the Apostle uses the Septuagint” (Romans 11:26), “our text has this… every tongue shall swear ” where Paul reads “confess” (Romans 14:11). …
ar.a: Sound — for the graded, two-sided claim, which is the honest one. Romans predominantly argues from a Greek text-form, and does so at load-bearing hinges: “not ashamed ” (Isaiah 28:16), “their sound ” (Psalm 19:4), the “ mind of the Lord” (Isaiah 40:13), “every tongue shall confess ” (Isaiah 45:23), a Septuagintal lean the ancient collators and the modern monographs alike report. What the thesis must be trusted to mean, and no more , is fixed by t…

ar.q: Zechariah 12:10 at John 19:37 — “whom they pierced”: does the pierced-Messiah proof follow the Hebrew against the Greek?
ar.c: “The Hebrew letters Daleth and Res , that is, D and R, are similar and are distinguished only by a small mark… For if it is read as Dacaru , it is understood to mean ‘they pierced or nailed’, but if the order is reversed, with the letters transposed, it is understood to mean ‘they danced’, as Racadu … However, the beloved disciple John, who drew wisdom from the heart of the Lord and was a Hebrew among the Hebrews, did not greatly care about what the Greek letters contained; but he translated word for word, as he had read it in Hebrew, and said that it was fulfilled at the time of the Lord’s pa…
ar.a: Sound. The interpretation this argument serves — that John 19:37 (with Revelation 1:7) reproduces a Hebrew-aligned form of Zechariah 12:10, “whom they pierced,” against the Old Greek’s “danced / mocked,” and so stands as the Gospels’ clearest MT-distinctive datum — holds, and is near-consensus. The catalog’s tag on the row is correct: John’s ἐξεκέντησαν is the Hebrew’s and not the Old Greek’s, the divergence arising from a dālet/rêš misreading ov…

The four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, Paul's Epistles to the Romans, 1–2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, and the Pastorals (1–2 Timothy, Titus), the Epistle to the Hebrews, the General Epistles (James, 1–2 Peter, Jude), and the Revelation of John are now worked row by row — the entire New Testament — every one of their explicit quotations (and, for Revelation, its handful of near-quotations) adjudicated against the Septuagint and the Masoretic Hebrew (and, where a divergence is load-bearing, the Qumran evidence), with th…

ds.t: Who Was Og of Bashan?
ds.q: Og is the giant king of Bashan whom Israel destroyed on the march to Canaan — and the one figure of the conquest the Hebrew Bible pauses to measure. He “went out against” Israel “to battle at Edrei,” and the LORD told Moses, “Fear him not: for I have delivered him into thy hand… thou shalt do to him as thou didst unto Sihon king of the Amorites” ( Numbers 21:33–35 ). His was a kingdom of “threescore cities… the region of Argob… which was called the land of giants” ( Deuteronomy 3:4–13 ), ruled from Astaroth in Edrei . Then comes the verse the whole later tradition turns on: “For only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of giants; behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron… nine cubits…

tl.w: The biblical portrait (Numbers 21; Deuteronomy 1–3; Joshua 12–13; the Psalms)
tl.t: Everything the tradition made of Og begins as a campaign notice.
