On the road north Israel turns “by the way of Bashan,” and “Og the king of Bashan went out against them, he, and all his people, to the battle at Edrei.” The verdict is Sihon’s over again: “the LORD said unto Moses, Fear him not… So they smote him, and his sons, and all his people, until there was none left him alive; and they possessed his land.” Deuteronomy repeats it and enlarges the kingdom — “threescore cities… all the region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan… which was called the land of giants” — and the Psalms fix him in Israel’s memory as one of the “great” and “famous kings” the LORD struck down: “Sihon king of th…

tl.w: The Septuagint (3rd–2nd century BC) — “of the Raphain… a bed of iron”
tl.t: The Greek translators, rendering Deuteronomy for Alexandrian Jewry, keep the datum but not the gloss. Where the King James would later say “the remnant of giants,” the Septuagint simply transliterates the Hebrew — “For only Og the king of Basan was left of the Raphain : behold, his bed was a bed of iron ( klīnē sidēra )… the length of it is nine cubits, and the breadth of it four cubits, according to the cubit of a man.” The word for “giants,” gigantes , that the Greek does use elsewhere for the Nephilim and Rephaim, is not used at this verse: the earliest translation leaves “of the Raphain” standing as an untranslated proper name. The bed, and its exact dimensions, pass into Greek unchanged…

tl.w: Josephus ( Antiquities of the Jews 4.5.3, c. AD 93) — the giant king and his iron bed at Rabbath
tl.t: The earliest datable treatment after the Bible turns the terse notice into a portrait. Retelling the war for a Greco-Roman readership, Josephus makes Og a marvel of stature and bearing — “Og had very few equals, either in the largeness of his body, or handsomeness of his appearance… a man of great activity in the use of his hands” — and then reads his size directly off the relic Deuteronomy names: “men could easily guess at his strength and magnitude when they took his bed at Rabbath, the royal city of the Ammonites; its structure was of iron, its breadth four cubits, and its length a cubit more than double thereto.” He takes the “bedstead” as literal furniture and the measure as the measure…

tl.w: Origen of Alexandria ( Homilies on Joshua 3, c. AD 240) — Og among the “kings of the contrary powers”
tl.t: The Christian reading begins allegorically. Preaching through Joshua, Origen contrasts the few kings Moses felled east of the Jordan with the many that fall once “Jesus” (the Greek Joshua) leads: “Sihon only… king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan, and the Amalekites, they cast down beyond the Jordan. But where Jesus leads the army, now five kings fall at once.” Og is read not as a curiosity of size but as one of the “kings of the contrary powers” — a spiritual adversary overthrown — the figural key the Fathers preferred to the metrology that fascinated Josephus and the rabbis. 5

tl.w: Eusebius of Caesarea ( Onomasticon , c. AD 325) — Og’s cities, “where giants dwelt”
tl.t: Eusebius, cataloguing the places of Scripture for pilgrims, pins Og’s kingdom to the real map of Roman Arabia and preserves the giant-tradition attached to it. Of Astarōth : “the ancient city of Og… where giants dwelled… located in the Batanea six miles from Adraa.” Of Edrai : “whence the gigantic Og, king of Basan… now there is Adra, a famous city of Arabia, twenty-four miles from Bostra.” The two towns Joshua gives “the remnant of the Rephaim” are, for Eusebius, findable ground — and their memory is still a memory of giants. 6

tl.w: Jerome (Commentaries on Isaiah, Micah, and Amos, c. AD 393–410) — Bashan the land of “confusion,” and the cedar-giant who is Sihon
tl.t: Jerome carries Og into the Latin West by way of etymology. Bashan, he explains, means “ignominy” or “confusion” — “Basan is a region in Arabia, over which Og ruled… interpreted as αἰσχύνη, that is, ignominy” — and there is “another confusion that leads to death, in which Og, the king of Bashan, once dwelt.” Reading Amos’s cedar-tall Amorite, though, Jerome is careful not to make him Og: the giant “lofty and strong like a cedar and an oak” whose “fruit” God broke “from above” is Sihon , Og’s brother-king of Heshbon — a distinction later giant-lore often blurs. 7

tl.w: Augustine of Hippo ( Expositions on the Psalms 135–136, c. AD 415) — Og “the heaper-together,” a figure of the devil
tl.t: Augustine, expounding the two psalms that name Og, presses the etymology all the way to the enemy of souls. On Psalm 136’s “And Og, the king of Basan”: “The ‘heaper-together,’ such is the meaning of Og, and, king of ‘confusion,’ which Basan signifies. For what else does the devil heap together but confusion?” On Psalm 135 he draws the moral from the slaughter of the mighty kings: “When you see what has been done to the wicked, take heed lest it be done to you… God… drove out the wicked.” Where Josephus saw a giant’s body, Augustine sees a name to be allegorized — Og the type of the accumulating adversary God casts out. 8

tl.w: The Venerable Bede ( Commentary on Genesis , on Genesis 14:5, c. AD 720) — “Rephaim in Greek are called Giants”
tl.t: Bede, reading the raid of the eastern kings, states plainly the equation the Septuagint had left implicit and hands it to the medieval West. At Ashtaroth-Karnaim — one of Og’s own cities — the kings “struck the Rephaim… Rephaim in Hebrew, in Greek are called Giants: in the singular number… a Rephaim is called a Giant. Now their land… Ashtaroth-karnaim… because indeed they were the dwellings of strong men.” The Rephaim of whom Og is “the remnant” are, for Bede, simply the Giants — and their city is the seat of “strong men.” 9

tl.w: The rabbinic tradition (Targum Pseudo-Jonathan; the Babylonian Talmud; Pirqei de-Rabbi Eliezer ; traditions from c. AD 200, redacted c. 500–800) — the antediluvian who outrode the Flood
tl.t: Jewish tradition made Og the great survivor. He is no mere Amorite but an antediluvian — brother of Sihon and, in one strand, a son of the fallen Watchers: “Sihon and Og were brothers… sons of Ahijah, son of Shamhazai,” and Rabbi Yoḥanan reads the fugitive “one that was saved” of Genesis 14:13 as “Og, who was saved from the punishment of the generation of the flood.” The Targum tells how: “Og came, who had been spared from the giants that died in the deluge, and had ridden protected upon the top of the ark, and sustained with food by Noah”; Pirqei de-Rabbi Eliezer adds that Og “sat down on a piece of wood under the gutter of the ark… he swore to Noah… that he would be their servant for ever,…

tl.w: The modern recovery: Og and the Ugaritic Rephaim (19th–21st century)
tl.t: The decipherment of the Ugaritic tablets from Ras Shamra opened a third reading of “the last of the Rephaim.” In the Ugaritic libation-prayer KTU 1.108 the god Rapiu — divine patron of the rpʾum , the cognate of the biblical Rephaim — is enthroned precisely “in Ashtaroth… in Edrei,” the very two cities Deuteronomy and Joshua assign Og; and a second liturgy (KTU 1.161) summons the rpʾum as the deified spirits of dead kings. On this line (first pressed by Baruch Margulis and built out by Michael Heiser and others) “Og… of the remnant of the Rephaim, who dwelt at Ashtaroth and Edrei” reads as at once a giant king and a shade , and Bashan — a region whose name puns on the word for “serpent” — as…

ds.t: Old-World Peoples in the Pre-Columbian Americas
ds.q: The Reformed pastor Douglas Wilson — a pointed critic of the Book of Mormon — states, in passing and on his own Reformed grounds, a belief that would sound at home in the very scriptures he rejects: “that King Solomon was behind the settlement of Central America.” His argument is one of feasibility: Captain Cook found people already waving from the beaches of Hawaii, and there are the statues of Easter Island “way the heck out there,” so somebody in antiquity knew how to cross open water — and if somebody could, then the crossing that (he holds) peopled Mesoamerica is no obstacle. Wilson is the modern front door to this page; he is also the tail of a tradition far older than he is.

tl.w: Bartolomé de las Casas weighs the idea — and doubts it (c. 1550)
tl.t: The tradition is often traced to the great Dominican defender of the Indians, Bartolomé de las Casas, but the ascription is a later legend, first spread by Juan de Torquemada. In his Apologética historia sumaria Las Casas in fact judged that circumcision and a handful of Hebrew-sounding words were no sufficient ground to make the Indians “descend from the Jewish people” — so he belongs at the head of this timeline not as the thesis's founder but as its first skeptic. 1

tl.w: Fray Diego Durán: the natives as the Ten Lost Tribes (c. 1581)
tl.t: The clean early proponent is the Dominican friar Diego Durán, raised among Nahuatl-speakers in Texcoco and Mexico City. He opened his Historia de las Indias de Nueva España with his own “opinion and suspicion” that the natives of New Spain descended from the Ten Lost Tribes of Israel, reasoning from a perceived likeness between the Aztec Aztlán-migration story and the Exodus, from the apocryphal exile of the tribes to a distant land in 2 Esdras, and from the Indians' own professed ignorance of their origin. 2

tl.w: José de Acosta answers by elimination: overland from Asia (1590)
tl.t: The decisive early counter-voice is the Jesuit José de Acosta , whose Historia natural y moral de las Indias (1590) rejected both the Lost-Tribes idea and any deliberate ocean crossing. Working by elimination, he argued that the first peoples had come overland from Asia, because the two landmasses must be “joyned and continued one with another in some part, or at the least, are very neere,” the country peopled gradually as hunting bands changed “by little and little their lands and habitations.” He dismissed the scriptural-migration route — the apocryphal Euphrates of 2 Esdras — as giving “no better passage” to the New World than Plato's “fabulous Atlantis.” His inductive guess, a century an…

tl.w: The 1650 cluster: Menasseh ben Israel and Thomas Thorowgood (1644–1660)
tl.t: The idea crossed from Catholic New Spain into Protestant and Jewish messianism on a single traveller's tale. On the sworn 1644 relation of Antonio de Montezinos — who claimed to have been led over the Andes to a hidden people reciting the Shema in Hebrew — the Amsterdam rabbi Menasseh ben Israel built The Hope of Israel (1650), which set out to prove “the place wherein the ten tribes at this present are … partly by the strange relation of one Anthony Montezinus,” making a worldwide dispersion (America included) a precondition of the messianic restoration — and a lever for readmitting Jews to England. 4 In the same year the English Puritan Thomas Thorowgood published Iewes in America, or, Pro…

The fullest early case in English came from a trader who had lived four decades among the Chickasaw, Cherokee, Choctaw, and Creek. James Adair devoted much of his History of the American Indians to some twenty-three “arguments” that the southeastern nations descended lineally from the Israelites — from their division into clans, their purity and mourning rites, their festivals, a supposed theocratic order, and a long list of claimed language parallels. The ethnography is still valued as among the best early records of those peoples; the Israelite thesis is not. 6

tl.w: Ethan Smith systematizes it for America: View of the Hebrews (1823)
tl.t: The Congregationalist minister Ethan Smith of Poultney, Vermont, gathered the scriptural prophecies and the ethnographic reports — Adair among his sources — into View of the Hebrews; or the Tribes of Israel in America (1823; enlarged 1825), the popular American synthesis of the Hebraic-origin view. It is also the book whose possible influence on the Book of Mormon, published seven years later and a few Vermont-New York counties away, has been debated ever since — a question weighed on its own at Did View of the Hebrews stand behind the Book of Mormon? (plausible: the milieu influence strong, direct dependence on this one book unproven). 7

tl.w: The Book of Mormon crystallizes the idea in scripture (1830)
tl.t: In March 1830 the tradition took scriptural form. The Book of Mormon presents Israelite migrants — the Jaredites from the Tower of Babel and the Lehites who left Jerusalem about 600 BC — as the founders of literate, metal-using civilizations in the ancient Americas. Whether that record survives the archaeological, genetic, and linguistic evidence is a large question of its own, weighed on the Book of Mormon and the material record ; on this timeline it marks the point at which the diffusionist idea became the charter of a new church. 8

tl.w: Lord Kingsborough spends a fortune to prove it (1830–1848)
tl.t: Edward King, Viscount Kingsborough, poured his inheritance into the nine elephant-folio volumes of Antiquities of Mexico (1830–1848), commissioning Agostino Aglio to copy the Mesoamerican codices scattered through the libraries of Europe expressly to prove the Mexicans descended from the Lost Tribes. He died in a Dublin debtors' prison, ruined by the cost. The thesis failed; the facsimiles endured — Aglio's copy of the Dresden Codex preserves readings later lost to damage of the original. 9

A related current placed the Lost Tribes not across the Atlantic but in Britain: John Wilson's Our Israelitish Origin (1840), later popularized by Edward Hine, held the Anglo-Saxons themselves to be Israel, traced by philological look-alikes. That four-century tradition has its own timeline ; it is noted here only to keep the two apart — British Israelism locates the tribes in Europe, not the Americas — though its fusion with the American strand shaped later movements. 10

The nineteenth-century American form of the tradition was the “Mound-Builder” myth — that a vanished, superior race, Israelite or otherwise Old-World, and not the ancestors of the living Indians, had raised the great earthworks of the Ohio and Mississippi valleys. The Smithsonian's Bureau of Ethnology set Cyrus Thomas to test it; after eight years of excavation his massive Report on the Mound Explorations concluded that the mounds were built by the ancestors of the historic Native American nations, and the “lost race” collapsed. Thomas had begun the work inclined to the vanished builders and was turned by his own evidence — the mainstream verdict ever since. 11 The same eastern mounds are we…

tl.w: The epigraphic diffusionists: Cyrus Gordon and Barry Fell (1971–1976)
tl.t: The twentieth-century revival ran on inscriptions. The Brandeis Semitist Cyrus H. Gordon defended the Bat Creek and Paraíba texts as genuine ancient Hebrew and Phoenician in Before Columbus (1971); the Harvard zoologist-turned-epigrapher Barry Fell read scattered New-World rock-markings as Celtic Ogham, Punic, and Iberian script in America B.C. (1976). 12 Specialists reject the whole corpus: the Bat Creek stone — the one genuinely excavated piece, and so weighed on its own page — closely tracks a line from an 1870 Masonic handbook, and Fell's “inscriptions” repeatedly proved to be plough-scars, glacial striae, or Native petroglyphs. This is the affirmative evidence Wilson's Solomonic thesis …

tl.w: Douglas Wilson revives it: Solomon in Central America (2026)
tl.t: At the modern tail stands the Reformed pastor Douglas Wilson, who — though a hard critic of the Book of Mormon — makes the same species of claim on his own grounds: “I have written elsewhere about my belief that King Solomon was behind the settlement of Central America.” His stated case is feasibility: Polynesians reached islands “way the heck out there,” so somebody in antiquity could cross open water. The interpretation the aside serves is weighed on its own page — weak as a general diffusionist thesis, unsupported in its specific Solomonic form. 14

ar.q: The Bat Creek stone: ancient palaeo-Hebrew, or a 19th-century forgery?
ar.c: The five letters to the left of the comma-shaped word divider read, from right to left, LYHWD, or “for Judea.” … The complete lack of the orange-colored silty-clay residue in any of the characters of the inscription is consistent with many hundreds of years of weathering in a wet earth mound. — J. Huston McCulloch, restating Cyrus Gordon's reading and reporting his own petrographic and radiocarbon findings. 1 The interpretation assessed here is that the Bat Creek stone carries a genuine ancient palaeo-Hebrew inscription — and so, in the hands of the diffusionists who cite it, that Old-World Se…
ar.a: Weak (sub-claim a: the inscription is genuinely ancient Semitic); unsupported (sub-claim b: it licenses the Old-World-settlement thesis). The Bat Creek stone deserves — and here gets — the fair, adversarial hearing its real provenance earns; it is not a self-evident fraud like its epigraphic neighbors, and McCulloch's word-divider and terminal-letter points are genuine complications to a letter-perfect copy theory. But the interpretation does not…

ar.q: Coca and nicotine in Egyptian mummies: pre-Columbian trans-Atlantic contact?
ar.c: … the first identification of cocaine, hashish and nicotine in Egyptian mummies … — the title finding of Balabanova, Parsche, and Pirsig's 1992 report. 1 The interpretation assessed here is the one that made the note famous far beyond forensic toxicology: that because cocaine comes from the coca plant and (as usually stated) nicotine from tobacco, both native to the Americas, their presence in Egyptian bodies of about 1000 BC is evidence of pre-Columbian trans-Atlantic contact — American plants reaching the Old World some 2,500 years before Columbus. It is the direct mirror of the “Old-World-i…
ar.a: Weak (the mummies evidence pre-Columbian trans-Atlantic contact), splitting into: unsupported for the nicotine sub-claim — nicotine has genuine Old-World botanical sources, so it is not contact evidence even if the chemistry is right — and weak for the cocaine sub-claim, the one substance that really is American-only. The cocaine result deserves, and here gets, the fair hearing its metabolite chemistry, GC/MS confirmation, and partial replication…

ar.q: The El Arenal chicken: a Polynesian bird in pre-Columbian Chile?
ar.c: The interpretation assessed here is that the El Arenal-1 chicken bones are archaeological evidence — faunal, not genetic-human — of a pre-Columbian Polynesian contact with the South-American coast. The chicken ( Gallus gallus ) is a Southeast-Asian domesticate that reached the Americas, on the standard account, only with the Spanish and Portuguese after 1500. A securely pre-Columbian chicken in Chile would therefore be a bird that crossed an ocean before Columbus — and because chickens were a core commensal that Polynesian voyagers carried across the Pacific, the natural reading is that Polyne…
ar.a: Contested. Keep the two sub-claims sorted. The dating sub-claim — a genuinely pre-Columbian chicken at El Arenal-1 — is well-grounded: the marine-reservoir objection was answered by sulphur-isotope data and the chronology was reconfirmed by a 2023 re-excavation. The Polynesian-origin sub-claim is genuinely disputed: the ancient-DNA sequence once read as a diagnostic Polynesian haplotype is a cosmopolitan lineage open to a contamination reading (T…

ar.q: Did genuine pre-Columbian Polynesia–South America contact occur?
ar.c: The interpretation assessed here is deliberately modest and precisely scoped: a genuine, human-mediated contact event occurred between Polynesians and Native South Americans at some point before 1492 . It is not the claim that South Americans peopled Polynesia (Heyerdahl's thesis, which the linguistic, archaeological, and genetic record refutes — Polynesia was settled west-to-east out of island Southeast Asia by Austronesian navigators), and it is not the claim that either side founded, seeded, or civilized the other. It is only that the two peoples met and mingled once, briefly, across the wi…
ar.a: Sound. That a genuine, human-mediated pre-Columbian contact occurred between Polynesians and Native South Americans is now well-grounded and, after two independent genome-wide studies converging on a thirteenth-to-fifteenth-century date, close to consensus — the strongest single line being direct ancient-DNA evidence from Rapanui skeletons carrying Native-American but no European ancestry. Keep the sub-claims sorted: the human-genetic case is sou…

ar.q: The Los Lunas Decalogue stone: ancient palaeo-Hebrew, or a modern carving?
ar.c: … the Decalogue inscription is clearly many times older than this [1930] graffito, and that 500 to 2000 years would not be an unreasonable estimate of its age … [its apparent freshness owing to its having been] chalked and scrubbed up [in modern times]. — the geologist George E. Morehouse, as reported by J. Huston McCulloch, arguing from the re-weathering of the incised grooves that the carving is ancient. 1 The interpretation assessed here is that the Los Lunas stone — a basalt boulder on the slope of Hidden Mountain, some 35 miles south of Albuquerque, carrying an abridged Ten Commandments i…
ar.a: Weak (sub-claim a: the inscription is genuinely ancient Semitic); unsupported (sub-claim b: it licenses the Old-World-settlement thesis). The Los Lunas stone gets the fair, adversarial hearing a real geologist's dating argument and a tenacious defender earn — but the interpretation does not hold on its best available case. The single most economical account of a boulder bearing the Masoretic Decalogue, cut in an alphabet that mixes archaic Hebrew…

ar.q: Mystery Hill (“America’s Stonehenge”): an ancient Old-World megalithic site, or a colonial New England farm?
ar.c: The megaliths of Mystery Hill … are the ruins of an ancient temple … The inscriptions are written in Ogam, Punic, and Iberian scripts. … The site was dedicated to Bel, the Phoenician sun-god. … Celtic peoples, together with Phoenician traders, had established a colony in New England. — the interpretation of the site advanced by Barry Fell in America B.C. (paraphrasing his running argument; the book reads the hill’s markings as Ogham and Punic, dedicates its central stone to the sun-god Bel, and reports one inscription as recording a Carthaginian prince’s annexation of part of Massachusetts). 1…
ar.a: Weak (sub-claim a: the structures are ancient Old-World construction); weak (sub-claim b: the markings are genuine ancient Ogham/Punic script); unsupported (sub-claim c: either licenses the Old-World-settlement thesis). Mystery Hill gets the fair hearing its scale and its genuine antiquity earn — the hill really was in use four thousand years ago, and Fell really did leave a puzzle worth adjudicating. But adjudicated, both believing readings fail…

ar.q: Did Old-World peoples trans-oceanically settle pre-Columbian Central America?
ar.c: I have written elsewhere about my belief that King Solomon was behind the settlement of Central America. Now if a learned scholar were to deign to give me the time of day on this question, he would just sniff and say that the consensus in the journals is that ancient man did not have the navigational ability to transit the Pacific. … when Captain Cook, harbinger of civilized man, representing all those who did know how to do it, arrived at Hawaii, right out in the middle of said Pacific, what did he find there? Who was waving at him from the beach? You guessed right . . . people . My argument …
ar.a: Weak as the general diffusionist thesis (Old-World peoples founded the pre-Columbian Central-American civilizations); unsupported in the specific Solomonic form Wilson advocates. Distinguish the sub-claims, because they do not stand or fall together. That trans-oceanic contact was feasible , and in scattered instances actual , is well-grounded — the Norse landfall and the AD-1200 Polynesian admixture prove it, and to that extent Wilson's “somebod…

ar.q: Where did Solomon’s fleet actually sail? Ophir and Tarshish located
ar.c: Three short passages describe Solomon’s maritime trade, and a rival reading turns on where they point. He “made a navy of ships in Ezion-geber, which is beside Eloth, on the shore of the Red sea, in the land of Edom,” crewed it with Phoenician sailors lent by Hiram of Tyre, and “they came to Ophir, and fetched from thence gold” ( 1 Kings 9:26–28 ; 2 Chronicles 8:17–18 ). Separately he “had at sea a navy of Tharshish… once in three years came the navy of Tharshish, bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks” ( 1 Kings 10:22 ; 2 Chronicles 9:21 ). 1 The mainstream reading places bo…
ar.a: Sound for the interpretation at issue: Solomon’s Ophir and Tarshish lay in the Old World, and his two fleets — the Red-Sea navy out of Ezion-geber bound south and east for Ophir’s gold, and the Mediterranean “navy of Tarshish” bound west for silver — sailed nowhere near the Atlantic. The precise pin for each name remains genuinely contested (Ophir: Arabia / the Horn / India; Tarshish: Tarsus / Sardinia / Tartessos, or a vessel-class), but that is…

ar.q: The Paraíba inscription: a genuine ancient Phoenician text, or an 1872 forgery?
ar.c: We are Sidonian Canaanites from the city of the Mercantile King. We were cast up on this distant shore, a land of mountains. We sacrificed a youth to the celestial gods and goddesses in the nineteenth year of our mighty King Hiram and embarked from Ezion-geber into the Red Sea. We voyaged with ten ships and were at sea together for two years around Africa. Then we were separated by the hand of Baal and were no longer with our companions. So we have come here, twelve men and three women, into … New Shore. Am I, the Admiral, a man who would flee? Nay! May the celestial gods and goddesses favour …
ar.a: Weak (sub-claim a: the inscription is a genuine ancient Phoenician text); unsupported (sub-claim b: it licenses the Old-World-settlement thesis). The Paraíba text gets the fair, adversarial hearing that a real Semitist's defense earns — but the interpretation does not hold on its best available case, and it is arguably the weakest of the three stones in this corpus, because it is not a stone at all. The single most economical account of a compete…

ar.q: Does the sweet potato evidence pre-Columbian human contact across the Pacific?
ar.c: The sweet potato is a New-World domesticate: it was bred from wild Ipomoea ancestors in tropical America, and at European contact it was grown nowhere in the Old World — except, unaccountably, across a broad sweep of Polynesia, from the Cook Islands to New Zealand to Hawaii to Rapa Nui. The interpretation assessed here is the long mainstream one, the “tripartite hypothesis”: the crop reached Oceania in three separate waves, the first of which — the “ kumara line” — was carried by Polynesian voyagers directly from north-western South America some centuries before Columbus, later joined by two p…
ar.a: Contested. That the sweet potato proves pre-Columbian human contact, taken as a solo knock-down, overreaches — the 2018 genome study shows a bare-presence natural-dispersal mechanism for the plant that cannot be ruled out, so the crop alone does not compel the conclusion. But the interpretation the argument serves — that the sweet potato is genuine evidence of human trans-Pacific contact — is strong and, on the full picture, probable. Keep the tw…

ds.t: The Condemnation of Origen
ds.q: Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) died in communion with the Church. He had been tortured under Decius and survived it, honoured as a confessor; he was the most productive and the most quoted Christian teacher of his age, and for a century afterwards the man whose commentaries every serious exegete in East and West worked from. Three hundred years later his name stands in a list of arch-heretics between Eutyches and the anathematized dead. This page asks how that happened, and whether it was fair.

tl.w: Origen marks out the open questions himself ( Peri Archōn , c. 229)
tl.t: Nearly everything later condemned comes from one work, written at Alexandria before Origen left it, and its preface is the first thing any fair account of the condemnation has to reckon with. Origen there divides Christian teaching in two. On some points “the holy apostles, in preaching the faith of Christ, delivered themselves with the utmost clearness”; on others they stated only that a thing is so, “leaving, however, the grounds of their statements to be examined into by those who should deserve the excellent gifts of the Spirit.” Into the second class he explicitly puts the origin of the soul — whether it “is derived from the seed by a process of traducianism… or whether it has any other…

The first sentence passed on Origen was not a verdict on his teaching. Sent to Greece “on account of a pressing necessity in connection with ecclesiastical affairs”, he travelled through Palestine “and was ordained as presbyter in Caesarea by the bishops of that country” — without the consent of his own bishop, Demetrius of Alexandria. Eusebius, who had read the papers and wrote a defence of Origen in six books, then declines to narrate what followed: “The matters that were agitated concerning him on this account, and the decisions on these matters by those who presided over the churches… demand a separate treatise.” 2 Behind the ordination lay a grievance fifteen years old. On an earlier st…

tl.w: Palestine declines to receive the sentence (from 231)
tl.t: The Alexandrian verdict was not universally received — the first and most important fact about it. Alexander of Jerusalem and Theoctistus of Caesarea, the bishops who had ordained him, “attended on him constantly, as their only teacher, and allowed him to expound the Divine Scriptures, and to perform the other duties pertaining to ecclesiastical discourse”; Firmilian of Caesarea in Cappadocia summoned him into his own province “for the benefit of the churches” and afterwards travelled to Judea to sit under him. 8 For the remaining two decades of his life Origen taught, preached, and wrote as a presbyter of the Palestinian church, and the bishops of three provinces treated the Egyptian senten…

tl.w: Tortured under Decius; dies in communion (250 – c. 253)
tl.t: In the Decian persecution Origen was arrested and tortured — “bonds and bodily tortures and torments under the iron collar and in the dungeon; and how for many days with his feet stretched four spaces in the stocks he bore patiently the threats of fire” — under a judge who “strove eagerly with all his might not to end his life.” He did not recant. 10 He survived, broken, and died a few years later at Tyre, where he was buried, in his sixty-ninth year. 11 No church had excommunicated him for his teaching; he died a confessor of the faith, and the next generation of Greek theologians — Dionysius of Alexandria, Gregory Thaumaturgus, Pamphilus, Eusebius — were his pupils or his pupils' pupils.

tl.w: Methodius attacks the doctrine, not the man (c. 290 – 311)
tl.t: The first sustained theological assault comes from Methodius, bishop of Olympus in Lycia, martyred at the end of the last persecution. Jerome's catalogue lists three anti-Origen works among his six titles — “an excellent work On the resurrection, against Origen and On the Pythonissa and On free will , also against Origen” — and this is the first point in the story at which an Origenist position , rather than Origen's person or his standing, is what is under attack. 12 The chief work, a dialogue on the resurrection called the Aglaophon , goes after the pre-existence of souls — Origen “said that the body was given to the soul as a fetter after the fall, and that previously it lived without a b…

tl.w: Pamphilus and Eusebius answer the charges from prison (c. 307–310)
tl.t: Pamphilus of Caesarea, presbyter and keeper of the library in which Origen's books had been collected, was arrested in November 307 and beheaded on 16 February 310; he spent the intervening months composing, with his pupil Eusebius, an Apology for Origen in five books, to which Eusebius added a sixth after his death. Only the first survives, in Rufinus's Latin of 397, and it is the earliest surviving inventory of the charge-sheet. Pamphilus enumerates nine accusations before answering them: that Origen holds the Son unbegotten; that the Son was emitted, as Valentinus taught; that Christ is a mere man, as Paul of Samosata taught; that Christ's acts were done “only in appearance, and by allego…

tl.w: Epiphanius makes Origen a heresy in his own right (c. 375–377)
tl.t: In the Panarion , his catalogue of eighty heresies, Epiphanius of Salamis gives Origen an entry of his own — heresy 64 — alongside the Gnostics and the Arians. This is the decisive formal step: a churchman who died in communion is now listed as a heresiarch under his own name, in the reference work every later heresy-hunter would consult. The catalogue's own index states the charges in one sentence that nearly every later list varies: the Origenists “reject the resurrection of the dead, represent Christ and the Holy Spirit as creatures, allegorize Paradise, the heavens and all the rest, and foolishly say that Christ's kingdom will come to an end.” The chapter itself is unusual for the genre …

tl.w: Evagrius Ponticus builds the system the sixth century will condemn (c. 383–399)
tl.t: The man who most shaped what was finally anathematized under Origen's name never judged Origen at all, and belongs on this timeline as its hinge rather than as one of his accusers. Evagrius Ponticus — a deacon of the Cappadocian circle, ordained by Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus and present at the Council of Constantinople in 381, who fled the capital in 382 and settled among the monks of the Egyptian desert until his death in 399 — took the boldest speculations of Peri Archōn and forged them into a tight, numbered metaphysics in his Kephalaia Gnostica . 20 Recovered in its unexpurgated Syriac form by Antoine Guillaumont in 1958, that work states, in Evagrius's own chapters, the whole scheme…

tl.w: Theophilus of Alexandria: the first synodical condemnation (399–403)
tl.t: Theophilus of Alexandria had preached against the monks who held that God has a human body — the view Origen's books were quarried to refute — and in 399 a crowd of them came to Alexandria and threatened his life over it. He bought his way out by giving them what they demanded: “I myself also disapprove of Origen's works, and consider those who countenance them deserving of censure.” 24 He then expelled the Origenist monks from the monasteries of Nitria, and in 400 convened a council at Alexandria whose synodical letter Jerome translated: “The books of Origen have been read before a council of bishops and unanimously condemned.” Eight errors are enumerated, said to be drawn mainly from Peri …

The question reached Augustine from Spain, not from Palestine. In 414 the priest Paulus Orosius came to Hippo to report that Priscillianism had been answered in his province with books of Origen's, and that the readers had swallowed the cure and the poison together; he set out six articles of what was being taught, among them that the world was made last of all so that souls which had sinned beforehand might be purged in it, and that the eternal fire is neither real fire nor eternal. Augustine's reply refuses the simple verdict. He grants that the province got “no small good from those books, in the very matter where the error is mortal” — the Trinity, where Priscillian was worst — and then …

tl.w: Vincent of Lérins: the great trial of the Church (434)
tl.t: By the fifth century the Latin verdict is settled enough to be used as a teaching example. Vincent of Lérins heads a chapter of his Commonitorium “The Error of Origen a great Trial to the Church” and makes him the type of the learned teacher whose gifts magnify his error: “this Origen, such and so great as he was, wantonly abusing the grace of God, rashly following the bent of his own genius…” — with the result that “very many were led astray from the integrity of the faith, not by any human excellencies of this so great man, this so great doctor, this so great prophet, but, as the event showed, by the too perilous trial which he proved to be.” 36 Vincent also records the mitigating suggesti…

tl.w: The Latin book-lists: Gennadius and the Decretum Gelasianum (c. 480 – c. 550)
tl.t: In the West the verdict next appears not as a trial but as an entry in a handbook, which is how it reached the Middle Ages. Gennadius, presbyter of Marseilles, turned the charges into flat dogmatic canons in his Book of Church Doctrines : the risen body will not be exchanged for another, “not according to Origen”, but the same corruptible flesh will rise incorruptible; after the resurrection and the judgement we are not to believe in a restoration to come, “which Origen raves about”, whereby demons or wicked men, purged as it were by torments, return to the angelic dignity in which they were created; and the souls of men are not from the beginning among the other intellectual natures nor cre…

tl.w: Justinian's edict to Menas: the charges become anathemas (543)
tl.t: The sixth-century revival of the quarrel was monastic and Palestinian, and its occasion was a fight between rival parties of monks rather than anything Origen wrote. An Origenist current owing more to Evagrius of Pontus than to Origen had settled in the Judaean lauras; Sabas of the Great Laura went to Constantinople in 531 to ask for imperial help against it and got nothing; his successor Gelasius expelled the Origenists from the Great Laura in 537 and they regrouped at the New Laura, while two of their party, Domitian and Theodore Askidas, were made bishops and stayed at court. The anti-Origenist monks drew up a memorandum, the papal representative at Constantinople carried it to the empero…

tl.w: The council of 553: the fifteen anathemas and the eleventh canon (5 May – 2 June 553)
tl.t: “Condemned by the Fifth Ecumenical Council” is the one thing most people know about Origen, and three separate things travel under it. The council itself was summoned for other business entirely: its subject was the Three Chapters — Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret of Cyrrhus, Ibas of Edessa — which Justinian had already condemned by edict and now wanted endorsed, and which Pope Vigilius, brought to Constantinople under guard in 546, would not endorse. Eight sessions ran from 5 May to 2 June 553 under Eutychius of Constantinople, with the pope absent and his name struck from the diptychs; the bishops issued fourteen anathemas against the Three Chapters, and Vigilius capitulated the followin…

tl.w: Maximus the Confessor rebuilds the system from inside (c. 628)
tl.t: The most serious answer Origen ever received came from a man who never named him. Writing about 628, some seventy-five years after the anathemas, Maximus the Confessor took up a phrase of Gregory Nazianzen — that we are “a portion of God” who have “flowed down from above” — and found it being read in the condemned sense. He states that reading fairly and at length before touching it: “According to the opinion of these people, there once existed a unity of rational beings, by virtue of which we were connatural with God, in whom we had our remaining and abode. In addition to this they speak of a ‘movement’ that came about, as a result of which the rational beings were variously dispersed, prom…

tl.w: The name in the later councils and the Byzantine lists (680–787 and after)
tl.t: Two subsequent ecumenical councils treat the matter as closed and name Origen in company that was to become fixed. Constantinople III (680–681) refers to “the fifth holy synod, the latest of them, which was gathered here against Theodore of Mopsuestia, Origen, Didymus and Evagrius”; 57 Nicaea II (787) anathematizes “the mythical speculations of Origen, Evagrius and Didymus, as did the fifth synod, that assembled at Constantinople.” 58 Both are ratifications by reference rather than fresh trials; but they establish that from the seventh century onward the Church read 553 as having condemned Origen personally, and they harden the Origen–Didymus–Evagrius triad into a formula. It is that formula…

Three centuries after the anathemas, the most learned reader in Constantinople was still working through the condemned books and the defences of them. Photius — later patriarch, then a layman compiling reading notes for his brother — devotes three notices of his Bibliotheca to the Origen file, and the mixture in them is the point. On Peri Archōn itself he is hostile and brief, giving a book-by-book table of contents with the objections inserted as they arise: “Read Origen's four books On First Principles … In this his statements are often blasphemous; thus, he asserts that the Son was created by the Father, the Holy Ghost by the Son… He also makes other strange and impious statements, indulg…

tl.w: The doctrines anathematized again, without the name (1082)
tl.t: The text that actually told a Byzantine congregation who the church's enemies were was not the acts of a council but the Synodikon of Orthodoxy , chanted every first Sunday of Lent from 843 onward. It names them at length — Arius “the first fighter against God and leader of the heresies”, Nestorius, Valentinus, Paul of Samosata, Sabellius, Eutyches, Dioscorus, Severus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, “and simply all heretics”. In the received text Origen is not among them, and neither are Didymus or Evagrius. 63 What happened instead is more interesting than a name on a list. In March 1082 the philosopher John Italos was tried at Constantinople, and eleven chapters against him were added to the Synodikon …

tl.w: The Latin schools: condemned in the handbook, quoted on every other page (12th century)
tl.t: The West inherited the opposite arrangement. There the name was formally condemned and the books were read continuously, because Rufinus and Jerome had put most of the homilies and commentaries into Latin before the quarrel closed — so that, as the standard English edition of Rufinus puts it, “a considerable part of the works of the great Alexandrian have floated down across the ocean of the Dark Ages, and, while lost in their native Greek, have in their Latin garb come to enrich the later civilization of the West.” 65 The clearest single specimen of the resulting arrangement is Peter Abelard's Sic et Non , the twelfth century's central textbook of theological method. Its prologue prints the…

tl.w: “Is Origen saved?”: Pico, Merlin, and the printed Origen (1486–1574)
tl.t: In December 1486 Giovanni Pico della Mirandola published nine hundred theses for public disputation at Rome. The last of the twenty-nine he offered on his own theological opinion reads: “It is more reasonable to believe that Origen is saved than to believe that he is damned.” 69 A commission appointed by Innocent VIII in February 1487 indicted thirteen of the nine hundred, and this was among them; Pico reports the censure in his own words — the masters said the conclusion was “rash and reprehensible, and savouring of heresy, and contrary to the determination of the universal Church” — and answered it with a treatise, the Disputatio de salute Origenis , laid out in seven articles of which the…

tl.w: Defended, censured again, and finally edited (1648–1759)
tl.t: The seventeenth century argued the case out in print, and it did not divide along the line one would expect. The fullest defence was a Jesuit's: Pierre Halloix's Origenes defensus (Liège, 1648) — which Rome then put on the Index donec corrigatur , the decree communicated to its author in 1650 and published in 1655. The roster of Origen's modern defenders drawn up later in the century by the Dominican Noël Alexandre — Pico, Merlin, Génébrard, Étienne Binet, Halloix — is a list of Catholics, and the sharpest early-modern hostility came from Protestants. 75 The exception is England, where a group around the Cambridge Platonists revived the condemned doctrines themselves. An anonymous Letter of …

The twentieth century largely reversed the verdict's terms, and it did so in a way worth stating precisely: not by pronouncing the condemned propositions orthodox — almost no one has argued that — but by arguing that the propositions condemned in 543 and 553 are sixth-century Origenism rather than Origen, and that his manner in the offending book was exploratory where his judges read it as dogmatic. The work was philological before it was theological, and the first landmark is a mistake. In 1913 Paul Koetschau published Peri Archōn in the Berlin corpus of the early Greek Christian writers. Rufinus had admitted omitting passages he took to be heretical interpolations; Koetschau concluded that…

ar.q: Did Origen’s allegory dissolve the literal and historical sense of Scripture?
ar.c: Sixthly, he so allegorises Paradise as to destroy historical truth, understanding angels instead of trees, heavenly virtues instead of rivers, and he overthrows all that is contained in the history of Paradise by his figurative interpretation. — Jerome, Against John of Jerusalem 7 , relaying the charge-sheet Epiphanius pressed against Origen, link . 1 That is the accusation in its sharpest form: Origen’s allegory does not merely add a spiritual sense on top of the history, it destroys the history — and, the charge continues, it does so wherever the letter is inconvenient, until nothing in the …
ar.a: contested. Taken as the accusers took it — that Origen’s allegory dissolves the historical sense of Scripture wherever the letter is inconvenient — the charge is a caricature, and the defense is strong against it: the threefold sense makes the “common and historical sense” the body on which everything else is raised, Origen states that the historically-true passages are “much more numerous” than the purely spiritual, he suspends the letter by a s…

ar.q: Was Origen condemned by a standard that did not exist in his lifetime?
ar.c: The holy apostles, in preaching the faith of Christ, delivered themselves with the utmost clearness on certain points which they believed to be necessary to every one, even to those who seemed somewhat dull in the investigation of divine knowledge; leaving, however, the grounds of their statements to be examined into by those who should deserve the excellent gifts of the Spirit… On other subjects, however, they merely stated the fact that things were so, keeping silence as to the manner or origin of their existence; clearly in order that the more zealous of their successors… might have a subje…
ar.a: contested. The historical spine of the argument is sound and is not seriously disputed: on the questions Origen was chiefly condemned for — the soul's origin, the mode of the risen body, the fate of the damned, the inner relations of the Trinity — the rule of faith of his day had defined nothing, he said so in his own preface and framed his treatment as inquiry, and men of unquestioned standing went on leaving the same questions open for generati…

ar.q: Did Rome in 400–401 condemn Origen's books only, and not the man?
ar.c: Anastasius, while declaring that Origen was entirely unknown to him, condemned the propositions extracted from his books. 1 — the standard handbook statement of what Rome did in 400–401. The assertion is that the Roman sentence, like the Egyptian and Cypriot synods of the same year, fell on a body of writing and not on the person of a presbyter a century and a half dead: propositions were rejected, reading was forbidden, and Origen himself was left where the fourth century had left him.
ar.a: weak as stated. The books-not-the-man reading is true of the Alexandrian and Cypriot synods of 400 and false of the Roman letters of 400–401, and the handbooks arrive at it by assimilating the one to the other. Anastasius condemned “they and their author” alike, and imputed to Origen a purpose to dismantle the apostolic faith. Two narrower claims in the neighbourhood do hold, and are worth keeping: that no canonical anathema on the person of Orig…

ar.q: Did the fifteen anathemas of 553 condemn sixth-century Evagrian Origenism rather than Origen?
ar.c: X. If anyone shall say that after the resurrection the body of the Lord was ethereal, having the form of a sphere, and that such shall be the bodies of all after the resurrection…: let him be anathema. XII. If anyone shall say that the heavenly Powers and all men and the Devil and evil spirits are united with the Word of God in all respects, as the Nous which is by them called Christ and which is in the form of God, and which humbled itself as they say…: let him be anathema. XIV. If anyone shall say that all reasonable beings will one day be united in one, when the hypostases as well as the nu…
ar.a: contested. The philological core is sound and is no longer seriously disputed: Guillaumont established that the fifteen anathemas of 553 track the Evagrian system of the sixth-century Palestinian monks and quote Peri Archōn nowhere, and the most distinctive condemned propositions — the spherical body, the nous -Christ, the final equality of every spirit with Christ — are demonstrably not in Origen's surviving text. To that extent the thesis holds…

ar.q: Did Origen teach universal restoration as a doctrine — and was it condemnable in his day?
ar.c: We think, indeed, that the goodness of God, through His Christ, may recall all His creatures to one end, even His enemies being conquered and subdued… for Christ must reign until He hath put all enemies under His feet. — Origen, De Principiis I.6.1 (c. 229) , link . 1 Three centuries later the ninth anathema of Justinian's edict to Menas condemned anyone who “says or holds that the punishment of demons and impious human beings is temporary and that it will have an end at some time, and that there will be a restoration of demons and impious human beings”; 2 the first of the fifteen anathemas of…
ar.a: contested. The historical half of the interpretation holds and is not seriously disputed: universal restoration was not a defined error when Origen taught it, it rests on a real and central scriptural chain (1 Corinthians 15:28; Acts 3:21; Colossians 1:20), and it kept reputable company for three centuries — decisively, Gregory of Nyssa taught the same conclusion from the same verse and was never condemned. To read the ninth anathema of 543 as th…

ar.q: Did Origen teach that “astronomy is the cause of events” — that the stars govern what happens?
ar.c: The accusation sits in the standing charge-list against Origen. In Photius’s ninth-century summary of an anonymous five-book Apology for Origen , the defender enumerates fifteen counts he means to answer as “mere slanders,” refuting each “by quotations from his writings”; the eighth is the charge “that astronomy is the cause of events” — standing, in the same breath, beside “that magic is not an evil” and beside transmigration and the denial of eternal punishment. 1 “Astronomy” here means judicial astrology — the reading of nativities and fortunes off the sky — and the charge is that Origen ma…
ar.a: weak. “Astronomy is the cause of events” ascribes to Origen the astral determinism he refuted more fully than any Father before him — the stars signify but do not cause , astral necessity would destroy free will and indict God, and the astrologer’s root error is mistaking the sign for its author ( Philocalia 23 = Commentary on Genesis III, on Genesis 1:14). The charge is not baseless invention: it distorts two real Origenist doctrines — that the …

ar.q: Was Origen's pre-existent soul of Christ a theological achievement — the full human soul Apollinaris denied and Chalcedon vindicated?
ar.c: The interpretation weighed here is that Origen's account of the soul of Christ is a genuine theological advance, wrongly swept up in his condemnation. In Peri Archōn II.6 Origen asks how the infinite Word could be joined to mortal flesh, and answers with a third term. One rational creature, of all those made at the beginning, clung to the Word with a love so total that it never cooled; that soul, “inhering, from the beginning of the creation… inseparably and indissolubly in Him,” becomes the medium of the incarnation: This substance of a soul, then, being intermediate between God and the flesh…
ar.a: contested. By the lights of the history of doctrine the argument is strong and largely granted: Origen is among the first to insist, deliberately and against his school's grain, that Christ assumed a complete rational human soul, he defends it as the very point most likely to trouble a reader, and that insistence is vindicated, not refuted, when Chalcedon confesses Christ “of a reasonable soul and body” against Apollinaris. The specialists are ri…

ar.q: Did Origen teach that the “coats of skins” (Genesis 3:21) are the mortal human body?
ar.c: In the fourth place, he interprets the coats of skins, with which Adam and Eve were clothed after their fall and ejection from Paradise, to be human bodies, and we are to suppose of course that previously, in Paradise, they had neither flesh, sinews, nor bones. — Jerome, Against John of Jerusalem 7 , the fourth of the eight Origenist errors Epiphanius had drawn up, link . 1 That is the charge in its sharpest form. It concerns not the pre-existence of the soul — weighed on its own page — but the origin of the body : that the flesh we now wear was a garment God fashioned for fallen souls, so tha…
ar.a: contested. That Origen connected the “coats of skins” of Genesis 3:21 with the soul’s descent into an earthly body — embodiment following upon the fall — can be read from his own surviving words, Against Celsus IV.40, and is corroborated by his reserve about the “entrance of souls into bodies” (V.29) and by Methodius’s refutation of Origenists who held the skins to be bodies around 300. To that extent the charge reports a real feature of his thou…

ar.q: Was Origen's condemnation driven by ecclesiastical politics rather than by his doctrine?
ar.c: [Theophilus] condemned Origen, who had been dead nearly two hundred years: not having this as his first object, but rather his purpose of revenge on Dioscorus and his brethren. — Socrates Scholasticus, Church History VI.10 , on Theophilus of Alexandria's synods of 400, link . 1 The interpretation weighed here generalizes Socrates's verdict on one node to the whole history: that Origen was condemned not because the Church came to a settled theological judgement against him but because, at each turn, his name was a usable weapon in a fight about jurisdiction, patronage, or power — the doctrine t…
ar.a: contested. The descriptive claim is strong: every institutional condemnation of Origen sits inside a quarrel about something other than his theology — Demetrius's jurisdiction, the campaigns against Chrysostom and the Tall Brothers, Jerome's reputation, the monastic war behind Justinian's edict and the Three Chapters intrigue behind the council of 553 — and contemporaries and modern historians alike say so. The advocated claim, that doctrine was …

ar.q: Did 553 condemn a school, or both extremes at once? Origen and Theodore in the same council
ar.c: If anyone does not anathematize Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Apollinarius, Nestorius, Eutyches and Origen, as well as their heretical books… let him be anathema. If anyone defends the heretical Theodore of Mopsuestia, who said that God the Word is one, while quite another is Christ… let him be anathema. — Second Council of Constantinople (553), the eleventh and twelfth of its fourteen anathemas . 1 Back to back in the council's own capitula stand the two names this page sets side by side: Origen of Alexandria, whose method was the allegorical reading of Scripture pressed to its boldest reach, …
ar.a: contested. The core observation is sound and worth making: the council of 553 anathematized Origen the allegorist and Theodore of Mopsuestia the literalist in adjacent anathemas of its own capitula, on wholly unrelated charges, so the reading of 553 as an anti-allegory or anti-Origen purge of an Alexandrian school cannot stand — a council hunting allegory does not condemn its greatest enemy. And the anachronism critique the timeline presses for O…

ar.q: Were Origen's condemned opinions offered as inquiry rather than assertion, so that the anathemas condemn a genre error?
ar.c: The cause of the diversity of opinion on these subjects is this, viz., that those subjects on which we discourse are treated by us with great solicitude and caution, in the manner rather of an investigation and discussion, than in that of fixed and certain decision. — Origen, De Principiis I.6.1 (c. 229) , link . 1 Origen introduces the restoration of all things — the doctrine the ninth anathema of 543 would condemn — with that sentence, and warns in the same breath that a reader “full of preconceptions and prejudices” may “judge these to be heretical… yielding… not so much to the convictions …
ar.a: contested. The descriptive half of the interpretation is sound and should be granted without grudging: Peri Archōn is a self-consciously exploratory book. Origen divides the faith into the plainly-delivered and the left-open, assigns his most-condemned speculations to the second class in the preface, flags them as “investigation and discussion” as he treats them, and expressly asks the reader to judge — and a hostile witness confirms the disclaim…

ar.q: Did the devil’s-salvation charge misrepresent Origen?
ar.c: …certain of these men who seek for matters of contention, ascribe to us and our teaching the blasphemy… namely, that the father of wickedness and perdition of those who shall be cast out of the kingdom of God can be saved; a thing which not even a madman can say. — Origen, letter to friends at Alexandria, as translated by Jerome, Apology against Rufinus II.18 , link . 1 The interpretation this page weighs is the one Origen states in his own defence and his modern defenders repeat: that the charge condemned by Theophilus in 400 and by Justinian in 543 — that Origen taught the devil himself will…
ar.a: contested. The charge in the form the councils enforced — that Origen positively taught the salvation of Satan, or that Christ will be crucified for the demons — does misrepresent him: he denied it explicitly, his book refers the devil’s conversion to the reader as an open question, and what he describes at the end is the destruction of a hostile will, not the enthronement of evil. To that extent the interpretation is sound, and the proponent who…

ar.q: Does Origen’s system require the devil’s final salvation?
ar.c: We think, indeed, that the goodness of God, through His Christ, may recall all His creatures to one end, even His enemies being conquered and subdued. For thus says holy Scripture, The Lord said to My Lord, Sit at My right hand, until I make Your enemies Your footstool. — Origen, De Principiis I.6.1 (c. 229) , link . 1 The interpretation weighed here is the one both Origen’s accusers and a strand of modern scholarship draw from that premise: that the architecture of Peri Archōn — one original unity, a universal fall, a restoration in which the end answers to the beginning — makes the ultimate …
ar.a: plausible. The interpretation is coherent, grounded in the primary text, and probably right in its measured form: Origen’s system does tend strongly toward the ultimate reconciliation of every fallen rational creature, the being called the devil among them. The restoration is said to reach “even His enemies”; the end is built to answer to a lost unity; the last enemy is destroyed by the removal of its enmity while its God-made substance persists;…

ar.q: Did Origen teach that God’s power is finite — and that creation is coeternal with God?
ar.c: If anyone says or holds that God’s power is finite and that he created [only] what he could grasp and comprehend, or that creation is coeternal with God, let him be anathema. — Justinian, edict to Menas (543), anathema 8 , tr. Richard Price . 1 The charge is older than the anathema. In his paschal letter for 402, translated into Latin by Jerome, Theophilus of Alexandria had already fastened both strands on Origen, quoting him: “God made as many things as he could grasp and hold in subjection to himself and control by his providence,” and concluding that “Origen, that pillar of truth, asserts t…
ar.a: contested. The charge bundles two inferences of unequal strength, and the honest verdict tracks the split. The eternal-creation half is genuinely Origen’s: he argued from divine immutability that God’s creating has no absolute beginning, and the objection that this makes the world necessary — and so compromises God’s freedom and edges toward coeternity — is a fair inference from his own premises, pressed by Methodius in his century and answered b…

ar.q: Did Origen teach that hellfire is the fire of a guilty conscience, not a material, external fire?
ar.c: Among the standing charges against Peri Archōn is that Origen emptied the eschatological threatenings of the Gospel by denying a real, external fire of punishment. On this reading the “everlasting fire,” the “furnace,” and the “outer darkness” are not places or substances a sinner is cast into, but images for an inward state: the fire is the burning of a guilty conscience, the memory of one’s own sins set before the eyes and tormenting the soul that made them. The interpretation weighed here is the plain one — that this charge reports something Origen actually taught — and, as with the ensoule…
ar.a: sound. That Origen taught the fire of hell to be a fire each sinner kindles from the fuel of his own sins — the guilty conscience forced to witness against itself, a purgative burning rather than a material fire prepared beforehand — is one of the charges that can be read straight out of his own text, Peri Archōn II.10 and Against Celsus V, and Jerome reported it faithfully. Trust the substance of the charge; qualify only what it is taken to prov…

ar.q: Was the first condemnation of Origen a disciplinary sentence rather than a verdict on his doctrine?
ar.c: He stands condemned by his bishop, Demetrius, only the bishops of Palestine, Arabia, Phenicia, and Achaia dissenting. Imperial Rome consents to his condemnation, and even convenes a senate to censure him, not—as the rabid hounds who now pursue him cry—because of the novelty or heterodoxy of his doctrines, but because men could not tolerate the incomparable eloquence and knowledge which, when once he opened his lips, made others seem dumb. — Jerome, Letter 33.4, to Paula (c. 384) , link . 1 The claim under weight is the sober core of this: that the sentence of c. 231–232 was passed on Origen's …
ar.a: sound. On the question actually at issue — what the sentence of c. 231–232 was passed for — the disciplinary reading is the only one the evidence supports, and it is the standing scholarly position. The occasion was an irregular ordination; the terms of both sittings concern residence, teaching licence and priestly rank; the sole additional charge named anywhere is the castration; and the neighbouring provinces treated the sentence as a matter of…

ar.q: Did Origen teach that the image and likeness of God was lost, no longer remaining in man after the fall?
ar.c: The eighth is Origen's cavil that the image and likeness of God, in which man was created, was lost, and was no longer in man after he was expelled from Paradise. — Jerome, Against John of Jerusalem 7 , the eighth and last of the Origenist errors Epiphanius had drawn up, link . 1 The charge is an anthropological one, and it stands apart from its neighbours on the same list — the coats of skins as the mortal body and the allegorized Paradise . Those concern how the body arose; this concerns what the fall destroyed — whether, on Origen’s account, the divine image survived Adam’s sin at all. The …
ar.a: weak. The charge that Origen taught the image and likeness of God to have been “lost, and no longer in man after he was expelled from Paradise” inverts his best-attested teaching. His governing distinction, stated in Peri Archōn III.6.1 and again in Against Celsus IV.30, is that man retains the image, given at creation, and must acquire the likeness, reserved for the consummation and won by imitation of God — the deficiency lies on the side of th…

ar.q: Is Epiphanius' story that Origen apostatized under persecution — the incense sacrifice, forced on him to escape sexual violation — credible?
ar.c: Epiphanius opens his heresy-entry on Origen with a life of him, and it is not Eusebius’s . He begins generously — son of the martyr Leonidas, tortured, defiant at the Serapeum — and then turns: But his deeds did not remain worthy of the prize till the end… With diabolical malice the workers of iniquity thought of mistreating him sexually and making that his punishment, and they secured a black to abuse his body. But Origen could not bear even the thought of this devil’s work, and shouted that, given the choice of either, he would rather sacrifice. Certainly, as is widely reported, he did not d…
ar.a: weak. As biography the incense-sacrifice story does not hold. In its favour there is only that Origen truly left Alexandria and never taught there again, that the kind of forced sacrifice it describes was a real feature of the persecutions, and that Epiphanius may transmit a genuinely independent Palestinian oral tradition rather than copying a book. That keeps the tale from being a bald invention with nothing behind it. But it is not enough to m…

ar.q: Did the “heretical interpolation” defence cut both ways — invoked to keep Gregory of Nyssa orthodox, refused to keep Origen’s book his own?
ar.c: Gregory of Nyssa taught the final restoration of all rational creatures, the devil included, and was never condemned for it — he was crowned “father of the fathers” by the seventh ecumenical council. Origen taught the same restoration, from the same verse (1 Corinthians 15:28, “that God may be all in all”), and was anathematized for it. Faced with the embarrassment of a saint who held a condemned doctrine, Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople (d. 733), wrote a treatise — the Antapodotikos , now lost but summarized by Photius in the Bibliotheca — arguing that Nyssa never really held it: the of…
ar.a: Contested. The comparandum is striking and true as far as it goes: the same “the offending passages are not authentic” move was reached for to keep Gregory of Nyssa orthodox and refused to keep Origen’s book his own, and the underlying asymmetry — one doctrine, one verse, opposite verdicts turning on whose reputation was at stake — is real evidence that the tradition judged the restoration by person, not by text. That much belongs to, and reinfor…

ar.q: Did Origen teach that “magic is not an evil” — that certain names have a real, natural power?
ar.c: Two of the standing charge-lists against Origen accuse him of holding, flatly, that magic is not an evil . In Photius’s ninth-century summary of an anonymous defence of Origen, the seventh of the fifteen counts the defender tries to answer is the charge “that magic is not an evil”; 1 and the synodical letter of the Alexandrian council of 400, translated into Latin by Jerome, lists among Origen’s eight chief errors the proposition “Magic, if real, is not evil” — set, tellingly, between the charge that “the stars are conscious of their own movements, and the demons know the future by their cours…
ar.a: contested. That Origen taught a real, natural power in certain names — the divine and angelic names above all, untranslatable without loss — is beyond dispute and argued in his own words ( Against Celsus I.24–25, V.45), and he does there defend “the so-called magic” as a coherent system rather than an empty superstition. To that extent the charge is grounded, strong by the lights of philology and history-of-religions. But the specific proposition…

ar.q: Did Origen teach reincarnation (the transmigration of souls)?
ar.c: In this place it does not appear to me that by Elijah the soul is spoken of, lest I should fall into the dogma of transmigration, which is foreign to the church of God, and not handed down by the Apostles, nor anywhere set forth in the Scriptures. — Origen, Commentary on Matthew XIII.1 (on Matthew 17:10–13) , link . 1 That is Origen’s own verdict on the doctrine, written at the one place where a reader might most expect him to embrace it — the Baptist whom Jesus calls Elijah “who is to come.” The interpretation weighed here is the corollary his defenders draw from it: that Origen was no reinca…
ar.a: sound. The interpretation holds. Origen rejected the transmigration of souls through successive earthly bodies openly and repeatedly — in the Commentary on Matthew (“foreign to the church of God”), the Commentary on John (the churchman “repudiates the doctrine of transcorporation as a false one”), and Against Celsus (a “folly” to be cured, distinct from “the metempsychosis of Plato”) — and he neutralised the Elijah/John text that reincarnationist…

ar.q: Was Origen himself anathematized by an ecumenical council?
ar.c: Recent studies have shown that these anathemas cannot be attributed to this council. — Norman P. Tanner’s standard edition of the conciliar decrees, printing the acts of 553 without the fifteen anathemas against Origen, link . 1 The interpretation weighed here is the canonical corollary usually drawn from that editorial judgement: that the Second Council of Constantinople — the Fifth Ecumenical Council — did not, as an act of the council in session, anathematize Origen. Two textual facts carry it. The fifteen anathemas, the fullest statement of what was condemned, belong (on this view) to a pr…
ar.a: contested. The argument is strong exactly where it is narrow and fails where it is made to prove too much. It is true, and now the majority editorial position, that the fifteen anathemas against Origen cannot be attributed to the recorded sessions of the Fifth Ecumenical Council, and arguable that Origen’s name in the eleventh canon is secondary — so the tidy statement that the council in formal session personally anathematized the man is not sec…

ar.q: Did Origen teach that God and all rational creatures are “of one and the same essence” — a creaturely consubstantiality that dissolves the line between Creator …
ar.c: The charge is Jerome’s, and he makes it the crescendo of his catalogue of Origen’s errors in Letter 124 to Avitus (c. 409–410), a section-by-section digest of the lost Greek Peri Archōn . Reaching the treatise’s closing recapitulation, Jerome renders Origen thus: God and His only-begotten Son and the Holy Spirit are of an intellectual and reasonable nature. But so also are the angels, the powers, and the virtues, as well as the inward man who is created in the image and after the likeness of God. From which I conclude that God and they are in some sort of one essence. — then pounces on the qua…
ar.a: weak. The interpretation — that Origen taught God and all rational creatures to be “of one and the same essence,” a consubstantiality dissolving the Creator/creature line — does not hold on its best case. Its one hard proof-text is an argument for the soul’s immortality whose whole force is participation , the relation that presupposes the participant is not what it shares in; Origen builds degree and diversity into it, hedges it with “in some so…

ar.q: Is it more reasonable to believe Origen saved than damned?
ar.c: It is more reasonable to believe that Origen is saved than to believe that he is damned. — Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the last of the twenty-nine theses he offered on his own theological opinion in the nine hundred Conclusiones published for public disputation at Rome in December 1486 (“Rationabilius est credere Origenem esse salvum, quam credere ipsum esse damnatum”). 1 The interpretation weighed here is the one Pico stated and defended, and it is worth stating precisely, because its force lies in its modesty. It is not the claim that Origen’s condemned doctrines are true; almost no one h…
ar.a: contested. The interpretation is genuinely disputed, with strong and irreducible cases on both sides, and — uniquely among the questions on this timeline — it concerns something no evidence can decide. Taken as Pico stated it, a comparison of reasonableness, it is well grounded: Origen died in communion, a confessor unbroken under torture, never tried in life for the doctrines later condemned; his gravest speculations were offered in questions th…

ar.q: Was the pre-existence of souls an open question when Origen taught it — so that the anathema of 543 judges him by a later rule?
ar.c: The apostles delivered themselves with the utmost clearness on certain points which they believed to be necessary to every one… but on other subjects they merely stated the fact that things were so, keeping silence as to the manner or origin of their existence… Whether the soul be derived from the seed by a process of traducianism, so that the reason or substance of it may be considered as placed in the seminal particles of the body themselves, or whether it has any other beginning; and this beginning, itself, whether it be by birth or not, or whether bestowed upon the body from without or no,…
ar.a: contested. The historical premise holds and is not seriously in dispute: there was no rule of faith on the soul's origin in Origen's day, he said so, no contemporary said otherwise, the first reaction to the doctrine was philosophical refutation rather than ecclesiastical sentence, and a Roman priest under interrogation in 400, a bishop consecrated in 410, and a bishop of Hippo writing in 415 all treated the question as unsettled. On that much th…

ar.q: Did Origen deny the resurrection of the flesh — and did he teach that risen bodies are spherical?
ar.c: Two charges travel together under one heading, and the argument weighed here is the modern defence that separates them. The first and blunter charge is that Origen denied the resurrection of the body outright — it stands fifth in the list a martyr answered around 307, and it is fifth again in Jerome’s eight-point indictment of 397: Origen “most openly denies the resurrection of the flesh and the bodily structure, and the distinction of senses.” 1 The second, sharper charge specifies the offending picture: that the risen body sheds its distinct members and becomes a round, luminous globe. Jerom…
ar.a: contested. The defence is sound on its two negative claims and overstated on its positive framing. It is right, and decisively, that the flat “Origen denied the resurrection” is false: he taught a real resurrection body, continuous with the earthly one, argued from 1 Corinthians 15, and said so against Celsus in Greek that no translator can be blamed for. It is right, too, that the spherical body of the 553 anathema is not his — it is a sixth-cen…

ar.q: Did Origen teach that Christ will be crucified again in the heavens to save the demons?
ar.c: …it may indeed be overbold to suppose that He will suffer in heaven; yet if there is spiritual wickedness in heavenly places… why need we fear to imagine a like occurrence in the upper world… so that the nations of all realms shall be saved by a passion of Christ? — Origen, as quoted by Jerome, Letter 124 to Avitus §13 , link . 1 This is the sharpest and most notorious charge in the whole catalogue against Origen, and it is more specific than the general accusation that he taught the devil’s salvation. The mechanism here is a repeated passion of Christ : that in a coming age Christ will suffer…
ar.a: weak. As a doctrine attributed to Origen, the second crucifixion does not hold. It is the hardest of the charges and the one with the most textual color — Origen really did float, in his own words, a saving passion “in the upper world,” and his picture of a Christ who laments and intercedes until all are gathered gives the motif a non-hostile root. That is enough to keep the charge from being a pure fabrication. But it is not enough to make it Or…

ar.q: Did Origen teach that the two Seraphim of Isaiah 6 are the Son and the Holy Spirit — and does the identification rank them among the creatures?
ar.c: The identification is stated flatly in the chapter of Peri Archōn that argues for the Holy Spirit’s divinity. Origen ascribes it to his teacher: My Hebrew master also used to say that those two seraphim in Isaiah, which are described as having each six wings, and calling to one another, and saying, “Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God of hosts,” were to be understood of the only-begotten Son of God and of the Holy Spirit. And we think that that expression also which occurs in the hymn of Habakkuk, “In the midst either of the two living things, or of the two lives, Thou wilt be known,” ought to b…
ar.a: contested. That Origen taught the two seraphim to be the Son and the Holy Spirit is beyond dispute: he states it in Peri Archōn I.3.4 and preaches it in the first Homily on Isaiah , so the charge is neither invented nor misattributed. Read as proof of a proto-Arian subordinationism it overreaches — Origen has it from “my Hebrew master,” deploys it to exhibit an undivided Trinity and the Son and Spirit as the ground of the knowledge of the Father,…

ar.q: Was Origen singled out? The condemned views measured against who else held them
ar.c: But He that becomes “all” things will be “in all” things too; and herein it appears to me that Scripture teaches the complete annihilation of evil… even from those evil spirits shall rise in harmony the confession of Christ's Lordship. — Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection (c. 380) , link . 1 That is Origen's conclusion — the restoration of all rational creatures, the demons included, argued from “that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28) — in the mouth of a bishop whom no council ever anathematized, whom the Second Council of Nicaea named among the holy Fathers and the …
ar.a: contested. Run the comparison the whole timeline invites — for each condemned view, who else held it and what happened to them — and it splits cleanly in two. The complaint is strong that enforcement was uneven, posthumous, and by person rather than by proposition: Gregory of Nyssa taught the identical restoration from the identical verse and was crowned “father of the fathers” by the council that condemned Origen for it; Clement, who taught Orig…

ar.q: Did Origen teach that the Son’s kingdom will come to an end?
ar.c: If anyone shall say that the heavenly Powers and all men and the Devil and evil spirits are united with the Word of God in all respects, as the Nous which is by them called Christ…; and [if anyone shall say] that the Kingdom of Christ shall have an end: let him be anathema. — the twelfth of the fifteen anathemas against Origen (553), NPNF2 XIV . 1 The charge is one of the oldest and most stable on the whole timeline. Epiphanius’s Panarion of the 370s already sums up the Origenist error in a single sentence — the Origenists “reject the resurrection of the dead, represent Christ and the Holy Spi…
ar.a: contested. The honest verdict splits the charge from the reading it serves. Origen genuinely does expound 1 Corinthians 15:24–28 to mean that Christ’s mediatorial kingdom is a dispensation “delivered up” to the Father, that the economy runs on his “end is like the beginning” axiom, and that his subordination of the Son sits under it — so the charge fastens on real text and real premises, not a phantom, and the same verse yielded an openly aboliti…

ar.q: Did Origen teach that the sun, moon, and stars are living, ensouled rational beings?
ar.c: The charge is one of the most heavily attested against Origen, and it hardens into a numbered anathema.
