In the edict Justinian sent to Menas of Constantinople in 543, the sixth anathema condemns anyone who “says or holds that heaven, sun, moon, stars, and the waters above the heavens are ensouled and rational powers.” 1 Ten years later the third of the fifteen anathemas against the Origenists condemns the view “that the sun, the moon and the stars are also reasonable beings, and that they have only become what they are because they turned towards evil.” 2 The proposition has two joints: that t…
ar.a: sound. That Origen taught the sun, moon and stars to be living, ensouled, rational beings whose souls pre-existed their luminous bodies is one of the few charges on the sixth-century list that can be laid straight against his own surviving words — Peri Archōn I.7 and Against Celsus V — and the accusers reported it faithfully. Trust the substance of the charge; treat with care only its packaging : the flat dogmatic wording overshoots a speculation…

ar.q: Was Origen's subordination of the Son a pre-Nicene idiom — so that reading him as an Arian is anachronistic?
ar.c: The charge answered here is that Origen subordinated the Son (and the Spirit below the Son) to the Father in a way the Church would later declare heretical. The texts cited for it are genuine. In the Commentary on John the Father alone is “Very God”: God on the one hand is Very God (Autotheos, God of Himself)… but… all beyond the Very God is made God by participation in His divinity, and is not to be called simply God (with the article), but rather God (without article). And thus the first-born of all creation, who is the first to be with God, and to attract to Himself divinity, is a being of …
ar.a: contested. By the lights of the history of doctrine the argument is strong: Origen's Trinitarian idiom is the shared ante-Nicene idiom, he is a genuine source of the eternal generation that Nicaea required, Athanasius cited him against the Arians by name, and to brand him an Arian is a retrojection that would equally brand Justin and Tertullian. On that the defence holds. By the lights of systematic theology it falls short of clearing him: the su…

ar.q: Did Origen teach an endless succession of worlds — and does it entail a second fall?
ar.c: …not then for the first time did God begin to work when He made this visible world; but as, after its destruction, there will be another world, so also we believe that others existed before the present came into being… It is not, however, to be supposed that several worlds existed at once, but that, after the end of this present world, others will take their beginning. — Origen, De Principiis III.5.3 (c. 229) , link . 1 Three centuries later the second anathema of Justinian’s edict of 543 and the fifteen anathemas of 553 turned this into a charge: the last of the fifteen condemns anyone who sa…
ar.a: contested. The core of the interpretation is sound and well-evidenced. Origen did teach a succession of ages, but he built it as providential and moral rather than fated, he ridiculed the Stoic doctrine of identical recurrence by name, and he aimed the whole sequence at a genuine terminus — God “all in all”, the last enemy destroyed, an incorporeal unity in which “there will no longer be any diversity.” The systematized “wheel of identical worlds…

ar.q: Can Origen be fairly judged at all, given how his text reaches us?
ar.c: …he “added or struck out whatever he chose, and changed things as he thought right, and published it abroad as if it were my work.” — Origen, in a letter “to certain intimate friends at Alexandria” complaining of the falsification of the record of a disputation, preserved by Rufinus , On the Falsification of the Works of Origen , link . 1 The interpretation weighed here generalises Origen’s own alarm into a verdict on the whole controversy: that the surviving evidence for what he taught is so systematically shaped by partisans on both sides — a defender who softened him, prosecutors who sharpe…
ar.a: contested. The skepticism is right about the letter and wrong about the substance, and the two verdicts are both firm, which is what makes it genuinely disputed rather than simply mistaken. On the exact wording of the condemned system — the fifteen anathemas, the spherical body, the propositions quoted as if lifted from his page — the caution is sound: Peri Archōn survives whole only in a translation that announced its own softening, its Greek re…

ds.t: The Origenist Controversy (Jerome and Rufinus)
ds.q: This is the story of a friendship that turned into one of the fiercest quarrels of the early Church. Jerome (c. 347–420) and Rufinus of Aquileia (c. 344/345–411) were the closest of friends in their youth — fellow ascetics who prayed, studied, and dreamed of the monastic life together — and both were, at first, ardent admirers of the great third-century theologian Origen. Twenty years later they were public enemies, trading apologies and invectives over whether Origen was a saint or a heretic and whose translations had betrayed the truth. The rupture drew in bishops, popes, and emperors, and it outlived both men.

tl.t: Rufinus was born about 344 or 345 at Concordia, in the territory between Aquileia and Altinum in north-eastern Italy, and was baptized about his twenty-eighth year in the monastic community at Aquileia. 1

At Aquileia a brotherhood of young ascetics formed around Jerome and Rufinus — with Bonosus, Hylas, and Heliodorus — the high point of the friendship. 2 Its sudden breakup scattered the friends; Jerome, driven east, later wrote to Rufinus of “that sudden whirlwind” that “dragged me from your side, severing with its impious wrench the bonds of affection in which we were knit together.” 3

tl.w: The friends part for the East; Rufinus goes with Melania (c. 372)
tl.t: When the company was scattered, Rufinus “joined the noble Roman lady, Melania, in her pilgrimage to the East,” while Jerome made his own way to Syria and the desert of Chalcis. 4

tl.w: Jerome's letters from Syria: come to me (374)
tl.t: From Antioch and the desert, Jerome wrote aching letters urging Rufinus — then in Egypt — to join him, longing to see his friend “more than the storm-tossed mariner looks for his haven,” and praising the newly-baptized Rufinus, to their mutual friend Florentius, as one made “white as snow.” 5

tl.w: Rufinus in Egypt, under Didymus the Blind (c. 373–380)
tl.t: For some six years Rufinus studied at Alexandria under Didymus the Blind and lived among the desert hermits, imbibing the lifelong devotion to Origen that would later divide him from Jerome; he suffered imprisonment and banishment under Lucius, the Arian bishop of Alexandria. 6

tl.w: The Mount of Olives; Rufinus ordained at Jerusalem (c. 379–386)
tl.t: About 379–380 Melania the Elder settled on the Mount of Olives, where Rufinus gathered and led a community of monks for some eighteen years; he was ordained priest at Jerusalem about 386, around the time Bishop John succeeded Cyril there. 7

tl.w: Jerome settles at Bethlehem: neighbours again (386)
tl.t: In 386 Jerome settled at Bethlehem with Paula, a few miles from Rufinus's monastery on the Mount of Olives. The old friendship was renewed — “though not apparently with all its former warmth” — and the two lived as friendly neighbours for some seven years, before the quarrel over Origen broke it apart. 8

tl.w: Atarbius comes accusing; Rufinus rebuffs him (c. 392)
tl.t: About 392 the monk Atarbius, a hunter of Origen's errors, came to Jerusalem pressing both Jerome and Rufinus to subscribe a repudiation of Origen. Jerome readily gave satisfaction; Rufinus refused him even an interview and “treated him with merited scorn” — an early sign that the two friends would end in opposing camps. 9

tl.w: Epiphanius preaches against Origen; the camps form (393–394)
tl.t: Visiting Jerusalem, Epiphanius of Salamis — who had already catalogued Origen as a heresy in his own right some twenty years earlier — ignited the quarrel: in the Church of the Resurrection, in the presence of the city's bishop John, he preached a pointed sermon against Origen's errors, aimed so plainly at John that the bishop sent his archdeacon to remonstrate. The camps hardened — Jerome with Epiphanius, Rufinus with John — and Rufinus stood “as the chief of a chorus of presbyters who applauded their own bishop and derided Epiphanius as a ‘silly old man.’” 10 Leaving the city, Epiphanius wrote John a letter — which Jerome himself rendered into Latin, and which survives as his Letter 51 — p…

tl.w: Paulinian ordained; Jerome breaks with his bishop (394)
tl.t: To free the Bethlehem monastery from John's jurisdiction, Epiphanius in 394 uncanonically ordained Jerome's brother Paulinian a priest within John's own diocese. John was enraged; the ordination, and Jerome's defence of it, opened the breach between Jerome and his bishop. 12

tl.w: The stolen translation, and Jerome's manifesto on translating (395)
tl.t: Epiphanius's letter was so admired that “all Palestine fought for copies of it,” and Eusebius of Cremona — a monk of Jerome 's Bethlehem house who had no Greek — begged him for a Latin version for his private use. Eighteen months later it was taken from his desk and carried to Jerusalem, where Jerome's opponents used it to charge him with falsifying his original: For a pretended monk — either bribed as there is much reason to believe or actuated by malice of his own as his tempter vainly tries to convince us — shewed himself a second Judas by robbing Eusebius of his literary property and gave to the adversary an occasion of railing against me. … What place of safety will be left us if we can…

About 396 Jerome poured the quarrel into a virulent tract, Against John of Jerusalem (addressed to Pammachius), answering John's complaints to Rome and heaping scorn on the bishop and, obliquely, on Rufinus — “your friends, who grin like dogs and turn up their noses.” So bitter was it that Jerome broke it off and left it unpublished once the situation changed. 15

tl.w: The reconciliation at the Holy Sepulchre (Easter 397)
tl.t: At Easter 397, before Rufinus set out for Italy with Melania, the breach was patched over — a gesture brokered amid the strife, with the influence of Theophilus of Alexandria and of Melania. As Fremantle tells it, “the two old companions who had been so long parted by ecclesiastical strife met together at the Church of the Resurrection at a solemn eucharistic feast, and joined hands in token of reconciliation, and … Jerome accompanied his friend some way on his journey before their final parting.” 16 Whether the reconciliation was a real healing of the friendship or a conditional truce that events soon overran is a question in its own right ; within a year the two would be at open war.

tl.w: Rufinus reaches Italy; Pinetum and Macarius (397)
tl.t: Late in 397 Rufinus returned to Italy with Melania and was welcomed by Paulinus of Nola. He settled for a time at Pinetum, near Terracina, where the monk Macarius pressed him — with a “persistence” that “even want of ability cannot resist” — to put Origen into Latin. 17

tl.w: Rufinus's Origen translations at Pinetum; the treatise On the Falsification (397)
tl.t: At Pinetum Rufinus translated the Apology for Origen written by the martyr Pamphilus, and “supplemented” the work “by a short treatise of my own” — his On the Falsification of the Works of Origen (the De Adulteratione ) — arguing that heretics had corrupted Origen's genuine text, so that a translator was entitled to prune the corruptions away. Whether that thesis holds — whether Origen's heresies were interlopers' insertions or his own teaching — is a question in its own right . 18

tl.w: The preface that named Jerome: the spark (397/398)
tl.t: Then, at Macarius's urging, Rufinus translated Origen's Peri Archon ( On First Principles ) — smoothing away, as he freely admitted, whatever he judged heretical interpolation. To his translation he prefixed a preface to Macarius that, without naming him, cast Jerome as his precedent: the translator who had already Latinized more than seventy of Origen's homilies and had done the very same softening: He has rendered into Latin more than seventy of Origen's homiletical treatises and a few also of his commentaries upon the apostle; and in these wherever the Greek text presents a stumbling block, he has smoothed it down in his version and has so emended the language used that a Latin writer can…

tl.w: The uncorrected papers: Eusebius of Cremona carries the charge through Italy (398)
tl.t: How the Peri Archon reached Jerome's Roman friends is itself disputed, and each side told it as a theft. By Rufinus 's account the translation was still unfinished and uncirculated when Eusebius of Cremona — the same monk whose desk had been robbed three years before, now “sent from their monastery to Rome” — obtained the draft and altered a sentence on the Trinity, so that where Rufinus had written “I will at once give you my reason for it” the copy read “as the Son does not see the Father, so the Holy Spirit also does not see the Son.” Eusebius recited the doctored line at Milan and, challenged, said a woman named Marcella had given him the copy. Rufinus's complaint was less that he had be…

tl.w: Jerome's answer: a literal Peri Archon , and a withheld olive branch (398)
tl.t: To expose the heresies Rufinus had softened, Jerome made his own strictly literal Latin Peri Archon and sent it to Rome with a furious open letter to Pammachius and Oceanus ( Letter 84), insisting that his old praise of Origen had been for the exegete only, never the theologian: “I have praised the commentator but not the theologian, the man of intellect but not the believer, the philosopher but not the apostle.” 23 He also wrote Rufinus a private, conciliatory letter ( Letter 81), protesting that when reconciled to a man he did not “while offering him bread with one hand, hold a stone in the other” — but he sent it by way of Pammachius, who “treacherously suppressed it,” so the olive branch…

tl.w: Anastasius succeeds Siricius; Rome moves against Rufinus (399)
tl.t: In November 399 Pope Siricius, who had befriended Rufinus, died, and Anastasius I succeeded him. The new pope was closer to Jerome 's Roman friends — the widow Marcella and the senator Pammachius — who now pressed the charge that Rufinus had smuggled Origen's heresy into the Roman church through his Latin Peri Archon . Marcella, Jerome wrote, “had the volumes of the Peri Archon brought in, and pointed out the alterations” the translator had made, until “letters were written … summoning the heretics to come and defend themselves, but they did not dare to come.” 26

tl.w: Theophilus purges Nitria; the Tall Brothers sail for Constantinople (400)
tl.t: The quarrel of two Latin monks now became an empire-wide campaign, and it was driven from Alexandria. Theophilus, who had once sheltered the Origenist monks, turned on them: in 400 he expelled the Origenists from the monasteries of Nitria and wrote to Jerome at Bethlehem to say so — “we have cut down with the prophet's sickle certain wicked fanatics who were eager to sow broadcast in the monasteries of Nitria the heresy of Origen” — and to enlist his pen. 27 Jerome answered with delight, reporting that the campaign had already told in the West: “The old serpent hisses no longer, but, writhing and disembowelled, lurks in dark caverns unable to bear the shining of the sun” — and that a priest …

At the “earnest request” of Theophilus of Alexandria — who had by now turned violently against the Origenism he once sheltered — a synod at Rome under Anastasius formally condemned Origen's errors, echoing the condemnations pronounced at Alexandria and, in 401, on Cyprus under Epiphanius. The tide had turned so far that within two years Jerome could say Origen stood condemned by the whole world. 31

Rather than travel to Rome to answer — “It was impossible for me to do this in person,” he pleaded, newly returned to his family after thirty years abroad — Rufinus sent Anastasius a written profession of faith. He confessed the resurrection of “this very flesh in which we now live,” a judgment to come in which even the devil would “receive as their portion the eternal fire,” and — on the origin of the soul , the point where he was most suspected — declared himself, after reading every view, “unable to hold any of them as certain and absolute.” As for Origen, he disclaimed the role of champion, resting on his work as a mere translator: I am not a defender or a champion of Origen; nor am I th…

From Aquileia, at the end of 400, Rufinus struck back with two books of an Apology addressed to his patron Apronianus. He turned the heresy-charge on his accuser: from Jerome's own Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians — the very work Jerome had held up as proof of his soundness against Origen — Rufinus argued that Jerome too had taught Origen's doctrines of the pre-existence of souls and the universal restoration: You made an exception in favour of the Commentaries on the Ephesians, in which you imagined that you had written more correctly. But even you must have seen … how like they are all through to Origen's views; and, indeed, how they contain something more extreme than the views …

tl.w: Anastasius's letter to John of Jerusalem (401)
tl.t: When John of Jerusalem wrote to Rome on Rufinus's behalf, Anastasius answered (401) by condemning the translation while pointedly leaving the translator to his conscience — “he must bring his conscience to the bar of the divine majesty” — and disowning any knowledge of him: I beg you to be assured of this, that he is so completely separate from all part or lot with us, that I neither know nor wish to know either what he is doing or where he is living. — Anastasius to John of Jerusalem, §6 . 34 Whether this amounts to the “formal summons and personal condemnation” of Rufinus that later handbooks describe — or only to a condemnation of the book , with the man left to his conscience — is a ques…

tl.w: Jerome's Apology against Rufinus , Books I–II (402)
tl.t: At the beginning of Spring 402, Pammachius and Marcella sent Jerome the chief heads of Rufinus's Apology — they could not obtain the full text — and pressed him to reply. From Bethlehem he answered with two books of his own Apology against Rufinus , addressed to those same friends; Book II took up and rebutted the Apology to Anastasius point by point. Jerome mocked Rufinus's translator's-plea and his professions of faith as evasions, and threw the charge of Origenism back where it began. 35

tl.w: Book III; Chromatius's plea; no reconciliation (402/403)
tl.t: A third book followed in 402/403, answering a now-lost private letter Rufinus had sent Jerome — one, by Jerome's account, that renewed the accusations and hinted darkly that its writer could, if he chose, produce facts to destroy his adversary. Bishop Chromatius of Aquileia begged both men to let the strife die; Rufinus, heeding him, made no public reply, but Jerome fired the last shot, closing with an olive branch clenched round a fist: We once were zealous in our praise of Origen; let us be equally zealous in condemning him now that he is condemned by the whole world. — Jerome, Apology against Rufinus, III.9 . Even Augustine wrote urging Jerome to peace; but the two old friends never recon…

tl.w: The Synod of the Oak; Jerome Latinizes the case against Chrysostom (403–405)
tl.t: The Alexandrian campaign ended by devouring a greater man than either of the two friends. Summoned to Constantinople to answer for his treatment of the Tall Brothers, Theophilus instead turned the proceedings against his host: at a synod held in 403 at a suburban estate called the Oak, John Chrysostom was condemned in his absence and deposed, and after a brief recall was exiled for good in 404. He died in exile in 407. 37 Theophilus then composed a violent invective against him and sent it to Jerome to be put into Latin for the West, resting the charge on Origenism — a charge his own synod had by then quietly dropped : But, not to speak of his other misdeeds, he has taken the Origenists into…

tl.w: Rufinus's Greek library goes into Latin (c. 401–406)
tl.t: The quarrel did not stop Rufinus 's pen. In these years at Aquileia the “loser” of the feud became one of the most consequential Greek-to-Latin translators the West would have: he rendered Eusebius's Church History for Bishop Chromatius (401, as a consolation amid the Gothic terror), adding two books of his own to carry the story on; Origen's Commentary on Romans (c. 405–406) for Heraclius; Origen's homilies on the Pentateuch and Joshua, again for Chromatius; works of Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus; and, for Gaudentius of Brescia, the Clementine Recognitions . Much of the Greek theology the Latin Middle Ages knew, it knew through the man Jerome had branded a heretic. 40

tl.w: Rufinus leaves Aquileia; Rome, and Melania's household (c. 408)
tl.t: After some nine years at Aquileia — and after the death of his patron Chromatius (c. 405) — Rufinus went to Rome as Alaric's Goths pressed into northern Italy, and attached himself to the religious household of Melania the Younger (granddaughter of the Melania who had brought him east long before), then preparing to leave Italy for the safety of the East. 41

tl.w: Jerome's literal version lost but for fragments (Letter 124 to Avitus, c. 409/410)
tl.t: Jerome's own literal translation of the Peri Archon does not survive intact; it is known only through the passages he later quoted, a decade on, in his Letter 124 to Avitus (c. 409/410), where he recalled that “about ten years ago that saintly man Pammachius sent me a copy of a certain person's rendering, or rather misrendering, of Origen's First Principles ” and asked for the true sense of the Greek. 42

tl.w: The sack of Rome; Rufinus flees to Sicily (410)
tl.t: When Alaric sacked Rome in August 410, Rufinus fled south with Melania's party toward Sicily, watching from across the strait as the Goths burned Rhegium. Even in flight he kept translating — he finished Origen's homilies on Numbers on the island. 43
Rufinus died in Sicily soon after, about 411 (some accounts round to c. 410). He and Jerome , the friends of Aquileia, were never reconciled. 44

tl.w: Jerome's cold epitaph: the scorpion and Grunnius (c. 411–414)
tl.t: Death did not soften Jerome. In the preface to his Commentary on Ezekiel — begun amid the news of Rome's fall and the deaths of Pammachius and Marcella — he greeted the passing of his old friend as the crushing of a venomous beast, Rufinus the “scorpion” now lying dead beneath the soil of Sicily (Trinacria), pinned like the buried giants of myth between Enceladus and Porphyrion: … a scar gradually covers a great wound: and Scorpius is pressed between Enceladus and Porphyrion and crushed by the Trinacrian soil, and the Hydra with many heads has at last ceased to hiss against us … — Jerome, Commentary on Ezekiel, preface (book I) . 45 He had long mocked Rufinus as “Grunnius” — the grunting pig…

tl.w: The other portrait: Palladius remembers Rufinus (c. 419–420)
tl.t: Almost everything above survives because Jerome wrote it down, and he is the more quotable man; but he is not the only witness. Palladius of Galatia, who had lived among the Egyptian and Palestinian monks and knew both households, wrote his Lausiac History about 419–420 — and took Rufinus 's side without hesitating. Of the twenty-seven years on the Mount of Olives he records: With her lived also the most noble Rufinus, from Italy, of the city of Aquileia, a man similar to her in character and very stedfast, who was afterwards judged worthy of the priesthood. A more learned man or a kinder than he was not to be found among men. — Palladius, Lausiac History XLVI.5 (on Melania the Elder) . 47 O…

ar.q: Did Pope Anastasius I formally summon Rufinus to Rome and personally condemn him as a heretic?
ar.c: At the instigation of Theophilus of Alexandria, Anastasius (pope 398–402) summoned Rufinus from Aquileia to Rome to vindicate his orthodoxy; but he excused himself from a personal attendance in a written Apologia pro fide sua . — “Rufinus, Tyrannius,” Encyclopædia Britannica (11th ed., 1911) . 1 In its strongest popular form the assertion has two parts: that Pope Anastasius I (399–401) issued a formal summons ordering Rufinus to appear at Rome and answer for his orthodoxy, and that he then personally condemned Rufinus as a heretic. The question here is whether either half survives the primary …
ar.a: Weak — for the strong “formal summons + personal condemnation” version. The primary record supports the milder reading on every disputed point: Anastasius condemned Origen and the translation, but left the translator to his conscience and professed not even to know where he was living; and Rufinus's Apology reads as a voluntary, rumour-prompted profession of faith, not a defendant's answer to a citation. The kernel of truth the strong claim infla…

ar.q: Was the Easter 397 reconciliation at the Holy Sepulchre a genuine healing of the friendship?
ar.c: Far be such conduct from these reverend persons. It is from your school that such actions proceed. You gave us all the signs of peace at our departure, and then threw missiles charged with venom from behind our backs. — Rufinus, in a now-lost private letter, quoted by Jerome, Apology against Rufinus, III.24 , link . 1 The assertion is that the hand-joining at the Church of the Resurrection at Easter 397 — before Rufinus sailed for Italy — was a true peace, one Jerome then broke by sending accusers after him to Rome. The question here is whether that reading holds: was the reconciliation a real…
ar.a: Weak — as a claim that the friendship was truly healed. The peace was conditional on Rufinus's orthodoxy, arranged amid a bishops' settlement rather than sought for its own sake, and broken within a year of the parting. Two narrower claims fare better and should be kept distinct from it: that the hand-joining was a sincere gesture in the moment is probable — both men recorded it as real, and Jerome's 398 olive branch shows he did not yet count th…

ar.q: Did Jerome himself once hold Origen's doctrines of pre-existent souls and universal restoration?
ar.c: You made an exception in favour of the Commentaries on the Ephesians, in which you imagined that you had written more correctly. But even you must have seen … how like they are all through to Origen's views; and, indeed, how they contain something more extreme than the views of which you demand the condemnation. — Rufinus, Apology against Jerome, II.28 , link . 1 The heart of Rufinus's counter-attack: Jerome had held up his own Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians (written c. 386) as proof that he opposed Origen — “read my Commentaries on the Ephesians, and you will acknowledge that I ha…
ar.a: Contested. By the historical and text-critical lights the charge is strong: Jerome's early Ephesians commentary really does relay the pre-existence of souls and the restitution of all things, with a sympathy his later self-defence conceals, and his anti-Origenism is a genuine reversal, not a lifelong constancy. As the categorical claim Rufinus's polemic drives at — that Jerome was an Origenist who dogmatically professed these doctrines — it is we…

ar.q: Were Origen's heterodox passages heretical interpolations rather than his own teaching?
ar.c: To license his “restoring” translation of Origen, Rufinus appended to his Latin Apology for Origen of the martyr Pamphilus a short treatise of his own, On the Falsification of the Works of Origen (the De Adulteratione ). Its thesis is that a learned and self-consistent author cannot have written flat contradictions of himself in “successive sentences”; where such contradictions appear, heretics have been at work: Whenever they found in any of the renowned writers of old days a discussion of those things which pertain to the glory of God so full and faithful that every believer could gain profi…
ar.a: Weak. As the general account of Origen's heterodoxy that Rufinus needed it to be — the premise that entitled him to prune and rewrite — the interpolation thesis does not hold. Origen's signature doctrines are integral to his system and present in his undisputed Greek; the surviving Greek shows Rufinus softening his author rather than removing intruders; his preface concedes the method; and Jerome's structural objection, that the thesis can absolv…

ar.q: Was Rufinus's draft Peri Archon interpolated before it reached Rome?
ar.c: Rufinus's Latin Peri Archon , at the place where Origen asks whether the divine nature is visible even to the Only-begotten, reads: “do not dismiss my answer as if it were impious or absurd, for I will at once give you my reason for it ” — and then goes on to the distinction between seeing (a property of bodies) and knowing (proper to intellectual natures). What was recited against him in Italy read otherwise: Well, in the place of the words which I had written, “I will at once give you my reason for it” they put the following words: “Do not dismiss my answer as if it were impious or absurd, f…
ar.a: Weak. On its best available case the interpolation charge does not stand. The sentence Rufinus disowned was not the kind of thing a forger had to invent: it was the most quoted line ever fathered on Peri Archon I.1, in Latin and in wide circulation for three years before the quarrel, so an unrevised draft rendering that passage literally would have looked much as the recited copy did. Rufinus's own Apology supplies the rest — his admission that h…

ar.q: Was Rufinus's doctrinal “smoothing” of Origen a defensible translation method, or was Jerome's literal fidelity the responsible one?
ar.c: Beneath the personal feud lay a genuine dispute about the ethics of translation. When Rufinus put Origen's Peri Archon ( On First Principles ) into Latin, he did not render the Greek as it stood: wherever he met a passage he judged heretical he silently corrected it, and he said so openly in his preface — his rule was to follow his predecessors and proceed to purge and pare away in his translation all the causes of stumbling which are to be found in the Greek works; and this he did in such a way that the Latin reader will find nothing in them which jars with our faith … Wherever therefore I ha…
ar.a: Contested. The methodological quarrel has no clear winner. On the question actually in dispute — how to translate a revered author whose orthodoxy is on trial — Jerome's principle is the sounder: a corrected text cannot honestly serve as evidence of the doctrine it has corrected, and his ideal of a version “without the patronage of the translator” is the responsible one, endorsed by scholarship ancient and modern. But that principle indicts Jerom…

ds.t: The Origin of the Soul
ds.q: Where does an individual human soul come from? Scripture says that God formed the first man of dust and “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” — but it never says plainly what happens at the conception of the second man, or the millionth. Three answers were given, and they are the axes of this timeline. Traducianism (from tradux , the layered vine-shoot by which a vine is propagated): the soul comes from the parents' souls as the body comes from their bodies, so that the whole race is one stock descending from Adam. Creationism : God makes each soul afresh out of nothing and joins it to the body He has formed in the womb. Pre-existence : souls were all made long ago, and enter bodie…

tl.t: Tertullian is the author of traducianism, and his Treatise on the Soul is the first sustained argument for it. Body and soul are conceived together and neither precedes the other: “both are conceived, and formed, and perfectly simultaneously, as well as born together; and… not a moment's interval occurs in their conception.” The soul is therefore a sprout from a root — it “has been derived from Adam as its root, and has been propagated among his posterity by means of woman” — so that “from the one (primeval) man comes the entire outflow and redundance of men's souls.” 4 His evidence is not exegetical but observational: we resemble our parents in disposition , not only in feature, and that li…

Origen supplies the third option and is candid that it is an option: the church's rule of faith, he writes in the preface to De Principiis , has not settled “whether it is derived from the seed by a process of traducianism… or whether it has any other beginning.” Into that acknowledged gap he puts pre-existence. Rational minds were made equal; freedom made them unequal; and a mind that cooled from the divine warmth became a soul — he derives psychē from psychesthai , to grow cold — and was placed in a body proportioned to what it had become. 6 The motive is theodicy: the inequality of human lots is not the Creator's arbitrariness but the residue of prior choice, so that even Jacob supplantin…

Lactantius is the first Latin to hold creationism explicitly and the first to say the surrounding question may be permanently insoluble: what the soul is , he writes, “is not yet agreed upon by philosophers, and perhaps will never be agreed upon.” On its origin he is not agnostic at all. Souls come from neither parent nor from both, “because nothing can depart from a slight and incomprehensible subject”; therefore “the manner of the production of souls belongs entirely to God alone.” The parents' whole contribution is the matter of the body; conception, moulding, and the breathing-in of life are God's. 8 He agrees with Tertullian on timing against the philosophers — the soul is present from …

Didymus , blind from childhood and for half a century the head of the catechetical school of Alexandria, is the one witness of standing to keep Origen's third option alive in the fourth century. Reading the Lord's “Adam, where are you?” he takes the fallen soul to have been “free from every place through incorporeality” and to have “come into a place” only once it “became attached to the body” — Origen's pre-cosmic descent, read out of Genesis 3. 10 That it was his own teaching and not merely a view he canvassed is confirmed by his pupil Jerome , who — sorting him as sound on the Trinity but astray “in trusting to Origen” — reports a treatise of Didymus holding that the pre-existent souls “h…

Gregory of Nyssa steers between the two options that frame the question in the Greek East — souls before bodies, or bodies before souls — and rejects both: “the doctrine of both, then, is equally to be rejected; but I think that we ought to direct our own doctrine in the way of truth between these theories.” Against pre-existence he presses that it slides into the pagan transmigration tales, fit for “the chatter of frogs or jackdaws”; against the literalist reading of Genesis 2:7 that makes the clay figure first, he answers that man is one , and so “the beginning of his existence is one, common to both parts,” lest a man be “antecedent and posterior to himself.” 12 His positive image is the …

Rufinus , defending himself before Pope Anastasius I against the charge of Origenism, gives the cleanest ancient statement of the three-way division — soul infused with the seed (he names Tertullian and Lactantius), or made new daily, or made long ago and planted in bodies (“the opinion of Origen”) — and then refuses to choose: “I declare in the presence of God that, after reading each of these opinions, I am up to the present moment unable to hold any of them as certain and absolute.” 14 The refusal is the point. Rufinus is treating the origin of the soul as an open question on which orthodoxy does not yet ride — and Jerome , mid-quarrel, treated that very refusal as evasion. 15 (His attrib…

Jerome is the West's decided creationist. Writing to Marcellinus and Anapsychia shortly after the sack of Rome he lays out the same taxonomy in five branches and marks his own view by the proof-text he attaches to it: are souls “daily created by God and sent into bodies, according to what is written in the gospel, My Father works hitherto, and I work ”? The rival he names is Tertullian's, which “Tertullian, Apollinaris, and the majority of the Western divines conjecture… so that as the body is the offspring of body, the soul is the offspring of soul, and exists on conditions similar to those regulating the existence of the inferior animals” — the sting being that traducianism levels man with…

Augustine is the great non-decider, and the reason the question mattered so much in the West. In On Free Will he had already enumerated four possibilities — souls propagated from Adam's; each newly made; pre-existing souls sent into bodies; pre-existing souls entering of their own accord — and deliberately argued in a way that would hold on any of them. He never advanced past that. In 415 he sent Jerome a whole treatise as a letter ( Letter 166), carried east by the priest Orosius, confessing “many are perplexed by questions concerning the soul, and I confess that I myself am of this number,” and pressing one difficulty above all: if God makes each soul new and sinless, whence the guilt for …

Cassian puts the creationist case on a proof-text that outlived the debate: Hebrews 12:9, which distinguishes “fathers of our flesh” from “the Father of spirits.” What could show more clearly, he asks, “that he laid down that men were the fathers of our flesh, but always taught that God alone was the Father of souls”? The mechanism is denied outright — “spirit does not beget spirit just as soul cannot procreate soul” — and God “makes them out of nothing whenever He pleases.” 21 The argument is a monk's, made in passing inside a conference on demons, which is itself a sign of where the question had got to by the 430s: in the Latin West, creationism was becoming the assumed answer. 22

Gennadius is the hinge from opinion to rule. His handbook of church dogmas states creationism as the church's teaching and names both rejected alternatives in one breath: souls were not all made at the beginning among the other intellectual natures, “as Origen imagines,” nor sown with the bodies through intercourse, “as the Luciferians, Cyril, and certain presumptuous Latins affirm”; rather the body alone is sown, and “the body being now formed, the soul is created and infused.” 23 Its influence came partly by accident: the book circulated for centuries under Augustine's name, so the West read Augustine's own permanent hesitation and a flat creationist canon as if both were his. 24

Anastasius II supplies the first papal intervention: a letter to the bishops of Gaul against people there who reasoned that “just as the parents transmit bodies to the human race from material dregs, so also they bestow the vital principle of the living souls.” Against them he argues from the same verse Jerome used — the Father's work has “not ceased even today” — and concludes that God “imparts souls.” 25 Its weight should not be overstated: it is a letter to a regional episcopate, not a conciliar definition, and it is preserved in the standard collections only in heavily abridged excerpt. What it shows is that by 498 traducianism in Gaul was something a bishop of Rome would write to suppre…

Justinian ends the third option by law. His edict against Origen opens with the pre-existence of souls and anathematizes precisely Origen's mechanism: whoever says that human souls pre-existed, “that they had previously been spirits and holy powers, but that, satiated with the vision of God, they had turned to evil, and in this way the divine love in them had died out… and they had therefore been condemned to punishment in bodies, shall be anathema.” 27 A fuller set of fifteen anathemas, opening with “the fabulous pre-existence of souls,” is transmitted with the Fifth Ecumenical Council of 553, though its relation to the council's own acts is disputed. Either way the effect was the same: aft…

John of Damascus fixes the settled Greek position in the handbook that became the East's standard summary. The reasoning soul God “bestowed upon him by His own inbreathing”; and against the remaining rival: “body and soul were formed at one and the same time, not first the one and then the other, as Origen so senselessly supposes.” 29 Gregory of Nyssa's simultaneity has become a formula, and the only named error is pre-existence. 30

Aquinas closes the Latin question with a metaphysical argument rather than a proof-text. Since the intellectual soul has an operation independent of the body it is subsistent; a subsistent immaterial thing cannot be produced by a power working in matter, so it “cannot be caused through generation, but only through creation by God.” Therefore “to hold that the intellectual soul is caused by the begetter, is nothing else than to hold the soul to be non-subsistent and consequently to perish with the body. It is therefore heretical to say that the intellectual soul is transmitted with the semen.” 31 Tertullian's inference is thus turned around: he had accepted a quasi-corporeal soul in order to …

ar.q: The condemnation of unbaptised infants as an objection to creationism
ar.c: I ask where can the soul, even of an infant snatched away by death, have contracted the guilt which, unless the grace of Christ has come to the rescue by that sacrament of baptism which is administered even to infants, involves it in condemnation? — Augustine, Letter 166 (to Jerome), ch. iii §6 , source (a.d. 415). The claim weighed here is that creationism — God making each soul afresh — cannot be reconciled with the church's practice and doctrine concerning infants who die without baptism, and that this counts as evidence against it. 1
ar.a: Contested. The objection is genuine, well-posed, and was never met in the terms its author set; it is the reason the West's most formidable theologian refused for thirty years to hold the view the West then adopted, and the reason he made his acceptance of it conditional. Against that, the answer eventually given is coherent, is held by the great majority, and blocks the sharpest version of the charge by denying that a directly created soul is th…

ar.q: “My Father works hitherto” as proof that God creates each soul afresh
ar.c: … are they daily created by God and sent into bodies, according to what is written in the gospel, My Father works hitherto, and I work ? — Jerome, Letter 126 (to Marcellinus and Anapsychia), §1 , source . The claim weighed here is that John 5:17 supplies scriptural warrant for creationism — that the “work” the Father is still doing includes, and is evidenced by, the making of a new soul for each person conceived. 1
ar.a: Weak. Not false, and not foolish: John 5:17 does what Jerome first needs it to do, which is to clear away the objection from God's sabbath rest, and it is fully compatible with the conclusion drawn from it. But a proof-text has to do more than be compatible with the thesis it is cited for. This one names no work in particular; the tradition that expounded it filled in providential conservation, not soul-making; its own argument is about the Son's…

ds.t: Original sin & the Fall
ds.q: Original sin is the doctrine of what Adam’s first transgression did to the rest of us — whether, and how, the fault of the garden reaches a newborn who has done nothing. All the ancient churches agree that something passed from Adam to his race; they divide sharply on what . Three answers were given. The first, which came to dominate the Latin West, is inherited guilt : every child is born already implicated in Adam’s sin — bearing not merely his mortality but his reatus , a real culpability that damns unless washed away, so that (in the Latin of Romans 5:12) all “sinned in him.” The second, kept by the Christian East, is inherited corruption only — “ancestral sin”: Adam bequeathed death, mo…

tl.w: Irenaeus of Lyons — the seed: we “offended in the first Adam” (c. 180)
tl.t: Irenaeus has no developed theory of transmitted sin, but he lays the corporate premise every later account builds on. In his scheme of recapitulation , the race is bound up in its head: what Adam did, humanity did, and what the “second Adam” undoes, He undoes for the race. God, he writes, is the one “whom indeed we had offended in the first Adam, when he did not perform His commandment. In the second Adam, however, we are reconciled, being made obedient even unto death.” The offense is ours in Adam; the reconciliation is ours in Christ. That solidarity — humanity a single stock that fell in one man — is the trunk from which both the Latin “inherited guilt” and the Greek “inherited death” wil…

tl.w: Tertullian — the vitium originis passed with the soul (c. 210)
tl.t: Tertullian gives the West its first mechanism. Because he holds that each soul is propagated from the parents’ souls as the body from their bodies ( traducianism , from tradux , the vine-shoot), the whole race descends from Adam as “the nascent sprout of a tree… derived from Adam as its root” — and the soul carries a fault with it. There is, he says, “an antecedent, and in a certain sense natural, evil which arises from its corrupt origin”: “the corruption of our nature is another nature.” Hence “every soul, then, by reason of its birth, has its nature in Adam until it is born again in Christ… and because unclean, it is actively sinful.” This is the vitium originis — a birth-fault, not merel…

tl.w: Origen — “the filth of birth” and infant baptism from the apostles (c. 248)
tl.t: Origen , in the Greek East, reads the newborn’s need from the practice of the church. Pairing Psalm 51:5 with Job 14:4 in its Septuagint form (“no one is clean from filth, not even if his life be of one day”), he infers that “whatever soul is born in the flesh is polluted with the filth of iniquity and sin”; and he takes the church’s baptizing of infants “for the remission of sins” as an apostolic tradition that would be “superfluous” unless there were something in the child to remit. On Romans 5, he reasons from solidarity as Hebrews reasons of Levi in Abraham’s loins: “all men who are born… were in the loins of Adam while he was still in paradise,” and so death “passed also into those who …

tl.w: Cyprian and the Council of Carthage — the “contagion of the ancient death” (253)
tl.t: Cyprian of Carthage , answering bishop Fidus for a council of sixty-six African bishops, gives one of the earliest Latin statements that the newborn contracts an inherited defilement. The infant, though it “has not sinned” by any act of its own, has “being born after the flesh according to Adam… contracted the contagion of the ancient death at its earliest birth”; in baptism “to him are remitted, not his own sins, but the sins of another.” The council’s point was practical — baptize the newborn without waiting for the eighth day — but the reason it gives is a doctrine of inherited stain, made the ground of urgency. The same African instinct will run straight into Augustine. 4 See the detail …

tl.w: Ambrosiaster — “all sinned in Adam as in a lump”: the Latin in quo (c. 375)
tl.t: The anonymous Roman commentator known as Ambrosiaster supplies the exegetical hinge of the whole Western doctrine. Reading Romans 5:12 in the Latin that renders Paul’s eph’ hō (ἐφ’ ὅ) as in quo — “ in whom all sinned” — he takes the “whom” to be Adam and draws the seminal conclusion: “all have sinned in Adam as though in a lump ( quasi in massa ). For, being corrupted by sin himself, all those whom he fathered were born under sin… we are all sinners, because we all descend from him.” This is the reading — grammatically a mistranslation, as the Greek relative is neuter/causal, not personal — that Augustine would build his case upon. Whether it can bear that weight is weighed on the Romans 5:1…

tl.w: Ambrose of Milan — “In Adam I fell… guilty as I was in him” (c. 387)
tl.t: Ambrose , whom Augustine would cite as a witness against the Pelagians, states the solidarity in the first person: “In Adam I fell, in Adam I was cast out of Paradise, in Adam I died; how shall the Lord call me back, except He find me in Adam; guilty as I was in him, so now justified in Christ.” On Luke he glosses Romans 5:12 with the same in quo : “all have died in Adam… death has passed upon all men, in whom all have sinned.” The Latin tradition is now speaking of guilt contracted in Adam, not merely mortality — the note the East will not sound. 6

tl.w: John Chrysostom — what passed from Adam is death, not guilt (c. 391)
tl.t: Preaching at Antioch, John Chrysostom reads the same verse the other way, and marks the great Greek divergence. Paul’s clause, he says, means only that Adam “having once fallen, even they that had not eaten of the tree did from him, all of them, become mortal.” What the race inherits is death — the whole consequence Chrysostom names is that all “become mortal” — not a personal guilt each newborn already carries. This is the Antiochene and broadly Eastern reading (Theodoret: each “receives the sentence of death not because of the sin of his first ancestor but because of his own sin”), and it is why the East, baptizing the same infants, would ground the rite in grace rather than in the remissi…

tl.w: Pelagius — sin by imitation, no inherited guilt (the provocation, c. 411)
tl.t: Pelagius and his follower Caelestius force the doctrine into the open by denying transmission outright. Adam harmed his posterity, on their account, only by setting a bad example: “as long as people sin as Adam sinned they die,” and a newborn, having done nothing, bears no sin at all — nature is not fallen, only imitated. Caelestius’s theses (that Adam’s sin “injured only himself, not the human race,” and that infants “are in the same state in which Adam was before the transgression”) were condemned at Carthage in 411, opening the controversy that would occupy Augustine for the rest of his life. 8 See the detail page: Pelagius (on the predestination timeline) .

tl.w: Augustine of Hippo — inherited guilt, concupiscence, and the “mass of perdition” (c. 412–430)
tl.t: Augustine of Hippo is the doctrine’s architect. Against Pelagius he welds the African tradition into a system: all were “bound by the chain of death in that one man in whom all men sinned, even though they added no sins of their own”; the transmission is by propagation, not imitation , carried through the disordered concupiscence of generation (“what is generated must be regenerated… what has been contracted may be remitted”); and the whole race is therefore one massa perditionis , a “mass of perdition” justly condemned, from which the elect are drawn as “vessels of mercy.” He makes the universal baptism of infants the decisive proof: since the church everywhere baptizes them “for the remiss…

tl.w: The Council of Carthage condemns Pelagianism — inherited sin made conciliar law (418)
tl.t: The plenary Council of Carthage of 1 May 418 (its canons soon confirmed by Pope Zosimus) fixed the African answer as binding doctrine. Its canons anathematize any who says that Adam was created mortal and “would have died… whether he had sinned or not sinned”; and, decisively, any who denies that newborn infants “derive from Adam original sin, which needs to be removed by the laver of regeneration” — adding that the church’s baptizing of infants “for the remission of sins” must be understood “in a true and not a false sense.” Inherited sin, real in the newborn and remitted by baptism, is now the law of the Latin church. 10

tl.w: The Second Council of Orange — the whole man changed for the worse (529)
tl.t: The Second Council of Orange , presided over by Caesarius of Arles and confirmed by Pope Boniface II, gave the settled Western statement. Adam’s sin, it teaches, harmed “the whole man… in body and soul,” passing to his posterity “by propagation, not by imitation” — the very phrase against Pelagius — and “death of the body, which is the punishment of sin,” together with the sin itself, “the death of the soul, passed through one man to the whole human race.” Orange thus canonizes Augustine on the reality and propagation of original sin (while, on predestination, stopping short of his hardest edge). 11

tl.w: John of Damascus — the Eastern road: inherited death, not inherited guilt (c. 730)
tl.t: John of Damascus , gathering the Greek fathers, states the settled Eastern view that the West never adopted. Adam’s transgression left the race “clothed about with death, that is, mortality and the grossness of flesh… condemned to death, and made subject to corruption” — the inheritance is death and corruption , the consequence Chrysostom had named. Crucially, the will is not enslaved: man remains “a creature endowed with free-will… master of his acts,” who “has the power to curb his appetite or to indulge it as he pleases.” There is no reatus handed down, no mass justly damned in Adam; this is the “ancestral sin” the Christian East still confesses, and the deepest fault line between the two…

tl.w: The Reformers — total depravity: a hereditary corruption that itself condemns (c. 1536)
tl.t: The magisterial Reformers pressed the Augustinian line to its sharpest form. John Calvin defines the thing directly: “Original sin, then, may be defined a hereditary corruption and depravity of our nature, extending to all the parts of the soul, which first makes us obnoxious to the wrath of God, and then produces in us works which in Scripture are termed works of the flesh.” The corruption is not partial but pervasive (“total” in extent, not intensity); it is itself culpable before God, not merely the soil of later sins; and it leaves the will bound until grace frees it — the point at which the Reformation’s doctrine of the Fall feeds directly into its doctrine of justification by grace alo…

tl.w: The Council of Trent — Rome’s decree on original sin (Session V, 1546)
tl.t: The Council of Trent , in its fifth session, fixed the Catholic doctrine against the Reformers. Adam by his sin “lost… holiness and justice” and transmitted to his posterity “sin, which is the death of the soul,” propagated “not by imitation, but by propagation.” Original sin is truly remitted by the grace of baptism — not merely covered or not imputed — and after baptism nothing that is properly and truly sin remains, though concupiscence , “the tinder of sin” ( fomes peccati ), stays behind: left “for the struggle,” it “cannot injure those who do not consent,” and Trent anathematizes calling it “truly and properly sin.” That last clause — concupiscence is sin (Reformers) or is not (Trent) …

ar.q: Does Romans 5:12 ( eph’ hō / in quo ) teach that all sinned “in Adam”?
ar.c: …all have sinned in Adam as though in a lump. For, being corrupted by sin himself, all those whom he fathered were born under sin. For that reason we are all sinners, because we all descend from him. — Ambrosiaster , Commentary on Paul’s Epistles , on Romans 5:12, link . The asserted reading: Paul’s clause “ in quo [ eph’ hō ] all sinned” means all sinned in Adam — a real, inherited implication in his sin (not merely inherited mortality, and not merely his bad example), so that the newborn bears a guilt drawn from its seminal head. This is the exegetical engine of the Western doctrine of origi…
ar.a: Contested. As a reading of Romans 5, the realist “all sinned in Adam” has a real anchor: the passage’s one-man/many logic and its Adam–Christ parallel do point to a corporate implication in Adam’s sin, and the seminal idiom has scriptural precedent (Hebrews 7). But its sharpest form — an inherited, personally-damning guilt — rests in its classic presentation on the Latin in quo (“in whom”), which over-specifies a Greek eph’ hō that is most natura…

ds.t: The Old Testament Canon (Is the Deuterocanon Scripture?)
ds.q: Is Tobit — and with it Judith, Wisdom, Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), Baruch, and 1–2 Maccabees, the books Catholics call the deuterocanon and Protestants the Apocrypha — part of the Christian Old Testament? For the first fifteen centuries there was no single fixed list to settle it, and the answer was given differently across time. The Greek Septuagint that the early church inherited included these books; many Fathers who knew the Hebrew (Melito, Origen, Cyril, Jerome) counted a narrower, Hebrew-sized canon and ranked the extra books below it; the African councils, Rome, Florence, Trent, and the Eastern Synod of Jerusalem affirmed them; the Reformers and the Reformed confessions excluded them. Th…

tl.w: The test case: dating Tobit (composed c. 200 BC)
tl.t: The dispute turns on a handful of books, and Tobit is the convenient bellwether, named on nearly every list below. Its own story is set in the eighth century BC: Tobit is a pious Israelite carried off to Nineveh in the Assyrian deportation that followed the fall of the northern kingdom (c. 722 BC). 1 But scholars date the book itself far later — to roughly 200 BC (a range of about 225–175 BC), on the absence of any trace of the Maccabean persecution and on geographical slips that betray an author writing centuries after the events he narrates. 2 That gap between narrative setting and date of writing is not peculiar to a "disputed" book: it is the very gap critical scholarship posits for cano…

The timeline opens not with a verdict but with a fact : the Greek Old Testament the early church inherited — the Septuagint — already contained Tobit, together with Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and 1–2 Maccabees. The three great fourth- and fifth-century Christian Bibles (Codices Vaticanus, Sinaiticus, and Alexandrinus) all carry Tobit among the Old Testament books, interleaved with the protocanonical ones rather than set apart. 4 This Greek Bible was "the most frequently used version of the Old Testament in the early Church," 5 and the New Testament's own scriptural citations follow it overwhelmingly — Archer and Chirichigno count 340 quotations agreeing with the Septuagint against only …

tl.w: The "Council of Jamnia" (c. 90 AD, Judaism): No — but no council
tl.t: The Jewish "No" to the deuterocanon is real but harder to pin to a date than the old story allowed. That story is the Council of Jamnia : a hypothesis Heinrich Graetz floated in 1871, that a rabbinic council sat at Yavneh about 70–90 AD and there closed the Hebrew canon, shutting out the Greek extras in reaction to the rise of Christianity. 7 Twentieth-century scholarship has largely abandoned it: Jack P. Lewis's "What Do We Mean by Jabneh?" (1964) showed that "canonicity was not the issue and the debate was not connected with Jabneh… No book is ever mentioned in the sources as being excluded from the canon at Jabneh," and F. F. Bruce judged it "probably unwise to talk as if there were a Cou…

tl.w: Josephus (c. AD 93, Judaism): No — a closed twenty-two-book Hebrew canon
tl.t: The single most-cited Jewish witness for a settled Hebrew canon writes within a few years of the supposed “Council of Jamnia.” Defending the antiquity of his nation against the grammarian Apion, the historian Josephus (c. AD 37 – c. 100) states that the Jews hold not “an innumerable multitude of books… disagreeing from and contradicting one another,” but “only twenty-two books, which contain the records of all the past times” and “are justly believed to be divine” — five of Moses, thirteen of “the prophets, who were after Moses,” and four of “hymns to God, and precepts for the conduct of human life.” 11 The reign of Artaxerxes (mid-fifth century BC) is the cutoff: the prophetic record runs “…

tl.w: Clement of Rome (c. 96 AD): Yes — earliest practical use
tl.t: Before any Christian canon- list exists, the disputed books are already at work in the church's own argument. Writing from Rome to quell a schism at Corinth, Clement — whose letter, 1 Clement , is among the earliest post-apostolic writings, usually dated to about 95–96 AD 15 — weaves a line of the deuterocanonical Wisdom of Solomon into his appeal in the same breath as the Gospel and the Psalms: "Who shall say unto Him, What hast thou done? or, Who shall resist the power of His strength?" — the words of Wisdom 12:12 and 11:21, set beside Matthew 24:35 and Psalm 19 with no mark of distinction. 16 Later he holds up "the blessed Judith," who, "exposing herself to danger," went out to the enemy …

tl.w: The Didache (c. 100 AD): Yes — an early practical use
tl.t: Between Clement and the canon-lists stands an anonymous document witness: the Didache , or Teaching of the Twelve Apostles , the primitive church-order manual usually dated near AD 100 (estimates run c. 50–150). 18 In its catalogue of moral duties it embeds a line of the deuterocanonical Sirach (Ecclesiasticus): "Be not a stretcher forth of the hands to receive and a drawer of them back to give" — the words of Sirach 4:31 — set in the same chain of commandments as a paraphrase of the apostolic charge to raise one's children "in the fear of God" (cf. Ephesians 6:4), with no mark of distinction. 19 Like Clement and Polycarp , it renders no canon-list and prefaces the maxim with no "it is writt…

tl.w: 4 Ezra (2 Esdras 3–14) (c. 100 AD, Judaism): No — a numbered twenty-four-book public canon, seventy esoteric books kept back
tl.t: An independent Jewish near-contemporary of Josephus gives the other first-century count. 4 Ezra — the Jewish apocalypse that forms chapters 3–14 of the composite book called 2 Esdras, written in the aftermath of the fall of Jerusalem and usually dated c. AD 100 20 — closes with a scene of canon-making: at God's command Ezra dictates for forty days until "ninety-four books" are written, whereupon the Most High divides them, "The twenty-four books that thou hast written publish, that the worthy and unworthy may read (therein): but the seventy last thou shalt keep, to deliver them to the wise among thy people." 21 The twenty-four made public is the standard rabbinic reckoning of the Hebrew Bibl…

tl.w: Polycarp of Smyrna (c. 125 AD): Yes — an early practical use
tl.t: A generation after Clement , and still before any Christian canon- list , the disputed books surface again as edifying maxims in the church's own exhortation. Writing from Smyrna to the church at Philippi — a letter usually dated c. 110–140 AD 23 — Polycarp urges, "When you can do good, defer it not, because alms delivers from death " — the saying of the deuterocanonical Tobit (Tob 4:10; 12:9), set in a chain of apostolic and prophetic phrases (1 Peter 2:12, 17 and 5:5; Isaiah 52:5) with no mark of distinction. 24 The force should not be overstated: Polycarp renders no canon-list and prefaces the maxim with no "it is written"; the Tobit line is woven in as authoritative counsel, not adduced …

tl.w: Rabbi Akiva ben Joseph (c. 130 AD, Judaism): No — the "external books" barred, the Hebrew borderline books kept in
tl.t: The sharpest named early-rabbinic voice on the canon is Rabbi Akiva (c. 50–135), the leading Tanna of the Yavneh generation. The Mishnah sets his name against the outside books: among those with "no share in the World-to-Come," he adds "one who reads external literature" — ha-sefarim ha-chitzonim , the books beyond the Hebrew canon (the word chitzonim , "outer," itself echoing Greek apokrypha ) — the earliest rabbinic ruling to name a whole category of writings and shut it out. 25 What that category covers is disputed already within the tradition: the Babylonian Talmud glosses the "external books" as sifrei minim , the books of heretics/sectarians (in the second century often Jewish-Christia…

The earliest Christian list of the Old Testament books comes from Melito , bishop of Sardis, who travelled East "to the place where these things were preached" to learn "accurately the books of the Old Testament" and sent the catalogue to his friend Onesimus; Eusebius preserved it verbatim. It is a Hebrew-sized canon: Tobit, Judith, Sirach, Baruch, and 1–2 Maccabees are all absent (so too Esther), and it closes at "Esdras." 29 The one word that might name a deuterocanonical book — "Wisdom," set right after "the Proverbs of Solomon" — is on the usual reading a second ancient title for Proverbs itself (the "all-virtuous Wisdom"), not the deuterocanonical Book of Wisdom, so the list most likely…

tl.w: The Muratorian Fragment (c. 170 AD): Yes — Wisdom only
tl.t: The same years yield a Western witness pointing the other way. The Muratorian Fragment — the oldest surviving list of New Testament books — counts, in the middle of its New-Testament reckoning, "the [book of] Wisdom, written by the friends of Solomon," ranking the deuterocanonical Wisdom of Solomon among the received writings. 31 That makes it the earliest Western witness that a disputed Old-Testament book was received as Scripture — but it is a cross-over witness, not an OT-list: it names only Wisdom (not Tobit, Judith, Sirach, Baruch, or Maccabees), and it files the book oddly among the New Testament , a sign of how unsettled the line between the Testaments still was. 32 Set beside Melito …

tl.w: Athenagoras of Athens (c. 177 AD): Yes — Baruch quoted as the inspired voice of the prophets
tl.t: A few years before Irenaeus , an Athenian philosopher-convert presses a disputed book into service as prophecy. Defending Christians against the charge of atheism in his Plea for the Christians (c. 177), addressed to the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus, Athenagoras calls the Hebrew prophets — "Moses or… Isaiah and Jeremiah, and the other prophets," who "lifted in ecstasy… by the impulses of the Divine Spirit, uttered the things with which they were inspired" — and strings together their utterances. The first he quotes, "The Lord is our God; no other can be compared with Him," is not protocanonical but the deuterocanonical Baruch (Baruch 3:35–36), set among the inspired words of the pro…

tl.w: Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 180 AD): Yes — the disputed books cited as prophetic Scripture
tl.t: A decade after Melito 's narrower list, and from the other direction, the great anti-Gnostic bishop of Lyons quotes the disputed books not as edifying maxims but as the words of named prophets . In Irenaeus 's Against Heresies (c. 175–189) the Greek addition to Daniel — the story of Susanna — is cited as words "to be found in Daniel the prophet ": "O thou seed of Canaan, and not of Judah, beauty hath deceived thee…" (Susanna 56, 52). 35 And a long passage of the deuterocanonical Baruch (Baruch 4:36–5:9) is adduced as genuine prophecy — " Jeremiah the prophet has pointed out… saying, 'Look around Jerusalem towards the east…'" — Baruch being reckoned in the Greek and Latin tradition an appendi…

tl.w: Clement of Alexandria (c. 200 AD): Yes — the disputed books cited with the "Scripture" formula
tl.t: With the head of the Alexandrian catechetical school the practical use hardens into an explicit citation formula . A generation after Irenaeus , Clement (c. 150–215; his Paedagogus and Stromateis written c. 198–203) quotes four of the disputed books the way he quotes Moses or the Gospel — introduced as “Scripture.” He cites Sirach 21:6 as “the Scripture which says, ‘And he that feareth the Lord will turn to his heart’”; Tobit 12:8 as “the Scripture which says, ‘Fasting with prayer is a good thing’”; Wisdom 2:12 as “Scripture… when it says, ‘Let us remove the righteous man from us’”; and a long passage of Baruch (3:16–19) as the words of “the Divine Scripture.” 37 He also strings Judith 8:27 …

tl.w: The Babylonian Talmud (c. 200 AD, Judaism): Two-edged — a Hebrew-sized enumerated canon ending in Chronicles, yet Sirach cited as Writings
tl.t: The fullest early Jewish articulation of the canon — and a witness that cuts both ways. A baraita preserved in the Babylonian Talmud , Bava Batra 14b , enumerates the Prophets and then the Writings — "… Daniel and the Scroll of Esther; and Ezra and Chronicles" — closing the whole of Scripture with Chronicles and listing none of the Greek extras. It is the single clearest ancient Jewish attestation of a Hebrew-sized, Genesis-to-Chronicles arrangement (the order on which the "from Abel to Zechariah" argument leans), and because a baraita is tannaitic material it is comparatively early, though it stands almost alone for a millennium. 39 Yet the same compilation, at Bava Kamma 92b , quotes Ben S…

tl.w: Hippolytus of Rome (c. 205 AD): Yes — the disputed books read as prophecy of Christ
tl.t: In the same decades, and from the West, the most learned teacher of the Roman church puts two of the disputed books to work as prophetic Scripture. Hippolytus (c. 170–235) opens his Expository Treatise Against the Jews by adducing — against his Jewish interlocutor — “the prophecy of Solomon, which speaketh of Christ”: the deuterocanonical Wisdom of Solomon (2:1, 12–20), the foretelling of the plot against the righteous one who “calleth himself the Child of God,” introduced with “the prophet says” and read as a Solomonic prophecy of the Passion. 42 And in Against Noetus he expounds the deuterocanonical Baruch (3:35–37) — “This is our God… afterward did He show Himself upon earth, and converse…

tl.w: Tertullian (c. 210 AD): Yes — the disputed books used, as prophecy and as example
tl.t: The first great Latin theologian, writing from Carthage, puts the disputed books to work in the same African church that would later enshrine them in conciliar form. Tertullian (c. 155 – c. 220) quotes the deuterocanonical Letter of Jeremiah (Baruch 6:3) as the very “words of Jeremias,” set beside Daniel 3 in his exhortation to martyrdom: the three youths “remembered also the words of Jeremias writing to those over whom that captivity was impending… Beware, therefore, that ye also do not be altogether like the foreigners… but say in your mind, Our duty is to worship Thee, O Lord.” 44 He ranks the Wisdom of Solomon among “our Christian authorities,” reading of God as “the searcher and witness…

tl.w: Origen of Alexandria (c. 240 AD): No — but keeps the Greek
tl.t: The greatest biblical scholar of the early church returns the timeline to a Hebrew-sized canon. In his Commentary on Psalm 1 , quoted by Eusebius, Origen lists the Old Testament books "as the Hebrews have handed them down" as twenty-two , the count of the Hebrew letters — Tobit, Judith, Sirach, and the Wisdom of Solomon all absent, and the Maccabees named only to be set "besides these." 48 Yet the same Origen will not surrender the longer Greek text the churches actually read: answering Julius Africanus, who challenged the story of Susanna as no genuine part of Daniel, he refuses to "reject as spurious the copies in use in our Churches" and appeals to the Providence that gave those Scripture…

tl.w: Cyprian of Carthage (c. 253 AD): Yes — the disputed books cited as “Holy Scripture”
tl.t: From the Latin West, and with the fullest formulae yet, the bishop and martyr of Carthage cites the disputed books exactly as he cites the Law and the Gospel. A generation after his fellow Carthaginian Tertullian , and a contemporary of Origen in the East, Cyprian (c. 200–258, bishop of Carthage from c. 248, martyred under Valerian) quotes Tobit 12:8 as what “Holy Scripture instructs us, saying” — “Prayer is good with fasting and almsgiving” 51 Sirach 2:1, 4–5 as what “Holy Scripture teaches and forewarns, saying,” 52 and the Wisdom of Solomon 3:4–8 — the martyrs “tried… as gold in the furnace” — as “the sacred Scripture.” 53 He gathers 1 Maccabees 2:62–63 under “Holy Scripture meets and war…

tl.w: Dionysius of Alexandria (c. 264 AD): Yes — the disputed books used as inspired Scripture
tl.t: The Greek East supplies a near-contemporary of Cyprian from the very school that produced the era's most careful canon-list. Dionysius (c. 190–264), pupil and successor of Origen as head of the Alexandrian catechetical school and bishop of Alexandria from c. 248, twice presses a disputed book into service as inspired Scripture. In his treatise On Nature , arguing against the Epicurean doctrine that the ordered cosmos arose by chance from random atoms, he answers the philosophers by appeal to Sirach : “listen to the divine oracles: ‘The works of the Lord are in judgment…’” (Sirach 16:26–27) — the deuterocanonical wisdom book introduced as ta theia logia , the very category of inspired utteran…

tl.w: Methodius of Olympus (c. 290 AD): Yes — Wisdom & Sirach handled as Scripture
tl.t: A second Greek witness, from outside the Alexandrian school, joins Dionysius on the “using” side. Methodius (c. 290; martyred c. 311), bishop of Olympus in Lycia and a pointed early critic of Origen , twice handles a disputed book as Scripture. In his major work, the Banquet of the Ten Virgins , debating the divine ordering of every birth, he brings forward Wisdom of Solomon 3:16 with the bare formula “the Scripture which says”: “As for the children of the adulterers, they shall not come to their perfection” — the deuterocanonical text introduced under the unqualified label he reserves for the protocanon. 59 And the Oration on Simeon and Anna — a work transmitted under his name but of contes…

tl.w: Lactantius (c. 310 AD): Yes — Sirach cited as “Solomon’s” testimony to the Word of God
tl.t: On the eve of Nicaea, the first Latin apologist for the faith presses a disputed book into christological service. Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), the rhetorician Constantine would set over his son’s education, builds in his Divine Institutes (c. 303–311) a case for the eternal Word made flesh and calls “Solomon” as its Old-Testament witness: “I came forth out of the mouth of the Most High before all creatures… and covered the whole earth with a cloud” — the words of the deuterocanonical Sirach (Ecclesiasticus 24:3–4), the self-speech of personified Wisdom — set immediately beside John 1:1, “In the beginning was the Word.” 61 The ascription to “Solomon” is itself a tell: Sirach, written by Jes…

tl.w: Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 320 AD): Both at once — transmits the Hebrew lists, yet cites the disputed books as Scripture
tl.t: The single figure who most embodies the era's tension stands on the eve of Nicaea. Eusebius (c. 260–339), bishop of Caesarea and father of church history, is the very channel through which the two great Hebrew-sized lists reach us — he preserves Melito 's catalogue ( Ecclesiastical History iv.26) and Origen 's "twenty-two, as the Hebrews have handed them down" (vi.25), the documentary backbone of the narrower-canon case. 62 Yet in his own apologetic works he uses the disputed books as Scripture. In the Praeparatio Evangelica (c. 313–320), having quoted the deuterocanonical Wisdom of Solomon — "she reacheth from end to end with full strength, and ordereth all things graciously" (Wisdom 8:1) —…

tl.w: Alexander of Alexandria (c. 321 AD): Yes — Sirach chained with Paul, Genesis & Isaiah as scriptural testimony
tl.t: The bishop who opened the Arian controversy — Alexander of Alexandria (d. 326), Athanasius ’s mentor and predecessor — weaves the deuterocanonical Sirach into the texture of his christology. In his encyclical against Arius (the letter to Alexander of Byzantium, c. 319–324), arguing that the eternal generation of the Word lies beyond inquiry, he chains in one breath Sirach 3:21 — “Seek not out the things that are too hard for you, neither search the things that are above your strength,” adduced as binding authority one is impious “not listening to” — with the Apostle Paul (“Eye has not seen…,” 1 Corinthians 2:9), God’s word to Abraham that he could not number the stars (Genesis 15:5), Sirach …

tl.w: The Council of Nicaea (325 AD): No recorded ruling — but a Judith report
tl.t: The first ecumenical council published no canon-list. Its twenty surviving canons and synodal letter concern the Arian and Melitian schisms, the lapsed, the date of Easter, and clerical discipline — not the books of Scripture. 67 It belongs on this timeline for one reason: it is the earliest council to which a verdict on a deuterocanonical book has ever been attributed. Eighty years later Jerome reports, in his Preface to Judith , that the council "is found… to have been counted" the deuterocanonical book of Judith "among the number of the Sacred Scriptures," and gives that as his reason for translating a book he otherwise ranked below the canon. 68 But the report will not carry a Nicene can…

tl.w: Aphrahat the Persian Sage (c. 337 AD): Yes — Maccabean history read as fulfilled prophecy
tl.t: The timeline reaches the Syriac East, beyond the Roman frontier. Aphrahat (c. 270–345), “the Persian Sage,” a bishop in the Sasanian empire whose Demonstrations are the earliest substantial body of Syriac theology, treats the Maccabean history as authoritative, prophecy-fulfilling Scripture. In Demonstration 5 ( Of Wars , dated by its author to AD 337) he declares Psalm 79 “fulfilled… when the venerable and aged Eleazar was slain, and the sons of the blessed Samuna, seven in number” — the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6:18–7:42 — alongside “Judas (Maccabeus) and his brethren.” 71 And, expounding Daniel 7, he reads the worm-eaten death of Antiochus — “he became sick with a grievous and evil sickness…

tl.w: Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 350 AD): No — but Baruch kept
tl.t: Catechizing the candidates for baptism at Jerusalem, Cyril recites an Eastern Old-Testament list of twenty-two books, the Hebrew-letter count, and draws the line sharply: "have nothing to do with the apocryphal writings… study earnestly these only which we read openly in the Church." Tobit, Judith, Sirach, the Wisdom of Solomon, and 1–2 Maccabees are all absent. 73 Yet the list is not the bare Hebrew thirty-nine: Cyril's single book of Jeremiah is reckoned "including Baruch and Lamentations and the Epistle " — two short deuterocanonical works folded in as appendices, exactly as the Greek manuscripts carried them — and he credits the whole Hebrew-sized canon to the Septuagint's seventy-two tr…

The first Latin Father to set out a canon-list returns the Eastern verdict in the West. In the prologue to his Tractatus super Psalmos (Expositions of the Psalms) Hilary reckons the Old Testament at twenty-two books, "according to the number of the [Hebrew] letters" — Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, and the Maccabees absent from the count — recording only that "to this some add Tobit and Judith to make twenty-four books." A Westerner who had spent his exile among the Greek bishops, he carries the Hebrew enumeration of Origen and Cyril into Latin a generation before Jerome would make that count the West's standard — though Hilary, like the others, still quotes the disputed books in his own arg…

tl.w: The Cheltenham List (c. 360 AD): Yes — an early African list with the deuterocanon
tl.t: From the same years, and the other direction, comes an anonymous Latin catalogue — the Cheltenham (or Mommsen) List , a stichometric table of the canonical books with their line-counts, most likely North African. Its Old Testament runs out the longer canon: the two books of Maccabees , Tobit , and Judith are enumerated among the Scriptures with the rest, and the whole is sealed by the Apocalypse's "four and twenty elders." 76 It is a Western witness to the deuterocanon a full generation before the African councils of Hippo and Carthage gave that same canon conciliar form — the reception Augustine would later state as a rule.

tl.w: The Council of Laodicea (c. 363 AD): No — a Hebrew-sized list, the deuterocanon absent but Baruch and the Epistle of Jeremiah kept
tl.t: From the Eastern, list-making side of the same years comes a conciliar canon of the region.
