A regional synod of Phrygian bishops meeting at Laodicea rules that "only the Canonical Books… of the New and Old Testament" may be read in church (canon 59), and in the much-disputed canon 60 appends a book-list whose Old Testament is the Hebrew twenty-two: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, and the two books of Maccabees are all absent, and only Baruch and the Epistle of Jeremiah are kept, folded into "Jeremiah" as Origen , Cyril , and Athanasius also count their Jeremiah. 77 It is the Eastern list-side answer to the West's Cheltenham List and African councils — the same generation, the opposite verdict…

tl.w: Athanasius of Alexandria (367 AD): No — but Baruch kept, in three tiers
tl.t: The most influential Eastern voice of the century sorts the books into a famous three-tier scheme. In his thirty-ninth Festal Letter Athanasius first lists the Old-Testament canon as the Hebrew twenty-two — Tobit, Judith, Sirach, the Wisdom of Solomon, and the Maccabees all absent — though his Jeremiah, like Origen 's and Cyril 's, carries Baruch and the Epistle of Jeremiah folded in. 79 Below the canon he sets a second rank — books "not indeed included in the Canon, but appointed by the Fathers to be read… for instruction in the word of godliness" — and there he files the deuterocanon proper: the Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Judith, Tobit, and (strikingly) even the protocanonical Esther ; bel…

tl.w: Basil of Caesarea (c. 379 AD): Yes — the disputed books cited as Scripture, though he leaves no list
tl.t: The eldest of the three Cappadocian Fathers stands on the "using" side of the divide his own circle is famous for narrowing. Basil (c. 330–379), bishop of Caesarea, draws up no Old-Testament canon- list , but across his works he quotes the disputed books as authority. In the Hexaemeron he clinches a lesson on the soul's instability with the bare formula reserved for the protocanon — "What Scripture says is very true, 'As for a fool he changeth as the moon'" — the words of the deuterocanonical Sirach (27:11); and a consoling letter grounds divine providence in the Wisdom of Solomon : the Lord "ordereth 'all things in measure and weight'" (Wisdom 11:20), set beside 1 Corinthians 10:13. 81 In O…

tl.w: Gregory of Nyssa (c. 380 AD): Yes — the disputed books cited as "the prophetical writing," as Baruch "delivered… by the Holy Scriptures," and as "the Scripture"
tl.t: The third Cappadocian joins his brother Basil on the "using" side of the divide. Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–395), bishop of Nyssa from 372, draws up no canon- list , but across his doctrinal and ascetic works he quotes three of the disputed books as inspired authority. In On the Making of Man (16.14, 379) he grounds the divine foreknowledge in the Greek addition to Daniel — the prayer of Susanna, "knoweth all things before they be" (Susanna 42 / Daniel 13:42) — introduced as the word of " the prophetical writing ." 83 In Against Eunomius (c. 380–383) he twice presses the deuterocanonical Baruch (3:37) into service as the prophetic proof of the Incarnation — "the God who was in the beginning, '…

An Eastern bishop, friend of the Cappadocians, casts the canon into verse. In his Iambics for Seleucus Amphilochius warns that "not every book is safe which has acquired the venerable name of Scripture" — some are "spurious and utterly unsafe, like counterfeit… coins" — and then recites a Hebrew-sized Old Testament that omits Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, and the Maccabees, and gives even Esther only as a book "some approve." 86 It is the Hebrew-canon posture of his fellow Cappadocian Gregory of Nazianzus , set to meter for memorizing.

tl.w: The Apostolic Canons (c. 380 AD): Yes — Judith, three Maccabees, Sirach commended
tl.t: The Eastern church's own canon-law collection returns a "Yes" of singular shape. Canon 85, the closing canon of the Antiochene Apostolic Canons appended to the Apostolic Constitutions , bids "the following books be esteemed venerable and holy by all of you" and lists, among the Old Testament, "[one of Judith;] three of the Maccabees," and urges the young to learn "the Wisdom of the learned Sirach." 87 Its canon runs wider than the later Catholic deuterocanon — it receives three books of Maccabees, not two — yet it names neither Tobit nor the Wisdom of Solomon: a reminder that the Eastern "longer" canon was never a single fixed list. (The same canon's New-Testament reckoning omits Revelation …

tl.w: The Council of Rome (382 AD): Yes — but on a sixth-century document
tl.t: The first Latin council-list to run out the full deuterocanon is ascribed to the Roman synod that met under Pope Damasus I in 382. Its canon-catalogue — the so-called "Damasine list" — gives the longer Septuagint Old Testament, filing Tobit, Judith, and 1–2 Maccabees among "the Histories" and Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) among the books of Solomon: the whole disputed deuterocanon received as Scripture, the same canon the African councils would enact a decade later. 88 But the verdict comes with a sharp caveat about its act : the list survives in no fourth-century text, only as a chapter of the Decretum Gelasianum , a compilation critical scholarship dates to the sixth century (this sit…

tl.w: Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 385 AD): No — but Wisdom & Sirach "useful," Baruch kept
tl.t: The great heresy-hunter of Salamis returns the Eastern verdict once more. In both the Panarion and On Weights and Measures , Epiphanius gives the Hebrew-sized canon — twenty-seven "recognized canonical books, but twenty-two when counted according to the letters of the alphabet of the Hebrews" — running them out in four "pentateuchs" plus Ezra and Esther, with Tobit, Judith, and the Maccabees all absent. 90 But his "No" is graded, like Athanasius 's before it: he names the two great Wisdom books — the Wisdom of Solomon and the Wisdom of Sirach — and rules them "of disputed canonicity," yet "helpful and useful," books that "were not kept in the chest, that is, in the ark of the covenant"; and …

tl.w: Ambrose of Milan (c. 387 AD): Yes — the disputed books cited as "Scripture" and "it is written," the bishop who shaped Augustine
tl.t: The great bishop of Milan supplies the weightiest Western "using" witness of the century — the man who catechized and baptized Augustine (at Easter 387), whose reception-canon would carry the day in the West. Ambrose (c. 339–397, bishop of Milan from 374) draws up no canon- list , but across his works he quotes the disputed books with the plain formulae he reserves for the protocanon. He grounds his grief for his brother in the deuterocanonical Wisdom of Solomon — "as Scripture says concerning him: 'He was taken away, lest that wickedness should alter his understanding'" (Wisdom 4:11); reads the deuterocanonical Baruch as the very speech of "the Lord," who "saying: 'Put off, O Jerusalem, the…

tl.w: Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 389 AD): No — the narrowest list, even Esther dropped
tl.t: The great Cappadocian theologian draws the Hebrew line hardest of all. His verse catalogue Concerning the Genuine Books of Divinely Inspired Scripture warns "let not extraneous books seduce your mind, for many malignant writings have been disseminated," and counts "twenty-two of the ancient books, corresponding to the number of the Hebrew letters." 95 Not only are Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, and the Maccabees absent — Gregory's list is narrower even than his neighbours', omitting Esther as well, the same omission Athanasius had hesitated over. The poem became a standard Eastern measure of the canon, carried into the medieval Greek canon-law collections. Yet even this strictest of the Fath…

tl.w: Jerome (c. 390 AD): No — the hardest line, even Baruch dropped
tl.t: The man who gave the Latin West its Bible draws the sharpest "No" on the timeline. In the Prologus Galeatus — the "helmeted" preface to his translation from the Hebrew — Jerome fixes the Old Testament at the Hebrew twenty-two and rules that "whatever is outside of these is set aside among the apocrypha. Therefore, Wisdom… and the book of Jesus son of Sirach, and Judith and Tobias, and The Shepherd are not in the canon." 96 He is harder even than the Eastern Fathers before him: where Cyril , Athanasius , and Epiphanius all folded Baruch into the canonical Jeremiah, Jerome omits it as "neither read nor found among the Hebrews," and it is he who supplies the very word — apocrypha — the later Pr…

tl.w: The African councils — Hippo & Carthage (393–419 AD): Yes — the deuterocanon in conciliar form
tl.t: For the first time the boundary is drawn by a council . The North-African synods gathered around Augustine and Aurelius of Carthage — Hippo in 393 (canon 36, the earliest canon-list any church council promulgated), re-enacted at Carthage in 397 and reaffirmed in 419 — each enact the rule "that besides the Canonical Scriptures nothing be read in church under the name of divine Scripture," and then list the books. Their Old Testament is the longer Septuagint canon: Tobit , Judith , and the two books of Maccabees named outright among the Scriptures, and the deuterocanonical Wisdom of Solomon and Sirach carried in "the five books of Solomon." 99 Where Athanasius a generation earlier had ranked e…

tl.w: John Chrysostom (c. 395 AD): Yes — an Antiochene preacher citing the disputed books as Scripture
tl.t: The greatest preacher of Antioch — the school usually invoked for the narrower, Hebrew-sized canon — reaches for the deuterocanon in the pulpit exactly as he reaches for Moses and Paul. Chrysostom adduces Sirach (4:1) "from the Divine Scriptures," cites Wisdom (11:23) under "it is written," ranks the Greek Susanna (Daniel 13:52) beside two Psalms as a scriptural instance, and sets Tobit (12:9) beside Paul and the Psalter on almsgiving. 101 102 103 104 The use rises to doctrine: against the Marcionite denial of a real Incarnation he presses Baruch (3:35–37) — "in the book of Jeremiah" — as a prophecy that "this is our God… He appeared upon the earth, and held converse with men." 105 He leaves…

tl.w: Augustine of Hippo (c. 397): Yes — the full canon, on the breadth of its reception
tl.t: The theological hand behind those councils sets out the same verdict under his own name. In On Christian Doctrine Augustine runs out a forty-four-book Old Testament that files Tobias , Judith , the two books of Maccabees , and the two of Ezra among the histories, and reckons Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus among the prophetical books — the longer Septuagint canon, with no second tier. 106 What carries the disputed books in is not a Hebrew enumeration but a rule of reception : "to prefer those that are received by all the catholic churches to those which some do not receive," weighing a book by the breadth and antiquity of its use. 107 That is the exact opposite test from Jerome 's Hebraica veritas…

tl.w: The Catalogue of Codex Claromontanus (c. 400 AD): Yes
tl.t: A stichometric book-list, copied into the sixth-century Greek–Latin Codex Claromontanus but reflecting an older (c. 300–400) table, gives the longer canon with line-counts: Tobit , Judith , the Wisdom of Solomon, the Wisdom of Jesus (Sirach), and the books of Maccabees all stand among the Old Testament books. 109 The list marks several disputed titles with a small dash — but those obeli fall on contested New-Testament books, not on the Old-Testament deuterocanon, which it carries without qualification: an early-Western "Yes" preserved, like the Damasine list , in a later codex.

tl.w: Sulpicius Severus (c. 403): Yes — Judith narrated within his epitome of "the sacred Scriptures"
tl.t: A Gallic aristocrat-turned-ascetic, friend and biographer of Martin of Tours , supplies a quieter Western datapoint: not a canon-list and not a proof-text, but a history . In his Sacred History ( Chronica , c. 403) Sulpicius Severus sets out to "give a condensed account of those things which are set forth in the sacred Scriptures from the beginning of the world… down to" his own day — an epitome of the biblical narrative whose contents are the canon he is summarizing. 110 Into that survey, alongside Esther and the post-exilic books, he folds Judith : "To this series of events it will be right that I should append an account of the doings of Judith; for she is related to have lived after the …

tl.w: Rufinus of Aquileia (c. 404): No — but "Ecclesiastical," read though not doctrinal
tl.t: Rufinus gives the cleanest, most systematic version of the middle position. In his Commentary on the Apostles' Creed he sorts the books into three named ranks. The Canonical Old Testament he lists is the Hebrew-sized canon — Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, and the Maccabees all absent, and Jeremiah named without Baruch. 112 Below it he sets a second tier, the books "our fathers call not 'Canonical' but 'Ecclesiastical'": the Wisdom of Solomon, the Wisdom of the Son of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), Tobit, Judith, and the Maccabees — "all of which they would have read in the Churches, but not appealed to for the confirmation of doctrine"; and below that the Apocrypha , which "they would not have rea…

tl.w: Innocent I (c. 405): Yes — the deuterocanon received from the see of Rome
tl.t: A sitting bishop of Rome restates the Western verdict. Answering a query from Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, on which books "really are received in the canon," Innocent I appends a canon-list whose Old Testament is the longer Septuagint form: Tobit , Judith , and the two books of Maccabees named outright among "the historical books," and the deuterocanonical Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) carried in "the five books of Solomon." 114 He files these books among the canon, with none of the "read but not canonical" qualification that Athanasius , Jerome , and Rufinus had attached to the very same titles — the Augustinian, reception-based posture rather than the Hebrew reckoning. 115 Coming a …

tl.w: John Cassian (c. 426 AD): Yes — Wisdom cited as "Scripture itself testifies," Baruch as "the prophet"
tl.t: The father of Western monasticism, carrying the desert tradition of Egypt into Gaul, cites the disputed books as Scripture and prophecy in the very work that shaped Latin monastic life. John Cassian (c. 360 – c. 435), whose Conferences ( Collationes , c. 426–429) report the teaching of the Egyptian abbots to the monks of Marseilles, introduces the deuterocanonical Wisdom of Solomon with the bare formula he reserves for Scripture: "as Scripture itself testifies: 'For God made not death, neither rejoices in the destruction of the living'" (Wisdom 1:13). 116 He quotes the deuterocanonical Baruch as the word of "the prophet" — "nor hear the words of the prophet: Why are you grown old in a strang…

tl.w: Vincent of Lérins (c. 434 AD): Yes — Sirach quoted among "the divine Oracles," bracketed with Proverbs and Ecclesiastes
tl.t: At the very hinge of the West's classic rule for telling catholic truth from heresy, a disputed book is named among "the divine Oracles." In his Commonitory (AD 434) Vincent of Lérins (c. 400 – c. 445), the Gallic monk whose "what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all" became the touchstone of orthodoxy, clinches his thesis that the faith may never be added to by stringing three wisdom-sayings together under one formula — "the divine Oracles cry aloud, 'Remove not the landmarks, which thy fathers have set,' and 'Go not to law with a Judge,' and 'Whoso breaketh through a fence a serpent shall bite him'" — and the middle of the three is the deuterocanonical Sirach (8:14), set withou…

tl.w: Junilius Africanus (c. 542 AD): No, tiered — a first class of "perfect authority" and a second of "middle authority," the deuterocanon demoted
tl.t: From Justinian's court comes the most systematic tiered canon of the age. Junilius , a North-African layman serving as quaestor sacri palatii at Constantinople, turned into Latin a Greek handbook of Scripture-teaching learned from Paul the Persian of the school of Nisibis, and near its start graded the books by authority: some "of perfect authority" ( perfectae auctoritatis ), the canonical class; some "of middle" authority ( mediae ), "added by many"; and some of none. 120 Into the second, "middle" rank he files the deuterocanonical Tobit, Judith, and Maccabees, and the Wisdom of Solomon — and, unusually, the protocanonical Chronicles, Job, Ezra, Esther, and Song of Songs with them — on the…

tl.w: The Synopsis of Sacred Scripture (c. 550 AD): No — but the deuterocanon "read," in Athanasius's tier
tl.t: A handbook transmitted under Athanasius 's name but later in date, the Synopsis Scripturae Sacrae repeats his graded verdict almost exactly. Its canonical Old Testament is the Hebrew-sized list, the disputed books absent; but it then sets out a second rank — books "not… canonical, but only read" to the catechumens — and there it files the deuterocanon: the Wisdom of Solomon, the Wisdom of Sirach, Esther, Judith, and Tobit. 122 It is Athanasius 's "appointed by the Fathers to be read" preserved into the sixth century — the disputed books neither canonized nor cast out, but kept as a middle, "read" rank.

tl.w: Gregory the Great (c. 590 AD): Yes, graded — quotes Wisdom, Tobit & Sirach as Scripture, yet calls 1 Maccabees "not canonical"
tl.t: The single sharpest "graded standing" datapoint on the timeline: a reigning bishop of Rome who cites the deuterocanon as Scripture with one hand and, of one book, withholds the word canonical with the other. In his Register III.53 Gregory the Great (c. 540–604) adduces the Wisdom of Solomon (1:11) as what "the Truth says through His Scripture" — "The mouth that lies slays the soul"; 123 and in the Book of Pastoral Rule (III.21) he ranges Tobit (4:17) and Sirach (12:4) together under "what is written," beside Luke and Matthew. 124 Yet in his great Morals on the Book of Job (XIX, §34), retelling Eleazar's death from 1 Maccabees 6, he pauses to qualify the source: "we are not acting irregularly…

tl.w: Isidore of Seville (c. 636 AD): No — Jerome's count, with a "fourth class" read
tl.t: The great encyclopedist of the Latin West restates Jerome 's Hebrew canon. In the Etymologiae (VI.9) Isidore divides the Old Testament into the three Hebrew classes — Law, Prophets, Sacred Writings — totalling twenty-two books (some, he notes, add Ruth and Lamentations to make twenty-four), with the deuterocanon outside the count. 126 But he then names a further class the Church "honors and proclaims" though it stands outside the Hebrew canon — Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus (Sirach), Tobit, Judith, and the Maccabees — the same graded posture, canonical-by-the-Hebrews / read-by-the-Church, that Rufinus and Jerome had handed him, carried into the medieval Latin schoolbooks.

tl.w: The Council in Trullo (Quinisext) (692 AD): Both and neither — conflicting canon-lists ratified en bloc
tl.t: The Eastern church's great disciplinary council issues no book-list of its own, but in its second canon confirms — together, without reconciling them — the canons of the earlier councils and Fathers, whose Scripture-lists contradict one another. Trullo ratifies "the eighty-five canons… in the name of the… Apostles" and the canons "at Laodicea in Phrygia… and those of Carthage… of Athanasius… of Amphilochius of Iconium" — but the Apostolic Canons and Carthage run the longer, deuterocanon-bearing Old Testament, while Laodicea , Athanasius , and Amphilochius rank the disputed books out or below. 127 As Percival notes, the earlier canons were "received in block," not adjudicated — so the East, i…

tl.w: Codex Amiatinus (c. 700 AD): Yes — the whole canon bound in one book
tl.t: The oldest surviving complete Latin Vulgate in a single volume — a pandect made c. 700 at the Wearmouth–Jarrow monastery in Northumbria — embodies the longer canon physically: Codex Amiatinus carries Tobit , Judith , Wisdom , Sirach , and the two books of Maccabees among its Old Testament books. 128 Yet the same manuscript prints the disagreement in its own front matter: its opening leaves diagram three rival canon-divisions — Jerome 's Hebrew-sized twenty-two, the Septuagint order, and Augustine 's longer list — so the very codex that hands the West the full deuterocanon also preserves, on its first pages, the Hebrew-sized schemes that disputed it.

tl.w: John of Damascus (c. 730 AD): No — the Hebrew canon, yet cites Wisdom as "the divine Scripture"
tl.t: The last of the Greek Fathers gives the Eastern Hebrew canon its closing classic statement. In An Exposition of the Orthodox Faith (IV.17) John of Damascus arranges the twenty-two books in four "pentateuchs" plus two — the deuterocanon outside the count — and names the Wisdom of Solomon and the Wisdom of Sirach only to rule them "virtuous and noble, but… not counted nor… placed in the ark." 129 It is the verdict of Epiphanius three centuries on, repeated almost word for word — the Eastern "No" still graded, still keeping the disputed books as honoured but uncanonical, two centuries before the Masoretic Text fixed the Hebrew table for good. Yet the witness is double, and the two halves stand …

tl.w: The Stichometry of Nicephorus (c. 810 AD): No — the deuterocanon ranked "disputed"
tl.t: A line-count catalogue attached to the Chronography of Nicephorus, Patriarch of Constantinople, gives the last great Eastern list before the medieval Hebrew codices. Its canonical Old Testament is the Hebrew-sized protocanon (Baruch folded into Jeremiah); the deuterocanon is not omitted in silence but sorted into a named lower rank of antilegomena — "those spoken against" — where the books of Maccabees , the Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach , Esther , Judith , Susanna , and Tobit are each listed with their line-counts. 131 It is the Synopsis 's graded "No" made into a formal three-tier inventory — canonical, disputed, apocryphal — the Eastern position carried to the threshold of the Byzantine Middl…

tl.w: The Masoretic Text (c. 1000 AD, Judaism): No
tl.t: The medieval Jewish standard text returns the Hebrew "No" in its definitive form. The Masoretic Text — the work of the Masoretes, scribal scholars of the seventh through tenth centuries who fixed the Hebrew Bible letter by letter, surviving in the tenth-century Aleppo Codex and the 1008/1009 Leningrad Codex — is "the authoritative Hebrew and Aramaic text of the 24 books of the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh) in Rabbinic Judaism," carrying the protocanonical books alone: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and the Maccabees have no place in it. 132 It did not decide the canon — it preserved the boundary the rabbinic stream had long since drawn (the "Council of Jamnia" marker) — but it gave that Hebr…

tl.w: The Glossa Ordinaria (c. 1130, the standard medieval glossed Bible): No — but Jerome transmitted, not an independent verdict: his prologues, carried in every Bible's front matter, ranking the disputed books "not in the canon"
tl.t: Through the long medieval lull the learned Hieronymian distinction has one great carrier, and it is not a council or a fresh verdict but a textbook . The Glossa Ordinaria — the standard glossed Bible assembled at the school of Laon in the early twelfth century (long misattributed to the ninth-century Walafrid Strabo, in fact the work of Anselm of Laon and his successors) and read "in every single center of theological learning" thereafter — carried, as front matter to Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, and the Maccabees, prologues declaring them outside the canon, read "for the edification of the people, not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical doctrines." 134 But those prologues are J…

tl.w: The Council of Florence (1442): Yes — the first ecumenical enumeration of the full canon
tl.t: After the long medieval lull the timeline reaches its first ecumenical verdict. In the bull Cantate Domino , the Bull of Union with the Copts, the Council of Florence professes that "one and the same God is the author of the old and the new Testament" and lists the books it "accepts and venerates" — and there, threaded into one undifferentiated list beside Genesis, Isaiah, and the Gospels, stand Tobit , Judith , Wisdom , Ecclesiasticus (Sirach), Baruch , and the two books of Maccabees . 137 It is the Augustinian, reception-based canon of the African councils and Innocent I — the disputed books levelled into the canon with none of the "read but not canonical" tier of Athanasius , Jerome , and…

tl.w: The Complutensian Polyglot (Cardinal Ximénez, c. 1520): No — the books "outside the canon" set apart, received "for the edification of the people," not for confirming doctrine
tl.t: On the very eve of the Reformation the Hebrew-canon distinction surfaces once more — in a cardinal's own Bible, under a pope's sanction. The Complutensian Polyglot , the first printed polyglot of the whole Bible, planned and financed by Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros (Ximénez), printed at Alcalá 1514–17 and published in 1522 with the sanction of Pope Leo X, sets the books outside the Hebrew canon apart from the rest. Its prologue Ad lectorem professes that these are "books outside the canon, which the Church receives for the edification of the people rather than for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical dogmas" ( libri extra canonem, quos Ecclesia potius ad aedificationem populi…

tl.w: Cardinal Cajetan (Thomas de Vio, 1532, Roman Catholic): No — two senses of "canonical": for edification, not for confirming faith — and Jerome is the measure
tl.t: Two years before Luther 's printed Bible, the distinction is stated once more — this time not in a preface but by one of Rome's foremost theologians, the cardinal who had examined Luther at Augsburg in 1518. Closing his Commentary on all the authentic historical books of the Old Testament (dedicated to Pope Clement VII, 1532) at the end of Esther, Cajetan writes that Judith, Tobit, the Maccabees, Wisdom, and Ecclesiasticus "are counted by St Jerome out of the canonical books, and are placed amongst the Apocrypha… as is plain from the Prologus Galeatus," and warns the "raw scholar" not to be disturbed at finding them called canonical in a council or a Father: "the words as well of councils as…

tl.w: Martin Luther (1534, Protestant): No — "not equal to Holy Scripture, yet useful and good to read"
tl.t: The Reformation reopens the question Florence thought closed, and answers it with Jerome 's "No" set in print. In his complete German Bible of 1534 Luther lifted Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and 1–2 Maccabees out of the Old Testament and gathered them — all but 1–2 Esdras, which he dropped — into a separate section between the Testaments under the heading "Apocrypha — that is, books which are not held equal to the Holy Scriptures, and yet are profitable and good to read." 144 The layout is the verdict, and it is the graded "No" of the Hebrew-minded Fathers made visible on the page: in his prefaces he commends Judith as "a fine, good, holy, useful book, well worth reading by us Chri…

tl.w: The Council of Trent (1546, Roman Catholic): Yes — the deuterocanon defined as canonical, under anathema
tl.t: The Counter-Reformation answers Luther by closing the question as dogma. In its fourth session, the first to take up doctrine, the Council of Trent declares that it "receives and venerates with an equal affection of piety, and reverence, all the books both of the Old and of the New Testament," and prints the list — Tobias , Judith , Wisdom , Ecclesiasticus (Sirach), Baruch , and the two books of Maccabees threaded among the rest with no second tier — the same receptive verb ( suscipit ac veneratur ) the Council of Florence had used a century before. 147 What sets Trent apart from every earlier "Yes" is the force: it anathematizes anyone who "receive not, as sacred and canonical, the said boo…

tl.w: The Thirty-Nine Articles (1571, Church of England): No — read "for example of life," not to establish doctrine
tl.t: The English Reformation answers Trent not with Luther 's heading but with Jerome 's rule, cited by name. Article VI of the Articles of Religion defines canonical Scripture as "those canonical Books of the Old and New Testament, of whose authority was never any doubt in the Church," lists the Hebrew-sized Old Testament book by book, and then files the deuterocanon in a separate rank: "the other Books (as Hierome saith) the Church doth read for example of life and instruction of manners; but yet doth it not apply them to establish any doctrine." 150 The list of those "other Books" is wider than Trent's: it brackets Tobias, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and 1–2 Maccabees together with the Gre…

tl.w: The Westminster Confession of Faith (1647, Reformed): No — the hardest line: "of no authority… than other human writings"
tl.t: The Reformed answer hardens the Anglican "No" into a flat exclusion. Chapter 1 of the Westminster Confession names the canon by inspiration — "all the books of the Old and New Testaments… All which are given by inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life" — and lists the Hebrew-sized thirty-nine Old Testament books (Genesis through Malachi) with the twenty-seven of the New. 152 The next section then rules on the disputed books with a force no earlier Protestant confession had used: "The books commonly called Apocrypha, not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of the Scripture; and therefore are of no authority in the Church of God, nor to be any otherwise approved, …

tl.w: The Synod of Jerusalem (1672, Eastern Orthodox): Yes — the Eastern counterpart to Trent
tl.t: The timeline closes in the East. A generation after Westminster, the Synod of Jerusalem — convened at Bethlehem by Patriarch Dositheus II to repudiate a Calvinizing confession that had circulated under the name of Cyril Lucaris, Patriarch of Constantinople — gave the Eastern Orthodox church its most authoritative modern ruling on the canon. The Confession of Dositheus names the books Lucaris had set aside as "Apocrypha" — the Wisdom of Solomon, Judith, Tobit, Bel and the Dragon, Susanna, the Maccabees, and Sirach — and declares them "genuine parts of Scripture," on a level "with the other genuine Books of Divine Scripture." 154 Its ground is not the Hebrew table but the delivering tradition …

ar.q: "Eye hath not seen…" (1 Corinthians 2:9): does Paul quote, as Scripture, an apocryphon outside the Old Testament canon?
ar.c: "But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him." — 1 Corinthians 2:9 (KJV). The formula kathôs gégraptai ("as it is written") is the standard New-Testament header for an Old-Testament citation; yet no canonical passage reads exactly this way. This is the firmest member of the cluster of New-Testament "strange quotations" for the wider-canon reading, because here — unlike the centerpiece at Ephesians 5:14 — a named Father actually pins the words to a specific apocryphal book. The argu…
ar.a: Weak. That Paul introduces with "as it is written" words found in no verbatim Old-Testament text is sound; the inference that he thereby quotes a non-canonical writing as Scripture is weak on its best case. The firmest patristic anchor for that reading — Origen's (and Ambrosiaster's) ascription to the Apocalypse/Secrets of Elijah — is contradicted by Jerome, who read the Hebrew and assigned the words to a paraphrase of Isaiah 64:4 , and rests on …

ar.q: Does "from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah" delimit the Hebrew Old Testament canon, excluding the Apocrypha?
ar.c: The argument runs as a short chain: The Hebrew Bible Jesus used ran Genesis to Chronicles — Chronicles, not Malachi, standing last. Abel's murder is recorded near the start of Genesis (Gen 4); the murder of a Zechariah is recorded near the end of Chronicles (2 Chron 24:20–22). So in naming "from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah" Jesus was citing the first and last martyrs of the canon — its opening and closing books — and thereby implicitly delimiting it, Genesis to Chronicles, excluding later books such as 1–2 Maccabees. 1 F. F. Bruce gave it its standard popular form: "when our Lo…
ar.a: Weak — as a demarcation of the canon. The interpretation that Jesus' "from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah" marks the limits of the Hebrew canon and thereby excludes the Apocrypha does not hold on its best available case. It rests on three premises each independently doubtful: that the saying functions as a canon-boundary (a reading unattested before Eichhorn in 1780, against an unbroken tradition that read it as a first-to-last marty…

ar.q: Did the early church accept the Apocrypha out of ignorance of Hebrew and the Hebrew canon?
ar.c: Two modern Protestant apologists give the thesis its sharpest form. James White, debating Gary Michuta on whether the Apocrypha is Scripture, traces the wider canon to a failure of knowledge: 1 Evidently some in the early church, ignorant of the Old Testament canon and the backgrounds of the people of Israel assumed that since some or all of the Apocryphal books appeared in their Greek translations then they must be canonical. Those early writers who knew the most about the Old Testament did not make this mistake. Remember, very few of the early church writers knew the Hebrew language. There i…
ar.a: Weak. As an account of why the church was familiar with the deuterocanon — a Greek-reading church whose Bible contained the books — the thesis names true facts. But as the explanation it is offered to be, that the wider canon is an artifact of linguistic ignorance rather than a considered judgment, it does not hold. Its load-bearing correlation — least educated in Hebrew endorsed, language-educated rejected — fails on both sides: the most Hebrew-…

ar.q: Had the word "apocrypha" drifted to mean "inspired-but-hidden" by the eve of Trent — so calling the deuterocanon "apocrypha" can't be read as rejecting it?
ar.c: For example, the word Apocrypha by the time of the 15th century had become so twisted—this is usually due to medieval writers who tried to make Jerome fit into an orthodox stance—that they would twist his words on calling the deuterocanonical books Apocrypha to mean something like "inspired scripture that is somehow hidden." By the time of the Council of Trent, the word Apocrypha had been so twisted that you would actually find fathers in the Council of Trent who argued for the full divinity and canonicity of these books, calling them Apocrypha . — Gary Michuta, The Great Debate IX: Is the Apo…
ar.a: Weak , in the form that does the apologetic work. The bare observation underneath it — that apocrypha is polysemous and its valence is author- and era-dependent, so a lone use of the word is not a knockdown — is true, but it is a different and much narrower claim, and it is weighed as sound on the "canon"-word page. The interpretation actually asserted here — that the term had drifted to "inspired-but-hidden" by the eve of Trent, evidenced by Tre…

ar.q: Was the apostles' Bible the Greek Septuagint — and does that make the deuterocanon canonical?
ar.c: The argument runs in two linked steps. First, a historical observation about which Bible the apostles used: "By the first century, the LXX was the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and so was the most frequently used version of the Old Testament in the early Church … the New Testament writers, when they quote from the Old Testament, usually quote from the Septuagint." — Catholic Answers , "In Which Passages Does Jesus Quote the Septuagint…?" The point is bolstered by the demonstrable cases where the New Testament follows a Greek reading against the Hebrew that became the Masoretic text, and by the …
ar.a: Contested. The interpretation is strong by one discipline's lights and weak by another's, which is just what a contested verdict marks. By the lights of textual and reception history, its core is sound and barely disputed: the apostolic Bible was a Greek Old Testament, and the New Testament's quotations follow its readings against the proto-Masoretic Hebrew, sometimes with the argument riding on the Greek (Acts 15 / Amos 9 is the textbook case). …

ar.q: Do the Apostolic Fathers show the deuterocanon used "commensurate with Scripture"? — Brabban's dissertation vs. Beckwith's survey
ar.c: So, what do we find in the Apostolic Fathers? I'd like to refer you to a doctoral dissertation written by R. J. Brabban, who, after an exhaustive study of the Apostolic Fathers, concludes that the Deuterocanonical books: "Were indeed known and used in a manner identical to those books now recognized as canonical or Scripture." … Brabban further concludes that the Deuterocanonical books are never refuted by the Apostolic Fathers, are never reduced to inferior sources, are never dismissed as inaccurate, are never treated as less than Scripture. — Gary Michuta, opening statement in The Great Deba…
ar.a: Contested. Split the interpretation in two. The modest reading — that the Apostolic Fathers drew on several disputed books (Wisdom, Judith, Tobit, Sirach) as authoritative, edifying, sometimes prophetic material from the first generation, so their later use is no late accretion — is sound , and Brabban documents it. The strong reading Michuta builds on Brabban — that the Fathers used the deuterocanon identically to canonical Scripture and never t…

ar.q: What divides Athanasius's "canon" and "read" tiers — function (evangelizing Jews vs. catechizing converts), not inspiration?
ar.c: Athanasius's thirty-ninth Festal Letter (367) sorts the Old-Testament books into three ranks: the canon proper (the twenty-two Hebrew-reckoned books), a middle tier of books "not… included in the Canon, but appointed by the Fathers to be read by those who newly join us, and who wish for instruction in the word of godliness" (Wisdom, Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, the Teaching of the Apostles , the Shepherd ), and a third tier of "apocryphal writings… an invention of heretics." The interpretation weighed here takes the modern two-bucket scheme (canonical-inspired vs. apocryphal-rejected) off th…
ar.a: Plausible. The interpretation's foundation is sound and its account of the read tier is probable: Athanasius does not divide his top two ranks by inspiration (he cites the lower books as Scripture in his own voice), and the middle tier is, by his own words and by Origen's parallel, catechetical instruction for newcomers — emphatically not the Protestant rejected-Apocrypha. Trust that much fully. The distinctive further claim — that the canon tier…

ar.q: Did Athanasius reject the deuterocanon — is his Festal Letter 39 a witness for the Protestant Old Testament canon?
ar.c: The argument runs from a single, famous document — the thirty-ninth Festal (Easter) Letter Athanasius issued in 367, the same letter that gives the first surviving list of the twenty-seven-book New Testament: Athanasius opens his Old-Testament catalogue by fixing the count at "twenty-two books… the number of the letters among the Hebrews," and names a Hebrew-sized list with no Tobit, Judith, Sirach, Wisdom of Solomon, or Maccabees. He then expressly files Wisdom, Sirach, Judith, and Tobit in a lower rank — "not… included in the Canon" — and denounces a third class, the "apocryphal" forgeries o…
ar.a: Contested. The headline question "did Athanasius reject the deuterocanon?" splits cleanly by sense, and the verdict follows the sense. As a claim about canonical status — that Athanasius's Festal Letter places the freestanding deuterocanon below the twenty-two-book canon, making him a genuine fourth-century Eastern witness against its canonicity — the argument is sound , and the careful proponents (White, Christie, Ortlund) state it accurately. A…

ar.q: Should Augustine's canon witness be discounted because he was "no biblical expert" and could not read Hebrew, unlike Jerome?
ar.c: The Christian Apologetics & Research Ministry (CARM) grants that the disputed books were received by a string of Western councils, then discounts that reception in two moves — a comparative-competence move and a not-universal move: 1 It is true that the Catholic Church accepted the Apocryphal books at earlier councils at Rome (A.D. 382), Hippo (A.D. 393), Carthage (A.D. 397), and Florence (A.D. 1442). However, these were not universal Church councils and the earlier councils were influenced heavily by Augustine, who was no Biblical expert, compared to the scholar Jerome, who rejected the Apocr…
ar.a: Weak. The argument's factual core is sound and is kept: Jerome was the superior Hebraist, Augustine read no Hebrew, and the African councils were regional and Augustine-shaped. But the discounting conclusion built on it does not hold. It impeaches Augustine for a competence his canon-argument never invoked — his test was breadth of churchly reception, not Hebrew enumeration, a standard for which reading Hebrew is not decisive — and it sustains "n…

ar.q: Did Augustine retract his view and rank the deuterocanon below the canonical Scriptures?
ar.c: In The Canon of the Old and New Testaments Ascertained (1826), the Old-School Presbyterian theologian Archibald Alexander — first professor of Princeton Seminary — grants that Augustine is the one early Father who "seems to favour the introduction of these six disputed books into the Canon," then reclaims him for the shorter canon on three counts: 1 These two last mentioned, he says, "are called Solomon's, on account of their resemblance to his writings; although it is known that one of them was composed by the son of Sirach: which deserves to be received among the prophetical books." But this…
ar.a: Weak. The interpretation — that Augustine retracted his high view of the disputed books and ranked them below the genuine Scriptures, so his witness should be discounted — does not hold on its best case. Its two factual props fail: the Retractations correct the authorship of the Wisdom of Solomon, not its canonicity, and the "read from a lower place / not as Holy Scripture" custom is the canonical-versus-ecclesiastical distinction of Jerome and R…

ar.q: Did Augustine accept the deuterocanon only because he mistakenly thought it stood in the Hebrew canon?
ar.c: In his 2014 debate with the Catholic apologist Gary Michuta, the Reformed apologist James White grants that Augustine accepted the disputed books, then turns him into a witness for the Protestant side by a counterfactual about Augustine's state of mind: 1 Augustine, however, disagreed. Augustine could not read Hebrew, and the manuscripts that he had contained these books but interestingly enough he is actually a witness for my side this evening. Why? Because though he accepted the Apocryphal books, he did so because he thought they were part of the Hebrew canon. If he had known what the Hebrew…
ar.a: Weak. The argument's true core — that Augustine read no Hebrew and held the Septuagint inspired — is real and worth keeping; it explains why his canon followed the Greek Bible. But the conclusion built on it, that his longer canon is an artifact of ignorance of the Hebrew table which a better-informed Augustine would have abandoned, does not hold, because it rests on a factual premise Augustine himself contradicts. In his own late words he states…

ar.q: Does the Bava Batra 14b baraita — the rabbinic "twenty-four books" — attest a pre-Christian, closed Hebrew canon?
ar.c: Answering the challenge that no Jewish source is ever quoted listing the books it receives as Scripture, James White adduces the enumerated canon-list preserved in the Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 14b : "The order of the books of the Prophets when they are attached together is as follows: Joshua and Judges, Samuel and Kings, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, and Isaiah and the Twelve Prophets… The order of the Writings is: Ruth and the book of Psalms, and Job and Proverbs; Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, and Lamentations; Daniel and the Scroll of Esther; and Ezra and Chronicles." — a baraita preserved in Ba…
ar.a: Weak — for the inference as pressed, that the Bava Batra 14b baraita witnesses a pre-Christian , closed, deuterocanon-excluding Hebrew canon. The positive datum the argument rests on is real and is its genuine strength: this is an actual named, ordered enumeration of a Hebrew-sized Scripture, the one thing a bare count like Josephus's does not supply, and it excludes the Greek extras. But the load-bearing move is the dating, and there the baraita…

ar.q: Do the Catholic canon councils contradict each other? — "Trent anathematizes Hippo and Carthage" and the conciliar-infallibility objection
ar.c: The inference comes in three escalating forms. James White put the sharpest version as a cross-examination dilemma in his 2004 debate with Gary Michuta: Given that Pope Innocent I and Pope Gelasius both affirmed the canon list of Hippo and Carthage, yet Trent and every pope since then has affirmed a different list that excludes the extra material in Esdras, which popes were right and which popes were wrong on this issue? — The Great Debate IX: Is the Apocrypha Scripture? (White vs. Michuta, 2004). 1 The "which were right and which were wrong?" frame already presupposes a conflict : if the list…
ar.a: Weak. The inference inherits a sound premise — the lists are genuinely not identical over the Greek 1 Esdras (weighed on the companion page ) — and then loads onto it more than it can carry. "Contradiction" requires one council to deny what another affirms, but Trent defined no proposition denying 1 Esdras: it withheld judgment on 3 Esdras (the Clementine appendix is a later editorial settlement, not a conciliar condemnation), so the most the rec…

ar.q: Is the canon "discovered, not decided" — a fact of reality the church recognizes rather than constitutes, so the Fathers' use of the deuterocanon was honest err…
ar.c: Pressing the point in 20 Questions with Pastor Mike , the Protestant teacher Mike Winger states the ontological view of canon plainly and then applies it to the deuterocanon: "there is no such thing as scripture that is no longer canon… the canon is simply a fact of reality… God inspired these books, they are canon whether you acknowledge them or not," and so of 1–2 Maccabees, "I think they never were at any point part of it, and were included in some people's lists mistakenly." 1 The structure of the argument is: Canonicity is a property a book has in virtue of being divinely inspired. Inspir…
ar.a: Contested. As a theological account of the nature of canon, the "discovered-not-decided" (ontological) view is coherent and well-represented — Kruger's self-authenticating model and Bruce's "canonicity follows authority" are its careful forms, and its core claim that the church recognizes rather than constitutes the canon is granted even by Catholic dogma. Whether canonicity is best located in that ontological fact or partly in the church's const…

ar.q: Does the deuterocanon dispute undermine sola scriptura — can Scripture settle its own table of contents?
ar.c: The argument runs from a fact this whole timeline establishes to a sweeping conclusion about authority: Sola scriptura makes Scripture the sole final authority for doctrine — what is "biblical" is the test of what may bind the conscience. But Scripture nowhere lists its own books: there is no inspired table of contents. The boundary of the Bible must therefore be received from somewhere outside Scripture — from the church, from tradition, from history. And that boundary is not even agreed: the deuterocanon dispute this timeline traces shows the table of contents genuinely contested among Chris…
ar.a: Contested — for the underlying tension; weak for the "whole experiment fails" conclusion. The serious form of the argument identifies something true and much-discussed: Scripture has no inspired table of contents, the canon cannot be derived from Scripture, and the deuterocanon dispute this timeline documents is a real, unresolved case of the table of contents being contested among Christians — a standing strain on sola scriptura that thoughtful …

ar.q: Does the Fathers' word "canon" (κανών) mean what the modern definition means — a closed, exclusive list of inspired books?
ar.c: The interpretation weighed here is a terminological one, pressed most carefully by the canon-list scholar John Meade: the words the Fathers used for Scripture shifted meaning over time, and "canon" especially did not always mean what it means now. The modern definition packs three things into one word — a list , that is closed (no additions), and exclusive to inspired books. Read that bundle back into Justin, Irenaeus, or Origen and you misdescribe what they were doing, because for them κανών did not yet name a table of books at all. The claim is not that the Fathers lacked Scripture or revere…
ar.a: Sound. The terminological claim is well-grounded and broadly agreed across confessional lines: the word canon developed, and the modern definition's bundle of "closed, exclusive, inspired list" is a fourth-century-and-later crystallization that should not be read back onto the earlier word. Kept in that calibrated form, it is a genuine corrective — and a two-edged one, trimming both the Protestant appeal to early "canon lists" and the Catholic ap…

ar.q: Were there “400 silent years” — no prophet at all between Malachi and Christ — closing the canon?
ar.c: A staple of the popular case against the deuterocanon is the “400 silent years”: that from Malachi (mid-fifth century BC) to the coming of Christ, God sent no prophet, so revelation paused and the Old Testament canon was already sealed before the deuterocanonical books were written. The cutoff is hung on Josephus, who bounds the divinely-credited books at the reign of Artaxerxes “because there hath not been an exact succession of prophets since that time.” Allen Parr presses it in its flat form: “Josephus is recognizing that Malachi was the last prophet inspired by God, and there were no other…
ar.a: Weak — for the literal “total silence” form and the canon-closure it is made to prove; the narrower premise underneath it is sound. That a recognized Jewish tradition held the classical prophetic succession to have ended with Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, and that the deuterocanon was written afterward, is true and well-attested, and a genuine datum for those books' graded standing — converging with the Hebrew-measure reading this timeline trac…

ar.q: Does a Father's quoting a book "as Scripture" prove he held it canonical — or must usage be weighed against his canon list?
ar.c: Much of the Catholic case for the deuterocanon is built from usage : Father after Father — Clement of Rome , Irenaeus , Clement of Alexandria , Cyprian , and more — cites the disputed books as "Scripture," as "it is written," as the voice of the prophets, to settle doctrine. The inference urged is: they quoted these books as Scripture, therefore they held them canonical. The interpretation weighed here, advanced by the Protestant Old-Testament scholar John Meade (co-author of the standard reference on the early canon lists), denies the inference. Citation-as-Scripture and canonical status are …
ar.a: Plausible. Take the principle in two halves. The distinction it rests on — that quoting a book "as Scripture" is a looser act than ranking it in a deliberate canon list, so a citation formula does not by itself prove a Father held the book canonical — is sound , and is the working method of the field's standard reference (Gallagher & Meade). Athanasius proves it: he excludes Wisdom, Sirach, and Tobit from his canon list and cites all three as Scr…

ar.q: Do the deuterocanonical books disclaim their own inspiration, excluding themselves from the canon?
ar.c: The argument runs: certain deuterocanonical books testify against themselves . Where a canonical prophet writes "Thus saith the LORD," these books instead apologize for their prose, describe themselves as condensations of other men's work, and admit that the age of prophecy was over. So — the argument concludes — the books make no claim to inspiration; indeed they quietly deny it, and a book that disclaims inspired status cannot belong in the canon. 1 Four passages are adduced: 2 Maccabees 15:38–39 — the author's closing apology: "And if I have done well, and as is fitting the story, it is tha…
ar.a: Weak — as a disqualifier. The interpretation that the deuterocanonical books disclaim their own inspiration, and so exclude themselves from the canon, does not hold on its best available case. The passages are genuine, but none is a statement about inspiration: the 2 Maccabees colophon and preface are a conventional authorial modesty formula and an editor's account of his method (the same self-conscious preface stands at the head of Luke); the Si…

ar.q: Do the deuterocanon's historical errors (the book of Judith) disqualify it from the canon?
ar.c: There's some problems with these books, there's historical errors in them. For instance, in the book of Judith … it says that Nebuchadnezzar reigned in Nineveh. How many of you guys remember where Nebuchadnezzar reigned? It was in the city of Babylon … But it has another problem. It also declares that Nebuchadnezzar was the king of the Assyrians — but he wasn't, he was the king of the Babylonians. It's so bad that some Catholic apologists trying to defend Judith have said "well it's an allegory." … It doesn't seem to be an allegory. — Mike Winger , How we got the OT Canon: Evidence for the Bib…
ar.a: Weak — as a disqualifier. The interpretation that the deuterocanon's historical errors exclude it from the canon does not hold on its best available case. What is sound is the narrower factual observation the argument starts from: read as literal history the book of Judith contains conspicuous anomalies — Nebuchadnezzar cast as "king of the Assyrians" reigning at Nineveh, set over a post-exilic second-temple Judea — and these should be conceded, …

ar.q: Did the fathers build doctrine only on the undisputed books — confining their proofs, in disputes with the Jews, to books both sides received?
ar.c: The principle, in its popular form, runs: let us only build doctrine on books that are not disputed — and we see the Fathers themselves doing this when they argue against the Jews, restricting their doctrinal proofs to the books the Jews also received (the protocanonical, Hebrew-canon books) and setting the contested books aside. Read this way, the practice is not merely a debating tactic but evidence of a considered canon-judgment: that the early church ranked the disputed books below the undisputed ones, fit to be read but not to establish a doctrine. The locus classicus offered for it is Je…
ar.a: Contested. The interpretation has a true core and an overstated reach, and the verdict tracks the split. Its core — that some Fathers distinguished books fit to confirm doctrine from books to be read for edification — is sound: Jerome states it, and the graded " ecclesiastical " tier embodies it. Its reach — that the early church followed a principle of building doctrine only on the undisputed books, practiced against the Jews, that shows it rank…

ar.q: Did the early church reject the deuterocanon as Scripture, making its later inclusion an accretion?
ar.c: The argument is a historical one, marshaled against the deuterocanon's canonicity: The earliest Christian Old-Testament lists — Melito's (c. 170), Origen's (c. 240), Cyril's, Athanasius's, Epiphanius's, Jerome's, Rufinus's — are Hebrew-sized: they either omit Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, and the Maccabees outright, or file them in a tier expressly below the canon. Therefore the primitive church did not reckon these books Scripture; their later reception (the African councils, Florence, Trent) is a development — an accretion onto an originally narrower canon. 1 Premise (1) is true and worth c…
ar.a: Contested. The early witness is genuinely divided, and the assessment turns on which form of the claim is weighed. As a claim about the Hebrew-conscious stream — that the most learned canon-watchers from Melito to Jerome ranked the deuterocanon below a Hebrew-sized canon, and that no undisputed universal reception of these books as fully canonical predates the fourth-century Western councils — the argument is strong, and it is the historical back…

ar.q: What did the "ecclesial / ecclesiastical" (read-but-not-canonical) category mean — a rank below the canon, or a catechetical subset within it?
ar.c: Several of the Hebrew-minded Fathers do not run a two-bucket scheme — inspired canon vs. rejected apocrypha — but a three -tier one, with a named middle category for books that are read in church yet kept off the canon list. Athanasius ( Festal Letter 39, 367) calls them books "not… included in the Canon, but appointed by the Fathers to be read by those who newly join us, and who wish for instruction in the word of godliness." Rufinus (c. 404) gives the rank its enduring Latin name: books "our fathers call not 'Canonical' but 'Ecclesiastical'… all of which they would have read in the Churches,…
ar.a: Sound. The meaning of the "ecclesiastical" category is not really in doubt once both proponents' true points are kept and their overstatements dropped. It is a genuine third rank — the Fathers coined a name for it because it fit neither of the outer two — defined by exclusion from the doctrine-proving canon yet honored with public reading and, in practice, with citation as Scripture. So Meade's structural reading is right (a real sub-canonical ra…

ar.q: Did the Hebrew canon end with Chronicles in Jesus' day — was a Genesis-to-Chronicles order established and dominant before the first century?
ar.c: The bookends argument turns on a chain whose first link is a claim about book- order : the Hebrew Bible ended with Chronicles; a Zechariah's murder is recorded near the end of Chronicles ( 2 Chron 24:20–22 ); so in naming "from the blood of Abel … to the blood of Zechariah" Jesus traced the canon from its first book to its last. Doug Wilson states the premise plainly — the saying gives "the A to Z, the table of contents — Genesis to 2 Chronicles," "the order … Jesus would have been familiar with." Roger Beckwith, the argument's scholarly anchor, is more careful: the saying "in all probability …
ar.a: Weak — for the form the bookends argument needs. The claim that the Hebrew Bible ran Genesis-to-Chronicles as an established, dominant order in or before the first century is not borne out by the surviving record. Across the first millennium no Chronicles-last sequence is dominant; the great majority of canon-lists and codices close on Daniel, Ezra, Esther, or Maccabees; and the authoritative Tiberian Hebrew manuscripts (Aleppo, Leningrad) place …

ar.q: Does Hebrews 11:35's allusion to 2 Maccabees 7 show the New Testament treats the deuterocanon as Scripture?
ar.c: "Women received their dead by resurrection. Some were tortured, refusing to accept release, that they might rise again to a better life" (Heb. 11:35). There is no episode in the protocanonical books of the Old Testament to which this passage might refer, but it has a direct parallel with an account in 2 Maccabees… Notice that [Luther] also removed Hebrews, the book which cites 2 Maccabees, to an appendix as well. — Jimmy Akin, Defending the Deuterocanonicals , EWTN . 1 Two claims are bundled here, and they want weighing apart. The first is a parallel : that Hebrews 11:35b has no protocanonical…
ar.a: Weak — for the canonicity inference; the allusion itself is sound . That Hebrews 11:35 alludes to the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 7 is true, granted across confessions, and a real refutation of the stronger Protestant claim that the apostles never so much as echo these books — and the proponent's survey premise, that the protocanon offers no parallel (the fiery furnace ends in deliverance, not martyrdom-for-resurrection), holds up. But the conclusion …

ar.q: Which Zechariah does Jesus name in "from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah" — and is he the Chronicles figure the "bookends" argument needs?
ar.c: The bookends argument runs: Abel's murder opens Genesis, a Zechariah's murder closes Chronicles, so "from the blood of Abel … to the blood of Zechariah" spans the Hebrew canon and excludes the Apocrypha. The second half of that span does its work only if the Zechariah Jesus names is the one in 2 Chronicles 24:20–22 — Zechariah son of Jehoiada, the priest whom King Joash had stoned "in the court of the house of the Lord ." He is, on the bookends reading, the last martyr in the last book. Doug Wilson, defending the argument, sees the danger plainly: if the Zechariah is the son of Berechiah and n…
ar.a: Contested. Which Zechariah Jesus names in Luke 11:51 // Matthew 23:35 was disputed in the early church and remains genuinely open, though not evenly balanced. Zechariah son of Jehoiada ( 2 Chron 24:20–22 ) is the most defensible answer and the probable one: his stoning in the temple court is the only such martyrdom in inspired Scripture, it matches "between the sanctuary and the altar" exactly, and the most rigorous interpreters — Jerome, Calvin,…

ar.q: Did the Council of Jamnia (c. AD 90) close or affirm the Hebrew Old Testament canon?
ar.c: A staple of the popular case for the Protestant Old Testament is the “Council of Jamnia”: that a formal rabbinic council sat at Yavneh (Jabneh) about AD 90 and there officially closed — or gave the final, authoritative affirmation to — the thirty-nine-book Hebrew canon, fixing for all time a Jewish Scripture that excluded the Greek “extras.” The point of invoking it is chronological: it furnishes a dated, first-century moment at which the Jews are said to have settled a closed, deuterocanon-excluding canon, which the church should then follow. Bible.org states it flatly: “The Council of Jamnia…
ar.a: Weak — for the claim that a Council of Jamnia closed or affirmed the Hebrew canon about AD 90. The “council” is Graetz's 1871 reconstruction, not an event the sources report; the rabbinic discussions assigned to Yavneh debated only whether two already-canonical books, the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes, “defile the hands” — a question within a settled Scripture, and one still live into the second century, the opposite of a closure; no source reco…

ar.q: Did later evidence undercut Jerome's grounds for a Hebrew-only Old Testament canon?
ar.c: The Jerome -versus- Augustine quarrel is the fault line this whole timeline traces: Jerome would measure the Old Testament by the Hebrew that the Jews kept, Augustine by the books the catholic churches received. The argument here is not the broad question "was the Hebrew-canon conclusion right?" — that is the live dispute the timeline runs end to end. It is the sharper, examinable thesis that Jerome's specific grounds were mistaken : that when one lays out the actual reasons the man gave, later scholarship has knocked the props away, so his "No" was right-sounding but wrongly reasoned. Jerome'…
ar.a: Sound , for the interpretation on its best available case: that Jerome's stated grounds for a Hebrew-only Old Testament rest on a historical premise later evidence has cut away. He wrote as though a fixed, authoritative Jewish canon already stood for the apostolic church to defer to — a settled "catalogue of Divine Scriptures" the Jews had ratified and from which they "exclude" these books. Modern scholarship has dismantled that picture, and larg…

ar.q: Did the Jews reject the deuterocanon — was the first-century Jewish canon closed and Hebrew-only?
ar.c: This is the umbrella under which a whole family of canon arguments shelters — the single most common popular case for the Protestant Old Testament. It is a syllogism: God committed His oracles to the Jews ( Romans 3:2 ); the Jews recognized a canon that excludes the deuterocanon; therefore the church should follow the Jewish canon and exclude those books. Its scholarly form is F. F. Bruce's: The books of the Apocrypha were not included in the Hebrew Bible, nor were they regarded as canonical by the leaders of official Judaism anywhere. Even Jews who wrote in Greek at the beginning of our era, …
ar.a: Weak — for the headline claim as stated. The minor premise of the most common deuterocanon-removal syllogism — that a closed, Hebrew-only Jewish canon already stood in the apostolic age and deliberately excluded these books — does not hold on its best case: the leading scholarship (Sundberg, Lim, McDonald, Barton) holds that no Jewish canon was yet fixed in the early first century; the Writings were still disputed inside Judaism into the second (…

ar.q: Were the Jews "entrusted with the oracles of God" (Romans 3:2), so the church should follow the Hebrew canon?
ar.c: The argument is a syllogism built on a single verse. Paul, listing the advantages of the Jew, writes: "What advantage then hath the Jew? … Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God." 1 From this the argument reasons: The "oracles of God" are the Old Testament Scriptures. God entrusted those Scriptures to the Jewish people — made them the custodians of His revelation, the keepers of the canon. The Jewish people recognized a canon — the Hebrew Bible, the later Tanakh — that does not include the deuterocanonical books. Therefore the Christian Old Testament …
ar.a: Contested — for the interpretation, with the proof-text itself weak. As a proof-text , Romans 3:2 does not hold: "the oracles of God" ( logia ) are God's utterances — the Law and the promises — not a catalogue of inspired books, as the word's New-Testament usage (Acts 7:38; Hebrews 5:12; 1 Peter 4:11) and the unbroken patristic exposition of the verse (Origen, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Aquinas) both show; the context is Israel's privilege and her …

ar.q: "Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water" (John 7:38): does Jesus cite, as Scripture, words found in no Old Testament book?
ar.c: "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." — John 7:38 (KJV). The clause "as the scripture hath said" ( kathôs eîpen hē graphē ) is a citation formula; the words that follow correspond to no single Old-Testament passage. As one sibling of the cluster headed by Ephesians 5:14 , the verse is sometimes enlisted to show that the New Testament cites, as Scripture, material outside any Old-Testament book. 1
ar.a: Weak. That "as the scripture hath said" at John 7:38 introduces words with no verbatim Old-Testament locus is sound; the inference that the New Testament thereby cites a source outside the Old-Testament canon is weak. No Father or scholar proposes a non-canonical writing here: the patristic and modern candidates are all canonical "living-water" texts (Proverbs, Zechariah 14:8, Isaiah, Ezekiel, the wilderness rock), best taken as a free, composite…

ar.q: Does Josephus's twenty-two-book count ( Against Apion 1.8) prove a closed, deuterocanon-excluding Hebrew canon?
ar.c: Around the close of the first century, defending the antiquity of his nation against the grammarian Apion, the Jewish historian Josephus tells a Roman readership that the Jews hold not "an innumerable multitude of books … disagreeing from and contradicting one another," but "…only twenty-two books, which contain the records of all the past times; which are justly believed to be divine … the time from the death of Moses till the reign of Artaxerxes … the prophets … wrote down what was done in their times in thirteen books. The remaining four books contain hymns to God, and precepts for the cond…
ar.a: Contested. The witness is strong by the historian's lights and short by the canon-historian's. What Josephus soundly establishes — a datable, late-first-century Jewish reckoning of twenty-two divinely-credited books, a Hebrew-sized table that did not count the deuterocanon among the inspired — is genuine and is the firmest single datum the Protestant case has on the Jewish side; it is real evidence for the Hebrew-measure reading this timeline tra…

ar.q: Does Jude's quoting 1 Enoch as prophecy (Jude 14–15) show the Old Testament canon was still open in the apostolic age?
ar.c: "And Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these, saying, Behold, the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints, To execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him." — Jude 14–15 (KJV), quoting almost verbatim 1 Enoch 1:9 ("Behold, he comes with ten thousands of his holy ones, to execute judgment upon all, and to destroy all the ungodly, and to convict all flesh of all the works of their ungodliness… and of all the h…
ar.a: Contested. That Jude formally quotes 1 Enoch as inspired prophecy (and leans on the Testament of Moses at v. 9) is sound and undisputed — the firmest instance in the New Testament of a Scripture-formula introducing a non-canonical work, conceded by Bauckham himself. But the interpretation it is pressed to serve — that the Old-Testament canon was still open in the apostolic age — is genuinely contested. Strong by one reading: a serious stream of s…

ar.q: "Therefore also said the wisdom of God" (Luke 11:49): does Jesus quote a written source outside the Old Testament canon?
ar.c: "Therefore also said the wisdom of God, I will send them prophets and apostles, and some of them they shall slay and persecute." — Luke 11:49 (KJV). The attribution formula "said the wisdom of God" introduces a first-person saying that appears in no surviving Old-Testament book; the words quoted in the Septuagint that elsewhere head Gospel citations are absent. As one sibling of the cluster headed by Ephesians 5:14 , the verse is enlisted to show the New Testament quoting, as authoritative, words with no canonical source — and, on the strongest form of the reading, citing a lost written wisdom…
ar.a: Weak. That Luke 11:49 ascribes to "the wisdom of God" a saying with no Old-Testament locus is sound, and its source is the least recoverable in the cluster; but the inference that Jesus thereby quotes a non-canonical writing as Scripture is weak. The patristic reading ( Ambrose , Bede) takes "the wisdom of God" to be Christ speaking in his own person — confirmed by the parallel at Matthew 23:34 , where Jesus says "I send" — and the dominant moder…

ar.q: Did Luther pave the way for the deuterocanon's removal?
ar.c: The "paved the way" line is what the "Luther removed the books" trope becomes once its bare form is corrected. Confronted with the fact that Luther's 1534 German Bible contains Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and 1–2 Maccabees — gathered between the Testaments under the heading "Apocrypha… not held equal to the Holy Scriptures, and yet… profitable and good to read" — the careful apologist no longer says Luther excised the books. The charge retreats to causation: Luther began it. He pulled the books out of the Old Testament proper, ranked them below Scripture, and quarantined them in an …
ar.a: Plausible — for the modest, causal core; the strong "naturally and inevitably led" form overstates. That Luther 's demotion-and-segregation of the deuterocanon was the originating step and a necessary precondition of its eventual removal is well-grounded: Luther created the separable "Apocrypha" category that the later Protestant Bibles carried and that the British and Foreign Bible Society's 1826 resolution finally deleted, and the sub-canonical…

ar.q: Did Luther reject 2 Maccabees in order to defeat the purgatory proof-text?
ar.c: The motive form adds a because to the demotion. Where the bare slogan says Luther took the books out, this version says he took 2 Maccabees out so that a doctrine he had decided to reject would lose its scriptural support. Jimmy Akin states it as a deliberate, doctrine-driven excision: Why would Martin Luther cut out this book when it is so clearly held up as an example to us by the New Testament? Simple: A few chapters later it endorses the practice of praying for the dead… Since Luther chose to reject the historic Christian teaching of purgatory… he had to remove that book from the Bible and…
ar.a: Weak — for the motive/causation claim that Luther rejected 2 Maccabees (and demoted the deuterocanon) in order to defeat purgatory and prayer for the dead. Luther's own printed answer to the proof-text is multi-pronged and explicitly argues the doctrine fails even granting the book's authority ("even were the book authoritative… at least one passage out of the chief books should support it"), so rejecting the book was not the mechanism by which h…

ar.q: Did Martin Luther remove the deuterocanonical books from the Bible?
ar.c: The trope is one of the most common in popular Catholic apologetics, the standing answer to the Protestant charge that Rome added books at Trent: it was not Rome that changed the Bible, the reply runs, but Luther who took the books out . Jimmy Akin's widely reprinted "Defending the Deuterocanonicals" states it plainly, and ties the removal directly to doctrine: The deuterocanonicals teach Catholic doctrine, and for this reason they were taken out of the Old Testament by Martin Luther and placed in an appendix without page numbers. And, on Tobit and 2 Maccabees specifically: Why would Martin Lu…
ar.a: Weak — for the "Luther removed (took out, cut out) the deuterocanon" framing. As a description of what happened the slogan does not hold: it confuses demoting and relocating a book with excising it. Luther's 1534 German Bible contains the deuterocanon — gathered into a separate inter-testamental section headed "Apocrypha… not held equal to the Holy Scriptures, and yet… profitable and good to read," each book given a preface and commended to read …

ar.q: Does 2 Maccabees 12:43–45 teach prayer and atoning offering for the dead?
ar.c: And when he had made a gathering throughout the company to the sum of two thousand drachms of silver, he sent it to Jerusalem to offer a sin offering, doing therein very well and honestly, in that he was mindful of the resurrection: For if he had not hoped that they that were slain should have risen again, it had been superfluous and vain to pray for the dead. And also in that he perceived that there was great favour laid up for those that died godly, it was an holy and good thought. Whereupon he made a reconciliation for the dead, that they might be delivered from sin. — 2 Maccabees 12:43–45 …
ar.a: Contested. The interpretation that 2 Maccabees 12:43–45 teaches and warrants prayer and an atoning offering for the dead is strong by one set of lights and weak by another, with no clear winner. By the plain sense of the text and the route of reception it is strong: the passage unmistakably narrates and approves an offering for the dead — even Luther granted as much — and the practice it warrants was the near-universal custom of the ancient Churc…

ar.q: Do the "52 ecclesiastical writers" and the Glossa Ordinaria show the shorter Hebrew canon was the medieval Western mainstream up to Trent?
ar.c: The argument's sharpest popular form is James White's, pressed against Gary Michuta in The Great Debate IX: Is the Apocrypha Scripture? (2004). Trent's fathers, White argues, ignored an overwhelming prior consensus: … surely they could not have been unaware of the long list of scholars down through the years who had rejected those books — some count as many as 52 major writers during that time period. Surely they knew that the Glossa Ordinaria introduced each book of the Apocrypha with the assertion that it was not a part of the canon. — James White, The Great Debate IX , 2004 . And again, gat…
ar.a: Contested. The medieval witness is genuinely divided, and the verdict turns on which form of the claim is weighed. As a claim about the Hieronymian stream — that a continuous, learned, Hebrew-canon-conscious current ran through the medieval Latin West, tiering the disputed books below the Hebrew canon from Jerome to Cajetan — the argument is sound , and it is conceded even by Catholic reference works (Metzger's "continuous succession"; the 1913 C…

ar.q: Does Melito's inquiry to Palestine refute the deuterocanon as apostolic tradition?
ar.c: "Melito of Sardis inquired of the church in Palestine concerning the Old Testament canon around AD 175. He discovered that the canon did not include the Apocryphal books. How can it be that he would inquire in Palestine if in fact the canon of the Old Testament including the Apocrypha was a matter of Apostolic tradition, as Trent had claimed?" — James White , in the form he presses in his 2014 Great Debate with Gary Michuta. The companion proponent Steve Christie states the list's content flatly: "Melito did not include any of the Deuterocanonical books in his Old Testament list, but only the …
ar.a: Weak — as an argument from the act of inquiry . Melito's having to inquire c. 175 is a real datum against the strong claim that the full canon was articulated, universally-possessed apostolic tradition from the start; it does not refute the deuterocanon as apostolic tradition in Trent's sense, because the inference equivocates between a circulated canon- list (which all sides grant developed over centuries, the New Testament included) and a recei…

ar.q: Did the deuterocanon confirm doctrine in conciliar argument before Trent? — the Wisdom of Solomon behind Nicaea's "Light from Light"
ar.c: The Catholic apologist Gary Michuta, surveying the councils and Fathers across the church's history, presses a single recurring datapoint against the Protestant "the books were never really used as Scripture / Trent first made them doctrine-bearing" line: that the disputed books were deployed to confirm doctrine — in dogmatic argument and at councils — long before 1546. His flagship instance is the Wisdom of Solomon and the Council of Nicaea: the council's description of the Son as "Light from Light" draws on the imagery of Wisdom 7:25–26, and Athanasius , defending the council in De Decretis …
ar.a: Plausible. The interpretation — that the deuterocanon functioned as doctrine-confirming Scripture in the church's conciliar and dogmatic argument long before the Council of Trent , exemplified by the Wisdom of Solomon ( 7:25–26 ) behind the Nicene "Light from Light" — holds on its best, modest case. A deuterocanonical book supplied the radiance/effluence imagery the fathers of Nicaea (325) used to articulate the Son's consubstantiality, and Athan…

ar.q: Does the absence of a recorded canon dispute between Jesus and the Jews prove a settled, shared Hebrew canon?
ar.c: The argument is the mirror of an expectation. If the deuterocanonical books really were Scripture, the apostles would have cited them as such; and if the Jews wrongly rejected books that belonged in the canon, Jesus — who never spared the Pharisees on their other errors — would have corrected them. We see neither. Since their recorded debates range across so much, the silence on the canon's extent is taken to show that no such dispute was live: Jesus and his opponents shared one settled, Hebrew-sized canon, which the apostolic church then received. James White presses both halves: "Nor do we f…
ar.a: Weak — as proof of a settled, shared canon. The interpretation that the missing canon-boundary dispute shows Jesus and the Jews shared a closed Hebrew-sized canon does not hold on its best case. It is an argument from silence that fits an unsettled canon as well as a settled one; it begs the question by assuming the very fixed Jewish canon that the leading scholarship (Sundberg, Lim, McDonald) says did not yet exist in the early first century; an…
