The man who gave the Helvidian reading its name — and whose treatise provoked the reply that created Jerome’s rival theory — is Helvidius , a layman of Rome who about 383 published a tract maintaining that the “brethren of the Lord” were the true sons of Joseph and Mary, born after Jesus, so that Mary was not ever-virgin. His aim was polemical: to check the age’s exaltation of virgin over married life by the example of the Lord’s own mother, who (he held) had gone on to bear children to her husband. His treatise is lost, surviving only where Jerome quotes it to refute it in The Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary, Against Helvidius — so his own words come to us at second hand and remain ⚠ un…

The reading that would govern the Latin West for a thousand years was minted in reply to Helvidius by Jerome , whose The Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary, Against Helvidius (c. 383) first advanced the Hieronymian theory: the brethren are the Lord’s maternal cousins , sons of “Mary of Clopas” the Virgin’s sister, so that “brother” means kinsman and the virginity of Mary and Joseph alike is preserved. He grounded it on the range of the word in Scripture — “In Holy Scripture there are four kinds of brethren—by nature, race, kindred, love” (of which the third, kinship, fits the brethren, as when Abraham calls his nephew Lot “brother”) — and on identifying “the Mary who is described as the mot…

From Alexandria, and in the same years Jerome was minting his cousins-theory at Rome, comes an Eastern voice reading the deniers’ own proof-text the other way: Didymus the Blind , the blind exegete who headed the Alexandrian catechetical school for half a century. In the treatise On the Trinity (c. 386) traditionally ascribed to him, he turns to Matthew 1:25 to illustrate the terms “first-born” and “only-begotten” and reads “until she brought forth her first-born son” as no bar to a virginity outlasting the birth: Mary “neither… marry anyone else, nor did she ever become the Mother of anyone else, but even after childbirth she remained always and forever an immaculate virgin.” 54 That places…

tl.w: Bonosus of Sardica and Jovinian — c. 390
tl.t: Two further Western voices rose against the perpetual virginity in the same decade as Helvidius , and J. B. Lightfoot files both in the Helvidian column of his conspectus — though he marks the second with a query, for they did not hold one position. Bonosus , bishop of Sardica in Illyria, is reported to have held the plain Helvidian reading, that Mary bore children to Joseph after Jesus; condemned by the synod of Capua (392), he left no text, so his teaching survives only in Lightfoot’s notice and the conciliar record and remains ⚠ unverified . 56 Jovinian — an anti-ascetic monk who taught at Rome, condemned by synods at Rome and Milan about 390 — is the better attested but the stranger witn…

The last of the great Latins to take up the brethren before Jerome’s reading swept the West is Ambrose of Milan , who devoted a treatise — On the Instruction of the Virgin and the Perpetual Virginity of Mary ( De Institutione Virginis , c. 392) — to refuting the deniers of the perpetual virginity, the party that had gathered around Bonosus of Sardica . Reaching the “brethren of the Lord,” Ambrose takes the Epiphanian line — “brother” is a wide term (Psalm 22:22; Romans 9:3), so “the brothers could be from Joseph, not from Mary” — and he even allows that one who looks into it “will find” this to be so; but he pointedly refuses to press the point: “We did not consider it necessary to pursue th…

The witness whose weight settled the question for the Latin West is Augustine , and with him Jerome’s new cousins-theory passes from a controversialist’s hypothesis into the standard reading. In his early Commentary on Galatians (on Galatians 1:19, c. 394, while still a presbyter) he left the alternative open — James “is to be understood either as [one] of the sons of Joseph by another wife” (the Epiphanian account) “or as of the kindred of Mary his mother” (the kinsman reading Jerome had pressed into the cousins-theory), committing to neither; but in his mature works he holds Jerome’s reading without wavering. 60 Expounding John 2:12 he lays it down as a rule of scriptural usage: “The kinsm…

The East’s point of transition is written across the works of a single father, John Chrysostom , who — as J. B. Lightfoot observed — “wrote both before and after Jerome’s treatise had become generally known, and his expositions of the New Testament mark a period of transition.” In the Antiochene homilies he is plainly Epiphanian : expounding Matthew 1:25 he defends the perpetual virginity (Joseph “knew her not till …” fixes only what was true before the birth, and “not even after this… could that righteous man ever have endured to know her”) and, asked in what sense the “brethren” are brethren, answers that they are so called only as Joseph was reputed husband — “How then… are James and the …

The first commentator to fall in behind Jerome’s new reading is Pelagius , who expounded Galatians 1:19 at Rome only a few years after Jerome — though which Pelagius did so is a textual question. His genuine note, recovered by Alexander Souter from beneath the later accretions, is terse and aimed at the deniers of the virginity: “Against those who say that blessed Mary had other sons — for we read that there were two apostles named James, one the son of Alphaeus and the other of Zebedee, neither a son of Mary or of Joseph; rather, they are called the Lord’s brothers from kinship ( de propinquitate ).” 65 That is the Hieronymian substance — Mary bears no later children, the brethren reduced t…

A Latin contemporary of Pelagius — Chromatius , bishop of Aquileia and friend of Jerome, Rufinus, Ambrose, and Chrysostom — meets the perpetual-virginity question not at the brethren but at the other great proof-text, the “until” of Matthew 1:25. Preaching on the verse in his Tractates on Matthew , he rebuts head-on the inference that “he knew her not till she had borne her firstborn son” implies Joseph knew her afterward: “not a few careless people insist on asking whether after the Lord’s birth the holy mother Mary had relations with Joseph. But this is not admissible on the grounds of either faith or truth… Far be it indeed that after the sacrament of so great a mystery and after the birt…

How settled the perpetual virginity had become in the Latin West by the 420s is shown not by a treatise defending it but by a retraction that simply confesses it. Leporius , a Gallic monk and priest who had taught Pelagian and proto-Nestorian errors about the person of Christ, was set right in Africa by Aurelius of Carthage and Augustine , and drew up under their eye a Document of Amendment ( Libellus emendationis , c. 426). Rehearsing the two births of the one Son, his confession names the Lord’s mother with the perpetual-virginity title as a fixed clause of the creed: Christ is “born of the Father before the ages, and in times most recent, made man of the Holy Spirit and the ever-virgin Ma…

That the Eastern flirtation with Jerome’s cousins-theory was a passing episode, not a conversion, is shown by Cyril of Alexandria , patriarch of the East’s chief see and roughly the contemporary of Theodoret , who reads the “brethren of the Lord” the old Epiphanian way. Expounding John 7:3–5, he explains the brethren’s unbelief by the low estimate they still had of Jesus, whom they reckoned a mere kinsman “in truth begotten of their father Joseph”; and pressing Jeremiah’s type “the house of thy father,” he fixes whose sons they were — “Very watchfully did the Prophet, having named His brethren, profitably add, The house of Thy father, lest they too should be supposed to have been of the bles…

The clearest Eastern statement of the Hieronymian reading — and the last witness to the original fourth-and-fifth-century controversy — is Theodoret of Cyrus , who, expounding Galatians 1:19 in his commentary on the fourteen Pauline epistles (c. 440), does what no earlier Greek father had done so plainly: he names the rival Epiphanian solution in order to reject it. James “the brother of the Lord” was not so by nature, and was “not, as some suppose, the son of Joseph by a previous marriage but the son of Clopas and cousin of the Lord. For his mother was the sister of the Lord’s mother” — the apparent brotherhood a double accident of the two Marys’ shared name and the families’ shared house. …

In the Latin West the same confession is preached from the pulpit by Peter Chrysologus (“golden-worded”), bishop of Ravenna and the most celebrated Italian preacher of his generation. In a sermon on the two Adams ( Sermon 117 , “The First Adam, and the Last Adam, Born of a Virgin”), setting the Virgin’s childbearing apart from that of ordinary women as a sign of God’s power rather than a work of nature, he presses Mary’s virginity through all three moments — conception, birth, and after: “Where are they who think that the Virgin’s conception and giving birth to her child are to be likened to those of other women?… The Virgin conceives, the Virgin brings forth her child, and she remains a vir…

The same Latin confession is spoken with the fullest doctrinal authority of the age by Leo the Great , bishop of Rome (440–461), whose dogmatic Tome would be acclaimed at the Council of Chalcedon in 451. Preaching on the Feast of the Nativity, he grounds Mary’s virginity in the “new character” of Christ’s birth — “not by intercourse with man but by the power of God was it brought about” — and states it through all three moments: “a Virgin conceived, a Virgin bare, and a Virgin she remained,” the reader to consider “not the condition of her that bare but the will of Him that was born.” 75 The virginity is, on Leo’s account, the very pattern of the Incarnation — “the uncorrupt nature of Him th…

What the Fathers had confessed the church now writes into the definition of the faith itself. The Second Council of Constantinople (553), the fifth ecumenical council, convened by Justinian to settle the Christological aftermath of Chalcedon, sets the perpetual virginity into a canon of the creed. Anathematizing those who deny the Word’s two nativities, its second capitulum names the mother of the second nativity as “the holy and glorious Mary, Mother of God and always a virgin ” (Greek aeiparthenos ): “coming down from heaven and being made flesh of the holy and glorious Mary, Mother of God and always a virgin, and born of her: let him be anathema.” 76 The title is not the council’s subject…

A century on, the Latin West states the doctrine with equal formality and greater fullness. The Lateran Council of 649 , a Roman synod of 105 bishops convened under Pope Martin I to condemn Monothelitism, devotes its third canon to Mary and confesses her ever-virgin through all three moments — before, in, and after the birth. The “holy Mother of God and ever Virgin and immaculate Mary… conceived of the Holy Spirit without seed… and… incorruptibly bore [Him], her virginity remaining indestructible even after His birth” — and denial is put under anathema: “let him be condemned.” 77 Where Constantinople II had named Mary aeiparthenos in a single clause, the Lateran canon spells the triple virgi…

The same settledness appears in the Latin West with Bede , the Northumbrian monk of Wearmouth–Jarrow, whose Commentary on Luke reads Mary’s reply to Gabriel — “How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?” (Luke 1:34) — as her reverent disclosure of a settled purpose of virginity. She “reverently expressed the purpose of her mind, that is, that she had decided to lead a virginal life” (Latin: propositum suae mentis reverenter exposuit, vitam videlicet virginalem se ducere decrevisse ) — “the first among women to devote herself to such great virtue.” Bede sets her question apart from Zachariah’s unbelief: she did not ask “How will I know this?” — a demand for a sign — but “How will this be?”, …

Three centuries on, the perpetual virginity is no longer argued but codified : John of Damascus — the last of the Greek Fathers, whose Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith (c. 743) gathered the settled dogma of the East into a system — devotes a chapter of it to the “ever-virgin” ( aeiparthenos ) Mother of God. He states the doctrine at its fullest reach: she “thus remains even after the birth still virgin, having never at any time up till death consorted with a man,” and answers the two stock objections from Matthew 1:25 exactly as the fathers before him. To “her first-born son” he replies that “he who is first-begotten is first-born even if he is only-begotten… the word ‘first-born’ mean…

The timeline’s medieval coda is Theophylact of Ohrid , a Byzantine archbishop and exegete who, six centuries after the fourth-century controversy, tries to fuse the two virginity-preserving readings. Commenting on both Matthew 13:55 and Galatians 1:19 he harmonizes the Epiphanian and Hieronymian accounts by the Mosaic levirate: “Cleopas and Joseph were brothers; when Cleopas died childless, Joseph raised up seed for him and begot him and his other brothers” — so James is the Lord’s reputed brother as Joseph’s natural son and his cousin as Clopas’s legal son, Joseph the natural and Clopas the legal father. 80 The Matthew comment spells the mechanism out: Clopas “died childless,” Joseph “took …

The vow-reading of Luke 1:34 gets its most dramatic medieval statement from Bernard of Clairvaux , the Cistercian abbot and “mellifluous doctor,” in the fourth of his early homilies In Praise of the Virgin Mother (the “ Missus est ” sermons). Where earlier witnesses simply assert that Mary’s “How shall this be done, because I know not man?” presupposes a vow, Bernard alone stages the objection the vow raises — how could a woman betrothed to Joseph have vowed never to know a man? — and answers it from inside Mary’s own supposed reasoning. She “doubts not the fact, but only inquires about the manner”; then, imagined as one already under vow, she reckons openly with the cost: “Since my Lord kno…

Two centuries later the doctrine is no longer defended but demonstrated : Thomas Aquinas , the great Dominican of the Latin schools, gives Mary’s virginity a whole question of his Summa Theologiae (III, q. 28), and in its third article condemns the Helvidian denial with scholastic finality — “without any hesitation we must abhor the error of Helvidius, who dared to assert that Christ’s Mother, after His Birth, was carnally known by Joseph, and bore other children.” He arrays four reasons: the denial derogates from Christ’s perfection as the Only-begotten; it insults the Holy Ghost, “whose ‘shrine’ was the virginal womb”; it dishonours the dignity of God’s Mother; and it imputes “extreme pres…

The first voice of the Reformation to speak for the doctrine is not Wittenberg’s but Zürich’s: Huldrych (Ulrich) Zwingli , in a sermon on the Virgin Mary preached in Zürich on 17 September 1522 ( Eine Predigt von der ewig reinen Magd Maria , printed 1524). He professes the perpetual virginity in the fullest terms — disclaiming that he has ever “thought, still less taught, or declared publicly, anything concerning the subject of the ever Virgin Mary, Mother of our salvation, which could be considered dishonorable, impious, unworthy or evil,” and confessing “with all my heart according to the word of holy gospel that this pure virgin bore for us the Son of God and that she remained, in the bir…

The doctrine’s most striking late witness is the Reformer who broke with Rome: Martin Luther , defending Mary’s perpetual virginity in That Jesus Christ Was Born a Jew (1523). He meets the Helvidian denial at the Matthean proof-texts and rejects it outright — the reading that “before they came together” and “knew her not till she had brought forth her first-born son” (Matthew 1:18, 25) imply Joseph knew Mary afterward is a “carnal” misreading, so that “one cannot from these words conclude that Mary, after the birth of Christ, became a wife in the usual sense; it is therefore neither to be asserted nor believed.” He answers it with the Fathers’ idiom-argument: the Scriptural “until” is “the c…

A second magisterial Reformer holds the doctrine, and more cautiously than Luther : John Calvin , expounding Matthew 1:25 both in his Harmony of the Evangelists and in a Geneva sermon on Matthew 1:22–25 (pub. 1562). His hinge is not a positive demonstration of the perpetual virginity but a denial that the text decides against it — “no just and well-grounded inference can be drawn from these words of the Evangelist, as to what took place after the birth of Christ,” for “first-born” is used “for the sole purpose of informing us that he was born of a virgin,” and Joseph’s knowing her not “till” the birth “is limited to that very time… What took place afterwards, the historian does not inform us…

The doctrine’s latest notable Protestant witness carries the Reformers’ line two centuries on: John Wesley , the Anglican priest and founder of Methodism, professing the perpetual virginity in A Letter to a Roman Catholic (Dublin, 18 July 1749). The letter is an irenic appeal — written to cool the sectarian hatred between Protestants and Catholics in Ireland — that sets out the creed of “a true Protestant” to show how much the two communions hold in common; and within its confession of the Incarnation Wesley affirms that Christ was “born of the blessed Virgin Mary, who, as well after as before she brought Him forth, continued a pure and unspotted virgin.” 90 The phrase “as well after as befo…

The timeline’s last witness is the scholar whose vocabulary frames the whole of it: J. B. Lightfoot , whose 1865 dissertation “The Brethren of the Lord” gave the three views their names and assembled the patristic catena this page still leans on. It is easy to read him only as the neutral adjudicator, but he was not neutral: weighing the solutions on the Scriptural notices, he abandons the Hieronymian reading — “there is not the slightest indication that the Hieronymian solution ever occurred to any individual or sect or church, until it was put forward by Jerome himself” — and comes down for the Epiphanian : “taking the scriptural notices alone, the Hieronymian account must be abandoned; wh…

ar.q: Does “brother” ( adelphos ) mean “cousin” in “the brethren of the Lord”?
ar.c: In Holy Scripture there are four kinds of brethren—by nature, race, kindred, love… Certainly Lot was not Abraham’s brother, but the son of Abraham’s brother Aram. — Jerome, Against Helvidius §16 (citing Genesis 13:8; he adds Jacob called “brother” of his uncle Laban, Genesis 29:15). 1 The Hieronymian reading of the “brethren of the Lord” (Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:3; John 7:5; Acts 1:14; 1 Corinthians 9:5; Galatians 1:19) stands or falls on this semantics: the brethren can be maternal cousins , sons of “Mary of Clopas,” only if the Greek word rendered “brother” ( adelphos ) will bear the sense “ki…
ar.a: Weak. The lexical claim taken narrowly — that adelphos can extend to a nephew or collateral kinsman — is sound, and it does neutralize any attempt to disprove the cousin-reading from the dictionary. But as a positive argument for reading the brethren as cousins it does not hold: the attested loose uses are all of a single known relationship named in direct speech, whereas the cousin-reading needs a group habitually and exclusively styled “brother…

ar.q: Does the separate word for “kinsman” ( suggenēs ) tell against the cousin-reading of “the brethren of the Lord”?
ar.c: Likewise, a word for kinsman/relative exists: suggenes , which is used 12 times in the New Testament elsewhere. It was not used to describe Jesus’ adelphos . — a common Protestant statement of the argument. 1 The point is a lexical-distinction move, and it is not the same as the “precise word for cousin” ( anepsios ) point weighed on the companion page . Its edge is that the Evangelists sometimes deploy suggenēs (“kinsman, relative”) in the same sentence as adelphos (“brother”), keeping the two apart: “call not thy friends, nor thy brethren ( adelphous ), neither thy kinsmen ( suggeneis ), nor…
ar.a: Weak. The datum is true — suggenēs exists, is common, and is co-listed with adelphos — and it belongs to the cumulative case against the Hieronymian reading. But as an independent argument it does not hold: it is an argument from silence, and the silence it leans on is broken by the Septuagint’s own adelphos -for-nephew (Lot; Jacob), the very idiom the New Testament writes out of. A category-list is not a rule of exclusion; the “restrict to New-T…

ar.q: Does the resurrection appearance to James (1 Corinthians 15:7) explain the brethren’s turn from unbelief to faith?
ar.c: A very short time before the Lord’s death His brethren refuse to accept His mission: they are still unbelievers. Immediately after His ascension we find them gathered together with the Apostles, evidently recognizing Him as their Master. Whence comes this change? Surely the crucifixion of one who professed to be the Messiah was not likely to bring it about… An incidental statement of St. Paul explains all; “Then He was seen of James.” At the time when St. Paul wrote, there was but one person eminent enough in the church to be called James simply without any distinguishing epithet — the Lord’s …
ar.a: Sound. On its load-bearing claims the argument holds. The “James” of 1 Corinthians 15:7 is, by the strong majority reading, the Lord’s brother; the appearance is bedrock-early, resting on the pre-Pauline creed and a named living witness, and is not to be waved off; and it supplies a natural cause for the otherwise puzzling turn of the brethren from unbelief (John 7:5) to faith (Acts 1:14), while marking James the Just as no member of the Twelve —…

ar.q: Were the brethren Mary’s own children? — the natural (Helvidian) reading
ar.c: The same names are repeated by the Evangelists in another place, and the same persons are there brethren of the Lord and sons of Mary. — Helvidius , as quoted in Jerome, Against Helvidius §15. 1 Where the argument pages grouped under the cousin theory weigh the rival readings from the rebuttal side — showing that “brother” need not mean cousin, that the completing identifications fail — this page asks the positive question they leave open: taken on its own evidence, how strong is the reading that the brethren were the children Mary herself bore to Joseph after Jesus? That is the Helvidian read…
ar.a: Contested. Judged as an interpretation on its own evidence, the Helvidian reading is strong where modern exegesis is strong: it is the plain sense of the recurring “his mother and his brethren,” it needs no auxiliary hypotheses, and it is the majority view among present-day scholars, conceded as such even by defenders of the perpetual virginity. But its positive support reaches only to literal household kinship — shared by the Epiphanian reading …

ar.q: Could two or three of the Lord’s brethren have been among the Twelve Apostles?
ar.c: Jerome himself claimed only that the brethren were the Lord’s cousins , sons of “Mary of Clopas” the Virgin’s sister. But the fuller reading that came to be taught bolts a further step onto that core: two of the brethren, James and Jude, are also numbered among the Twelve Apostles — James the Lord’s brother identified with the apostle “James son of Alphaeus” (Matthew 10:3), and Jude the Lord’s brother with the apostle “Jude of James” (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13); some completers add Simon as a third. J. B. Lightfoot states the requirement and then presses the objection: But again: the Hieronymian th…
ar.a: Sound. As an interpretation of the New Testament data — that the Lord’s brethren were not members of the Twelve — the argument holds, and holds on the mainstream side: five converging notices (John 7:5; Acts 1:14; James’s resident office; Jude 17; the never-used designation) range the brethren consistently outside the apostolic college, and modern criticism has generally abandoned the older identification of the brethren with apostles. No single …

ar.q: Is Clement of Alexandria’s witness to Mary’s virginity undermined by textual unreliability — that it survives only in an expurgated sixth-century Latin translat…
ar.c: “Clement of Alexandria initially appears to support Mary’s perpetual virginity ( Stromata , Book VII, ch. 16), but as Juniper Carol acknowledges, we cannot completely trust the document because the Greek original is lost, and the Latin version dates to the 6th century and was written specifically to correct offending sentiments: ‘We cannot rely absolutely on this text, since it is a [6th century] translated adaptation [by Cassiodorus], with the expressed intention of expurgating anything that might be offensive…’” — Thorncrown Ministries, “Roman Catholics and Their Queen, Part 4” (2017), quoti…
ar.a: Weak. The textual-reliability objection does not hold as leveled. Its one sound element — that Clement’s Adumbrationes survive only in Cassiodorus’ edited Latin, so cannot be trusted “absolutely” — is a caution about a text the objector is not actually quoting: he cites the Greek Stromateis VII.16 while borrowing a caveat that Carol aimed at the Latin notes on the epistles, conflating two distinct works. Where the caveat does bite (the Jude note)…

ar.q: Is Mary’s perpetual virginity positively grounded in the “consecrated womb / new tomb” typology and the shut gate of Ezekiel 44:2 — not merely in ascetic devalu…
ar.c: …it is not altogether correct to represent this belief as suggested solely by the false asceticism of the early Church which exalted virginity at the expense of married life. It appears in fact to be due quite as much to another sentiment which the fathers fantastically expressed by a comparison between the conception and the burial of our Lord. As after death His body was placed in a sepulcher ‘wherein never man before was laid,’ so it seemed fitting that the womb consecrated by His presence should not thenceforth have borne any offspring of man. It may be added also, that the Epiphanian view…
ar.a: Plausible. The positive typological rationale is coherent, ancient, and genuinely more than ascetic prejudice — Lightfoot’s historical point is sound and Origen gives it a firsthand spine — and it is not ruled out. But it is a fittingness argument resting on an accommodated proof-text, so it adorns and corroborates the doctrine rather than establishing it; the doctrine must be carried, if at all, on the historical and exegetical grounds weighed i…

ar.q: Was the cousin theory a novelty without earlier witness — one Jerome himself let go?
ar.c: Of the three historic readings of “the brethren of the Lord,” the Hieronymian — that they were the Lord’s maternal cousins, sons of “Mary of Clopas” the Virgin’s sister — is the last to appear, and it appears all at once, in Jerome ’s Against Helvidius (c. 383). The argument here is that this timing is telling: the reading was a novum devised for the polemical occasion, resting on Scripture alone with no earlier writer to vouch for it, and held by its own author with a grip that visibly slackened over his later works. J. B. Lightfoot, who gave the three views their names, built the case on fiv…
ar.a: Contested. The argument bundles a strong claim with a weaker one, and they should be scored apart. The historical core — that the cousin theory has no witness before Jerome and was a fourth-century novelty — is well-grounded and close to consensus: the pre-Jerome timeline knows only the Epiphanian and Helvidian options, the sole alleged early prop (the “Papias” fragment) is spurious and depends on Jerome, Jerome himself, eager for authorities, co…

ar.q: Does Jesus entrusting Mary to John (John 19:26–27) show she had no other sons?
ar.c: Our Lord in His dying moments commended His mother to the keeping of St. John; “Woman, behold thy son.” The injunction was forthwith obeyed, and “from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home” (John 19:26,27). Yet according to the Helvidian view she had no less than four sons besides daughters living at the time. Is it conceivable that our Lord would thus have snapped asunder the most sacred ties of natural affection? — J. B. Lightfoot, stating the argument in its modern form. 1 At the crucifixion Jesus sees his mother and the beloved disciple standing by and says, “Woman, behold thy…
ar.a: Contested. As support for the perpetual virginity the entrustment to John is a real argument, not an empty one: the permanence of the arrangement, and its survival past the brethren’s conversion and settlement in Jerusalem (Acts 1:14), genuinely tell against Mary’s having other sons to keep her, and this is why the fathers reached for it and Lightfoot pressed it hardest. But it does not hold as a proof . The brethren’s unbelief and apparent absen…

ar.q: Were the brethren Joseph’s sons by a former marriage? — the Epiphanian reading on its merits
ar.c: … these brethren were in fact sons of Joseph by a former wife, before he espoused the Virgin; and… they are therefore called the Lord’s brethren only in the same way in which Joseph is called His father. — J. B. Lightfoot, defining the reading he adopts. 1 Where the companion page asks the positive question of the rival reading — taken on its own evidence, were the brethren the children Mary bore after Jesus ? — this page asks the symmetric one: taken on its own evidence, how strong is the reading that they were Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage, no blood-kin of Mary at all? That is the Epi…
ar.a: Contested. Judged as an interpretation on its own evidence, the Epiphanian reading is strong exactly where the patristic record is strong — it is the earliest and only pre-Nicene solution, uniform in the East, plausibly Palestinian in root — and it is exegetically unstrained, giving “brother” its natural sense and losing nothing to the reputed-kinship objection. Against the Hieronymian cousin-theory it wins outright. But it is weaker where modern…

ar.q: Is the Epiphanian reading weakened by making the brethren only reputed kin — or does Joseph’s reputed fatherhood license calling his sons the Lord’s “brethren”?
ar.c: Both kinship readings that preserve Mary’s perpetual virginity — the Hieronymian (cousins) and the Epiphanian (Joseph’s sons by a former wife) — deny that the “brethren of the Lord” were Jesus’ own uterine brothers. The Helvidian reading (Mary’s later children) is often urged to have, at least, the advantage of naturalness: it alone gives the brethren a real relationship to Jesus, a shared mother, so that “brother” carries its plainest sense. On the Epiphanian view the brethren share with Jesus neither mother nor blood at all — only a reputed, legal father in Joseph — and the objection is that…
ar.a: Sound. The objection that the Epiphanian reading makes “brother of the Lord” an empty or strained title is answered in full: Joseph’s own reputed fatherhood, used of him in Scripture by Mary and by the Evangelist with no thought of denying the virgin birth, licenses the parallel reputed fraternity of his sons, and this is the very rationale the earliest fathers give. As a rebuttal it holds, and it removes the Helvidian reading’s one intuitive adv…

ar.q: Does the perpetual virginity “have its origin in gnosticism, not Christianity”?
ar.c: “Are you aware that such doctrines as perpetual virginity and bodily assumption have their origin in gnosticism, not Christianity, and have no foundation in apostolic doctrine or practice?” — James White, “Reposting a Top Ten List on Roman Catholicism” (Alpha and Omega Ministries). 1 The move is a historical-origins thesis, distinct from the timing objection weighed at the companion “late invention” argument : not merely that the dogma was defined late, but that the belief itself is a Gnostic import — the glorification of virginity and disparagement of the body flowing from Gnostic asceticism …
ar.a: Weak. As an origins-thesis the charge does not hold on its best available case. Its one defensible element — that the doctrine’s earliest literary elaboration belongs to a second-century current of Syrian asceticism that prized virginity — is real, and keeps the verdict off unsupported ; but that element is not what White claims. He names gnosticism , where the scholarship names encratism/asceticism — a distinct thing — and he infers non-Christia…

ar.q: Do the brethren’s traceable family line — Jude’s named grandsons — support reading “brother of the Lord” as literal kinship?
ar.c: The Gospels name Jude (Judas) among the four “brethren of the Lord” (Mark 6:3 ∥ Matthew 13:55), but tell us nothing of what became of him or his family. The earliest historical tradition does. Hegesippus , a Palestinian Hebrew Christian who gathered the traditions of the Lord’s kindred around 175 and whose words survive only where Eusebius quotes them, reports that in the reign of Domitian two grandsons of Jude were still living. Eusebius sets down the story, quoting Hegesippus’ own words for its heart: Of the family of the Lord there were still living the grandchildren of Jude, who is said to…
ar.a: Sound. On the interpretation it is actually offered for — that “brother of the Lord” is a designation of literal family kinship — the argument is well-grounded and unrefuted, and rests on the strongest kind of evidence this whole question affords: the earliest historical (as opposed to legendary) witness, a Palestinian who gathered the family’s own traditions, reporting a named, dated, geographically-located family line, with a critic of the trad…

ar.q: Does Hegesippus’ usage tell against the cousin-theory — or can “ dēuteron ” (HE 4.22.4) mean “a second cousin”?
ar.c: Hegesippus (c. 175), the earliest historical witness on the Lord’s kindred, is a linchpin of the modern debate because he keeps two relationships verbally distinct. James and Jude are the Lord’s brother ( adelphos ); Symeon, who succeeded James as bishop of Jerusalem, is the Lord’s cousin ( anepsios ), being the son of Joseph’s brother Clopas. 1 Since the Hieronymian reading makes the “brethren of the Lord” the sons of “Mary of Clopas” — that is, cousins, of the very family of Clopas to which Symeon belonged — a witness who reserves “cousin” for Symeon and “brother” for James and Jude, and nev…
ar.a: Sound. On the more probable grammar — “the second [bishop],” with the office expressed in the same sentence and the idiom fixed by H.E. iii.22 — Hegesippus preserves a real distinction between the Lord’s cousin Symeon and the Lord’s brethren James and Jude, and so, as Lightfoot and Bauckham both conclude, his evidence “must be held to count against the Hieronymian view.” 3 The “second cousin” counter is coherent and has a respectable translation …

ar.q: Does the two-word Greek “until” of Matthew 1:25 ( heōs hou ) imply Mary bore other children?
ar.c: The literary evidence suggests that the Greek speaker of Matthew’s time would have understood the phrase heōs hou to imply cessation of the action of the main clause after the action of the subordinate clause. — the thesis of Eric Svendsen, Who Is My Mother? (2001), as he states it. 1 This is the modern, linguistically-armoured form of the oldest Helvidian proof-text. Helvidius (c. 383) pressed Matthew 1:25 — Joseph “knew her not till ( heōs hou ) she had brought forth a son” — as implying that he knew her afterward. The classic reply (Jerome’s, weighed on the companion page “Do the infancy ph…
ar.a: Weak. As a proof that the Greek of Matthew 1:25 implies Mary bore other children — or even that she and Joseph later had relations — the argument does not hold. It earns one fair correction: the classic parallels are the one-word heōs , and the companion page on the infancy language notes as much. But the conclusion does not follow. The two-word heōs hou is used with no change of state in the very Koine the Evangelist wrote — Psalm 72:7, read exa…

ar.q: Do the identifications that complete Jerome’s cousin-theory hold? (Alphaeus = Clopas; “Jude of James”; “James the little”)
ar.c: Jerome himself advanced only that the “brethren of the Lord” (Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:3; John 7:5; Acts 1:14; 1 Corinthians 9:5; Galatians 1:19) were sons of “Mary of Clopas” the Virgin’s sister — His maternal cousins . The fuller Hieronymian reading that came to be taught, in which two or three of the brethren are also apostles numbered among the Twelve, needs three further identifications bolted onto Jerome’s core: Alphaeus = Clopas — the father of the brethren (Clopas, John 19:25) is one man with Alphaeus the father of the apostle “James son of Alphaeus” (Matthew 10:3), on the supposition tha…
ar.a: Weak. The three identifications are jointly required to turn Jerome’s cousins into named apostles, yet each is a later graft on his theory and each is the less-probable reading on its own evidence: Clopas and Alphaeus are distinct names, “Jude of James” is more naturally “son,” and “the little” is a mark of stature, not a rank implying two Jameses. As positive support for the Hieronymian reading the chain therefore fails; it lends the cousin-iden…

ar.q: Do “till she brought forth” (Matt 1:25) and “firstborn son” (Luke 2:7) imply Mary bore other children?
ar.c: From this he endeavours to show that the term first-born is inapplicable except to a person who has brothers, just as he is called only begotten who is the only son of his parents. — the argument as Jerome states it, Against Helvidius §10. 1 The Helvidian reading of the “brethren of the Lord” — that they were true sons of Joseph and Mary, born after Jesus — rests in part on two phrases from the infancy narratives. Matthew says Joseph “knew her not till she had brought forth” her son (Matthew 1:25); Luke calls Jesus Mary’s firstborn son (Luke 2:7). Helvidius pressed both: a man who “knew her no…
ar.a: Weak. As a positive argument that the infancy language implies Mary bore other children, the case does not hold. Both phrases are neutral on the question they are asked to settle: “till” establishes only that there was no union before the birth (the standard force of heōs hou , as Michal, the raven, and “lo, I am with you… till the end” all show), and “firstborn” is a consecration term fixed at birth, applicable to an only child no less than to t…

ar.q: Does the shared manner of death — both stoned in Jerusalem — support identifying James the Lord’s brother with the apostle James son of Alphaeus?
ar.c: The completed Hieronymian reading identifies James the Lord’s “brother” — James the Just, first bishop of Jerusalem — with the apostle “James the son of Alphaeus” among the Twelve (Matthew 10:3). Beside the philological props weighed on the companion page (Alphaeus = Clopas; “Jude of James”; “James the little”), a historical datum is sometimes adduced as extra confirmation: the two men are reported to have died in the same manner and place — each stoned to death in Jerusalem . Two men of one name, sharing so specific a death, are taken to be one man. James the Just / the Lord’s brother: stoned…
ar.a: Weak. The manner-of-death parallel looks like independent circumstantial confirmation but is not. Its sole source for the apostle’s stoning is a spurious, “blundering” apostle-catalogue that, in the same breath, treats James the Lord’s brother and James son of Alphaeus as two men; the apostle-notice is best explained as a stereotyped back-formation from the famous martyrdom of James the Just rather than a second independent event; and the two acc…

ar.q: Are “James the little” and Joses (Mark 15:40) the Lord’s brothers James and Joses? (Bauckham’s two impediments)
ar.c: Every version of the Hieronymian (cousin) reading, however much machinery it strips away, rests on one identification at the base. The companion pages weigh the props that make the brethren apostles among the Twelve (Alphaeus = Clopas, “Jude of James,” “James the little” as a comparative) and the John 19:25 punctuation that makes their mother the Virgin’s sister — and the theory’s strongest modern form (Josef Blinzler’s) discards them all. What no form of the reading can shed is the first link: that the “James and Joses” named among the Lord’s brethren (Mark 6:3: “the brother of James, and Jos…
ar.a: Weak. The identification of the Lord’s brothers James and Joses with the “James the little and Joses” of Mark 15:40 is the one premise every form of the cousin-reading must keep, and on Bauckham’s two impediments it is the less-probable reading: the Jerusalem leader is not credibly “the little,” and the mother of two equally-prominent sons is not credibly the mother of James-and-lesser-Joses. On the better account, Mark’s epithet does the opposit…

ar.q: Is a never-consummated (“Josephite”) marriage unbiblical — does 1 Corinthians 7 forbid a permanently celibate Joseph and Mary?
ar.c: … their teaching is, no, they got married but they never consummated the marriage, which is considered a wonderful thing in this scripture… 1 Corinthians 7 talks about how you’re not supposed to stay celibate in marriage — that’s not how it works, this is bad for marriage. You want to stay celibate, then stay single. — Mike Winger, “Unbiased stuff the Catholic Church teaches” (2015), at about 57:23–59:37. 1 A companion form of the objection is pressed by GotQuestions.org from Matthew’s wording: “Matthew also makes a point of telling us that Joseph ‘took Mary home as his wife’… Matthew’s reader…
ar.a: Weak. As a disproof of the perpetual virginity the “a never-consummated marriage is unbiblical” objection does not hold on its best available case. Its two supports both give way: 1 Corinthians 7 forbids only unilateral deprivation and expressly permits abstinence by consent while positively commending celibacy, and the premise that consummation is what makes a marriage is denied by the classical account of marriage-by-consent (Augustine, with Ep…

ar.q: Was Jude the Lord’s brother the apostle Thomas, Jesus’ physical twin?
ar.c: The brethren-question asks who the “brethren of the Lord” — James, Joses, Simon, and Jude (Mark 6:3) — really were. One proposed answer folds the fourth of them, Jude, into a different figure: the apostle Thomas . In the East Syrian church of Edessa and its region the apostle was known not as “Thomas” simply but as Judas Thomas — so in the title of the Gospel of Thomas , throughout the Acts of Thomas and the Book of Thomas the Contender , in the Curetonian Syriac of John 14:22, in the Abgar legend Eusebius reports ( H.E. 1:13), and in Ephraem. 1 Since the name “Thomas” renders the Aramaic word…
ar.a: Weak. There is a real tradition here to reckon with — an old and distinctive East Syrian name, “Judas Thomas,” and a genuine ancient interpretation of it as “the twin” — so the claim is not baseless, and it is rightly weighed rather than waved off. But on its best available case the interpretation it is marshalled for — that Jude the Lord’s brother was the apostle Thomas, Jesus’ physical twin — does not hold. The twin-of-Jesus motif is confined t…

ar.q: Does Jude 1’s “brother of James” denote literal kinship, or a figurative brotherhood (gloss, spiritual fraternity, or “co-worker”)?
ar.c: The letter of Jude names its author only once, in its opening words: Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James, to them that are sanctified by God the Father, and preserved in Jesus Christ, and called… — Jude 1 . 1 The author does not call himself the brother of the Lord — only the brother of James . Who is he, and what does “brother of James” mean? Richard Bauckham — himself holding the perpetual virginity on the Epiphanian reading — catalogues the identifications that have been proposed and argues that the phrase settles the matter in favour of literal kinship. 2 The majority r…
ar.a: Sound. On the interpretation it is actually offered for — that “brother of James” in Jude 1 denotes literal family kinship, not a figurative, spiritual, honorific, or “co-worker” brotherhood — the reading is the mainstream one and well-grounded. The phrase is an identifier , and it identifies by relationship to the one James who needed no epithet; the idiom ( adelphos + a personal name) is the ordinary New-Testament language of kinship; and the a…

ar.q: Does the Epistle of Jude’s christological vocabulary — the title “Master” ( despotēs ), tied to the desposynoi — support the letter’s authenticity, that it was …
ar.c: Like its companions from Jude’s learned exegesis and his knowledge of the Testament of Moses , this argument reaches the literal-kinship case for the brethren through the letter’s authenticity : its author names himself “ brother of James ” ( Jude 1 ), so a genuine Jude who could write it is a real member of the family group the Gospels name — James, Joses, Jude, Simon ( Mark 6:3 ). Where the exegesis argument reads authenticity off Jude’s method and the Testament argument off his knowledge of a source , this one reads it off Jude’s christological vocabulary . The case is Richard Bauckham ’s —…
ar.a: Contested. The argument has two parts, and they fare differently. Its foundation — that the four christological titles recoverable for the relatives’ circle are the four found in Jude, and that the rarest of them, christological despotēs , is otherwise unattested in the first century yet presupposed by the very name desposynoi — is well-grounded and locates the letter’s idiom securely in the kin-circle of Palestinian Jewish Christianity; it genui…

ar.q: Does the Epistle of Jude’s learned, Palestinian pesharim-style exegesis support the letter’s authenticity — that it was written by Jude the Lord’s brother?
ar.c: The whole literal-kinship case for the brethren rests, in part, on the letter of Jude being a real artifact from within Jesus’ own family: its author names himself “ brother of James ” ( Jude 1 ), and a genuine Jude who could write that is a real member of the family group the Gospels name — James, Joses, Jude, Simon ( Mark 6:3 ). So the letter’s authenticity — whether it was really written by Jude the Lord’s brother, or is a later pseudepigraph — bears on the brethren question. And here Richard Bauckham — himself holding the perpetual virginity on the Epiphanian reading — mounts an argument f…
ar.a: Contested. The argument has two parts, and they fare differently. Its foundation — that Jude 4–19 is an elaborate, formal work of Palestinian Jewish exegesis in the manner of the Qumran pesharim, written early and probably drawing on 1 Enoch in Aramaic — is well-grounded, detailed, and widely accepted; it is close to a settled result, and it genuinely excludes the picture of Jude as a late, Hellenistic, Gentile forgery. But the conclusion the arg…

ar.q: Does the Lukan genealogy’s origin in Jude’s circle — its Enochic structure resting on the two Enoch data Jude deploys — support the Epistle of Jude’s authentici…
ar.c: Like its companions from Jude’s learned exegesis , his knowledge of the Testament of Moses , and his christological vocabulary , this argument reaches the literal-kinship case through the letter’s authenticity : its author names himself “ brother of James ” ( Jude 1 ), so a genuine Jude who could write it is a real member of the family group the Gospels name — James, Joses, Jude, Simon ( Mark 6:3 ). But it differs from those three in kind . They read authenticity off features internal to the letter — its method, its sources, its vocabulary. This one argues from an external document: the geneal…
ar.a: Plausible. The observation at the argument’s heart is genuine and arresting: the Lukan genealogy carries an Enochic scheme whose two indispensable foundations — the seventy generations of 1 Enoch 10:12 and Enoch’s seventh place — are exactly the two Enoch data that the letter of Jude, alone among first-generation Christian writings, deploys. That double convergence securely locates both documents in one narrow milieu: an early, Palestinian, Enoch…

ar.q: Does the Epistle of Jude’s knowledge of the obscure Palestinian Testament of Moses (Jude 9) support the letter’s authenticity — that it was written by Jude the …
ar.c: Like the argument from Jude’s learned exegesis , this one reaches the literal-kinship case for the brethren through the letter’s authenticity : its author names himself “ brother of James ” ( Jude 1 ), so a genuine Jude who could write it is a real member of the family group the Gospels name — James, Joses, Jude, Simon ( Mark 6:3 ). Where the exegesis argument reads authenticity off Jude’s method , this one reads it off Jude’s knowledge of a specific, obscure source . The case is Richard Bauckham ’s — himself holding the perpetual virginity on the Epiphanian reading. Jude 9 alludes to a story …
ar.a: Contested. The argument has two parts, and they fare differently. Its foundation — that Jude 9 alludes, without explanation, to the lost ending of the Palestinian Testament of Moses , a source so little known that the early church at large (the Alexandrian Fathers, the author of 2 Peter) did not possess it — is well-grounded and locates the letter securely in first-century Palestinian Jewish Christianity; it genuinely excludes the picture of Jude…

ar.q: Is the perpetual virginity a late invention — a dogma “defined nearly 2,000 years after Christ,” unheard of by early Christians?
ar.c: “Have you thought through the entire complex of doctrines and dogmas relating to Mary, and how unbiblical and a-historical they are? Do you really believe that dogmas defined nearly 2,000 years after the birth of Christ represent the actual teachings of the Apostles? … Are you aware of the origin of these doctrines… and how do you explain how it is you must believe these things de fide , by faith, when generations of Christians lived and died without ever even having heard of such things?” — James White, “Reposting a Top Ten List on Roman Catholicism” (point 2, the Marian point). 1 The point r…
ar.a: Weak. As a charge against the perpetual virginity specifically, the argument does not hold on its best available case. Its one sound element — that the formal dogmatic definition postdates the apostolic age — is true of almost every conciliar doctrine and is the ordinary grammar of development, not a symptom of invention; and the vivid “nearly 2,000 years” figure belongs to the Immaculate Conception (1854) and the Assumption (1950), which the obj…

ar.q: Does 1 Corinthians 9:5 — the “brothers of the Lord” as married travelling apostles, a known class — support reading “brother of the Lord” as literal kinship?
ar.c: Only once in his letters does Paul mention the brothers of Jesus other than James, and the reference is, at first sight, merely incidental. Arguing that he has the right (though he waives it) to be supported by his converts, he lines himself up with the other missionaries who enjoy that right: Have we not power to lead about a sister, a wife, as well as other apostles, and as the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas? — 1 Corinthians 9:5 . 1 Richard Bauckham — himself holding the perpetual virginity on the Epiphanian reading — argues that this “at first sight merely incidental” verse “proves very i…
ar.a: Sound. On the interpretation it is actually offered for — that “brother(s) of the Lord” denotes a real, recognized class of the Lord’s literal kin, married men known well enough to serve Paul as a byword for apostolic standing — the argument is well-grounded and unrefuted, and it rests on the best kind of evidence the whole question affords: an undesigned, incidental notice in an undisputed letter of Paul, written within a generation of the event…

ar.q: Do the shared names (James, Joses, Simon) across two families make a kinship reading of the brethren incredible — or is the coincidence unremarkable given the t…
ar.c: The kinship readings of “the brethren of the Lord” — both the Hieronymian (the brethren are maternal cousins, sons of “Mary of Clopas”) and the Epiphanian (they are Joseph’s sons by a former wife) — posit a second household standing alongside the family of Joseph and Mary. And the Gospels give both households overlapping names: the Lord’s brethren are “James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas” ( Matthew 13:55 ; Mark 6:3 ), while the second Mary at the cross is “the mother of James the little and of Joses” (Mark 15:40) and the family of Clopas yields a Symeon (Simon). A stock reply to the kinship…
ar.a: Sound. As a rebuttal the argument holds on its own terms and is confirmed from a quarter Lightfoot did not have: the name-pool of first-century Palestinian Jewry was tiny and top-heavy, James, Joses, and Simon sat at or near its summit, and the repetition of those names across two kindred families is unremarkable — predicted, if anything, by the onomastic data and by ordinary naming custom. The naming objection to the kinship readings therefore c…

ar.q: Does the “Papias” fragment give early (pre-Jerome) support for the cousin theory?
ar.c: A short Latin extract, headed with the name Papias , lists the several Marys of the Gospels and makes the Lord’s brethren the sons of “Mary the wife of Clopas or Alphaeus” — the cousin-identification at the heart of the Hieronymian reading. Printed by Grabe ( Spicilegium II.34) and Routh ( Reliquiae Sacrae I.16) among the remains of Papias of Hierapolis (fl. c. 110), it runs: Maria mater Domini: Maria Cleophae, sive Alphei uxor, quae fuit mater Jacobi episcopi et apostoli et Symonis et Thadei et cujusdam Joseph: Maria Salome uxor Zebedei mater Joannis evangelistae et Jacobi: Maria Magdalene: i…
ar.a: Unsupported. As early evidence for the cousin theory the fragment collapses on every count: the manuscript is fourteenth-century, its one relevant sentence is copied almost word for word from Jerome (so it is later than the theory it is offered to attest, not earlier), the real Papias’s silence — and the tradition’s — tells decisively against it, and its author is the eleventh-century lexicographer Papias, not Papias of Hierapolis. It is not a we…

ar.q: Does the present tense of “I know not a man” (Luke 1:34) — read as a Semitic participle of permanent condition — prove Mary had vowed lifelong virginity?
ar.c: A grammatical argument, widely copied across popular apologetics, is drawn from the exact form of Mary’s verb in Luke 1:34 — “How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?” The Greek is ándra ou ginóskō (“a man I do not know”), a present indicative ; the argument holds that this present tense expresses not a passing fact (“I have not known a man”) but a continuous, settled disposition — and that it renders a Hebrew or Aramaic active participle , yodaat (“knowing”), which names a lasting or permanent condition. The reconstructed underlay offered is ki enneni yodaat ish . As Warren Carroll states …
ar.a: Weak — as a proof of a vow , which is the interpretation it is marshaled to serve. Keep the two questions apart. Is the grammatical datum sound? Largely yes: the present tense is unusual against the Old Testament idiom, and the participle behind it does carry a durative, forward-leaning sense — the argument’s linguistic core is defensible, and it is a real gain over reading the clause as a bare statement of present fact. Does it establish a lifel…

ar.q: Does Psalm 69:8’s “my mother’s children” prove Mary bore other children?
ar.c: “I am become a stranger unto my brethren, and an alien unto my mother’s children.”… This verse also teaches the virgin birth of Christ. A very strange phrase for the psalmist to use is “…and an alien unto my mother’s children”—not His father’s children because Joseph was not His blood father; His siblings were half-brothers and half-sisters. — Koinonia House, “The Life of Christ in Psalm 69” . 1 The argument runs in three steps. Where “brother” ( adelphos ) is lexically elastic and so open to the cousin- or stepbrother-reading (weighed at “Does adelphos mean cousin?” ), Psalm 69:8 is said to b…
ar.a: Weak. As an interpretation the Psalm 69:8 proof-text does not hold on its best available case. Its premise — that a messianic psalm may be read as Christ’s first-person speech clause by clause — is refuted by the psalm itself (v. 5’s confession of sin; the traitor’s inheritance of v. 25 at Acts 1:20), so the inference from “Psalm 69 is messianic” to “v. 8 predicates Mary’s children of Jesus” is invalid. Even conceded, the verse yields only the es…

ar.q: Do the traditional names of Jesus’ sisters — Mary and Salome — preserve genuine early memory?
ar.c: The Gospels record that Jesus had sisters — “are not his sisters here with us?” (Mark 6:3 ∥ Matthew 13:56) — but never name them. Post-canonical tradition does: the best-attested names are Mary and Salome . Epiphanius gives them as the two daughters of Joseph by his first wife ( Panarion 78:8:1; 78:9:6), the same reconstruction that anchors the Epiphanian view that the “brethren” were Joseph’s children by a former marriage. 1 Two witnesses earlier than Epiphanius can be read to carry the same names. The Gospel of Philip — a Valentinian work of probably the third century — states: “There were t…
ar.a: Plausible. Bauckham’s statistical argument is the strongest single piece of evidence that any part of the extra-canonical family tradition rests on real Palestinian Jewish-Christian memory. It is not an argument from authority or from piety but from independent onomastic data: Salome’s near-absence from the diaspora makes it genuinely unlikely that a Gentile inventor would have chosen it, and the tradition’s failure to spread beyond one branch fi…

ar.q: Is the second-century stepbrother tradition genuine historical memory or a construct protecting Mary’s virginity?
ar.c: The wiki’s timeline shows the Epiphanian reading — the “brethren of the Lord” are Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage, no blood-kin of Mary — as the earliest attested solution to the brethren-question, running from the Protevangelium of James and the Gospel of Peter (c. 150) through Clement , Origen , and Eusebius . This argument asks the sharper question that the timeline’s bare chronology cannot settle: does that early attestation amount to evidence that the brethren really were Joseph’s sons by a former wife — a memory of the family’s actual make-up — or only to evidence that the belief wa…
ar.a: Contested. The question is genuinely disputed, with a strong case on each side and no decider in the evidence — the defining shape of a contested rating. For the memory reading: the stepbrother tradition is the earliest attested solution by a wide margin, it is early enough that reliable tradition survived, and its earliest carriers assume rather than argue it, as if drawing on something older than themselves. For the construct reading: it travel…

ar.q: Is Tertullian the earliest Helvidian — did he teach that Mary bore children after Jesus?
ar.c: It is easy to run together two things Tertullian says, and the whole question turns on prising them apart. He treats the birth of Christ in two registers — the manner of Mary’s childbearing, and the identity of the brethren — and he is explicit on the first, silent (or only suggestive) on the second. The manner of the birth (explicit). Against heretics who played on the paradox “a virgin and yet not a virgin,” Tertullian draws the line himself: “although she was a virgin when she conceived, she was a wife when she brought forth her son. Now, as a wife, she was under the very law of ‘opening th…
ar.a: Contested. Keep the two claims apart and the verdict follows. That Tertullian denied Mary a virginity outlasting the birth is secure — his own words settle it, and even his critics concede it — so he is firmly no witness for the perpetual virginity in its developed ( in partu ) form. That he positively taught the Helvidian reading of the brethren is the more probable reading of him but remains an inference : strong by the plain sense of “brother”…

ar.q: Does John 19:25 make “Mary of Clopas” the Virgin’s sister — two sisters both named Mary?
ar.c: Jerome’s Hieronymian reading makes the “brethren of the Lord” the sons of “Mary of Clopas” and identifies that Mary as the Virgin’s own sister , so that the brethren are the Lord’s maternal cousins . That sisterhood hangs on a single verse. John 19:25 names the women at the cross: “Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene.” Read in its received punctuation, the clause “his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas” is a single apposition — the sister is Mary of Clopas — so the verse names only three women. Combined …
ar.a: Weak. The maternal cousinhood Jerome asserts requires John 19:25 to make “Mary of Clopas” the Virgin’s own sister — and that requires two sisters both named Mary, which is, as Lightfoot rightly judged, most improbable. The early versions (Peshito, the Jerusalem Syriac lectionary, the Thebaic) and the couples-arrangement of the Greek all point to four women, on which reading the Virgin’s sister is unnamed (plausibly Salome) and Mary of Clopas is n…

ar.q: Does Mary’s reply to Gabriel — “How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?” (Luke 1:34) — imply she had taken a vow of perpetual virginity?
ar.c: Mary is betrothed to Joseph ( Luke 1:27 ) and is told she will conceive and bear a son ( Luke 1:31 ) — that is, in the ordinary course, that she will begin a family with her husband. Yet she answers with a question that treats her virginity as an obstacle : Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man? — Luke 1:34 . On the ordinary reading — a betrothed woman who will in the normal course consummate her marriage — the question is puzzling: she of all people would know how a child is conceived. The argument infers that it makes sense only if Mary never intended to “…
ar.a: Contested. The two forms of the claim fare differently, and the fair verdict tracks the steelman rather than the popular overstatement. The strong form — that Luke 1:34 discloses a formal, absolute vow of perpetual virginity already sworn — is weak : it is anachronistic to a Judaism with no such institution, it strains the betrothal it must explain, and even its defenders reach it only by the two-stage construction that concedes no absolute vow p…

ds.t: The Pillars of Seth
ds.q: According to a tradition first written down by the Jewish historian Josephus (c. AD 93–94), the righteous descendants of Seth were the inventors of astronomy — "that peculiar sort of wisdom which is concerned with the heavenly bodies, and their order" — and, warned by Adam's prophecy that the world would be destroyed once by fire and once by water, they inscribed their discoveries on two pillars, one of brick and one of stone , so that whichever catastrophe came, the knowledge would survive. The stone pillar, Josephus adds, still stood "in the land of Siriad" in his own day. This page follows that legend of antediluvian wisdom preserved through the Flood — where it came from, and what later …

tl.t: Josephus gives the legend its classic form in the Antiquities of the Jews (I.2.3). Seth's posterity, virtuous men, "were the inventors of that peculiar sort of wisdom which is concerned with the heavenly bodies, and their order"; and foreseeing on "Adam's prediction that the world was to be destroyed at one time by the force of fire, and at another time by the violence and quantity of water, they made two pillars, the one of brick, the other of stone," inscribing their discoveries on both so that one would outlast whichever destruction came — the stone pillar, he reports, still "remains in the land of Siriad to this day." 4 Josephus himself preserves, elsewhere in the same book, the rival ac…

Isidore carries the legend into the Latin West. His universal chronicle, the Chronica , reports "as Josephus reports, some men, who knew that they were about to die by either fire or water, inscribed their discoveries on two columns made of brick and stone," the stone columns said to "remain in Syria to this very day." Isidore tells it generically, of "some men," and lodges it one entry below his notice of the Cainite Jubal , "from the line of Cain," inventor of music before the flood — the two ingredients a later hand would fuse. (The legend is not in his better-known Etymologies , which carries only the Cainite-music note.) 6

George Syncellus , a monk of Constantinople, carries the legend into the Greek/Byzantine chronicle-tradition — and his Chronography is the single conduit through which the two closest pagan cognates of the pillars story survive. He alone preserves the Egyptian fragment of the (pseudo-Manethonian) Book of Sothis , whose sacred antediluvian knowledge was inscribed "upon the columns set up in the Seriadic land , by Thoth, the first Hermes," and re-transcribed after the deluge — the same region-name (Josephus's "land of Siriad") and the same before-and-after-the-Flood logic; and he alone preserves Berossus's Babylonian parallel, the antediluvian writings buried at Sippar before the flood and dug…

George Kedrenos (Latin Cedrenus ) gives the legend its fullest surviving Greek form — and gives it, pointedly, back to Seth himself . In the primeval-history opening of his Synopsis Historion , "Seth gave names to the seven planets, and comprehended the lore of the movements of the heavens. He also prepared two pillars, one of stone and one of brick, and wrote these things upon them… He also devised the Hebrew letters." Where Josephus credits Seth's posterity collectively and Isidore tells it of "some men," Kedrenos names Seth as discoverer, planet-namer, pillar-builder, and inventor of the alphabet. He writes a little before the Latin Comestor would reassign the same pillars to the Cainite …

Peter Comestor 's Historia Scholastica — the "school Bible" of the medieval West, surviving in some 800 manuscripts and the great conduit for Josephus's material — retells the pillars and cites Josephus by name, yet makes the decisive change: he ascribes them not to Seth's line but to the Cainite musician Jubal . "He wrote it on two columns, the whole of it on each, as Josephus says — one of marble, the other of brick — of which the one would not be washed away by the flood, the other not dissolved by fire." With Comestor the pillars of Seth become, in the West, the pillars of Cain's line. 9

Ranulf Higden 's Polychronicon — Englished by John Trevisa in 1387 — carries both forms. Its main text keeps the plain Josephan version, "men" who foresaw fire and flood and "closede hem in tweie greet pileres i-made of marbyl and of brend tyle"; but in the chapter on Jubal several manuscripts splice in Comestor's Cainite retelling verbatim. The one chronicle thus documents the legend's two streams — the older generic/Sethite and the medieval Latin Cainite — and it is the Polychronicon that the later Masonic "Old Charges" (the Cooke MS) would quarry. 10

ar.q: Is the pillars-of-Seth legend a displaced Enoch tradition?
ar.c: …although Josephus refers to Seth and his progeny, some features of the "two stelae" story allude to peculiar roles and situations which Jewish lore traditionally associates with the seventh antediluvian patriarch Enoch. — Andrei A. Orlov, "Overshadowed by Enoch's Greatness: 'Two Tablets' Traditions from the Book of Giants to Palaea Historica ," marquette.edu/maqom . The thesis is not that Josephus muddled the two names — he plainly writes "Seth" — but that the functions his Sethites perform (discovering "the science of the heavenly bodies and their order," writing that science down, and inscr…
ar.a: Plausible. Take the two questions apart. That Josephus's Sethite pillars carry roles that Jewish lore gives to Enoch — heavenly astronomy, its inscription, and its preservation through fire and water on paired durable media — is well-grounded and effectively mainstream: the celestial-scribe function is Enoch's in Jubilees , the Astronomical Book, and the Book of Giants, and the two-media survival device is told of Enoch himself in the Palaea Hist…

ar.q: Is the fire-and-water double-destruction an ancient tradition?
ar.c: …Adam might foretell a conflagration and a deluge, which all antiquity witnesses to be an ancient tradition… — William Whiston, translator's footnote to Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews I.2.3. Whiston's point is that the two-pillars story does not require Josephus to have made up its premise: the belief that the world would be destroyed once by fire and once by water was already old and widespread when Josephus wrote it down. If that is right, the legend's central framing device — a pair of durable media hedged against a pair of catastrophes — is a shared inheritance, not an ad hoc invention.…
ar.a: Sound. The narrow claim the argument serves — that the fire-and-water double-destruction is an ancient, independently attested tradition rather than Josephus's invention — is well-grounded and effectively mainstream. Plato frames it as old Egyptian priestly lore, Berossus and the Stoics give it the great-year machinery of ekpyrosis and kataklysmos , and the first-century Life of Adam and Eve carries the full Jewish version, Sethite frame and pair…

ar.q: Is Josephus's pillars-of-Seth report historical?
ar.c: Of Josephus's mistake here, when he took Seth the son of Adam, for Seth or Sesostris, king of Egypt, the erector of this pillar in the land of Siriad, see Essay on the Old Testament, Appendix, p. 159, 160. — William Whiston, translator's footnote to Antiquities of the Jews I.2.3 (1737 translation), ccel.org . Whiston, having translated Josephus's report that the Sethite stone pillar "remains in the land of Siriad to this day," appends two objections to it — the one quoted here, that Josephus mistook Seth son of Adam for the pillar-erecting Egyptian king Sesostris , and a second, that a stone p…
ar.a: Contested — strong as tradition-history, weak as a report of fact, and its best-known refutation misfires. Distinguish the two questions the story runs together. As a tradition — antediluvian discoveries preserved through catastrophe on paired durable pillars, kept by a righteous line — the legend is genuinely ancient and coherent, with independent Babylonian (Berossus) and Egyptian (Manetho / the Hermetic Book of Sothis ) analogues; on that leve…

ar.q: Is the pillars-of-Seth legend the pious inversion of the Watchers' antediluvian astrology?
ar.c: The summary frames the whole doctrine as one half of a pair — "the same knowledge, two origins: impious revelation or righteous discovery" — with the impious half represented by the fallen-angels aetiology ( 1 Enoch 8; Tatian; Tertullian), in which rebel Watchers teach mankind the forbidden science of the stars. But there is a closer impious mirror still: a tradition that preserves antediluvian celestial knowledge in the same physical form the Sethite legend uses — carved on durable stone, surviving the Flood, recovered afterward — except that here the knowledge is the Watchers' illicit astrol…
ar.a: Plausible. Take the two questions apart. That the pillars-of-Seth device has an impious mirror — the same celestial-knowledge-carved-on-stone-and-surviving-the-Flood motif, told of the Watchers' illicit astronomy and the transgressing Cainan — and that this impious version ( Jubilees , 2nd c. BC) is the older of the two, is sound and documented. On that narrow point the summary's "impious revelation vs. righteous discovery" pairing is not merely …

ar.q: Is the Sethian-Gnostic Seth tradition a cognate of the antediluvian-pillars legend?
ar.c: In the Three Steles of Seth … the traditional two steles, or tablets of stone and brick, on which Seth was said to have preserved from destruction by flood or fire the vast sum of astrological lore revealed to him (cf. Josephus Jewish Antiquities 1.67.1–71.5) have now become three steles recording doxological hymns. — John D. Turner, introduction to The Three Steles of Seth , in Marvin Meyer (ed.), The Nag Hammadi Scriptures (HarperOne, 2007), p. 523. The claim of this page is that the Sethian-Gnostic literature — a body of 2nd–3rd-century texts built entirely around Seth as heavenly savior an…
ar.a: Sound as a cognate / reception claim; conjectural as a direct-dependence claim. Keep the two apart. That the 2nd–3rd-century Sethian-Gnostic corpus reworks the same Seth + elect-race + saving-knowledge + water-and-fire-survival complex the pillars legend carries is well-supported: the Apocalypse of Adam runs the seed of Seth through destruction by water (Noah/Deucalion) and then by fire, sulphur, and asphalt; the Gospel of the Egyptians has Seth …

ar.q: Is the Surid pyramid-legend a cognate of the Sethite antediluvian-pillars tradition?
ar.c: Three hundred years before the flood, Surid had a dream in which it seemed that the earth overturned… and the stars fell and collided against each other with a terrible crash… [The priests] engraved on these monuments all sayings of the wise. They wrote on every surface of the pyramids, the ceilings, foundations, and walls, all the sciences familiar to the Egyptians… the figures of the stars… the science of talismans, mathematics, architecture — all the sciences of the world. — al-Maqrizi (d. 1442), al-Khiṭaṭ , retelling the older Coptic-Arab Surid narrative, trans. in Jason Colavito, "Al-Maqr…
ar.a: Sound as a cognate claim; conjectural as a descent claim. Keep the two apart. That the medieval Arab-Coptic Surid legend is a branch of the same antediluvian-knowledge-survival motif as the pillars of Seth is well-supported and close to demonstrable: it shares the tradition's whole skeleton (celestial foreknowledge → inscription on catastrophe-proof stone → survival of a doubled fire-and-water destruction), it names as builder the very Hermes–Idr…

ds.t: The Power of the Name
ds.q: From its first pages the church believed that the Name has power — above all the name of Jesus. Demons flee at it, the sick are healed by it, prayer is offered in it, converts are baptized into it, and salvation is found in no other. “There is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Acts 4:12); God has “given him a name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:9–11). This page traces how that conviction — that to invoke the Name is to lay hold of the One named, and that the Name itself is effectual in exorcism, prayer, baptism, and devotion — developed and was disciplined across the centuries, from the New Tes…

tl.w: Justin Martyr — the name of Jesus crucified routs demons (c. 160)
tl.t: Justin is the earliest father to make the exorcistic power of the Name a public, verifiable argument. Four times he appeals to a fact he says his hearers can check with their own eyes: demons are “overcome and subdued” when Christians exorcise them “in the name of Jesus Christ, crucified under Pontius Pilate,” and “the power of whose name even the demons do fear” is a present, ongoing power — grounded not in the exorcist but in what the Father gave the Son through “the dispensation of His suffering.” 11 Writing to the Roman authorities he makes it empirical: “numberless demoniacs throughout the whole world, and in your city,” are healed by “Christian men exorcising them in the name of Jesus …

tl.w: Irenaeus of Lyons — the church works in the Name, not by incantation; the Gnostic misuse of secret names (c. 180)
tl.t: Irenaeus states the doctrine’s whole tension inside one work. On the positive side, the church “calling upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” drives out demons, heals the sick, and (he claims) has even raised the dead — “in the name of Jesus Christ, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate,” done freely and for the benefit of others, “neither practising deception upon any, nor taking any reward.” 14 And he draws the boundary himself: the church works these things “ not … by means of angelic invocations, or by incantations, or by any other wicked curious art,” but by prayer and the plain invocation of Jesus — and it is this Name, “but not that of Simon, or Menander, or Carpocrates, or of any …

tl.w: Tertullian of Carthage — the demons compelled to confess and flee at the naming of Christ; a public courtroom proof (c. 197)
tl.t: Tertullian turns the exorcistic power of the Name into a standing dare to the Roman magistrates. Bring any demoniac before the tribunal, he writes: the possessing spirit, “bidden to speak by a follower of Christ,” will confess itself a demon, and — for “all the authority and power we have over them is from our naming the name of Christ” — will leave the body it holds, “Fearing Christ in God, and God in Christ… So at our touch and breathing… they leave at our command the bodies they have entered, unwilling, and distressed, and before your very eyes put to an open shame.” The power is not a formula the operator commands but the dread of “Christ as Judge” — and Tertullian heads off the obvious …

tl.w: Origen of Alexandria — the fullest theory of why a name has power; names natural, not conventional (c. 248)
tl.t: Origen gives the most developed patristic account of the doctrine — the theory the earlier witnesses assumed and the later ones inherit. Answering Celsus’s gibe that it makes no difference whether God be called Zeus, or Sabaoth, or Ammon, he argues that the nature of names is “a deep and mysterious subject”: names were given “by nature,” not “by arrangement,” so that a power is lodged in the very sounds — “it is not the things signified, but the qualities and peculiarities of words, which possess a certain power.” Hence the Hebrew divine names — Sabaoth, Adonai, “the God of Abraham, of Isaac, of Jacob” — are “possessed of great power” and make “even demons… vanquished,” yet render them into …

tl.w: Cyprian of Carthage — demons adjured by the Name confess and are cast out; the pagan gods unmasked as the spirits it expels (c. 250)
tl.t: Cyprian is the Latin voice beside Origen at mid-century, pressing the practice the Greek had theorized. The demons, he writes, “when adjured by us through the true God, at once yield and confess, and are constrained to go out from the bodies possessed” — smitten, howling, and confessing “whence they came,” the spirit driven out “even as the faith of the sufferer comes in aid, or the grace of the healer effects.” He turns the datum apologetically, first against the idolater and then against the persecutor Demetrianus, whom he dares to come and hear his own gods “betraying what they are”: the very spirits the pagan venerates “as lords” are the ones that, at a Christian’s voice and “the power o…

tl.w: Athanasius of Alexandria — the Name’s power made an apologetic proof of the Resurrection and the Godhead of Christ (c. 318)
tl.t: Athanasius keeps the doctrine intact but turns it to a new use. Where the earlier witnesses wield the Name in exorcism, he marshals its power as public evidence : since “actions, and power over men, belong to the living only,” the plain fact that “where Christ is named… all idolatry is deposed” and every spirit “on barely hearing it flies and disappears” proves that the One named is not dead but risen — “and especially… God.” 25 The demons themselves are pressed into the proof: they would not obey a dead man, yet “if they be manifestly expelled by the naming of His name… He is not dead,” for the spirits “see… that He is God, and hence they fly and fall at His feet.” The argument turns histor…

tl.w: Cyril of Jerusalem — the liturgical face of the doctrine: the exorcisms of the catechumenate, the renunciation of Satan, and baptism “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (c. 350)
tl.t: Cyril gives the doctrine its liturgical face.
