Where the earlier witnesses argue the Name’s power in public exorcism and apology, Cyril, catechizing the baptismal candidates at Jerusalem, shows it enacted in the church’s rite of initiation. Through Lent the convert is exorcised again and again: “receive with earnestness the exorcisms… without exorcisms the soul cannot be purified” — and when “the exorcists inspire terror by the Spirit of God… the hostile demon flees away.” 28 On the night of baptism the candidate turns to face the West, “the region of sensible darkness,” and with arm outstretched “as though [Satan] were present” renounces him aloud — “I renounce thee, Satan” — the renunciatio…

tl.w: John Chrysostom — the doctrine’s central thesis in one sentence: “not the Name does anything, unless it be spoken with faith”; the renunciation and the sign of the cross as everyday armour (c. 400)
tl.t: Chrysostom states the whole doctrine in a single flat sentence. Preaching on the sons of Sceva, he explains the vagabond exorcists’ rout in one line — “then not the Name does anything, unless it be spoken with faith” — and guards it from the obvious misreading, insisting the demon is made to own Christ (“Jesus I know, and Paul I know”) before it is loosed on the men, “that there may not seem to be any slight put upon the Name of Jesus”: the collapse is “not any weakness of the Name, but all owing to the imposture of those men,” who worked “by way of trade” as Simon Magus had sought the Spirit “for the sake of merchandise.” 31 He presses the same boundary in his catechetical preaching, agains…

tl.w: Augustine of Hippo — the great Latin hinge: the idols fall where Christ is named, the church exorcises rather than propitiates, and the anatomy of the licit and illicit sign (c. 415)
tl.t: Augustine is the Latin doctor who states both poles of the doctrine in their sharpest Western form — the voice the timeline had been missing between the Greek fathers’ exorcistic argument and the medieval Western devotion. On the positive side he takes up the apologetic proof Athanasius had pressed — that where Christ is named the idols fall: “the Christian religion is overthrowing all lying figments… in order that the grace of the true Saviour may deliver men from those gods which man has made” — and he sharpens the exorcistic claim into an anti-theurgy argument against the Platonists who would placate the spirits: men of God cast out the hostile power “by exorcising it, not by propitiating…

tl.w: Diadochos of Photike — the Name turns inward: the continual invocation “Lord Jesus” in the heart (c. 486)
tl.t: With Diadochos the doctrine pivots from expelling demons to holding the Name. Where the earlier witnesses argue the exorcistic power of the Name, the fifth-century bishop of Photike gives the praying intellect the Name as its whole occupation: “For the complete fulfillment of its purpose we should give it nothing but the prayer ‘Lord Jesus’… Let the intellect continually concentrate on these words within its inner shrine… Those who meditate unceasingly upon this glorious and holy name in the depths of their heart can sometimes see the light of their own intellect.” The invocation is grounded not in technique but in the Spirit — “no one can say ‘Lord Jesus’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corin…

tl.w: John Climacus and the Sinai tradition — the Name bound to the breath; the strongest weapon in heaven or earth (c. 630)
tl.t: At Sinai the inward “Lord Jesus” is joined to the body’s own rhythm. The abbot John Climacus, in the Ladder of Divine Ascent , makes the invocation a thing of every breath: “Let the remembrance of Jesus be present with your every breath. Then indeed you will appreciate the value of stillness” 39 — the line that gives the practice its other name, hesychasm (from hesychia , stillness). And he draws the old exorcistic power of the Name inward to the ascetic’s warfare: “Flog your enemies with the name of Jesus, for there is no stronger weapon in heaven or earth.” His Sinai successor Hesychios teaches the same — the heart that “breathes and invokes, endlessly and without ceasing, only Jesus Chris…

tl.w: Bernard of Clairvaux — the sweetness of the Name: “light, food, medicine”; the fountainhead of the Western Holy Name devotion (c. 1140)
tl.t: In the Latin West the power of the Name takes an affective turn: its sweetness . Preaching on the Song of Songs’ “thy name is as ointment poured forth” (1:3), the Cistercian abbot Bernard of Clairvaux reads the Name of the Bridegroom as oil with a threefold property — “it gives light, it nourishes, it anoints… When preached it gives light, when meditated it nourishes, when invoked it relieves and soothes”: light, food, and medicine. 41 He gives the whole devotion its most quoted line — “Write what you will, I shall not relish it unless it tells of Jesus… Jesus to me is honey in the mouth, music in the ear, a song in the heart” — and presses the Name as a remedy for every ill of the soul: the…

tl.w: Gregory Palamas — the theological charter of the Jesus Prayer; the “single-phrased” invocation defended (c. 1340)
tl.t: What Diadochos and Climacus transmitted, Palamas defended. When the Calabrian Barlaam ridiculed the Athonite monks who invoked the name of Jesus with bowed head and controlled breath, the archbishop of Thessalonica vindicated the whole method — naming, in his own voice, the “single-phrased Jesus Prayer,” in which “the intellect’s noetic activity is easily ordered and purified.” 43 The body, he argued, is no obstacle to prayer but is drawn into it — it is “not out of place to teach people, especially beginners… through control of breathing” — and he quotes the inherited hesychast method he is defending: “Have no other occupation or meditation than the cry of: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, h…

tl.w: Bernardine of Siena — the Western Holy Name devotion; the IHS tablet charged as idolatry and vindicated (c. 1420)
tl.t: In the Latin West the Name took a public, civic form. The Franciscan preacher Bernardine of Siena made devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus the centre of his missions, raising at the climax of each sermon a tablet painted with the monogram IHS in a blaze of golden rays and exposing it for the crowd’s veneration — and persuading the warring cities of Italy to strike the arms of their factions from wall and gateway and set the sacred initials there instead. He preached the Name as “the glory of preachers, because the shining splendor of that name causes his word to be proclaimed and heard.” 45 The devotion drew the very charge this whole timeline turns on: he was accused of “having introduced a …

tl.w: The Holy Name confraternity and feast — the Western devotion institutionalized: the Society of the Holy Name, the universal feast, and the Jesuit monogram (c. 1564)
tl.t: What Bernardine carried into the public square the Western church made a standing institution. The devotion to reverence the Name and to check its abuse was fixed as the charge of a church-approved confraternity — the Dominican Society of the Holy Name, whose object is “to beget due love and reverence for the Holy Name of God and Jesus Christ” and to suppress blasphemy, tracing its commission to the Second Council of Lyons (1274) and Gregory X’s letter to Blessed John of Vercelli, taking organized form in Didacus of Victoria’s Confraternity of the Holy Name of God against blasphemers, and approved by Pius IV (1564) and reserved to the Dominicans by Pius V’s Decet Romanum Pontificem (1571). 4…

tl.w: The Way of a Pilgrim — the Jesus Prayer carried to a lay and Western readership (c. 1860)
tl.t: The monastic practice reaches the laity in an anonymous Russian narrative. Its wanderer, arrested by St Paul’s “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17 — the very text that had launched Diadochos’s teaching), is taught by a starets the continual invocation of the Name: “The continuous interior Prayer of Jesus is a constant uninterrupted calling upon the divine Name of Jesus with the lips, in the spirit, in the heart… at all times, in all places, even during sleep. The appeal is couched in these terms, ‘Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me.’” 50 He is to say it “three thousand times a day,” then six, then “twelve thousand times a day,” until the counted Prayer becomes the self-acting praye…
