Longevity and stature are given together as marks of a world before the Flood. 1 If that is a memory of something real rather than a literary …
ar.a: Weak — as evidence that the antediluvian lifespans are historical, while the prediction itself comes in. Both halves of that are meant. Traditions of a long-lived, taller first age are genuinely widespread and genuinely structured; India supplies them in their most explicit form, in Jain cosmology's descending aras and in the yugas, from outside the Near Eastern transmission routes that account for the Mesopotamian and Greek material. That is a r…

ar.q: Is the Durupınar formation Noah's Ark?
ar.c: The object is real and deserves meeting at its strongest. On the southern slopes above Doğubayazıt in far-eastern Turkey — in the volcanic uplands about 29 km south of Greater Ararat's summit, at roughly 2,000 m elevation — lies a large, smooth, boat-shaped outline in the earth: a pointed "bow," a blunt "stern," raised sides curving around a lower interior, and a striking bilateral symmetry. Local report has it emerging after heavy rains and earthquakes in May 1948; it was noticed by a Turkish army captain, İlhan Durupınar, on aerial photographs taken during a NATO mapping mission in October 1…
ar.a: Weak — as the claim that the Durupınar formation is the remains of Noah's Ark. The whole case rests on a boat-shaped outline that a doubly-plunging syncline produces on its own; the metal-detector "iron fittings" are natural limonite and magnetite, the "petrified timbers" are metamorphosed peridotite, and the "anchor stones" are local volcanic rock, while a younger limestone cross-cuts the supposed hull. The ground-penetrating-radar "decks and co…

ar.q: Do the Easter Island Moai require a lost technology or a lost civilization to carve and move?
ar.c: On Rapa Nui — Easter Island, one of the remotest inhabited specks on Earth — stand the moai: on the order of nine hundred monolithic human figures, torsos with oversized heads, carved between roughly the thirteenth and seventeenth centuries. Almost all were cut from a single quarry, the crater wall of Rano Raraku, and the scale is genuinely arresting. The average statue runs about four metres and some twelve or thirteen tonnes; the largest ever raised on a platform, Paro , stood close to ten metres and about 82 tonnes, with a separate red topknot ( pukao ) of some ten tonnes hoisted onto its h…
ar.a: Weak — for both sub-claims. The carving claim mistakes the stone: Rano Raraku's soft tuff was worked with basalt toki that survive in the quarry by the thousand, in a worksite frozen at every stage of manufacture, and needs no lost technology to explain. The transport claim is the real puzzle and is answered by the real evidence: the "walking" hypothesis converges the Rapa Nui oral tradition, the forward-leaning D-shaped road moai, the purpose-bu…

ar.q: Are the Eastern US mounds the "pyramids" of a lost 2,000-year civilization revealed by LiDAR?
ar.c: Over roughly two years the explorer and Maya Exploration Center research associate Luke Caverns says he has used publicly-available airborne-LiDAR data to identify and map "well over 100" previously-uncharted sites across the Eastern United States, and he insists on describing them as cities, villages, pyramids, palaces and geoglyphs . In a 2026 post he wrote that "calling these anything short of ‘Pyramids’ is a disservice to the civilizations that ruled over the American East for over 2000 years," and set as one of his goals for the year to "shed light on the great & sophisticated civilizatio…
ar.a: Weak — as the claim that the eastern earthworks are the "pyramids" of an unknown, lost, sophisticated civilization revealed by LiDAR. The concessions are real and are entered before the verdict. LiDAR has genuinely rewritten the map of pre-Columbian complexity elsewhere, so the expectation that uncharted earthworks remain under the eastern canopy is reasonable, not fringe; and the mound cultures the argument gestures at were authentically sophist…

ar.q: Did predynastic Egypt's hard-stone vases require lost machining technology to make?
ar.c: Two things are true and are the whole basis of the argument. The first is the material. From the Badarian and Naqada periods (roughly 4000–3000 BC) and into the Early Dynastic, Egyptian craftsmen worked vessels not only in soft travertine ("alabaster") but in granite, diorite, basalt, and the tough greywacke and siltstone of the Wadi Hammamat — stones at Mohs 6–7, harder than a copper tool and unworkable by any chisel. The second is the output. These were made by the tens of thousands: nearly forty thousand stone vessels were found stacked in the galleries beneath Djoser's Step Pyramid alone, …
ar.a: Weak — as the claim that predynastic Egypt's hard-stone vases required a lathe, machine tooling, or a technology beyond their own capacity. The process is understood in its main lines and attested at every step by material that has been dug up: abrasion rather than carving, with loose quartz sand harder than the copper; tubular drilling and sawing that leave diagnostic cores and striations; hollowing of closed forms with crescent flints and weigh…

ar.q: Are the post-Flood "giants" a warrior category rather than a surviving lineage?
ar.c: The problem the other two readings solve by mechanism, this one dissolves by lexicon. On the deflationary reading, "Nephilim" and gibborim are not the name of a bloodline that must be got from one side of the Flood to the other. They are category words — the fallen ones, the mighty men, the warriors, the outsized enemy — that a later writer or speaker can apply to any formidable population without asserting descent. The conquest-era clans are then simply Canaanite peoples, some of them genuinely tall, described in the idiom the tradition had for formidable predecessors; and the spies' claim in…
ar.a: Sound — as an account of the post-Flood problem. The reading is where the weight of scholarship sits, and it earns that position on the text rather than on authority. The clause that generates the problem is spoken by men the narrative is condemning for speaking it, and it stands beside a self-declared figure of speech in the same sentence. The catalogue of giant peoples in Deuteronomy 2 is ethnographic throughout — territories, neighbours, alter…

ar.q: Does the peer-reviewed SAR-Doppler scan really reveal undiscovered structures inside the Great Pyramid?
ar.c: The 2022 paper is careful about what radar cannot do — and then claims to have done it anyway by an indirect route. Its abstract concedes the penetration problem, proposes reading background-seismic micro-movements instead, and states the result in the strongest possible terms: … due to the poor penetrating action of electromagnetic waves inside solid bodies, the capability to observe inside distributed targets is precluded. … The present work describes an imaging method based on the analysis of micro-movements on the Khnum-Khufu Pyramid, which are usually generated by background seismic waves…
ar.a: Weak. The interpretation this page rates — that the 2022 micro-movement SAR-Doppler method can bear the internal reconstruction of the Great Pyramid it advertises — is genuinely stronger than its viral Khafre sibling, and the difference is worth stating precisely so the rating is not read as a wave-off. It cleared peer review; it does not depend on the impossible deep-penetration physics that sinks the underground-city claim; and it rests on a pr…

ar.q: Do satellite-radar scans reveal a buried city and a twin Sphinx beneath Giza?
ar.c: There are two layers here, and they must be kept apart. The peer-reviewed layer is modest and honest about its own limits: … due to the poor penetrating action of electromagnetic waves inside solid bodies, the capability to observe inside distributed targets is precluded. … [We propose] an imaging method based on the analysis of micro-movements on the Khnum-Khufu Pyramid, which are usually generated by background seismic waves … Khnum-Khufu becomes transparent like a crystal when observed in the micro-movement domain. — Filippo Biondi and Corrado Malanga, "Synthetic Aperture Radar Doppler Tomo…
ar.a: Unsupported for the flagship claim, weak for its companion — and the split is worth stating precisely, because it is not a wave-off. The 2022 Remote Sensing paper is a real, peer-reviewed piece of work that says something careful and small. What went viral in 2025 is a different object: an unreviewed, un-ground-truthed reading that pushes an imaging technique hundreds of metres past what its own physics allows, produces a lost city and a "Hall of…

ar.q: A recent single global Flood predicts a synchronous worldwide sediment horizon — is there one?
ar.c: Grant the premise this timeline grants: a Flood happened. Now add the specific model that makes the sharpest prediction — a single deluge, global in extent, within the last several thousand years, which destroyed the land life of the earth and then drained. Such an event moves an enormous quantity of sediment and drops it. It should therefore have left one contemporaneous deposit, recognisable on every continent, occupying the same position in every sequence : a worldwide horizon with the same event on both sides of it — a world before, a world after. This is a genuinely risky prediction, and …
ar.a: Weak — as a prediction of the young single-date global model. The prediction was well framed and the test is a fair one, run with tools that have found exactly this kind of horizon when it existed: the end-Cretaceous iridium anomaly is a synchronous worldwide layer, it was predicted, looked for, and found. The Flood horizon is not there. What the record holds instead is many local sequences correlated by fossils, isotopes and magnetic reversals, …

ar.q: Do Göbekli Tepe and Karahan Tepe attest a lost pre-Flood civilization?
ar.c: The object is genuinely extraordinary and should be met at its strongest. On a hill above the Harran plain in south-eastern Turkey, and at its sister mound Karahan Tepe some thirty-five kilometres east, people who had no pottery, no metal, no writing, and — on the excavators' reading of the plant and animal remains — no domesticated crops or herds raised rings of carved T-shaped limestone monoliths up to five and a half metres tall and sixteen tonnes in weight, beginning around 9500 BC. At Karahan Tepe, excavated by Necmi Karul from 2019 under the Turkish "Taş Tepeler" ("Stone Hills") programm…
ar.a: Weak — as the reading that Göbekli Tepe and Karahan Tepe attest a lost pre-Flood civilization , whether identified as Eden, as the Watchers' work, as a deliberately buried antediluvian world, or as the observatory that recorded the Vulture-Stone comet. The datum underneath is sound but modest: monumental complexity does precede agriculture here, and it does bear on this reconstruction's theme that early society is older and more capable than assu…

ar.q: Does Göbekli Tepe's pre-agricultural monumentality fit a pre- or post-Flood world?
ar.c: Göbekli Tepe is a hill of stone enclosures above the Harran plain, ringed with carved T-shaped monoliths up to five and a half metres tall, raised by people with no pottery, no metal, no writing and — on the excavators' reading of the plant and animal remains — no domesticated crops or herds. On the conventional chronology it stands from roughly 9600 to 8000 BC, which is to say it is monumental architecture built before agriculture rather than after it. 1 The argument assessed here is that this datum belongs to the primeval history of Genesis — that Göbekli Tepe is the work of a world on one s…
ar.a: Weak — as evidence bearing on a Flood horizon. The argument needs Göbekli Tepe's conventional date to be wrong by about seven thousand years, and the site's genuinely open questions do not supply that. The backfill problem is real and is why the Enclosure D wall plaster date is the one that matters — plaster belongs to the standing structure, so it dates construction rather than burial; the typological late end is soft by centuries; the contempor…

ar.q: Does the Great Pyramid's precision require lost technology or a builder older than Dynasty 4?
ar.c: The Great Pyramid of Giza — the tomb-complex of the Fourth-Dynasty king Khufu, built around 2560 BC and, at an original height near 146 metres, the tallest structure on earth for nearly four thousand years — is the flagship of the "lost technology" case. The argument gathers a set of real metrological facts, each impressive on its own, and reads their sum as a signature no bronze-and-stone-age culture could leave. Five features carry the weight. The base is almost perfectly level: the platform on which the pyramid sits varies by only about two centimetres across a footprint of some five and a …
ar.a: Weak — as the claim that the Great Pyramid's leveling, alignment, concavity, casing, and coffer required a lost technology to make; and weak separately, and on stronger ground, as the claim that the monument is older than Dynasty 4. The concessions owed are real and are made in full. The base leveling and the cardinal alignment are precision achievements of a very high order, not overstated by their admirers on the point of accuracy, and they des…

ar.q: Is Pharaonic Egypt the heir of a now-buried "Green Sahara" civilization?
ar.c: On the reading pressed by Michael Button — fullest in "The Green Sahara Collapse: The Migration that Changed Humanity" (the Limitless podcast, November 2025), and touched on in his appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience #2368 and his own channel — the Sahara we know as the largest hot desert on Earth was, through the early and middle Holocene, a savanna of grassland, lakes, rivers, and megafauna. Across those millennia it filled with cattle-herding peoples who left rock art, cemeteries, and standing-stone monuments, accumulating generation on generation of social, ritual, and technical develop…
ar.a: Contested — as the claim that Pharaonic Egypt is the heir of a now-buried Green Sahara civilization. The thesis is strong by one discipline's lights and weak by another's, which is what makes it contested rather than weak or sound. By the lights of Holocene climate science and migration archaeology it is largely right : the Sahara was green and peopled, it held real monument-building cattle-cult societies, its desiccation drove a documented exodu…

ar.q: Is the Gulf of Khambhat sonar site a 9,500-year-old submerged city?
ar.c: In December 2000 oceanographers from India's National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT), running a routine marine-pollution survey in the Gulf of Khambhat — the older maps call it the Gulf of Cambay — some 20 km off the Gujarat coast, recorded side-scan sonar returns showing, under roughly 30–40 m of water, regularly spaced geometric shapes strung along two buried palaeo-channels. On the maximal reading these were the remains of a drowned city: press accounts described a settlement about five miles long and two miles wide, and the sonar features were read as dwellings on a grid, a "granary,…
ar.a: Weak — as the claim that the Gulf of Khambhat sonar site is a man-made city, and weak again, at the joint everything hangs on, as the claim that it is ~9,500 years old. The concessions are made in full: NIOT's dredges did recover a real assemblage from that seabed, some of it plausibly cultural; the wood really is old; and post-glacial sea-level rise genuinely drowned Holocene coastlines off Gujarat, so submerged early coastal occupation off Indi…

ar.q: Is Gunung Padang a 25,000-year-old buried pyramid?
ar.c: Gunung Padang is a terraced hilltop site above the village of Karyamukti in the Cianjur regency of West Java: five stepped terraces climbing a promontory, buttressed with dry-stone retaining walls, reached from the valley by a long stone stair, and paved and walled with thousands of prismatic stone columns. The conventional reading is that it is a punden berundak — an Indonesian stepped ancestral sanctuary — one of the largest of its kind, raised in the late prehistoric period. The argument here is far larger. A team led by the geologist Danny Hilman Natawidjaja surveyed the hill with ground-p…
ar.a: Weak — as the claim that Gunung Padang is a buried man-made pyramid, and weaker still, and on the ground the retraction names, as the claim that its construction reaches ~25,000 BP. The concessions are made in full, because a fair hearing requires them: the hill has real internal structure that the geophysics detected; the terrace columns were genuinely gathered and stacked by people; and a paper should not be retracted for reaching an unwelcome …

ar.q: Does Homo juluensis , the "large-head" hominin, attest the Nephilim?
ar.c: In December 2024 a new archaic human made the news under a name that translates as "large head people," and the identification followed within days: here at last is the material basis for the Nephilim of Genesis 6:4 and for the Anakim and Rephaim who descend from them — not a folk memory and not a hoaxed skeleton, but a distinct, unusually endowed human-like population known from excavated bone and published in a first-rank journal. The claim assessed here is that Homo juluensis supplies that basis.
ar.a: Weak — as an identification, on its best available case. The rating is not "unsupported," and the difference matters: unlike the giant-skeleton corpus, there is a real object here, measured and published, and the measurement is as impressive as advertised. But the inference from it fails at each joint independently. The type material contains no postcranial bone, so it makes no claim about height; the closest comparanda at 1800 ml stood about 165…

ar.q: Did Liangzhu's jades require technology beyond Neolithic capacity to make?
ar.c: Two things about Liangzhu jade are true and are the whole basis of the argument. The first is the material. Nephrite sits at about 6–6.5 on Mohs' scale and is exceptionally tough as well as hard; it does not flake like flint and it does not chisel. Nothing softer than quartz will mark it. The second is the work. From the Yangtze delta between about 3300 and 2300 BC come squared cong tubes with true bores, bi discs drilled perfectly round, and surfaces polished to a mirror — some nine-tenths of all surviving Neolithic cong and bi , produced by a culture with no metal. The showpiece is the objec…
ar.a: Weak — as the claim that Liangzhu jade required machine tooling or a technology beyond Neolithic capacity. The manufacturing process is understood in its main lines and is attested at every step by material that has been dug up: abrasion rather than carving, with loose sand harder than nephrite; string and blade sawing; tubular drilling from both faces; grinding and polishing with corundum and, on the finest surfaces, diamond; and hand incision w…

ar.q: Does the Jishi Gorge outburst flood (c. 1920 BC) supply the historical kernel of China's Great Flood?
ar.c: On 5 August 2016 Wu Qinglong and sixteen collaborators published in Science a paper whose title states the thesis: "Outburst flood at 1920 BCE supports historicity of China's Great Flood and the Xia dynasty." Sarah Allan, who answered it the following year, summarises the argument fairly and at first hand: A great lake was formed after an earthquake caused a landslide in the upper reaches of the Yellow River. The eventual breach of the barrier resulted in a flood originating at Jishi 積石 Gorge in present-day Qinghai Province, in about 1920 BCE. This flood breached the natural levees of the Yell…
ar.a: Weak — as the identification of the Jishi Gorge outburst flood with the flood of Yu. Two independent failures, either of which would be sufficient. The dating fails: independent radiocarbon and OSL work by several teams, before and after the 2016 paper, puts the Jishi Gorge dammed lakes in the eighth-to-sixth millennia BC and finds them already drained by about 5.60 ka BP, with the Lajia destruction a separate seismic-and-mudflow catastrophe some…

ar.q: Is the Kailasa temple at Ellora far older than its eighth-century date?
ar.c: Cave 16 at Ellora, in the Charanandri hills of Maharashtra, is not a building. It is a temple that was left behind when a hillside was taken away: three trenches were cut down into the basalt scarp to isolate a block, and the block was then worked from the summit downward into a two-storey Shiva temple with its shikhara , its Nandi pavilion, its gateway, its cloistered courtyard walls, its free-standing victory pillars and its life-size elephants — every one of those elements being rock that was never removed. The Archaeological Survey of India calls it "the largest single monolithic excavatio…
ar.a: Weak — as the claim that Kailasa is significantly older than its eighth-century date, and weak separately as the claim that its scale exceeds eighth-century capability. The concession comes first because it is genuine and because this page would be worthless without it. Of the monuments examined in this group, Kailasa has the softest anchor: no dedicatory inscription, an attribution resting on grants issued about forty years later and physically …

ar.q: Do the "lathe-turned" pillars of the medieval Deccan imply machining beyond their period?
ar.c: Three sets of objects are usually put together, and they do share a single visual signature: rotational symmetry in stone, on a scale and to a finish that looks industrial. The Hoysala temples of Karnataka — Chennakeshava at Belur, Hoysaleshwara at Halebidu, Keshava at Somanathapura — stand on porches of cylindrical, bell-bodied, deeply fluted pillars whose ring-grooves run true all the way round; the technique is so characteristic that the standard architectural literature simply calls them "lathe-turned," and one description of the construction has it that "lathe-turned cylindrical pillars a…
ar.a: Weak — as the claim that these works are significantly older than their dates and reflect a lost or pre-Flood technology; and weak separately as the claim that their manufacture exceeds the attested medieval toolkit. The deepest form of the claim — that the turning capacity was antediluvian know-how carried through the Flood, not a redated artifact — is coherent for so late a maker (the Deccan dynasties are post-Flood on every reckoning, heirs an…

ar.q: Does "mature creation" — a world made with the appearance of age — neutralize the material record's old dates?
ar.c: The classic statement is Philip Henry Gosse's Omphalos (1857), written to reconcile geology with a young Creation. Gosse's premise is that organic life is a closed circle — egg to animal to egg — with no natural starting point, so that creation can only be "a sudden sovereign act of power, an irruption into the circle." Wherever the "irruption" is placed, the created organism necessarily carries the implied marks of antecedents that never existed: Adam a navel, the first trees growth-rings, the starlight already in transit. Gosse coins a pair of terms for the two kinds of past a creature's bod…
ar.a: Weak as a defeater of the dating record — and, importantly, not false : it cannot be disproved, and that is exactly its defect. As metaphysics the restricted form is coherent and even unanswerable at the creation-instant; as a tool for relocating Göbekli Tepe or the Flood horizon it fails, because the disciplined version cannot reach a post-Creation record of events , and the version that can is unfalsifiable, dissolves the very reconstruction it…

ar.q: Is the Mesopotamian flood corpus independent corroboration of a historical Flood?
ar.c: The argument is one of the oldest and most widely repeated in popular apologetics: the Babylonians, who had no motive to confirm the Hebrew Scriptures, tell the same story. A flood sent by the gods; one warned man; a great vessel; his family and the animals aboard; a grounding on a mountain; birds sent out to test the waters; a sacrifice on landing. Two cultures with no interest in agreeing agree — therefore something happened. Stated as an evidential claim, it is that the Mesopotamian flood corpus ( the Sumerian flood story , Atra-ḫasīs , and Gilgamesh Tablet XI ) constitutes independent extr…
ar.a: Weak — as independent corroboration of a historical Flood. The three texts are not three witnesses. The flood episode of Gilgamesh was copied from Atra-ḫasīs with the seam still showing in the received line 49, and the Sumerian, Akkadian, and Hebrew versions share the plot in sequence — the mark of one tradition transmitted, not of several parties reporting one event. An argument from agreement needs the agreeing parties to be independent, and he…

ar.q: Do the Missoula / Channeled Scabland megafloods support flood geology and a global Genesis Flood?
ar.c: Uniformitarians were theoreticians who, because of stubborn adherence to dogma, thwarted the understanding of Washington's scabland. … We learn that catastrophist interpretations need to be brought back into geology so that we can understand correctly the formation of the Earth's landscape. — Steven A. Austin, "Washington Scablands and the Lake Missoula Flood" (Institute for Creation Research, 2005), link . Two moves are bundled and should be kept apart: that the Scabland saga shows an anti-catastrophist consensus can be wrong for decades (an epistemic point), and that the Missoula flood is a …
ar.a: Plausible — as the modest claim that catastrophic megafloods are real, geologically legible, and were wrongly dismissed by an anti-catastrophist consensus. Bretz's vindication is genuine, the scale of the Missoula floods is not in doubt, and the field's own leading authority concedes that ruling out catastrophe a priori "is contrary to the logic of science." Flood geology is entitled to that point, and it is the honest partial concession this str…

ar.q: Is Monte Sierpe (the "Band of Holes") a purpose-unknown feature of a lost antiquity?
ar.c: On a dry ridge in the Pisco Valley of southern Peru, near the village of Humay and some thirty kilometres inland from the coast, thousands of pits are dug into the hillside in a continuous band that climbs the slope for about a kilometre and a half. The site is called Monte Sierpe, "serpent mountain." The recent drone survey counts roughly 5,200 holes — older popular accounts run the figure as high as six or seven thousand — each on the order of one to two metres across and half a metre to a metre deep, many stone-lined, laid out in a strip averaging some nineteen metres wide and broken into a…
ar.a: Weak. The true kernel is conceded in full: Monte Sierpe is a real, large, deliberate, and genuinely singular earthwork whose function was uncertain for the better part of a century, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. But the argument the mystery is made to serve — that an unexplained purpose points past the Inca to a lost or pre-Inca antiquity — conflates two separate questions and fails on the one that matters. The band's date and cult…

ar.q: A real widespread Nephilim phenomenon predicts authenticated material remains — are there any?
ar.c: Grant the premise: the Nephilim were a real phenomenon, and — this is the model under test — a physical one, a population of people substantially larger than ordinary humans, present in the Levant across a datable historical period. Numbers 13 has them as tribes with names and towns; Deuteronomy 2 supplies two more with local names for each; Joshua 11 leaves a remnant in three named Philistine cities. This is not a single prodigy. It is peoples, in places, over centuries. Peoples in places over centuries die and are buried where they lived. The prediction is therefore osteological and specific…
ar.a: Unsupported — as a prediction of the widespread-physical-giants model. The prediction was the right one to make and was well posed: peoples living in named places over centuries leave burials, femora survive, and stature is straightforwardly recoverable from them. The search has been run at a scale the argument cannot dismiss — 6,098 measured prehistoric skeletons across the Near East and Europe from 10,000 to 1000 BC, modelled into stature surfa…

ar.q: Did Og survive the Flood by clinging to the ark?
ar.c: … except Og, king of Bashan, who sat down on a piece of wood under the gutter of the ark. He swore to Noah and to his sons that he would be their servant for ever. What did Noah do? He bored an aperture in the ark, and he put (through it) his food daily for him, and he also was left, as it is said, "For only Og, king of Bashan, remained of the remnant of the giants" (Deut. 3:11). — Pirqei de-Rabbi Eliezer 23, Sefaria . The interpretation assessed here is a survival mechanism for the post-Flood giants that runs outside the hull: Og, an antediluvian giant, rode out the deluge clinging to the ark…
ar.a: Weak — not unsupported. The legend is genuinely ancient, is advocated, and answers a real exegetical crux from the very verse that creates it; a reading with that pedigree is not nothing, and its non-global variant is a coherent (if separately contested) way to relieve the tension. But as an account of a giant surviving the Flood it does not hold on its best available case. Genesis 7:23 says Noah "only remained alive," which is exactly what a sur…

ar.q: Is Og's "iron bed" (Deuteronomy 3:11) evidence of a giant?
ar.c: Deuteronomy 3:11 records that Og of Bashan, "the last of the Rephaim," left an iron bedstead "nine cubits was the length thereof, and four cubits the breadth of it, after the cubit of a man," still on display "in Rabbath of the children of Ammon" when the notice was written. 1 The argument assessed here is the material one: that this is the giant tradition's hard datum — an object of stated dimensions, publicly exhibited, from which the stature of its owner can be read off. Nine cubits at the ordinary Hebrew cubit of about 45 cm is roughly 4.1 metres ; four cubits, about 1.8 m across.
ar.a: Weak — as material evidence of gigantism. The notice is genuine and concrete, and the tradition plainly does present Og as enormous; on the wiki's own reading the dimensions are a sound literary parallel to the cultic bed of Marduk. But four separate things stand between the verse and a giant's body. The object is reported, not recovered: no excavation, no collection, no measurement by anyone. It is furniture, and royal furniture is sized to rank…

ar.q: Do Ollantaytambo's monoliths require lost technology or a pre-Inca origin?
ar.c: Ollantaytambo, at the western end of the Sacred Valley some sixty kilometres from Cusco, is one of the great Inca sites and still a living town on the original grid. Rising above it is Temple Hill, and on its highest terrace stands the object the argument is about: the Wall of the Six Monoliths , six upright slabs of rose-coloured porphyry (a rhyolite), each on the order of fifty tons, set side by side and separated by thin, protruding stone ribs — a wall so finely finished that, as at every such site, a blade will not enter the vertical joints. It is the surviving fragment of an unfinished Te…
ar.a: Weak — as the claim that Ollantaytambo's monoliths, alcove marks, and stepped masonry required a lost technology to make; and weak separately, though given its fairest hearing, as the claim that the finest of it is pre-Inca work the Inca inherited. Its subtler form — that the fitting capacity , not the wall, was inherited from before the Flood — fares no better and in fact worse: the Andean stone tradition has no phase reaching even the long Sept…

ar.q: Do the Giza pyramids map Orion's Belt, and do they date to 10,500 BC?
ar.c: … the three pyramids were an unbelievably precise terrestrial map of the three stars of Orion's belt — the two larger pyramids, Khufu and Khafre, being in an almost perfect diagonal line, with the third and smaller pyramid, that of Menkaure, offset slightly to the east… exactly as the smallest of the three stars of Orion's belt, Mintaka, is offset to the east of the strong diagonal formed by the other two. — Robert Bauval's statement of the correlation. On the theory, Khufu (the Great Pyramid) maps Alnitak, Khafre maps Alnilam, and the smaller, offset Menkaure maps the fainter, offset Mintaka;…
ar.a: Weak — both sub-claims, and the separation is the finding. Take the correlation first. There is a real visual resemblance between the bent pyramid line with its small offset member and the bent Belt with its faint offset star, and there is a real Old-Kingdom cult of Osiris as the constellation Sah/Orion; together these make a loose intended Orion association at Giza genuinely plausible, and it would be overreach to rate that away. But the strong …

ar.q: Is the Osireion at Abydos far older than Seti I — a megalith he found and claimed?
ar.c: Behind the L-shaped limestone temple that Seti I raised at Abydos, and at a markedly lower level, stands a structure that does not look like anything else of the Nineteenth Dynasty. The Osireion is a subterranean hall built of colossal rough-faced monoliths — red granite and quartzite brought from Aswan, some blocks put at around a hundred tonnes — arranged as a rectangular "island" carrying two rows of five massive square pillars, ringed by a channel that fills with groundwater, so that the central platform sits in water. It lies roughly fifteen metres below the floor of the temple in front o…
ar.a: Weak — as the claim that the Osireion is significantly older than Seti I and was found and appropriated by him, and weak separately in its predynastic rainfall-erosion form. The concession is genuine and this page would be dishonest without it. The masonry contrast between the cyclopean granite of the Osireion and the decorated limestone of Seti's temple is not an illusion, and it was strong enough that Naville, a real Egyptologist who cleared th…

ar.q: Do elongated skulls attest a non-human / Nephilim morphology?
ar.c: The first and initial results of DNA testing of Elongated Human Skulls of Paracas Peru have finally come in, and suggest that these people, who died out 2000 years ago had genetic attributes, to some degree, not found in Homo Sapiens, Neanderthal, or Denisovans. — Brien Foerster, Hidden Inca Tours . The mortuary bundles of the Paracas culture of Peru's south coast (c. 800 BC – AD 100) preserve skulls whose braincases are dramatically elongated. The claim assessed here is that this elongation, together with a set of reported anatomical anomalies and an "unknown" mitochondrial signature, exceeds…
ar.a: Weak. The interpretation — that the Paracas skulls attest a non-human or Nephilim morphology — does not hold on its best available case. The elongation is artificial cranial deformation of a kind documented worldwide and, at Paracas specifically, in nearly the entire population of a culture whose deliberate cranial modification extended even to surgical trepanation. The anatomical anomalies are either known consequences of binding (the suture and…

ar.q: Do Puma Punku's andesite H-blocks require lost machining technology or a pre-Flood origin?
ar.c: On the high altiplano south of Lake Titicaca, at about 3,850 metres, sits Puma Punku (Pumapunku), a terraced platform mound at the edge of the Tiwanaku complex — and it is genuinely among the most startling stonework anywhere. Two things are on the ground. There are giant slabs of red sandstone: the largest is about 7.8 metres long, 5.2 wide and just over a metre thick, an estimated 131 tonnes, and a second runs near 85 tonnes, both part of the platform's stone floor. And there are the smaller pieces of grey andesite — the facing, the gateways, and above all the famous "H-blocks," so called fo…
ar.a: Weak — for both sub-claims. The manufacturing claim, that Puma Punku's andesite demanded a machine technology beyond a Bronze-Age Andean state, is refuted the way Sacsayhuamán's is: not by argument but by reproduction. Protzen and Nair made the H-block finish with stone tools, abrasion and sand; the unfinished blocks and hammerstones sit at the quarries; the one unusual feature, the poured cramps, is ordinary Andean metallurgy; and the most caref…

ar.q: A recent eight-person bottleneck predicts a detectable genetic signature — is it there?
ar.c: Genesis 7:13 names the passengers: Noah, his wife, his three sons, and their three wives — eight people, and the text is emphatic that they were all. Take that literally, and place it a few thousand years ago, and the genetic consequences are not vague. The three sons carry only their parents' alleles, so the founding pool is five genetically distinct individuals: Noah, his wife, and three daughters-in-law. That caps the whole species at ten alleles at any autosomal locus , four mitochondrial lineages (the four women), and one Y-chromosome lineage (Noah). Everything human beings now carry must…
ar.a: Weak — as a prediction of the young literal-eight model. The model's genetics are admirably precise and therefore genuinely testable: five distinct founders, ten alleles per autosomal locus, four maternal lineages, one paternal, a few thousand years ago. What the genome shows instead is coalescence depths two orders of magnitude older, mitochondrial and Y ancestries that are both far too old and not contemporaneous with each other, and no recent …

ar.q: Is the Richat Structure (Eye of the Sahara) the site of Plato's Atlantis?
ar.c: The Richat Structure — the "Eye of the Sahara" — is a set of concentric rings about 40 km across in the desert of west-central Mauritania, prominent enough to be a landmark for orbiting astronauts. On the identification pressed by Jimmy Corsetti of the YouTube channel "Bright Insight" (reviving a 2011 documentary, Visiting Atlantis ), it is the physical site of Plato's Atlantis. The mapping he presses is detailed: the Richat's alternating ridges are Plato's rings of land and water around the citadel (Corsetti reads "three rings of water, two rings of land," with an opening toward the sea to th…
ar.a: Weak — as the claim that the Richat Structure is the site of Plato's Atlantis. The concessions are made in full, and they are real: the concentric-ring resemblance is genuinely striking, the African siting is in the right direction "beyond the Pillars," and a green early-Holocene Sahara with elephants is no fantasy. That is enough to make the claim worth weighing — and it does not survive the weighing. The Richat is a Cretaceous igneous dome erod…

ar.q: Do Sacsayhuamán's polygonal walls require lost technology or a pre-Inca origin?
ar.c: The object is genuinely extraordinary, and the argument should be met at its strongest. Above Cusco run three terraced zigzag ramparts, up to about eighteen metres high and some five hundred and forty metres long, faced with irregular many-sided blocks fitted without mortar so closely that the standard trope — a knife blade, a sheet of paper, a credit card will not enter the joint — is, at the visible face, true. The largest blocks stand over four metres tall and are estimated at well over a hundred tons, with the most-cited figures running to roughly a hundred and twenty-five; and the stone i…
ar.a: Weak — as the claim that the polygonal masonry of Sacsayhuamán and Cusco required a lost technology to make; and weak separately, though given its fairest hearing, as the claim that the finest of it is pre-Inca work the Inca inherited. Its subtler form — that the fitting capacity , not the wall, was inherited from before the Flood — fares no better and in fact worse: the Andean stone tradition has no phase reaching even the long Septuagint horizo…

ar.q: Did a solar-plasma outburst — not a comet — end the Ice Age and destroy a lost civilization? Robert Schoch's Solar-Induced Dark Age
ar.c: Schoch's thesis, in his own site's framing, is that solar outbursts or coronal mass ejections sent “ plasma hitting the surface of Earth ” that “could heat and fuse rock, incinerate flammable materials, melt ice caps” and drive rapid climate warming, and that “electrical discharges hitting the surface of Earth may have been responsible for the vitrification … of ancient stone structures.” 1 The full argument runs: the Younger Dryas cold snap ended, on Greenland ice-core evidence, with extraordinary abruptness (“possibly within an incredible three years”); the trigger was not a comet but an “ag…
ar.a: Weak — the interpretation that a solar-plasma outburst ended the Ice Age, fused monuments, was recorded in petroglyphs, and destroyed an advanced civilization. Rated by its three layers: The narrow climatology (a solar event drove the terminal-Pleistocene transitions) is weak : the specific coronal-mass-ejection-as-terminator mechanism has essentially no peer-reviewed support, the abrupt warming it is invoked to explain is already accounted for b…

ar.q: Did a second angelic incursion after the Flood reseed the Nephilim?
ar.c: Genesis 6:4 reports that "There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that , when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them." 1 Numbers 13:33 then finds the sons of Anak "of the giants" in Canaan, generations after a Flood in which — on the text's own account — every human being outside the ark died. The interpretation assessed here takes the "and also after that" to reach past the Flood, and fills the gap with a repetition of the original transgression: divine beings came down a second time, took human wives a second time, and the resul…
ar.a: Plausible — and plausible is a real rating here, not a polite dismissal. The clause is genuinely there, the iterative force of yābōʾû is granted even by scholars arguing the other side, and the reading is the only one of the three that leaves both the Flood's totality and Numbers 13:33's pedigree standing as written. It is not weak, and it is not refuted by the bare fact that it requires supernatural agency. What keeps it short of probable is the…

ar.q: Do the Serapeum of Saqqara's granite boxes require lost machining technology or a pre-Flood origin?
ar.c: Under the desert north of the Step Pyramid at Saqqara runs a rock-cut gallery some three hundred and fifty metres long, its walls lined with alcoves, and in twenty-three of those alcoves — with one more stranded in the corridor — sits a colossal box. Each is a single block of hard stone, mostly the rose granite of Aswan quarried eight hundred kilometres to the south, a few of diorite or basalt; each has a separate flat lid; and each is large enough to walk into. A representative example runs about 3.8 metres long, 2.3 wide and 2.3 high, with a body of some thirty-eight tonnes and a lid of twen…
ar.a: Weak — for both sub-claims. The manufacturing claim, that the boxes required a machine technology beyond dynastic Egypt's, is built on un-instrumented spot-checks by a single advocate that no independent survey has ever confirmed; the finish is genuinely fine, but "fine, by hand, at the top of a long abrasive tradition" fits the evidence, and the rough exteriors, the attested sand-and-copper toolkit, and Egypt's documented granite-working and geo…

ar.q: Is the near-simultaneous rise of civilizations a signature of a single post-Flood dispersion?
ar.c: The advocacy case is put most crisply by young-earth writers (creation.com's "All at once"): Genesis has one post-Flood people, gathered at Babel, scattered "abroad upon the face of all the earth" in a short span. Many of the dispersing groups would have carried the accumulated know-how of a settled, building, organising society; wherever they landed, cities would therefore appear to spring up "suddenly," with no local evolutionary run-up — while groups that carried none of it "started again" at a primitive level for later researchers to fit into a gradualist scheme. On this reading the near-s…
ar.a: Weak — as a reading of the observed synchrony, though not unsupported, and with one honest fit inside it. The puzzle is genuine and mainstream concedes it; the urban-civilization cluster (c. 3000 BC outward) does fit the Septuagint post-Flood window, and that leg is conceded. But the interpretation as a whole does not beat parallel independent development on its best case. The end-of-Ice-Age climate stabilisation supplies a strong worldwide commo…

ar.q: A global Flood predicts single-point post-Flood faunal radiation — does biogeography show it?
ar.c: Genesis grounds the ark "upon the mountains of Ararat," and the animals go out of it. On the global-ark model that is a single release point for the entire terrestrial fauna of the earth, a few thousand years ago. The prediction follows directly and admits of no vagueness: the present distribution of land animals should be a radiation from one point in eastern Anatolia . Diversity should broadly decrease with distance and difficulty from that point; the animals of remote regions should be a subset of those nearer; and, because dispersal takes generations and generations leave dead animals, the…
ar.a: Weak — as a prediction of the global-ark model. The prediction was clean and checkable: one release point, therefore a radiation, therefore route fossils. Biogeography instead partitions the world into provinces whose boundaries follow ancient continental configurations — marsupials in Australasia and the Americas, lemurs in Madagascar, a total faunal change across twenty miles of deep water at the Wallace Line — and the intermediate fossils that…

ar.q: Does the Great Sphinx's weathering push it far older than dynastic Egypt?
ar.c: The most prominent weathering pattern seen on the body of the Sphinx and on the walls of the Sphinx enclosure is, in my opinion, primarily due to precipitation (rainfall) … Such weathering, I believe, takes thousands of years to develop, and its presence on the Great Sphinx indicates that the core body of this structure predates the time of Khafre. — Robert M. Schoch, "Redating the Great Sphinx of Giza" . The deep, undulating, vertical-fissured profile of the enclosure walls is read as rainfall erosion, which requires a much wetter climate than dynastic Egypt's — and therefore a date millennia…
ar.a: Contested — and the split is the finding. Rate the water-erosion redating as a geological question and it is genuinely open: Schoch's rainfall reading of the enclosure is a real, peer-reviewed observation, reached independently by Reader and Coxill, and answered not by consensus but by rival mechanisms (haloclasty, atmospheric-moisture salt weathering, differential erosion of soft and hard limestone beds) that are themselves not decisive. Strong …

ar.q: Do the Sumerian King List's antediluvian reigns preserve a memory of a pre-Flood age?
ar.c: The Sumerian King List does something no other cuneiform document does: it treats a deluge as the hinge of a chronology rather than as a story. Eight kings hold kingship in five cities before the flood, 241,200 years between them; "then the flood swept over"; then "the kingship had descended from heaven" a second time, at Kish, and the reigns begin their long slide toward humanly plausible lengths. 1 That is the architecture of Genesis 5–11 — long-lived antediluvians, a flood, a restart of the line — in an independent tradition. The argument assessed here presses the further step: that the ant…
ar.a: Weak — as evidence of a preserved memory of a pre-Flood age. Two facts carry the verdict. The antediluvian reign-figures are whole multiples of the sexagesimal šár and ner , with the total an exact 67 šár : they were produced inside a numbering system, which is why no conversion recovers a plausible original from them. And the oldest surviving recension of the list, copied under Shulgi in the Ur III period, begins at Kish with no flood and no ant…

ar.q: Does the Ta Prohm "stegosaurus" carving attest dinosaur–human coexistence?
ar.c: Ta Prohm — the Rajavihara, "monastery of the king" — is a Buddhist foundation of Jayavarman VII in the Angkor complex, dedicated in 1186 to the king's mother, whose likeness was carved in the guise of Prajnaparamita. Its stele is one of the great administrative documents of the Khmer empire: 12,640 people resident, 3,140 villages assigned to its upkeep, gold dishes and Chinese silk in its treasury. The temple is also covered in animals. On a doorway pilaster in Gopura III, east of the central sanctuary, runs a vertical strip of circular medallions, each holding a creature. 1 One of them is odd…
ar.a: Weak — as the claim that the Ta Prohm roundel depicts a stegosaur observed from life, and so attests dinosaur–human coexistence. The concessions are real and are the reason this is a page rather than a dismissal. The resemblance is genuine, and the first to say so in print were guidebook authors with no stake in the question, one of them a distinguished epigraphist of Angkor. The developed version of the argument is field research: Woetzel went t…

ar.q: Does the Taurid complex deliver a recurring impact cycle remembered in myth?
ar.c: Halloween, like death festivals worldwide in late October-early November, reflects the trauma inflicted by the Taurid Meteor stream. — George Howard, "Halloween & the Taurid Meteor Stream," summarizing Randall Carlson's thesis at The Cosmic Tusk (31 October 2019). Carlson develops it at length in his "Cosmic Lessons: The Day of the Dead" series, where the point of the calendar is that the November Taurid radiant lies almost on the Pleiades, so that the festivals of the dead mark the season Earth crosses the densest part of the stream. The astronomical foundation under the folklore is stated by…
ar.a: Contested — the astronomical core (the Taurid complex as a coherent, fragmenting stream with a resonant swarm of impactors). The stream and its Encke association are secure; the strong coherent-catastrophism form is a real but minority hypothesis now leaning against its advocates as the predicted large swarm fails to appear in successive searches, while its most testable claim — the 2032 and 2036 encounters — is still open. Contested is the hones…

ar.q: Is Woolley's Ur "flood deposit" the biblical Flood?
ar.c: In 1929, digging below the Royal Cemetery at Ur, Leonard Woolley's workmen cut through some three metres of clean, artefact-free water-laid silt at a depth of about twelve — and then struck occupation debris again beneath it. A sterile band that thick, sealed between two levels of human life, meant an inundation deep enough to end a world and long enough to resettle a river's whole load. Woolley said so, and the wires carried it around the planet as the discovery of Noah's Flood. 1 The claim assessed here is the one the public took away and that still circulates: the Ur silt is the physical si…
ar.a: Weak — but the reason is extent, not date. Woolley's Ur stratum cannot be the biblical Flood because Eridu, seven miles from Ur, was searched for the same deposit and has none: the Ur flood was not even regional, and a local inundation that spared the next tell cannot be the region- or world-covering deluge the claim needs. That defeater holds on every chronology, which is why it — and not the much-repeated "six centuries too early" — carries the…

ar.q: Do the Sanskrit epics' vimanas and divine weapons remember a lost pre-Flood technology?
ar.c: The Sanskrit epics are full of flight and full of fire. Ravana keeps a self-moving aerial palace, the Pushpaka, which Rama flies home in at the end of the Ramayana; the gods travel in cars that go where they will; and the great warriors of the Mahabharata discharge named weapons — the Brahmastra, the Brahmashira, the Narayanastra, the Agneya — which are invoked by formula and which consume armies, scorch the earth and cannot be recalled once loosed. Drona gives his son the Brahmashira with the instruction never to use it, least of all against men, because it is "capable of consuming the whole …
ar.a: Unsupported — as the claim that the vimanas and astras of the Sanskrit epics attest a real lost technology surviving from a pre-Flood world; and weak , separately, as the narrower claim that the epic tradition preserves memory reaching to an antediluvian horizon. The concessions are worth stating plainly, because they are the only reason this is a page rather than a footnote. The epics' oral prehistory really does run behind the text that fixes i…

ar.q: Do the Wadi al-Hitan desert whale fossils corroborate a global Flood?
ar.c: Wadi al-Hitan — the "Valley of the Whales" — lies in the Western Desert of Egypt, some 150 km south-west of Cairo, hyperarid and roadless, and it holds the richest concentration of fossil whales on the planet: hundreds of skeletons of the archaic archaeocetes Basilosaurus isis (up to some 18 m) and Dorudon atrox , together with sea cows, sharks, sawfish, turtles, crocodiles, bony fish, and the shells of a shallow-marine invertebrate fauna. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005 — Egypt's first natural listing — for preserving, better than anywhere on earth, the late-Eocene tr…
ar.a: Weak — as the claim that the Wadi al-Hitan whales are evidence a single global Flood put marine life in the desert. The observation is real and the wonder is earned, but the reading fails on the physical record. The beds preserve an in-place marine ecosystem — articulated skeletons, a whale with juvenile prey and fish in its gut, bite-marked calf skulls, a nursery age-structure, in-situ biogenic sediment structures, and an ordered succession thro…

ar.q: Is the Yonaguni Monument a man-made structure or a natural formation?
ar.c: The object is real and genuinely striking, and the argument should be met at its strongest. In 1986 Kihachiro Aratake, a local diving operator scouting for hammerhead sharks, found off the southern tip of Yonaguni — the westernmost inhabited island of Japan, some 100 km east of Taiwan — a great terraced mass of rock rising from about 25 metres of water to within a few metres of the surface, roughly 100 metres long and some 25 metres tall. Its most-photographed face is a stack of broad flat terraces and sheer walls meeting in clean right angles, so that the whole reads at a glance as a stepped …
ar.a: Weak — as the strong claim that the Yonaguni Monument is a deliberately quarried, human-built monument (a stepped pyramid with roads, temples and a stadium); plausible — as the modest claim that it is a natural formation ancient people used or lightly modified. The concessions are real and are made in full. The object is genuinely arresting — the terraces and right angles do read as architecture to the eye, and Kimura is a serious field geologist…

ar.q: Did a Younger Dryas cosmic impact (c. 12,900 BP) destroy a lost civilization and seed the world's flood myths?
ar.c: Around 12,800 years ago … a comet made a series of catastrophic impacts on the great ice cap that then covered North America. … The result was a global cataclysm of epic proportions in the aftermath of which the survivors of a lost civilization of prehistoric antiquity settled amongst the hunter-gatherer peoples of the earth, seeking to pass on to them the benefits of their knowledge. — Graham Hancock, Magicians of the Gods (2015), publisher's page . The scientific foundation Hancock builds on is stated in the paper that launched the debate: an object "several kilometers in diameter" struck or…
ar.a: Contested — the scientific impact hypothesis. This is a live, front-rank dispute that leans skeptical without being closed. On the proponents' side stand a real and independently replicated platinum anomaly, a real climate reversal and extinction pulse, and a serious "premature rejection" counter-narrative. Against them: the nanodiamond proxy is largely refuted as misidentified graphene, the microspherules replicate in some laboratories and not o…

ds.t: The Flood and the Nephilim: the evidence under competing scenarios
ds.q: The other Genesis 6–9 pages on this wiki either ask who believed what ( the sons of God and the Nephilim , the historicity of the Flood ) or weigh each artifact on its own merits with the premises held open ( the material record , the dating of the Flood ). This page does something different: it fixes a whole bundle of presuppositions — a "scenario" — and then reads the same body of evidence straight through under each, to see what that scenario gets for free, what it must pay for, and what it simply cannot explain. The three scenarios weighed here are all believing readings; the mainstream naturalistic reading is not a scored column but the neutral baseline the linked premises-open pages al…

xs.t: Each scenario is a spelled-out set of commitments with a bill — the specific results that must hold true for it, and what would break it — not a mood or a label. Three axes could in principle vary independently: the biblical chronology (how many years Genesis 5 and 11 put between Creation and the Flood), the Flood's extent (geographically global, anthropologically universal, or a local inundation that peoples elsewhere survived), and whether the antediluvian genealogy is read as a closed chain that fixes Creation a few thousand years before the Flood or an open one that leaves the pre-Flood age a long, floating interval. In practice three believing bundles are each genuinely advocated and ab…

Each row is one item of evidence, scored under every scenario into one of four buckets: ✓ fits (positively expected — a win) · ○ neutral (consistent but non-discriminating) · △ costs a date (fits only if a named dating result is wrong) · ✗ unexplained (a residue the scenario cannot absorb even granting its premises). Each row links the full argument page, which keeps its own neutral assessment; the cells report only how that evidence reads conditional on each bundle. Evidence A — LXX + inheritance B — young-earth C — open antediluvian age Göbekli Tepe (pre-pottery megaliths, c. 9600 BC radiocarbon) 7 △/✗ — predates even this scenario's Creation (c. 5500 BC); fits only if the Enclosure-D radi…

The honesty floor of a scenario ledger: for each bundle, what it still cannot explain (✗), and how many independent datings it must overturn (△) — and whether those failures share one mechanism (correlated) or are ad hoc. The tallies below are read from the worked rows above and grow as the ledger is extended; the friendly bundle is shown beside its bill, not apart from it. Scenario A Scenario A's ✗ residue : no authenticated Nephilim remains despite its own prediction; the continuous Egyptian and Mesopotamian sequences that run unbroken across its own c. 3300 BC Flood horizon with no bottleneck to eight; a deep-time monument (Göbekli Tepe) sitting before its Creation horizon; no positive ma…

What follows is a coherence-and-cost accounting , not a proof of any bundle. Reading the most evidence for free does not make a framework true, and carrying a large bill does not make one false — a scenario could in principle be correct and still owe more than the present record lets it pay, and the material shelf is only one axis of a question that also has textual, theological, and philosophical dimensions this page does not weigh. What the ledger can say honestly is which framework the material evidence sits easiest under, which leaves the largest unpaid residue, and whether each one's costs are a single correlated claim or a scatter of independent ones. Scenario B leaves the largest resi…

ds.t: The problem of evil (theodicy)
ds.q: It is the oldest objection to belief in God: if God is perfectly good and all-powerful , why is there evil? The pagan schools sharpened it into an inconsistent triad — God is good, God is omnipotent, evil exists — and pressed that no two of the three seem to leave room for the last. This page traces how the church answered across time, earliest witness first. The answers fall into a few enduring lines, and it helps to keep two distinctions in view throughout. The first is between moral evil (the wrong that wills do) and natural evil (the suffering that merely befalls — disease, disaster, death). The second is between a defense — showing only that the triad is not self-contradictory, that a g…

tl.t: Irenaeus gives the earliest sustained Christian answer, and it is a “soul-making” answer before the name. Against the Gnostics, who blamed a defective creator, he lodges moral evil in the free creature: God “made man a free [agent] from the beginning… to obey the behests of God voluntarily, and not by compulsion… for there is no coercion with God.” 1 And he answers the objection “why not make man unfallable?” developmentally: God “could have made man perfect from the first, but man could not receive this, being as yet an infant,” 2 and one cannot knowingly choose the good without knowing its contrary — experience yields “a surer and an undoubted comprehension” than mere opinion. 3 Evil is th…

Origen builds the first complete Christian theodicy, and every later Greek move is already in it. Moral evil lodges wholly in the free rational creature: to blame outward things is to say “we are like pieces of wood, or stones, which have no motion in themselves,” whereas reason assents or refuses, so the blame “wholly lies” on us. 4 His distinctive contribution is to answer the inequality objection — why are creatures so unequally placed, if one just God made them all? — as God's justice : the “diversity among rational creatures” derives “not from the will or judgment of the Creator, but from the freedom of the individual will,” the just wage of the creatures' own prior choices, so the Crea…

Lactantius, the “Christian Cicero,” preserves the sharpest ancient statement of the problem — the fourfold dilemma he ascribes to Epicurus: God “either wishes to take away evils, and is unable; or He is able, and is unwilling; or He is neither willing nor able, or He is both willing and able… from what source then are evils?” 7 He answers by breaking the last horn: God is able to remove evils but does not, “because He at the same time gives wisdom… unless we first know evil, we shall be unable to know good… no traces of virtue remain in man, the nature of which consists in enduring and overcoming the bitterness of evils.” 8 A painless world would be a virtueless one; the permission of evil i…

Basil the Great supplies the two moves that organize the classical answer. First, evil is no thing : “it is equally impious to say that evil has its origin from God… Evil is not a living animated essence; it is the condition of the soul opposed to virtue, developed… on account of their falling away from good.” 9 Second, moral evil is self-authored: “do not… imagine that there is an original nature of wickedness. Each of us… is the first author of his own vice… evil… has no other origin than our voluntary falls.” 10 With no evil substance to blame and a free will to bear it, God is in no sense evil's author — the Greek form of the privation-plus-freedom answer.

Basil's younger brother carries the same two moves and adds a third. Evil is no substance but a defect: “there is no evil other than wickedness… all wickedness has its form and character in the deprivation of the good; it exists not by itself… it is the non-existence of the good that is so denominated.” 11 It arises not in God but in the free creature: “No growth of evil had its beginning in the Divine will… it is not God Who is the author of the present evils, seeing that He has ordered your nature so as to be its own master and free.” 12 Gregory's own contribution answers the Manichee's harder question — why make man at all, foreseeing the fall? — from providence: God “knew what was going …

Between the Cappadocians and Augustine stands the greatest preacher of the age, whose answer is pastoral rather than metaphysical: he asks not what evil is but what it can do to a soul . In the homily That Demons Do Not Govern the World he insists that God's very chastisements are no argument against providence but its highest expression — “not only when he confers benefits but even when he chastises God is good and loving… his chastisements and his punishments are… the greatest form of his providence,” a physician's bitter medicine. 14 He resolves Amos 3:6 and Isaiah 45:7 by dividing evil in two: the “really evil” — sin, which God does not author — and what “is not evil, but is called so, f…

Augustine, a former Manichee who had once made evil a rival dark substance, gives the Latin West its enduring synthesis. Evil is no nature but the corruption of one: it is “nothing else than corruption, either of the measure, or the form, or the order, that belong to nature… when incorrupt it is good; but even when corrupt, so far as it is nature it is good.” 17 That answers what evil is; the why is providential greater good: God “judged it better to bring good out of evil, than not to permit any evil to exist.” 18 Moral evil itself he traces to the created will and nowhere higher: its cause is “not efficient, but deficient… the will itself is not an effecting of something, but a defect,” so…

The anonymous Christian Neoplatonist writing under the name of Paul's Athenian convert gives the privation answer its most rigorous ancient form. Evil is nothing positive: “The Evil is not from the Good, and if it is from the Good, it is not the Evil” — a cause makes only what is like itself, as fire cannot make cold, so there are not two warring first principles. 21 Evil “has not a subsistence, but a parasitical subsistence, coming into being for the sake of the Good, and not of itself”; it is “privation and failure, and want of strength… and being itself nothing in any manner of way whatever.” 22 And it never escapes providence, which “uses even evils which happen for the benefit… and prov…

Boethius, a Roman senator awaiting execution on a false charge, wrote the most-read theodicy of the Latin Middle Ages. Lady Philosophy answers the complaint that the wicked flourish along two joined lines. Metaphysically: because the omnipotent God can do no evil, “evil is nothing,” 24 and the wicked, forsaking the good that is the end of all things, forfeit real being — “that only is which maintains its place and keeps its nature” 25 — so their apparent triumph is in truth “the indubitable weakness of the bad.” 26 Providentially: what looks like the rule of chance is the unfolding in time (Fate) of one changeless divine reason (Providence), “seated in the Supreme Being, which disposes all t…

The last of the Greek fathers gathered the settled Eastern answer into a textbook. All three moves appear in crisp formulae. Evil is no substance but “absence of goodness, just as darkness also is absence of light”; 28 moral evil is self-authored — the devil, “made good by the Creator, became of his own free-will the inventor of evil”; 29 and providence governs all “partly according to good-will… and partly according to permission,” 30 so that God positively wills the good and merely permits the evil He bends to remedial ends. Death itself is no work of God but of the fall: “God did not create death… its origin is in Adam's transgression.” 31 His definitions became the fixed reference of Eas…

Aquinas locks the whole inherited answer into one system — the reference statement Leibniz and the moderns would argue with. Evil is no nature but a defect: “it must be that by the name of evil is signified the absence of good” — and, sharpening the fathers, not every absence but only the privation of a good due to a thing (blindness is evil in an animal, not a stone). 32 Because a privation is nothing positive, it has “no formal cause… neither… a final cause” and only an accidental agent-cause: good is the cause of evil merely by a defect, in the moral case a will that fails to hold to its rule. 33 So everything real in a sin traces to God, first cause of all being, but its defect does not:…

Calvin closes the long gap between the schoolmen and the moderns, and he does it by hardening the one seam the fathers had left soft — the line between what God wills and what He merely permits . His doctrine of universal providence denies that God ever idly allows: God “holds the helms and overrules all events,” so that “nothing happens but what he has knowingly and willingly decreed,” and “fortune and chance are heathen terms.” 36 To answer only that God permits evil is, he says, “the merest trifling” — yet God, employing even the deeds of the wicked and of Satan, “contracts no taint from their impurity,” because in one act done by many the reasons differ and the guilt lodges in the creatu…

Between the confessional age and the Enlightenment stands the skeptic who set the modern problem its terms. Bayle, a Huguenot refugee in Holland, argued in his Dictionnaire historique et critique (1697) — in the articles “Manichéens,” “Pauliciens,” and “Rorarius” — that the problem of evil simply defeats reason. Monotheism is the simpler and more elegant hypothesis a priori ; but faced with the world’s actual mixture of good and evil, “the manner in which evil was introduced under the empire of a sovereign being, infinitely good, infinitely holy, and infinitely powerful” is found “not only inexplicable, but even incomprehensible,” and every objection to God’s permitting it “is more agreeable…

Leibniz gives the constructive tradition its most confident modern form — and its name: his 1710 Essais de Théodicée coin the word “theodicy” (a “justification of God”) for the whole enterprise. 41 God, surveying every possible world His wisdom could conceive, freely actualized the best of all possible worlds : “if there were not the best ( optimum ) among all possible worlds, God would not have produced any,” and its evils are the unavoidable price of the greatest attainable good — “a lesser good is a kind of evil if it stands in the way of a greater good.” 42 He sorts evil into three kinds — metaphysical (the mere imperfection of any finite creature), physical (suffering), and moral (sin),…

The optimism drew its most famous assault not from a philosopher but from a satirist. Voltaire’s Candide, ou l’Optimisme (1759) follows the endlessly-battered Dr Pangloss — teacher of “metaphysico-theologico-cosmolo-nigology” — as he insists through plague, war, and earthquake that “there is no effect without a cause, and that, in this best of all possible worlds, the Baron’s castle was the most magnificent of castles”; the maimed Candide can only ask, “If this is the best of possible worlds, what then are the others?” 44 Behind the comedy lay a real argument, made already in the Poème sur le désastre de Lisbonne (1756) — subtitled An Inquiry into the Maxim, “Whatever Is, Is Right” — which V…

tl.w: The modern debate — Hume and the analytic reply (from 1779)
tl.t: After Leibniz the initiative passes to the critics. Hume’s Dialogues concerning Natural Religion (1779) revive the Epicurean trilemma in its sharpest modern form — “Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? then is he impotent… Is he both able and willing? whence then is evil?” — as the standing objection to natural religion. 46 In the twentieth century the debate splits. The logical problem (J. L. Mackie, 1955) charges that God and evil are outright contradictory; 47 Alvin Plantinga’s free-will defense (1974) — the modern, modal form of the fathers’ free-will answer — is widely held to have shown the triad at least consistent. 48 John Hick’s Irenaean soul-making theodicy (1966) revives I…

ar.q: Leibniz’s best of all possible worlds — is this the optimal world, and was God bound to create it?
ar.c: Leibniz’s 1710 Théodicée — the work that coined the word theodicy — presses the greater-good answer to its most confident possible form. God’s intellect contains infinitely many possible worlds , each complete down to the last detail; His goodness inclines Him to create, and His wisdom to create the best ; and since (Leibniz holds) there is a uniquely best among them, that is the one He made: Now this supreme wisdom, united to a goodness that is no less infinite, cannot but have chosen the best… if there were not the best ( optimum ) among all possible worlds, God would not have produced any. …
ar.a: Weak. Leibniz’s best-of-all-possible-worlds thesis does not hold on its best available case. Its keystone — that there is a uniquely best possible world — is unproven and most likely incoherent (for any world a better is conceivable, as for any number a greater), and it is denied by the tradition’s own foremost greater-good theologian, Aquinas , who holds God can always make a better world. The necessity it adds — that a perfect God is bound to a…

ar.q: The evidential problem of evil — does gratuitous suffering make God improbable?
ar.c: The evidential (or “inductive,” or “probabilistic”) problem of evil is a different argument from the logical one, and William Rowe is careful to separate them. He concedes the logical problem: “Some philosophers have contended that the existence of evil is logically inconsistent with the existence of the theistic God. No one, I think, has succeeded in establishing such an extravagant claim.” What remains is “the evidential form—as opposed to the logical form—of the problem of evil: the view that the variety and profusion of evil in our world, although perhaps not logically inconsistent with th…
ar.a: Contested. The evidential argument is the strongest and most durable form of the problem of evil, and it is honestly weighed as genuinely undecided rather than as either a proof or a failure. Its logic is valid, it sidesteps the free-will defense by asking about probability rather than possibility, and its data — the vast mass of apparently gratuitous suffering, the fawn among it — are real and not dissolved by any theodicy that locates the point…

ar.q: The greater-good theodicy (and the felix culpa ) — does God permit evil to draw a greater good?
ar.c: The greater-good theodicy is the most general constructive answer on the timeline, and the one the others defer to. It does not name a particular good (that is the work of the soul-making, free-will, and privation lines); it states the form the answer takes. God, being omnipotent and wholly good, would permit no evil at all — unless His power and goodness were such that from the evil He permits He can draw a good greater than the good a world without that evil would hold. The permission of evil is therefore not a failure of goodness but its instrument: evil is not merely outweighed (a greater …
ar.a: Plausible. The greater-good theodicy is the master principle the constructive tradition is built on, and as a framework — and in its defense form — it is close to secure: it is the correct logical shape of any theodicy, and its coherence is not in serious doubt, so a bare inconsistency charge cannot touch it. It has genuine content, not merely form: the felix culpa gives it a central Christian instance (the redemption as the good drawn from the F…

ar.q: Horrendous evils and the goodness of God — can only God defeat the worst evils?
ar.c: The analytic debate that Mackie began, Adams argued, had stayed too abstract — trading God against “evil” in general and passing over the concrete worst of it. She fixes attention instead on a distinguished class she names horrendous evils : evils the participation in (the doing or suffering of) which gives one reason prima facie to doubt whether one’s life could (given their inclusion in it) be a great good to one on the whole. — Marilyn McCord Adams, “Horrendous Evils and the Goodness of God”. 1 Her examples are the atrocities that seem to ruin a life from the inside — the torture of a child…
ar.a: Plausible. Rate the two halves apart, as Adams’s own influence divides them. The diagnostic — that horrendous evils cannot be defeated by the generic goods of the greater-good and soul-making theodicies, which are the wrong size for the job, and that any answer must be a good to the sufferer that defeats rather than merely balances the horror — is near- sound and is now common ground; it is the strongest single reason those theodicies are rated o…

ar.q: The logical problem of evil and the free-will defense — does it answer Mackie?
ar.c: The logical problem of evil , in J. L. Mackie’s 1955 statement, is not that evil makes God unlikely but that the theist’s own beliefs are logically inconsistent : “God is omnipotent; God is wholly good; and yet evil exists,” and “if any two of them were true the third would be false.” 1 The charge is the hardest possible one: not that the theist is probably wrong, but that no possible reason could reconcile an omnipotent, wholly good God with any evil at all, so belief is incoherent from the start. Alvin Plantinga’s free-will defense ( God, Freedom, and Evil , 1974) replies that the triad is c…
ar.a: Sound. As an answer to the logical problem of evil the free-will defense holds up, and by something close to consensus: it needs only the possibility that God could not actualize moral good without moral evil, that possibility suffices to defeat an inconsistency charge, and the very philosophers who pressed the charge — Mackie in 1982, Rowe in 1979 — conceded that it does. The compatibilist counter (God could make free creatures who always choose…

ar.q: Stump’s narrative (Thomistic) theodicy — is suffering the means to the sufferer’s own union with God?
ar.c: In Wandering in Darkness: Narrative and the Problem of Suffering (2010) Eleonore Stump reconstructs and defends the theodicy she finds in Thomas Aquinas. On the Thomistic value-theory she adopts, the best thing for any human person — her deepest flourishing and her heart’s truest desire — is union , a personal relationship of love, with God. But such union is impossible while a person’s will is internally divided against the good; the will must first be healed and integrated. Suffering, on this account, can be the means by which that healing happens — and God is justified in permitting it when…
ar.a: Contested. Stump’s narrative theodicy is the most fully developed contemporary answer to meet the person-centred demand that a justifying good be a good to the sufferer : God permits an adult’s suffering when it is the best available means to her own greatest good, union of love with God, either by averting the worst (self-willed separation from God) or leading to the best. It is grounded in a real Thomistic value-theory and defended with unusual…

ar.q: Natural evil and the fallen-powers (cosmic-fall) reading — is nature’s disorder the work of rebel spirits?
ar.c: Every theodicy of the will — the free-will defense, the fathers’ self-authored evil, the soul-making answer — is aimed first at moral evil, the wrong that wills do. Natural evil is the harder case: the fawn burned in a forest fire, the parasite that blinds, the earthquake, and above all the whole predatory order — a creation “red in tooth and claw” for hundreds of millions of years before any human will existed to be blamed. The retrospective move that pins this on the human fall (no death before Adam) founders on that antiquity. The fallen-powers reading makes a different move: it extends the…
ar.a: Contested. Keep the two questions apart. As a possibility deployed by a defense , the fallen-powers reading is sound and is rated so on the free-will defense page: it need only be possible, it is, and this wiki does not dismiss it for being supernatural. As a positive theodicy of natural evil — the claim adjudicated here — it is genuinely disputed. It is unrivalled at giving natural evil a responsible author other than God and coheres tightly wit…

ar.q: Natural evil as the penalty of the human Fall — did death and predation enter through Adam’s sin?
ar.c: The evolutionary theodicy takes the predatory order as intrinsic to creation; the fallen-powers reading blames rebel spirits.
