ar.a: Contested. That early rabbinic Judaism suppressed a divine-Messiah, "two powers in heaven" reading of Daniel 7 is a serious, well-sourced thesis with named proponents on both sides and no clear winner — the wiki's standard for contested . Trust the bedrock: two-powers was a real rabbinic heresy-category (Segal), Daniel 7's plural thrones were one of its battlegrounds, and Akiba's second-throne reading was publicly rebuked and re-glossed — a genui…

ds.t: Who Was Rahab of Jericho?
ds.q: Rahab is the Canaanite harlot of Jericho who saved the two Israelite spies — and, on the strength of one confession, was saved herself when her city fell. Scripture introduces her without apology: Joshua’s men “came into an harlot’s house, named Rahab, and lodged there” ( Joshua 2:1 ). When the king’s search closes in she hides them under the flax on her roof, sends the pursuers off on a false trail, and then makes the confession the whole later tradition turns on: “I know that the LORD hath given you the land… for the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath” ( Joshua 2:9–11 ). She strikes a bargain for her family, lets the spies down by a cord through her window, and …

tl.t: Everything the later tradition made of Rahab grows from two chapters of Joshua. She is named at once for what she is — the spies “came into an harlot’s house, named Rahab” — and the narrative neither excuses the trade nor lets it define her. When Jericho’s king sends to seize the men, Rahab hides them under the flax drying on her roof and turns the search aside with a lie (“there came men unto me, but I wist not whence they were… whither the men went, I wot not”). Then, alone among her people, she reads the war rightly: “I know that the LORD hath given you the land… for the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath.” She has heard how the LORD dried up the Red Sea and de…

tl.w: The New Testament: faith, works, and the genealogy of Christ (c. AD 60–90)
tl.t: The New Testament takes up Rahab three times, and each writer puts her to a different use. Matthew sets her in the genealogy of the Messiah — “Salmon begat Booz of Rachab” — one of the four women (with Tamar, Ruth, and “her that had been the wife of Urias”) whose irregular or Gentile stories the evangelist chose to name in the royal line, so that the harlot of Jericho stands four generations above David and, through him, in the ancestry of Christ. Hebrews ranks her among the heroes of faith, immediately after the fall of the walls: “By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace.” And James, pressing the opposite edge of the sam…

tl.w: Josephus ( Antiquities of the Jews 5.1.2, c. AD 93) — the harlot recast as an innkeeper
tl.t: The earliest datable treatment of Rahab after the Bible already begins to rehabilitate her. Retelling the Jericho episode for a Greco-Roman readership, Josephus silently drops the harlotry: the spies lodge not in a brothel but in “a certain inn,” and Rahab is its keeper — “they were in the inn kept by Rahab.” She hides the men, is spared with her family “who had fled to her inn,” and Joshua “gave her certain lands immediately, and had her in great esteem ever afterwards.” The Greek word is katagōgion , a lodging; the word for harlot never appears. This is the fountainhead of the “innkeeper, not harlot” reading that the Targum and Rashi would fix in Jewish tradition — and the exact opposite o…

tl.w: Clement of Rome ( First Epistle to the Corinthians 12, c. AD 96) — the fountainhead: the scarlet thread a prophecy of the blood of the Lord
tl.t: The Christian reading begins with the earliest surviving Christian writing outside the New Testament, and it begins already at full stretch. Clement praises Rahab twice over — “on account of her faith and hospitality, Rahab the harlot was saved” — and then reads the scarlet thread itself as a prophecy: the spies gave her the sign of a scarlet thread, “and thus they made it manifest that redemption should flow through the blood of the Lord to all them that believe and hope in God.” His conclusion sets the pattern for four centuries: “You see, beloved, that there was not only faith, but prophecy, in this woman.” The scarlet cord is no mere rescue-token but a deliberate foreshadowing of the blo…

tl.w: Justin Martyr ( Dialogue with Trypho 111, c. AD 160) — the blood of Christ that saves the harlots of all nations
tl.t: Arguing the Scriptures with the Jew Trypho, Justin makes the same figure sharper and wider. The scarlet thread the spies gave Rahab “manifested the symbol of the blood of Christ, by which those who were at one time harlots and unrighteous persons out of all nations are saved, receiving remission of sins, and continuing no longer in sin.” Independent of Clement, Justin adds the note that would dominate the tradition: “out of all nations” makes Rahab the type not merely of a saved sinner but of the saved Gentile — and he presses the reading as a proof drawn from the Hebrew Scriptures themselves. 6 Full detail »

tl.w: Irenaeus of Lyons ( Against Heresies IV.20.12, c. AD 180) — the three spies and the scarlet sign
tl.t: Irenaeus folds Rahab into his great argument that one God speaks across both Testaments. Rahab the harlot, “a Gentile, guilty of all sins,” received the three spies — “doubtless [a type of] the Father and the Son, together with the Holy Spirit” — and when the city fell at the seven trumpets she “was preserved… together with all her house, through faith of the scarlet sign.” He ties the thread to the Passover and the exodus, and seals it with the Lord’s own word to the unbelieving: “The publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of heaven before you.” The trinitarian reading of the spies is his own flourish, one later Fathers would vary (Jerome makes the spies the mission to Jew and Gentil…

tl.w: Origen of Alexandria ( Homilies on Joshua 3, 6, 7, c. AD 240) — Rahab the Gentile church, outside whose house none is saved
tl.t: Origen draws the figure out to its fullest early form. The scarlet sign is the blood of Christ and nothing else — “no other sign would have been accepted, except the scarlet-colored one that carried the sign of blood… there was no salvation for anyone except in the blood of Christ.” Rahab’s house is the church: “if anyone wants to be saved, let him come into the house of this one who was once a prostitute… Outside this house, that is, outside the church, no one is saved.” And the harlot herself becomes the redeemed bride — “once she was a prostitute, but now ‘a pure virgin, to one man’ she has been united, ‘to Christ.’” Origen’s reading of the house as the one ark of salvation would shape Cy…

tl.w: Cyprian of Carthage ( Epistle 75, c. AD 255) — Rahab’s house is the one Church
tl.t: Cyprian turns the figure to his own fight over the unity of the Church. Rahab “bore a type of the Church”: she was told to gather her father, mother, and kindred into her house, “and whosoever shall go out of the doors of thine house into the street, his blood shall be upon him” — so “they who will live, and escape from the destruction of the world, must be gathered together into one house alone, that is, into the Church.” What Origen read spiritually, Cyprian makes an ecclesiological rule: there is no salvation outside the one house, the one Church. 9 Full detail »

tl.w: Cyril of Jerusalem ( Catechetical Lectures 2.9, c. AD 350) — the pattern of salvation by repentance
tl.t: To Cyril, instructing catechumens, Rahab is less a figure than an example — the proof that no sinner is beyond repentance. “Fix your eyes, woman, upon Rahab, and look for salvation for yourself too. For if she who openly and publicly practiced fornication was saved through repentance…” And Cyril catches a fine point in her confession: she said only “the Lord, your God, is God in heaven above and on earth below” — “your God,” not daring to call him “her God, because of her wantonness.” The reading is penitential where the Alexandrians’ is typological, and it would feed the church’s long use of Rahab as the sinner’s hope. 10 Full detail »

tl.w: John Chrysostom (homilies on Repentance, Matthew, and Hebrews, c. AD 390–407) — the pearl in the mire
tl.t: Chrysostom returns to Rahab again and again, and fuses every strand. She is “a pearl mixed up in mire, like gold thrown in mud, the rose of piety hidden in thorns”; her confession is faith taken “on her lips”; and she “is a prefigurement of the church, which was at one time mixed up in the prostitution of the demons and which now accepts the spies of Christ.” On her place in the genealogy he draws the great conclusion: Matthew named “Ruth also and Rahab, the one an alien, the other an harlot,” so that “thou mayest learn that He came to do away with all our ills. For He hath come as a Physician, not as a Judge.” And to slack Christians he holds her up as a rebuke: it would be “disgraceful, if…

tl.w: Jerome ( Letter 52 and the Homilies on the Psalms , c. AD 400) — the scarlet cord handed to the Latin West
tl.t: Jerome carries the whole figure into Latin. The scarlet cord is “a mystic reference to the shedding of blood” which “the harlot Rahab (a type of the church) hung in her window that she might be saved.” The two spies are the mission to Jew and Gentile — “one to the circumcised; the other to the Gentiles, Peter and Paul” — so the harlot who takes them in is “the church gathered together from the Gentiles.” Even her name preaches: it means “a broad space” or “pride,” and she who “walked the broad, spacious road to death… was later converted unto humility.” This is the reading the medieval West would inherit. 12 Full detail »

tl.w: Theodoret of Cyrus ( On Divine Providence and the Interpretation of Hebrews , c. AD 450) — faith over lineage
tl.t: Theodoret makes Rahab the standing rebuke to confidence in descent. A foreigner and a prostitute, she “relied solely on their reputation, accepted their religion, abandoned her own beliefs”; her “lawlessness of life did not prevent salvation; faith covered the wounds of sin.” He marvels that the Spirit set “a foreign woman and prostitute” beside “Moses, Abraham, Noah, Enoch, and the other saints… to establish the power of faith and repress the Jews’ conceit” — and he keeps the old figure alongside the new: “as she was given the scarlet cord as a sign of salvation, so the church through the Lord’s blood enjoyed the eternal goods.” 13 Full detail »

tl.w: The rabbinic tradition (Targum Jonathan and the Babylonian Talmud; traditions from c. AD 200, redacted by c. 500) — the proselyte who married Joshua
tl.t: Jewish tradition ran the opposite way from the Christian, and further. Where the Fathers kept “harlot” to magnify grace, the Targum of the Prophets rendered the Hebrew zonah as pundeqita , an “innkeeper,” and Rashi followed it (“a lady innkeeper… who sold various kinds of foodstuff”) — the reading Josephus had already assumed. And where Scripture leaves her simply “dwelling in Israel,” the Talmud drew her all the way in: Rahab “converted and married Joshua,” and from her descended “eight prophets who were also priests… Neriah, Baruch, Seraiah… Jeremiah… Hilkiah,” and “Huldah the prophetess” besides. She is numbered among the four women of surpassing beauty in the world (Sarah, Abigail, Rahab…

tl.w: The Venerable Bede ( Commentary on the Catholic Epistles , on James 2:25, c. AD 710) — justified by works, written into the genealogy
tl.t: Bede gathers the two New Testament strands — the faith of Hebrews and the works of James — and hands them to the Latin Middle Ages. Reading James, he asks “was not Rahab the harlot also justified by works when she received the messengers?” and answers with her whole reward: “a sinful woman, a foreign woman, who nevertheless by acts of mercy, by the duty of hospitality, even at the risk of her life, received the servants of God… was deemed worthy to be justified from sins, to be numbered among the citizens of the people of Israel… to be inserted in the genealogies of our Lord and Saviour.” The harlot’s faith, her works, and her place in Christ’s line are made one. 15 Full detail »

ar.q: Was Rahab a harlot, or an innkeeper?
ar.c: A lady innkeeper. According to Targum Yonasson, an innkeeper who sold various kinds of foodstuff. — Rashi on Joshua 2:1 , Sefaria . The claim is that the Hebrew word describing Rahab ( zonah ) means, or should be read as, “innkeeper” rather than “prostitute” — that the tradition of Rahab the harlot rests on a mistranslation or a slander, and she was in fact simply the keeper of a lodging.
ar.a: Weak , as a replacement for “harlot.” The Hebrew zonah , the Septuagint’s pornē , and the New Testament’s twice-repeated “the harlot” settle the plain sense, and the “innkeeper” reading is a demonstrable later softening by sources with a motive to soften. What survives is only the modest, plausible residue that she may also have kept a lodging — the two roles are not exclusive — which takes nothing from the word Scripture chose and the whole trad…

ar.q: Did Rahab marry Joshua and become the ancestress of priests and prophets?
ar.c: Eight prophets, who were also priests, descended from Rahab the prostitute… Rabbi Yehuda said: So too, Huldah the prophetess was a descendant of Rahab the prostitute… For Rahab converted and married Joshua. — Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 14b , Sefaria . The claim is that Rahab became a proselyte, married Joshua son of Nun, and through that marriage became the ancestress of a line of men who were both priests and prophets — Jeremiah, Hilkiah, Baruch, and the rest — and of Huldah the prophetess.
ar.a: Weak , as history. The married-to-Joshua tradition has no scriptural warrant, is contradicted by the one canonical record of Rahab’s marriage (to Salmon of Judah), and rests on a genealogy built backward from later priest-prophets. It is a revealing and honourable piece of Jewish reception — the measure of how fully the tradition adopted the Canaanite convert — but a theological honour, not a fact about Rahab.

ar.q: Is the Rahab of Matthew 1:5 the same Rahab of Jericho?
ar.c: And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth; and Obed begat Jesse. — Matthew 1:5 (KJV), Matthew 1:5 . The claim is that the “Rachab” whom Matthew names as the wife of Salmon and mother of Boaz — and so an ancestress of David and of Christ — is the harlot Rahab of Jericho.
ar.a: Plausible, and probably right. That Matthew’s “Rachab” is the harlot of Jericho is almost certainly the evangelist’s intent — the four-women pattern, the lack of any rival Rahab, and the trivial spelling variant settle it. The genuine chronological gap does not defeat the identification; it shows only that the genealogy telescopes generations, as ancient genealogies do. The identity holds; the generation-count is selective.

ar.q: Is the scarlet cord a type of the blood of Christ?
ar.c: Moreover, they gave her a sign to this effect, that she should hang forth from her house a scarlet thread. And thus they made it manifest that redemption should flow through the blood of the Lord to all them that believe and hope in God. — Clement of Rome, First Epistle to the Corinthians 12 , newadvent.org . The claim is that the “line of scarlet thread” Rahab bound in her window ( Joshua 2:18–21 ), the sign that spared her house when Jericho fell, was a divinely-intended type of the blood of Christ by which the church is redeemed.
ar.a: Sound as a typological figure; overstated in its maximal form. The scarlet-cord = blood-of-Christ reading is one of the best-pedigreed types in the patristic corpus, dense in its Passover parallel and unbroken from Clement of Rome onward, and it deserves the church’s confidence as a figure. What it cannot claim is that Scripture itself institutes or foretells it: the reading is apostolic-era inference, not apostolic citation, and its baroque elab…

ds.t: The Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist
ds.q: When the Church gathers to "break bread," what is received? Real Presence is the belief that, in the Eucharist, the consecrated bread and wine are — not merely symbolize — the body and blood of Christ, so that the communicant truly partakes of the Lord himself. The conviction is among the oldest in Christian worship and, for most of the Church's history, went without serious challenge; the disputes that fill this page are mostly about how Christ is present, and only in the last five centuries about whether the presence is real at all.

tl.t: Writing on his way to martyrdom, Ignatius is the earliest witness after the apostles. He marks out the Docetists precisely by their refusal of the Eucharist: they "abstain from the Eucharist and from prayer, because they confess not the Eucharist to be the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins, and which the Father, of His goodness, raised up again" ( Smyrnaeans 7). 4 Longing for martyrdom, he writes that he desires "the bread of God, the heavenly bread, the bread of life, which is the flesh of Jesus Christ … and … the drink of God, namely His blood" ( Romans 7). 5 And he calls the one bread the Church breaks together "the medicine of immortality, and the antidote wh…

Defending Christian worship to the emperor, Justin gives the earliest surviving explicit statement that the consecrated elements are not ordinary food. Of the food "called among us the Eucharist" he writes that "not as common bread and common drink do we receive these; but in like manner as Jesus Christ our Saviour, having been made flesh by the Word of God, had both flesh and blood for our salvation, so likewise… the food which is blessed by the prayer of His word… is the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh" ( First Apology 66). 7 The Incarnation is his warrant: as the Word truly took flesh, the food consecrated by his word truly is that flesh and blood. In the Dialogue with Tr…

Against the Gnostics, who scorned the flesh, Irenaeus makes the Eucharist an argument for the goodness and resurrection of the body — and in doing so becomes the first father to be explicit about a change in the elements. The bread "which is produced from the earth, when it receives the invocation of God, is no longer common bread, but the Eucharist, consisting of two realities, earthly and heavenly; so also our bodies, when they receive the Eucharist, are no longer corruptible, having the hope of the resurrection" ( Against Heresies IV.18.5). 9 When "the mingled cup and the manufactured bread receives the Word of God," he writes, "the Eucharist of the blood and the body of Christ is made," …

In The Instructor ( Paedagogus ), Clement treats the eucharistic cup as efficacious, not merely commemorative. "The blood of the Lord is twofold," he writes, "and to drink the blood of Jesus, is to become partaker of the Lord's immortality." 11 The mingled cup of water and the Word "is called Eucharist, renowned and glorious grace; and they who by faith partake of it are sanctified both in body and soul." 12 Clement writes as an allegorist — wine, water, blood, and Word are layered symbols for him — yet the efficacy he ascribes to the Eucharist (immortality, and the sanctification of the whole person, body as well as soul) is realist in force.

In North Africa, Tertullian witnesses to the church's handling of the consecrated elements. Listing the settled customs that rest on tradition rather than explicit Scripture — the baptismal renunciations, offerings for the dead, the sign of the cross — he records that the faithful receive the Eucharist "from the hand of none but the presidents" and "feel pained should any wine or bread, even though our own, be cast upon the ground" ( De Corona 3). The grief at a fallen fragment is reverence owed not to ordinary food but to a holy thing — the practical corollary of a real presence, and the earliest witness here to how the elements were treated as Christ's body. 13

Answering the pagan Celsus — who urged thank-offerings to the demons set over the things of this world — Origen sets against it the Christian's thanksgiving to the Creator: "we also eat the bread presented to us; and this bread becomes by prayer a sacred body, which sanctifies those who sincerely partake of it" ( Against Celsus VIII.33). 14 Origen is the boldest allegorist of the early fathers and elsewhere spiritualizes the eating of Christ's flesh; yet here the bread becomes — and becomes it by prayer , a consecratory act — "a sacred body" that sanctifies the worthy communicant: efficacy, not bare remembrance.

The first Latin witness here, Cyprian argues the church's realism from a disciplinary quarrel: writing against the "Aquarians," who used water alone in the cup, he insists the mingled cup is the blood of Christ. Because "that was wine which He called His blood," it follows that "the blood of Christ is not offered if there be no wine in the cup, nor the Lord's sacrifice celebrated with a legitimate consecration unless our oblation and sacrifice respond to His passion" ( Epistle 62.9). 15 The Eucharist is for him a true sacrifice — "the Lord's passion is the sacrifice which we offer" — which the ordained priest re-presents: he "offers a true and full sacrifice… when he proceeds to offer it acc…

Explaining the sacraments to the newly baptized, Cyril gives the patristic realism its first sustained catechetical form. In the lecture On the Body and Blood of Christ he tells them to "consider… the Bread and the Wine not as bare elements, for they are, according to the Lord's declaration, the Body and Blood of Christ… Judge not the matter from the taste, but from faith be fully assured" ( Mystagogic 4.6). 17 Walking them through the liturgy, he locates the change at the invocation of the Spirit over the gifts, "that He may make the Bread the Body of Christ, and the Wine the Blood of Christ; for whatsoever the Holy Ghost has touched, is surely sanctified and changed" ( Mystagogic 5.7) — an…

In The Great Catechism Gregory gives the Greek fathers' strongest change-of-substance statement. The Body Christ took was maintained by bread and yet "transmuted to the dignity of Godhead" by the indwelling Word; "rightly, then, do we believe that now also the bread which is consecrated by the Word of God is changed into the Body of God the Word" — and changed "at once… by means of the Word," not by being eaten (ch. 37). 19 He coins a verb for it — God "transelements" ( metastoicheiōsis ) "the natural quality of these visible things to that immortal thing" — the sharpest patristic term for a re-constitution of what the elements are, which later Western writers read as anticipating transubsta…

In his mystagogical sermons Ambrose gives the Latin West its sharpest early statement of a conversion of the elements: "this is not what nature made, but what the blessing consecrated… because by blessing nature itself is changed" ( On the Mysteries 9.50). 20 He fixes the moment and cause of the change on the words of institution: "Before the blessing of the heavenly words another nature is spoken of, after the consecration the Body is signified… Before it is consecrated, it is bread; but when the words of Christ have been spoken, it becomes the body of Christ" ( On the Mysteries 9.54; On the Sacraments 4). 21 It is the seed of the medieval Western account of consecration that Trent would de…

The Antiochene preacher Chrysostom reaches for the most concrete language of any of these witnesses. Standing the reader before the altar in his Treatise on the Priesthood , he marvels that "He who sitteth on high with the Father is at that hour held in the hands of all, and gives Himself to those who are willing to embrace and grasp Him" (3.4). 22 Preaching on Paul's "communion of the blood," he identifies the contents of the cup with the blood of the cross — "this which is in the cup is that which flowed from His side" — and asks, "what is the bread? The Body of Christ" ( Homilies on First Corinthians 24). 23 His realism is homiletic, in the service of awe and of worthy reception, but it i…

No father is claimed so evenly by both sides of the later dispute. To the newly baptized Augustine says plainly that "the bread is the body of Christ, the cup is the blood of Christ," bidding them "be what you see, and receive what you are" ( Sermon 272); and expounding "fall down before His footstool" he draws the sharpest realist corollary before the medievals — the flesh given to eat is the very flesh born of Mary, so that "no one eateth that flesh, unless he hath first worshipped … we sin in not worshipping" ( Expositions on the Psalms 98.9). 24 Yet the same Augustine makes John 6's "eat my flesh" his textbook example of a figure — a command that, taken literally, "seems to enjoin a crim…

Against a sect who held that the consecrated Eucharist lost its power if kept and consumed on a later day, Cyril insists the presence does not lapse with time: "Christ is not altered, nor is his holy body changed, but the power of the consecration and his life-giving grace is perpetual in it" ( Letter to Calosyrius ). It is the realism of Irenaeus carried to its next question — not only that the bread becomes the body, but that it remains so when the assembly disperses — the premise of eucharistic reservation. 26

Writing the great summa of Greek theology, John gives the Eastern tradition its most emphatic pre-medieval statement of the Real Presence — and fills the long gap in the surviving Western record between Cyril of Alexandria and the Carolingians. In the chapter "Concerning the holy and immaculate Mysteries" he teaches that "the bread itself and the wine are changed into God's body and blood," "supernaturally changed by the invocation and presence of the Holy Spirit" — the Eastern epiclesis emphasis of Cyril of Jerusalem carried forward. He denies outright that they are "merely figures of the body and blood of Christ (God forbid!) … for the Lord has said, 'This is My body,' not, this is a figur…

After a long silence in the surviving Latin record — the Greek East meanwhile teaching the realism John of Damascus had just gathered up — the Carolingian West produced the first full-length Latin treatise on the Eucharist, and with it the sharpest pre-scholastic statement of the Real Presence. The abbot of Corbie, Paschasius , presses the realist tradition to a strict identity: what is received on the altar is "the true body of Christ, which was crucified and buried," made present by the priest's consecration "with the word of Christ through the Spirit" ( De Corpore et Sanguine Domini , c. 831). The eucharistic flesh, he teaches, is the very flesh born of the Virgin — the Incarnation the pa…

At the same abbey and the same king's request, Ratramnus answered his confrere with the great medieval counter-witness. The elements are Christ's body and blood in figura , "in a figure" — the sacrament of the body, distinguished from the historical body born of Mary — received spiritually by faith; and yet they are "not mere empty figures, or naked signs." His "figure" is the Augustinian sign that truly bears its reality, not a bare token; his treatise — revived in the eleventh century and later prized by the Reformers — is the standing alternative to Paschasius 's identity-realism. That two monks of one house could disagree so sharply shows the ninth-century West had no settled scholastic …

Master of the school of Tours, Berengar revived Ratramnus's line and denied a material change: after the consecration the bread and wine remain, and are the "sign" or "sacrament" of Christ's body — "the reality of the sign" received by faith, not the flesh physically present on the altar. Condemned at a string of synods, he was forced in 1059 to swear an oath that the faithful "crush" Christ's body "with their teeth" — a formula so grossly physical that later theology quietly retired it — and in 1079 a milder one introducing "substantial conversion." The reaction to his denial produced the very language that would harden into the defined dogma. 30

The council convoked by Innocent III gave the verb its first dogmatic, conciliar use. Its opening confession of faith professes that Christ's body and blood are "truly contained in the sacrament of the altar under the forms of bread and wine, the bread being changed ( transsubstantiatio ) by divine power into the body, and the wine into the blood" — and, in the same sentence, reserves the confecting to "the priest who has been duly ordained." It is the point at which the medieval West made the word official, a century before Trent , binding the Real Presence and the ministerial priesthood in a single dogmatic clause. 31

Aquinas supplies the account of how that Lateran IV had named but left unexplained. In the Summa Theologiae (III, q. 75) he holds that the substance of the bread and wine does not remain; that "the whole substance of the bread is changed into the whole substance of Christ's body," a conversion so unlike any natural change that it must be "called by a name of its own, 'transubstantiation'"; and that the sensible accidents (appearances) remain. His Aristotelian exposition is the philosophical machinery Trent presupposes — and the reason the "medieval-innovation" thesis is half right about the philosophy and wrong about the ancient faith it formalizes. 32

The Reformation breaks the long realist consensus, and Zwingli of Zürich is the fountainhead of the memorialist reading. The "is" of "This is my body," he held, means signifies : the bread and wine are signs that represent Christ's body and call his once-for-all sacrifice to mind — "those things are called the body and blood of Christ which are the symbols of the true body." Christ's true body ascended and sits at the Father's right hand, so it is received "by the contemplation of faith," not "masticated with our mouth and teeth." He made "the flesh profiteth nothing" (John 6:63) the linchpin of his case, and at the Marburg Colloquy (1529) he and Luther agreed on fourteen of fifteen articles…

Luther broke with Rome over much, but not over the reality of the presence. Against Zwingli he insisted the consecrated bread and wine are the true body and blood of Christ, present "in and under" the elements, on the plain force of the words of institution — "distinct, clear… words, which certainly are no trope." At Marburg he chalked Hoc est corpus meum on the table and refused the Swiss the hand of fellowship. His reading is sacramental union , not transubstantiation: he left the substances of bread and wine standing — "I do not argue whether the wine remains wine or not… let it be with the wine as God wills" — grounding the presence in the Word rather than in a change of substance. 34

Calvin of Geneva took the middle road between Zwingli's memorial and Luther's bodily presence. Christ is truly received in the Supper, he taught, but spiritually : the Holy Spirit lifts the believer up to feed on the body and blood of the ascended Christ in heaven, so the elements remain bread and wine yet are no bare signs but efficacious instruments — the Supper conveys its grace "not by presenting a vain or empty sign, but by there exerting an efficacy of the Spirit." Against Zwingli the sign "truly exhibits" what it signifies; against Rome and Luther there is no local, carnal presence in the elements; and of the mode he confessed he "rather feel[s] than understand[s] it." His spiritual-p…

Answering the Reformation, Trent 's thirteenth session defines the realist line as transubstantiation — "a conversion… of the whole substance of the bread into the substance of the body of Christ" — and draws out its worship corollary: because Christ "the true God" is wholly present, "all the faithful of Christ may… render in veneration the worship of latria… to this most holy sacrament," reserving it, venerating it, and bearing it in procession, on pain of anathema to any who would call such adoration idolatry (Session 13, chs. 4–6 and Canon 6). It is the dogmatic terminus of the reverence-and-reservation thread that runs from Tertullian and Cyril. 36

ar.q: Augustine's sign and figure: was he a symbolic witness against the Real Presence?
ar.c: No father is quoted more often on both sides of the eucharistic dispute than Augustine . The memorialist tradition rests a large part of its patristic case on him: he makes "eat my flesh" his textbook example of a figure , distinguishes the outward sacramentum from the inward res , and tells his hearers "believe, and thou hast eaten already." If the greatest of the Latin fathers read the discourse figuratively, the claim that the early Church was uniformly realist collapses. So: does Augustine's sign-and-figure language make him a witness against the Real Presence — a proto-memorialist — or is…
ar.a: Contested. Augustine cannot be made a clean witness for either side, and the honest finding is that both readings capture something real in him and neither captures all of him. His sign-and- figure language is genuine and load-bearing, so the enlistment of him for a crude physical presence fails; his realist statements — the bread that is the body, the flesh that must be adored — are equally genuine, so the enlistment of him for memorialism fails…

ar.q: "Guilty of the body" and "not discerning the Lord's body": is 1 Corinthians 11:27–29 an independent witness to the Real Presence?
ar.c: Where the hinge argument weighs the discourse of John 6 and the words of institution, this page isolates a third proof-text usually left in the background: Paul's warning to the Corinthians. "Whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord … For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body" (1 Corinthians 11:27–29). 1 The realist claim is that this language is too heavy for a symbol : one does not become "guilty of the body and blood" of a person by …
ar.a: Plausible. 1 Corinthians 11:27–29 is a genuine and often-underweighted witness on the realist side: the guilt "of the body and blood," the physical judgment of v. 30, and the Church's uniform treatment of the elements as a holy thing to be guarded all sit more easily with a real presence than with a memento. But the strong form — that the passage independently establishes the Real Presence — overreaches, because the pivotal phrase "discern the bo…

ar.q: Does "the flesh profiteth nothing" (John 6:63) refute the realist reading?
ar.c: Midway through the Bread of Life discourse, after the hearers stumble over "eat my flesh," Jesus says: "It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life" (John 6:63). 1 The memorialist reads this as the discourse's own retraction: Jesus himself pulls back from the literal flesh-eating and reframes the whole teaching as spiritual — so "this is my body" must likewise be figurative. Is John 6:63 that key? The parent argument weighs the whole New Testament hinge ; this page weighs the single verse most often pressed …
ar.a: Weak. As the memorialist's decisive counter-text — the verse that dissolves the realist reading of John 6 — the argument does not hold. The dominant patristic construal, corroborated by the Johannine idiom of "flesh," is that "the flesh profiteth nothing" concerns a carnal manner of understanding, or flesh considered apart from the life-giving Word, and so never denies that the flesh given is real; it denies only a fleshly way of receiving it. Th…

ar.q: Is the Real Presence taught by the New Testament, or is the language symbolic? (John 6 and the Words of Institution)
ar.c: The Real Presence stands or falls on a single exegetical hinge: when Jesus says "my flesh is meat indeed" (John 6:55) and "this is my body" (Matthew 26:26), is he speaking literally — the bread he gives is his flesh — or figuratively — the bread represents his body, as "I am the door" and "I am the true vine" use "am" for "signify"? Every later dispute over the mode of the presence (transubstantiation, sacramental union, spiritual feeding) presupposes that the presence is in some sense real; the memorialist denies even that. This page weighs the New Testament case for and against, not the medi…
ar.a: Contested. This is the textbook case of a genuinely disputed interpretation: strong by the lights of historical reception and the discourse's own rhetoric (which favor a real, not merely symbolic, presence), weaker when pressed to settle the precise mode , and met by a figurative reading that has a real internal anchor in John 6:63 and in Jesus' metaphorical idiom. The realist reading is, on balance, the better fit for the first-century and patri…

ar.q: Was the earliest Christian Eucharist a psychedelic sacrament continuous with the Mysteries? (Muraresku)
ar.c: The witnesses on this timeline take the Eucharist to be, in some sense, the body and blood of Christ; the arguments on the New Testament words weigh whether that presence is real or symbolic. A different kind of claim cuts under both: that the Supper's original content and power were pharmacological — that the earliest Christians drank a psychoactive, visionary wine, an inheritance from the pagan mystery cults, and that the Church later purged the drug and the memory of it. On this reading the "immortality" the Fathers ascribe to the cup (Ignatius's "medicine of immortality") was once a litera…
ar.a: Weak. As an account of the Eucharist's origin the thesis does not hold on its best available case. The narrow premise — that ancient wine could be psychoactive and that a cult drink or two may have been — is defensible and should not be dismissed; but it is doing all the work, and it does not reach Christianity. The load-bearing claim (an original, later-suppressed psychedelic Eucharist) rests on no direct archaeochemical, textual, or liturgical …

ar.q: "This is my body": does the copula establish a Real Presence, or is "is" a figure of speech?
ar.c: The words of institution — "Take, eat; this is my body … this is my blood of the new testament" — stand in all three Synoptics and in Paul (Matthew 26:26–28; Mark 14:22–24; Luke 22:19–20; 1 Corinthians 11:23–25), and are the single sentence most often produced as the knock-down proof of the Real Presence. 1 The realist reads the copula as identity: the bread is his body. The memorialist reads it as Huldrych Zwingli did — "is" for "signifies," est = significat — so the bread represents his body. The wider hinge (John 6, Paul's realism, the patristic reception) is weighed on the hinge page ; thi…
ar.a: Contested. Taken by itself — the question this page isolates — "This is my body" does not establish the Real Presence, and it does not refute it: the underlying Aramaic omits the copula, the Passover haggadah and Jesus' "I am" idiom supply ready figurative models, and yet the early Church heard the words as identity without strain. The realist reading is, on balance, the better fit for the first-century and patristic evidence — but that verdict r…

ar.q: Is transubstantiation a medieval innovation, or the patristic realism made precise?
ar.c: The realist witnesses on this timeline — from Ignatius to Ambrose — speak of the elements as Christ's body and blood, and several speak of a change . But the precise dogma the Council of Trent defined in 1551 has a specific shape: a conversion of the whole substance of the bread into the substance of Christ's body, the accidents (appearances) alone remaining. That vocabulary is Aristotelian, and it enters the record late. So the memorialist and much Protestant historiography press a historical thesis: transubstantiation is a medieval invention , read back onto the Fathers who knew nothing of i…
ar.a: Contested. The dispute is genuine and turns on an ambiguity in its own key word. If "transubstantiation" denotes the scholastic theory of how Christ becomes present — substance, accidents, the term, the instantaneous conversion — then it is a medieval development, and the innovation thesis is sound to that extent. If it denotes the realist conviction of what is received — that the consecrated elements are truly changed into and are the body and b…

xs.t: The doctrine rests on four bodies of New Testament text: The Bread of Life discourse — "Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you … For my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed" (John 6:53–58), with the qualifying word "It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing" (John 6:63). 1 The Words of Institution — "Take, eat; this is my body … this is my blood of the new testament" (Matthew 26:26–28; Mark 14:22–24; Luke 22:19–20, which adds "this do in remembrance of me"). 2 Paul's "communion of the body and blood" — "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?" (1 Corinthians 10:16) — …

ds.t: The Veneration of Relics
ds.q: May a Christian honour, touch, kiss, and pray at the bones and possessions of the saints — or is this the worship of dead matter? From the second century the church kept the remains of its martyrs, gathered them as treasures, built altars over them, and reported miracles at their shrines; by the eighth century a council required relics in every altar, and the medieval West filled with them. The Catholic and Orthodox traditions defend the practice as the relative honour ( dulia ) due the friends of God, distinct from the worship ( latria ) owed God alone; a line of critics from the Gallic priest Vigilantius to Calvin answered that it is idolatry dressed as religion — and, in fact, a trade rid…

tl.t: The earliest Christian relic-cult text. When Polycarp of Smyrna was burned, the church of Smyrna gathered his charred bones — “more precious than the most exquisite jewels, and more purified than gold” — and laid them where the community could return each year to “celebrate the anniversary of his martyrdom.” The same letter records the pagans' fear that the Christians would “worship” the martyr, and answers with the line the whole later debate rests on: “For Him indeed, as being the Son of God, we adore; but the martyrs… we worthily love.” Devotion to the relics, and the worship/love distinction, appear together at the outset. 1

tl.w: Victricius of Rouen’s theology of the relic (c. 396)
tl.t: The earliest sustained theology of relics in the Latin West. Welcoming a gift of relics from Ambrose of Milan, Victricius answered the age's live objection — how can a saint's power sit in a scrap of bone no bigger than a fingertip? — with the striking thesis that, because the martyr is joined to the indivisible, omnipresent God, the whole saint is present in every particle : “There is nothing in relics which is not complete… a reminder of perfection, not the injustice of division.” Yet he keeps the guard — the martyr is what God is “by gift, not by property” — so the honour paid the fragment is not the worship due God by nature. It supplies the metaphysic (the “whole in the part”) on which …

The classic patristic defence — and, because Jerome quotes his opponent, the fullest early record of the case against. The Gallic priest Vigilantius had attacked the cult as a pagan survival: “Why do you kiss and adore a bit of powder wrapped up in a cloth?” Jerome answers that no one worships the martyrs (“Madman, who in the world ever adored the martyrs?”), that the honour redounds to Christ whose servants they are, that emperors and the bishop of Rome carry and enshrine relics without sacrilege, and that the relics put demons to flight. It is the Reformation debate four centuries early. 3

tl.w: Augustine and the relics of St. Stephen (c. 426)
tl.t: When the relics of the protomartyr Stephen reached Roman Africa, Augustine recorded a wave of miracles at their shrines — a blind woman given sight, the dead raised, nearly seventy cures at Hippo in under two years — granting that “even now miracles are wrought… by the… relics of His saints.” Yet he guards the line as sharply as anyone: “to our martyrs we build, not temples… but monuments… it is to God, not to them, he sacrifices.” He is the fullest early witness to relic-miracles and the most explicit that they are not the worship of the dead. 4

tl.w: The Second Council of Nicaea requires relics in every altar (787)
tl.t: The council that restored the images also legislated the relics. Its seventh canon decrees that relics be placed in every church consecrated without them, and that any bishop who henceforth consecrates a church without relics “shall be deposed, as a transgressor of the ecclesiastical traditions.” Relic-veneration passes here from custom to conciliar law — the rule behind the Catholic altar-relic and the Orthodox antimension . 5

The sharpest Reformation attack. Calvin argues in principle that “the desire for relics is never without superstition, and… usually the parent of idolatry”; and in fact that the relics of Europe are a mass of frauds — enough “true Cross” to “form a whole ship's cargo,” every apostle with “more than four bodies,” rival heads of John the Baptist from Amiens to Rome. He revives Vigilantius's charge with the full Reformed doctrine of worship behind it. 6

Against the Reformers, the Council of Trent , in the same last-session decree that reaffirmed the images, defined that “the holy bodies of holy martyrs… are to be venerated by the faithful,” and condemned those who deny it. At the same time it conceded the Reformers' factual point, ordering that “all superstition shall be removed, all filthy lucre be abolished,” and that new relics be approved by the bishop. This is the Catholic charter that fixes the confessional divide to this day. 7

ar.q: Does Elisha's bones raising the dead (2 Kings 13:21) warrant the veneration of relics?
ar.c: “And it came to pass, as they were burying a man, that, behold, they spied a band of men; and they cast the man into the sepulchre of Elisha: and when the man was let down, and touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet.” — 2 Kings 13:21 (KJV). The argument: Scripture itself records that the physical remains of a holy man carried life-giving power — a corpse touched Elisha's bones and rose. If God worked resurrection through a prophet's bones , then a saint's relics are not “worthless dust” but vessels God may honour and use; the honouring of relics has a biblical warran…
ar.a: Plausible. As warrant for the reality of relic-power — that a holy person's remains may be a channel of God's miraculous action — the text is a sound and genuinely biblical precedent, and the Fathers who cite it read it fairly. As warrant for the developed veneration-cult it proves less: it shows God honouring a saint's bones, not the faithful venerating them, so the inference to the practice is coherent but not compelled. The honest verdict trac…

ar.q: Do Paul's handkerchiefs (Acts 19:11–12) warrant the veneration of relics?
ar.c: “And God wrought special miracles by the hands of Paul: So that from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out of them.” — Acts 19:11–12 (KJV). The argument: cloths that had merely touched Paul's body carried healing and exorcising power to the sick — the New Testament's own warrant for contact-relics (later called brandea ), objects sanctified by contact with a holy person. If God worked miracles through Paul's sweat-cloths, the honouring of relics is apostolic, not pagan.
ar.a: Plausible. As the Scriptural warrant for contact-relics — that God may work through objects sanctified by touch with the holy — the text is sound and hard to dismiss. As warrant for the veneration of relics it proves less: the miracles are called special, the cloths touch a living man, and the sick use rather than venerate them. So it grounds the reality of relic-power firmly and the cult only by extension — the same shape as its OT companion.

ar.q: Does the fraud and multiplication of relics discredit the cult?
ar.c: “If we were to collect all these pieces of the true cross exhibited in various parts, they would form a whole ship's cargo. The Gospel testifies that the cross could be borne by one single individual; how glaring, then, is the audacity now to pretend to display more relics of wood than three hundred men could carry!” — Calvin , A Treatise on Relics (1543). This is Calvin's in-fact argument, kept distinct from his in-principle one (that honouring relics is idolatry — weighed at “Is venerating relics dulia or idolatry?” ). The thesis here: even granting that venerating a genuine relic could be l…
ar.a: Contested. As history the argument is strong: the duplication and the trade were real, the provenance of most relics is unverifiable, and the strong-devotion-to-every-relic form of the cult cannot survive it — a point the Catholic tradition itself conceded and moved to reform. As a discrediting argument it overreaches: the leap from “many relics are fake” to “the practice is illegitimate” trades on the genetic fallacy and on collapsing abuse into…

ar.q: Is venerating relics dulia or idolatry?
ar.c: “Madman, who in the world ever adored the martyrs? who ever thought man was God?” — Jerome, Against Vigilantius 5. The defenders' claim: to venerate a relic is not to worship it. The honour paid a martyr's bones is dulia (the relative honour due the holy), which passes to the saint and through the saint to God; it is not the latria (adoration) reserved to God alone. So the practice is not idolatry, and the charge rests on a confusion of honour with worship.
ar.a: Contested. By the tradition's own lights — honour is not worship, reverence to the holy dead is biblical, and the sacrifice is reserved to God — the veneration of relics is a coherent dulia , and the flat charge of idolatry overreaches. But the Reformed objection is not answered by the theology alone: the honour paid a relic attaches directly to matter, the lived cult demonstrably slid into the superstition its critics named, and the “honour pass…

ds.t: Did the early church permit remarriage? (the deprecation of digamy)
ds.q: May a Christian whose husband or wife has died marry again? The early church answered, almost with one voice, in a single divided breath: yes — but the single life is better . Remarriage after a spouse’s death (“digamy”) was held lawful and no sin, yet everywhere deprecated as the lesser state; the twice-married were barred from the clergy and, in the East, penanced before readmission to communion. This page traces that “permission-with-deprecation” across time, earliest witness first — from Paul’s two-sided rule, through its mainstream restatement in Hermas, Clement, and Origen, its hard pole in Athenagoras and its outright prohibition in Tertullian, the canon law of Neocaesarea, Laodicea, …

tl.t: Paul sets the terms the whole tradition inherits. He permits the widowed to remarry — a widow “is at liberty to be married to whom she will; only in the Lord,” and is “no adulteress” if she does — and positively wills that “the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house.” 1 Yet he rates the single state the “happier” one, calls remarriage a concession to those who “cannot contain,” and bars the twice-married from church office and the widows’ roll. 2 Permission with a preference: the tension every later witness leans one way or the other upon.

The earliest post-apostolic answer reproduces Paul’s balance in one sentence. Asked whether a widow or widower who remarries sins, the angelic Shepherd replies: “There is no sin in marrying again… but if they remain unmarried, they gain greater honour and glory with the Lord.” 3 No hint that the second marriage is shameful, let alone fornication — the mainstream mean from which Tertullian later departs.

Athenagoras is the hard pole before Montanism. An unimpeachably catholic apologist, he tells the emperors that a man should “be content with one marriage; for a second marriage is only a specious adultery,” and that “he who deprives himself of his first wife, even though she be dead, is a cloaked adulterer.” 4 The adultery-language is a rhetorical intensifier applied to a concededly lawful act — but it shows the severe reading was current, and catholic, a generation before the New Prophecy, not a Montanist coinage; whether it was actually mainstream , or the lone severe pole against Hermas and Clement, is weighed in the Arguments below.

Clement holds the balanced middle against two errors at once. In Stromateis III he answers the Gnostic encratites, who forbade all marriage as evil, and the libertines, who thought conduct indifferent — keeping second marriage lawful as “the apostle allows… from sympathy” to those who “burn,” while preferring continence and the widow who “remains as she is.” 5 Toleration and preference together — and the prohibition of marriage flatly labelled an encratite heresy.

Tertullian alone turns the deprecation into a ban. His early To His Wife still grants that the apostle “permits marrying” and urges (not commands) widowhood; but in the later, openly Montanist On Exhortation to Chastity and On Monogamy the counsel hardens into a prohibition, and the remarriage of a widow or widower is classed as “a species of fornication.” 6 Forced to reckon with Paul’s plain permission, he does not out-argue it but overrides it — the Paraclete has “abrogated an indulgence which Paul granted” — and even claims the Greek of 1 Cor. 7:39 was corrupted to widen the license (a charge weighed, and found unsupported , in the Arguments ). 7 Whether this is a severe reading of a real…

Origen keeps Clement’s mean and reasons out its sharpest tension. Remarriage after widowhood is “no reproach” and lawful; yet the twice-married are shut out of church office — a bar Origen frankly finds hard to justify against a chaste digamist, since “some who have been married twice may be much better than those who have been married once,” and files, with Paul’s other indulgences, among the “laws given by concession to human weakness.” 8 The marriage is allowed; it simply belongs to the weaker, not the perfect, Christian.

The deprecation now hardens into canon law — but in a form that proves the point. A presbyter may not even attend a digamist’s wedding-feast, “for, since the digamist is worthy of penance, what kind of a presbyter shall he be, who… sanctioned the marriage?” — yet the digamist is a penitent, not a fornicator, and his marriage stands, the church “never” reputing second marriages “illicit.” 9

Laodicea softens the penance and, in doing so, states the rule as plainly as any canon: communion is restored “to those who have freely and lawfully joined in second marriages… after a short space… in prayer and fasting.” 10 The word “lawfully” is decisive — the deprecation preserved, the prohibition refused.

Basil fixes the eastern discipline in numbers: a year’s penance for a second marriage, three or four for a third. Only the third and further unions draw the sharp word — “no longer… marriage at all, but… polygamy; nay rather… limited fornication” — and even those penitents are received back. 11 Where Tertullian denied the name “marriage” to the second union, Basil withholds it only from the third.

Ambrose is the careful Latin mean. In Concerning Widows he presses the honour of perpetual widowhood as hard as anyone, yet draws the line Tertullian crossed: “I do not forbid second marriages, only I do not advise them,” for the second marriage is one “which the precepts of the Apostle certainly do not condemn.” 12 Lawful, but not expedient — the distinction Tertullian collapsed, kept firmly apart.

Jerome is the test case. The age’s fiercest champion of virginity, he quarried Tertullian’s monogamist works and pressed the denigration of marriage so hard in Against Jovinianus that friends withdrew the book from circulation — yet at the decisive point he refuses to cross where Tertullian crossed: “I do not condemn second, nor third, nor, pardon the expression, eighth marriages.” 13 When even Jerome, who followed Tertullian furthest, draws back at calling remarriage sin, the ban is shown to be a step past the church’s severity, not its expression.

Augustine states the settled Latin verdict and names the man who overstepped it. In On the Good of Widowhood he refuses to condemn any lawful marriage — “I dare neither to condemn any marriage” — and faults “Tertullian… whilst with railing tooth he attacks second marriages, as though unlawful, which the Apostle with sober mind allows to be altogether lawful.” 14 The single life is the greater good honoured by the submission of a real good — “despise, not condemn” — not a good purchased by branding the other evil.

Trullo crystallizes the East’s discipline and names its principle: a blend of Roman “exact perfection” and Constantinopolitan “kindness and consideration,” so “that neither gentleness fall into licence, nor severity into harshness,” renewing the bar on the twice-married from the clergy. 15 Over the next two centuries the rule fixed into its final Eastern form — first marriage the norm, second a penanced concession, third tolerated under limits, a fourth absolutely forbidden — tested and settled by the tetragamy of the emperor Leo VI and the Tomos of Union (920). 16

ar.q: Was the Greek of 1 Corinthians 7:39 corrupted to widen the remarriage license?
ar.c: Let us plainly know that, in the Greek original, it does not stand in the form which (through the either crafty or simple alteration of two syllables) has gone out into common use, “But if her husband shall have fallen asleep,” as if it were speaking of the future, and thereby seemed to pertain to her who has lost her husband when already in a believing state. If this indeed had been so, licence let loose without limit would have granted a (fresh) husband as often as one had been lost. — Tertullian, On Monogamy 11, ANF vol. 4 . 1 The verse as the church received it reads: “The wife is bound by…
ar.a: unsupported. As a claim about the text, the charge has nothing behind it. The Greek of 1 Cor. 7:39 is uniform across the witnesses; the apparatus records no variant bearing on the tense or the scope of the permission; and Tertullian’s own appeal to the Graeco authentico is best read as correcting a Latin rendering, not as reporting a corrupted Greek exemplar — a reading confirmed by the fact that no editor of the Greek New Testament, ancient or m…

ar.q: Was the severe “second marriage is adultery” reading a mainstream position before Montanism?
ar.c: …a person should either remain as he was born, or be content with one marriage; for a second marriage is only a specious adultery. “For whosoever puts away his wife,” says He, “and marries another, commits adultery”… For he who deprives himself of his first wife, even though she be dead, is a cloaked adulterer. — Athenagoras, A Plea for the Christians 33, ANF vol. 2 . 1 The interpretation weighed here is the historical thesis the deprecation-of-digamy timeline flags at Athenagoras: that the strict view — second marriage as a kind of adultery — was a mainstream Christian position before the ris…
ar.a: plausible. The thesis is right in its defensive core and overstated in its reach. That the severe “second marriage is adultery” language predates the New Prophecy, and comes from an impeccably catholic apologist writing to the emperors about 177, is sound — the reading is no Montanist coinage, and the deprecation it heightens is older still and partly scriptural. But the claim that it was therefore mainstream outruns the evidence: Athenagoras is …

ds.t: The Resurrection of the Body
ds.q: The Christian hope is not that the soul survives death but that the body rises. Both ancient creeds fix it as an article of faith — the Apostles' Creed confesses "the resurrection of the flesh " ( carnis resurrectionem ), the Nicene "the resurrection of the dead " — and the Church has always held that at the last day the dead are raised bodily, never to die again. What the Church has had to work out across time is the harder question of the nature and identity of the risen body : in what sense is it the same body that died?

tl.t: Paul lays down the text every later camp reads. Against Corinthians who asked "how are the dead raised up? and with what body do they come?" he answers with the analogy of the seed: "that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die," and God gives it a body of his choosing — "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." The risen body is continuous with the one sown ("this corruptible must put on incorruption") yet transfigured ("sown in dishonour…raised in glory"); and he adds the crux the whole debate turns on: "flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption" (15:50). 1

Justin — in the fragments On the Resurrection — states the same-flesh reading bluntly against those who "say that there is no resurrection of the flesh": "the resurrection is a resurrection of the flesh which died," and it rises "entire," God being able to "collect again the decomposed members of the flesh, and make the same body as was formerly produced by Him." The flesh is God's own handiwork, made "in the image of God," and therefore saved with the soul; Christ's own bodily rising — he "let them handle Him," and ate before them — is the proof that the body, not the soul only, rises. 2

Athenagoras , in the earliest surviving Christian treatise devoted wholly to the subject, argues the resurrection from God's power and will : reuniting "bodies that are dead, or even entirely dissolved into their elements, so as to constitute the same persons" is a work the Creator "can perform, and can will, and such as is worthy of Him," for the God who made the body from nothing "knows…whither each of the dissolved particles" has gone. He meets the era's stock objection — that bodies eaten by beasts or (in famine) by other men cannot be reassembled — by arguing that alien matter never truly becomes part of a body, so the same person's own parts are reconstituted; and he grounds the whole …

Irenaeus , in Against Heresies Book 5, defends the flesh's resurrection against the Gnostic denial and answers the crux verse head-on. If the flesh is not saved, he argues, "then neither did the Lord redeem us with His blood, nor is the cup of the Eucharist the communion of His blood" — the very bodies "nourished" by Christ's body and blood must rise. And "flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God" does not exclude the substance of the flesh: "flesh and blood" names those who lack the Spirit, and the flesh is not what inherits but what is inherited — taken up by the life-giving Spirit "into the kingdom of God," "not repudiating…the substance of flesh, but showing that into it the Spi…

Tertullian , in On the Resurrection of the Flesh , gives the identity-of-substance reading its fullest and most insistent form: "the very same flesh which was once sown in death will bear fruit in resurrection-life — the same in essence, only more full and perfect; not another, although reappearing in another form." Paul's "spiritual body" marks "a difference of honour, not of nature"; change is not destruction ("a thing may undergo a complete change, and yet remain still the same thing"), so "the substance of the flesh will still be preserved safe." The identity is required by justice itself — it would be "unjust…for one substance to do the work, and another to reap the reward" — and so "th…

Origen , in On First Principles and Against Celsus , gives the great third-century alternative to the same-flesh reading. What rises is genuinely a body — “What is that which died? Was it not a body? It is of the body, then, that there will be a resurrection” — but a spiritual body “educed” out of the animal one, not the same corpse resuscitated. He lodges its identity in a persisting bodily principle, a “germ…which is always safe in the substance of the body” that raises the scattered matter “as the power which is in the grain of wheat…restores the grain into a body having stalk and ear.” He rejects both the pagan caricature that Christians expect “the same bodies, without a change to a hig…

Methodius , in his dialogue On the Resurrection (the Aglaophon ), mounts the first sustained rebuttal of Origen and reasserts the identity of the same flesh. He “cannot endure the trifling of some who…do violence to Scripture” to make “the resurrection… without flesh…by allegorizing”; the “coats of skins” signify mortality, not the body; and man, “composed of soul and body,” must rise as the composite. Like Irenaeus he reads “flesh and blood cannot inherit” as the carnal impulse, not the substance of the flesh, citing Justin for the same. Against Origen's form he presses that “there is no resurrection of the form without the flesh” — the form is a quality of the flesh and cannot outlast it, …

Cyril of Jerusalem , catechizing baptismal candidates on the Jerusalem creed's article “the resurrection of the flesh ,” gives the same-flesh reading its mid-fourth-century catechetical form. “The root of all good works is the hope of the Resurrection,” and “faith…in the Resurrection of the dead, is a great…doctrine of the Holy Catholic Church,” though “Greeks contradict it, Samaritans disbelieve it, heretics mutilate it.” Reading Paul's demonstratives (“ this corruptible must put on incorruption”), he states the identity plainly: “this body shall be raised…the very same body, though by putting on incorruption it shall be fashioned anew,—as iron blending with fire becomes fire” — the same fl…

Ambrose , in the funeral oration for his brother Satyrus ( De excessu fratris II, circulated as On the Belief in the Resurrection ), gives the same-flesh hope its fourth-century Latin form — the bridge from Tertullian to Augustine . He rests it on “three grounds… reason, analogy from universal example, and the evidence of what has happened, since many have risen”: reason, because the body acted with the soul and so must rise to be judged; analogy, from a nature that everywhere dies and rises; and evidence, from the Gospel raisings. The risen flesh is the very same substance — “we shall be the same persons as we were,” “flesh…restored from flesh, bone from bone, blood from blood” — and he rea…

Gregory of Nyssa , in the deathbed dialogue with his sister Macrina ( On the Soul and the Resurrection ), defines the resurrection as "the reconstitution of our nature in its original form" — the Edenic pattern, not the body as it lay dying. He is firmly same-substance on the matter: "the identical atoms (belonging to each soul) reassembling together in the same order as before," the simple soul never wholly losing its bond with its own scattered dust. He presses the flux objection himself — the living body is a flame "always passing itself along," so a resurrection of "the same" body would raise "a crowd" (infant, youth, and old man at once) — and answers it with Paul's seed: the grain must…

Jerome , in To Pammachius Against John of Jerusalem (c. 397) and Letter 84 (c. 400) — both weapons of the Origenist controversy — is the fiercest Latin champion of the resurrection of this same flesh . His wedge is the word itself: the Origenists will confess “the resurrection of the body ” but never “of the flesh ,” and “all flesh is body, but not every body is flesh” — so the vaguer word smuggles in an ethereal body under an orthodox sound. Against it he presses the return of the very members: “after the resurrection we shall have the same members which we now use, the same flesh and blood and bones,” for Scripture condemns not their substance but their works. Because the members return, s…

tl.w: The Apostles' Creed — "the resurrection of this flesh" (Rufinus, c. 404)
tl.t: The article of the creed. The older Western baptismal creed confesses not "the resurrection of the dead " (the Nicene ἀνάστασιν νεκρῶν) but "the resurrection of the flesh " ( carnis resurrectionem ), and Rufinus of Aquileia 's Commentary on the Apostles' Creed is the earliest full exposition of why. "Flesh" is the word the Gnostics could not say — "Valentinus altogether denies the resurrection of the flesh, so do the Manicheans" — so the creed nailed it to the font. Rufinus's own church sharpened it further, to "the resurrection of this flesh": the confessor signs his own forehead as he says the word, confessing the rising of the very body he stands in, "not a confused or foreign body but it…

Augustine , in the last book of The City of God (Book 22), gives the identity-of-substance reading its settling Latin form and, uniquely, presses it into a series of concrete questions on the character of the risen body. What rises is the very same flesh, "transformed from the oldness of the animal body into the newness of the spiritual body … but still flesh, not spirit"; God can "recall all the portions which have been consumed by beasts or fire, or … evaporated into the air," so even eaten flesh reverts to its first owner "like a pecuniary loan." All rise at the prime of life — the age of Christ, "about … thirty"; both sexes are kept, for "the sex of woman is not a vice, but nature," and …

John of Damascus , in An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith IV.27 ("Concerning the Resurrection"), gives the settled Byzantine synthesis — the Greek East's counterpart to Augustine 's Latin one, filling the long gap between the fourth-century Greek fathers and Aquinas . Resurrection is by definition "the re-union of soul and body," and it is "this very body, which is corruptible and liable to dissolution, that will rise again incorruptible" — the same flesh remade, proved by Lazarus ("not another body but the very one that was corrupt") and by the palpable risen Christ ("a spirit hath not flesh or bones, as ye see Me have"). He answers the dispersal objection as Athenagoras and Cyril did…

tl.w: The medieval councils fix the same flesh (Fourth Lateran, 1215; Second Lyons, 1274; Benedictus Deus , 1336)
tl.t: The high-medieval councils raise the same-flesh reading from patristic consensus to dogmatic definition, filling the interval between John of Damascus and Aquinas . The Fourth Lateran Council (1215), in the confession Firmiter credimus that opened it against the Cathar dualists, defined that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead and render to each according to his works, “all of whom will rise again with their own bodies which they now bear” ( qui omnes cum suis propriis resurgent corporibus quae nunc gestant ) — the identity of the risen body with this present flesh made an article of faith. The Second Council of Lyons (1274), in the profession of faith the emperor Michael VIII …

Aquinas , in the Summa contra Gentiles (IV.79–89) and the Summa Theologiae Supplement (qq. 75–86), gives the same-flesh tradition its most rigorous form. The risen body is numerically identical — "we cannot call it resurrection unless the soul return to the same body… otherwise… it will not be a resurrection, but rather the assuming of a new body" — but its identity is secured by the returning soul, not by retained matter. On the flux problem that vexed the whole tradition he is decisive: a living body's matter is already in constant flux ("as fire… is called numerically one because its species persists, yet wood is consumed and new wood is applied"), yet the man stays one; so the rational s…

John Calvin , in the final (1559) Latin Institutes III.25 ("Of the Last Resurrection"), carries the same-flesh hope into the Reformation — the Protestant leg of a tradition that runs unbroken from the fathers. Reading Paul's demonstratives, he lays a finger on the present body: " this corruptible must put on incorruption," so a change of quality in this flesh, not a substitute, is what is promised — "he very plainly affirms that no new bodies are to be fabricated." He rejects as "equally monstrous" the error "of those who imagine that the soul, instead of resuming the body with which it is now clothed, will obtain a new and different body" (against the ancient Manichees and the spiritualist …

tl.w: The Reformed confessions fix the same flesh (Heidelberg Catechism, 1563; Westminster Confession, 1646)
tl.t: The Reformed confessions codify Calvin 's reading for catechesis and church order — the Protestant counterpart to the way the medieval councils raised the patristic consensus into dogma. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563), expounding the creed's "resurrection of the body," confesses that "not only my soul after this life shall be immediately taken up to Christ its head; but also, that this my body, being raised by the power of Christ, shall be reunited with my soul, and made like unto the glorious body of Christ" (Q&A 57) — the same demonstrative finger on the present flesh. And the Westminster Confession (1646) gives numerical identity its sharpest confessional form anywhere: "all the dead sha…

Oscar Cullmann , in the Ingersoll Lecture Immortality of the Soul or Resurrection of the Dead? The Witness of the New Testament (Harvard, 1955; published 1958), gives the bodily hope its landmark twentieth-century statement — and the diagnosis Wright would later inherit: that the New Testament hope of resurrection is something wholly different from, and incompatible with, the Greek immortality of the soul . His opening image fixes the contrast — "Like Jesus, Socrates has his disciples about him on the day of his death; but he discourses serenely with them on immortality. Jesus, a few hours before His death, trembles and begs His disciples not to leave Him alone." Socrates can be calm because…

N. T. Wright , in The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003) and Surprised by Hope (2008), recovers the bodily hope against a modern disembodied piety of "going to heaven when you die." "Resurrection" in the ancient world, he argues, always meant new bodily life — "something that everybody knows doesn't happen" — which the whole pagan world denied; the Christian claim was its reversal, not the survival of the soul. Heaven is a "temporary resting place," not the final destiny, which is "to be bodily raised into the transformed, glorious likeness of Jesus Christ" in a renewed creation. And Paul's "spiritual body" ( sōma pneumatikon ) he reads, with the older tradition, as a body animated by the…

ar.q: Does the "chain-consumption" (cannibalism) objection defeat the resurrection of the same body?
ar.c: what kind of body is that which, after being completely corrupted, can return to its original nature, and to that self-same first condition out of which it fell into dissolution? — the pagan critic Celsus, quoted in Origen, Against Celsus V.14, link . The advocated interpretation is that a resurrection of the numerically identical particles is impossible, and so the same-flesh doctrine fails. The sharpest form is not the mockery of a rotted corpse reassembled ("a hope…which might be cherished by worms") but the chain-consumption case: if a man's flesh is eaten — by fish, by beasts, or by anoth…
ar.a: Weak — as a defeater of the resurrection of the body. The chain-consumption objection is real, ancient, and, steelmanned into the general problem of material flux and matter shared across many bodies over time, genuinely fatal to one version of the doctrine: the crude claim that the risen body is the numerically identical particles reassembled. Against that target a bare appeal to omnipotence fails, because the same particle in two bodies is a co…

ar.q: Is the risen body the same material flesh that died? (the identity-of-substance reading)
ar.c: believe that the very same flesh which was once sown in death will bear fruit in resurrection-life — the same in essence, only more full and perfect; not another, although reappearing in another form. — Tertullian, On the Resurrection of the Flesh , ch. LII, link . The advocated interpretation is that the body raised at the last day is numerically the same flesh that died — the same substance, not merely a body of the same kind or a soul re-embodied afresh. Paul's "spiritual body" marks a change of glory and quality, not of nature: the corruptible flesh is remade incorruptible, whole and ident…
ar.a: Sound. The identity-of-substance reading — that the risen body is the believer's own flesh, the same body that died, transfigured rather than replaced — is the historic mainstream, confessed in the older creed, held by the whole anti-Gnostic and Latin tradition, and well grounded in the plain sense of 1 Corinthians 15:53, Philippians 3:21, and the risen body of Christ. It absorbs its hardest counter-text (1 Cor 15:50) from within Paul's own gramm…

ar.q: What will the risen body be like? (Augustine's City of God 22 questions)
ar.c: we gather this conclusion, that in the resurrection of the flesh the body shall be of that size which it either had attained or should have attained in the flower of its youth, and shall enjoy the beauty that arises from preserving symmetry and proportion in all its members. — The City of God , Book XXII, ch. 20, link . The advocated interpretation is a single, connected picture of the risen body: it is numerically the same flesh that died, raised as a "spiritual body" (a change of glory, not of substance); it rises whole and personally identifiable; it stands at the prime of life — the age of…
ar.a: Plausible. As one connected reading of 1 Corinthians 15, Philippians 3:21, and Luke 20:35–36, the glorified-same-flesh body — whole, identifiable, healed of defect, its sex retained — is coherent, text-grounded, and became the mainstream Western picture; on its central claims it is as strong as the identity-of-substance reading it rests on. What keeps it short of "sound" is that its more concrete determinations, chiefly the resurrection age of ab…

ar.q: Is the resurrection future and bodily, or "already past"? (2 Timothy 2:18)
ar.c: …Hymenaeus and Philetus; who concerning the truth have erred, saying that the resurrection is past already; and overthrow the faith of some. — 2 Timothy 2:17–18 (KJV), link . The interpretation weighed here is the one Paul is opposing: that the resurrection is not a future, bodily event at the last day but a present, spiritual reality already accomplished — so that no bodily rising remains to be hoped for. The mainstream Christian confession, traced on this doctrine's timeline and fixed in both creeds ("the resurrection of the flesh" / "of the dead"), is that the dead rise bodily at the last d…
ar.a: Weak. As a denial of a future bodily resurrection, the "resurrection is past already" reading does not hold on its best available case. Its steelman — the genuinely Pauline language of a rising already begun in the believer (Romans 6, Colossians 2–3, Ephesians 2) — establishes an inaugurated, spiritual resurrection, but not the elimination of the bodily one; the same writers place a still-future rising "at his coming," "at the last trump," and "a…

ar.q: Does everyone rise bodily, or only the saved? (the resurrection of the unjust)
ar.c: …there shall be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust. — Paul before Felix, Acts 24:15 (KJV), link . The interpretation advanced here is the historic mainstream: at the last day every human being who has died is raised bodily — the wicked no less than the righteous — and only then , standing again in the body, is each brought to judgment and sent to his final state. The resurrection of the body is thus a universal event, not a privilege of the saved; the sorting of the risen into life and condemnation is a distinct, subsequent act.
