In the letter to Studius he has Jesus write a prophetic oracle disowning the accusers: "What did He write except the prophetic saying: 'Earth, earth, write that these men have been disowned,'" a line Ambrose refers to Jeremiah's oracle against the doomed king Jechoniah, and develops into an earth/heaven contrast — the accusers' names written on the ground, the names of the faithful written in heaven. 4 In the companion letter to Irenaeus he reads the gesture differently: Jesus wrote with the same finger that had writt…

Jerome supplies the answer that would prove the most durable — and the most popular ever since: Jesus wrote the accusers' own sins. Against the Pelagians he writes that Jesus, stooping, "began to write with his finger on the ground the sins, to be sure, of those who were making the accusation, as well as the sins of all mortal beings, according to what is written in the prophet, 'Those who depart from you shall be written in the earth'" (Jeremiah 17:13). 6 This is the fountainhead of the enduring "he wrote their sins" reading.

Augustine, by contrast, pointedly declines to name the words and reads the act itself as sign. In the Tractates on John the writing marks the passage from law to grace: the Law "was written with the finger of God; but written on stone because of the hard-hearted. The Lord now wrote on the ground, because He was seeking fruit" — grace sown on fruitful soil against law graven on barren stone. His scene ends not with a decoded message but with a famous image: the two left alone, "the wretched woman and Mercy." 7 The most influential Latin father on the passage is the one who refused to say what was written. He is also the earliest to explain the passage's textual history: in a later work on adu…

Bede folds two readings together. The writing shows that this was the very one "who once wrote the Ten Commandments of the law on stone with his finger, that is, by the action of the Holy Spirit"; and the second stooping he reads practically — "by directing his look elsewhere he might give them the freedom to go away," foreseeing that the accusers, astounded, "would be more inclined to depart quickly than to ask him more questions." He adds the moral: that Jesus wrote both before and after his verdict teaches us to examine ourselves before and after we correct a neighbour. 9

Alcuin turns the gesture wholly moral and allegorical, dropping the question of content altogether: "The ground denotes the human heart, which yieldeth the fruit either of good or of bad actions: the finger jointed and flexible, discretion." The scene instructs us, seeing faults in our neighbours, "not immediately and rashly to condemn them, but after searching our own hearts to begin with, to examine them attentively with the finger of discretion." 10

tl.w: The scribes: "the sins of every one of them" (9th century onward)
tl.t: Some copyists resolved the silence by writing the answer into the text. In a cluster of (mostly Byzantine) witnesses — the uncial U (Nanianus) and a string of minuscules (73, 95, 331, 364, 413, 658, 700, 782, 1592), with 264 placing it at the first writing (8:6) rather than the second, 652 adding it only in the margin, and some Armenian copies — the verse gains after "the ground" the words ἐνὸς ἑκάστου αὐτῶν τὰς ἁμαρτίας — "the sins of every one of them" — so that it now states outright that Jesus wrote "the sins of each one of them." (Metzger's own list also cites the uncial Π, but that manuscript is in fact lacunose right through John 8:6–39 and so cannot witness the gloss at all.) Metzger…

The one Byzantine commentator to reach the passage reaches it only to bracket it. Euthymius records that everything from John 7:53 to 8:12 is, "in the accurate copies, either not found or marked with an obelus, because these things seem spurious and added," and then expounds the story as edifying — but never asks what Jesus wrote. He is the terminus Metzger has in mind in the line that "no Greek Church Father prior to Euthymius Zigabenus" comments on the passage; the Greek East's characteristic response to the scene is text-critical doubt, not reconstruction — though his note, in a commentary largely compiled from earlier exegetes, is almost certainly older than he is. 12

By the thirteenth century the answers were being catalogued as a set. Bonaventure lays them out: "Augustine responds that He wrote what He spoke. But Ambrose says that He wrote: 'Earth, earth, write down the rejected men,' and this is drawn from Jeremiah chapter twenty-two. The Interlinear Gloss says that He was writing 'their sins.' Others say that He was writing letters in which each one could read his own sins." He registers the Greek puzzle too — "some say that it was not found in the ancient Greek books, because John added it after the Gospel was completed" — and, asking why Jesus wrote with his finger, gives the deflating literal answer alongside the mystical one: "The reason is litera…

Aquinas gives the same menu and, unusually among the ancients and medievals, weighs it: "Some say that he wrote the words of Jeremiah: 'O earth, earth, listen — write down this man as sterile.' According to others, and this is the better opinion, Jesus wrote down the very words he spoke... However, neither of these opinions is certain." He then reads the choice of the ground itself three ways: that those testing him "would be written on the earth" (Jeremiah 17:13) while the just are "written in heaven"; that writing signs on earth figures the miracles wrought in the flesh he assumed; and that the soft earth, against the stone tablets of the old Law, shows "the sweetness and the softness of t…

Calvin closes the speculative era by refusing it. Those who "conjecture that he wrote this or the other thing," he holds, "do not understand his meaning" — and he declines even Augustine's ingenious law-and-grace reading of the gesture. The stooping and writing showed the accusers only how "unworthy they were of being heard," as a man addressed by another might "draw lines on the wall, or ... turn his back ... to show ... that he was not attending to what was said." The content is not the point, and the search for it is misdirected. 15

A learned minority has nonetheless kept reconstructing, now on legal and ritual rather than allegorical grounds. T. W. Manson (1953) proposed that Jesus was miming Roman criminal procedure, in which a magistrate wrote out his sentence before reading it aloud — going through the form of a verdict worded so that it could not be executed, and so escaping the trap as he escaped the tribute question; F. F. Bruce followed him, taking the written words to be those of verse 7 itself. 16 J. D. M. Derrett (1963) argued instead that Jesus wrote words of the Torah against false witnesses — from Exodus 23, "put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness" (23:1b) and "keep thee far from a…

Most modern reference works judge the content unrecoverable and left blank by the Evangelist's own design. C. K. Barrett finds no point in asking after the inscription's content, since the writing itself enacts Jesus' refusal to sit as judge; Barnabas Lindars and George Beasley-Murray likewise read the gesture as a sign of unwillingness to engage, indifferent to any words; Gail O'Day puts the pole most sharply — the very act of writing is what matters, and readings that try to recover its content miss the point of Jesus' nonverbal response; and Craig Keener dismisses even the ingenious guess that Jesus wrote the commandment against coveting (turning it on the accusers) as, at best, speculati…

ar.q: Did Jesus write the accusers' sins on the ground?
ar.c: "But Jesus, stooping down, began to write with his finger on the ground," the sins, to be sure, of those who were making the accusation, as well as the sins of all mortal beings according to what is written in the prophet, "Those who depart from you shall be written in the earth." — Jerome, Dialogue against the Pelagians 2.17 (c. 415), newadvent.org . 1 The reading is that the withheld words of John 8:6, 8 were the accusers' own sins — or, in a common variant, their names — written out so that each, reading his guilt in the dust, dropped his stone and left. It is the single most widespread ans…
ar.a: Contested. Judge the interpretation on its best case — the Jeremiah 17:13 intertext, held independently by Ambrose and Jerome — and it is coherent, ancient, and not ruled out: the ground-writing plausibly belongs to the register of "written in the earth" over against "written in heaven." But that is a claim about the gesture's symbolic key, not proof of its literal content; the further, popular specification that Jesus inscribed the accusers' own…

ar.q: Did Jesus write Torah verses against the false witnesses?
ar.c: Derrett's reconstruction turns on a physical constraint of his own devising: a person stooped over the ground, scratching with a finger from a low, seated posture, could form no more than about sixteen Hebrew characters in a line. 1 Using that self-imposed ceiling as a filter — it disqualifies any longer candidate text — he reconstructs the withheld content as two short clauses of the Torah's law on witnesses: the first writing (8:6) was Exodus 23:1b — "you shall not join hands with a wicked man to be a malicious witness" — and the second (8:8) was Exodus 23:7a — "keep far from a false charge"…
ar.a: Weak. Keep the two questions apart. The interpretation Derrett's argument serves — that the episode arraigns the accusers under the Torah's law of witnesses, so the real defendants are the men holding the stones — is well grounded, carried by Jesus' spoken invocation of the first-stone rule (Deut 17:7) and the surrounding testimony-motif, and it does not depend on Derrett at all. But the argument as Derrett states it is a claim about the writing …

ar.q: Is the story of the woman taken in adultery (John 7:53–8:11) original to John's Gospel?
ar.c: The evidence for the non-Johannine origin of the pericope of the adulteress is overwhelming. — Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament , 2nd ed. (1994), 187. 1 The interpretation weighed here is the mainstream text-critical verdict that John 7:53–8:11 — the woman taken in adultery, the scene whose central gesture this doctrine tracks — was not part of the Gospel as the Evangelist wrote it, but a later insertion of an independently-circulating story that scribes eventually settled into John. The question is deliberately narrow: not whether the incident happened, and no…
ar.a: Sound — as a claim about textual origin. That John 7:53–8:11 was not part of the Gospel the Evangelist wrote, but a later insertion of an old, independently-circulating story, is the near-universal verdict of critical editors from Tregelles to the present, and it rests on as strong a convergence of external and internal evidence as the discipline offers. The Augustinian excision theory and the Byzantine-majority defense are the two live counter-c…

ar.q: Did Jesus mime a Roman magistrate's verdict?
ar.c: I have for some time thought that the action of Jesus might be explained from the well-known practice in Roman criminal law, whereby the presiding judge first wrote down the sentence and then read it aloud from the written record. … Jesus by this action says in effect: "You are inviting me to usurp the functions of the Roman Governor. Very well, I will do so; and I will do it in the approved Roman manner." He then stoops down and pretends to write down the sentence, after which he reads it out … Jesus defeats the plotters by going through the form of pronouncing sentence in the best Roman styl…
ar.a: Weak. The interpretation is clever and has a respectable following, and it rests on a genuinely strong foundation — Jeremias's reading of the scene as a Roman-vs.-Moses trap parallel to the tribute question. But that foundation carries the weight by itself; Manson's specific added mechanism does not hold. He evidences the "magistrate writes his sentence" custom only from Roman provincial tribunals and then transplants it into a Jewish Temple cour…

ar.q: Does the writing allude to the Numbers 5 ordeal of the suspected adulteress?
ar.c: It was the office of the priest, when he tried a suspected wife, to stoop down and gather the dust off the floor of the sanctuary; which when he had infused into the water, he was to give the woman to drink. — John Lightfoot, Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae , on John 8 (1671). 1 The reading is that Jesus, stooping to write in the Temple dust before an accused adulteress, evokes the ordeal of the suspected wife (the sotah ) in Numbers 5:11–31 — the one rite in the Law that joins an accused woman, a written curse, and the dust of the sanctuary floor. In Numbers 5 the priest takes "holy water in an…
ar.a: Plausible. This is the strongest of the modern reconstructions on thematic grounds: it alone gathers all three of the scene's distinctive features under one biblical rite, and its "the accuser must be sinless" hinge is a substantive parallel to Jesus' spoken condition, not a coincidence of props. That makes it a coherent, not-ruled-out allusion worth taking seriously. But it stays short of established, because everything that would make the ordea…
